# 04 — CESR and the Wire {#04-cesr-wire}

## Thesis {#04-thesis}

CESR (Composable Event Streaming Representation) is not a serialization convenience layered on top of KERI; it is the external interop contract that makes the whole stack verifiable at all. Its single defining property is text-binary concatenation composability — the guarantee that any set of self-framing primitives concatenated in the text domain can be converted en masse to binary and back with zero loss and zero re-parsing (CESR spec > Composability, L5; CESR spec > SAD Path Signatures, L1390). Everything an adversarial reviewer needs to understand about "the wire" follows deductively from that one property plus one arithmetic fact — that 24 is the least common multiple of Base64's 6 bits per character and a byte's 8 bits (CESR spec > Conversions, L196). From those two roots come the sizing math, the code-table taxonomy, the count/group codes, the version strings, the cold-start tritet discipline, and the crypto-agility mechanism by which a post-quantum algorithm claims an unused code slot without desynchronizing a parser that predates it. The recurring reviewer error is to treat CESR as "just Base64 with type tags," to reach for `=` padding or JCS-style lexicographic canonicalization, or to assume the encoding is an implementation detail a maintainer may simplify freely. Each of those is a wire-interop defect that keripy's own test suite will not catch, because the failure is in an external contract with keria, signify-ts, and every other implementation on the network (00-lens.md, claim 5; 30-invariants.md > A).

This section separates what the spec and the reference implementation enforce (well-established) from what is reserved, in flux, or a known landmine (uncertain/contested), and flags where a claim rests on a load-bearing assumption.

## Status {#04-status}

In this chapter "normative" means CESR's standardizing line, `main` at `bad6edd84` (2026-08-28), and unmarked claims are [spec]. For the post-quantum [spec-next] claims in this chapter, the uncertainty that attaches to any forward-branch text is now concrete: as of 2026-10-03 an open, unmerged pull request proposes to revert them from `v1.1` ([section 5.7](#04-pq-in-practice)).

---

## 1. What CESR fundamentally is, and the priors it corrects {#04-what-cesr-is}

CESR is a dual text-binary encoding format whose unique property is text-binary concatenation composability (CESR spec > SAD Path Signatures, L1390; CESR spec > Composability, L5). This is the root claim; the rest of the format is derived from it.

Three corrections to outsider priors are worth stating at the top, because they are the tells of someone who has not read the spec.

### CESR is not crypto-only {#04-not-crypto-only}

CESR is not crypto-only. "The CESR protocol... is not limited to merely encoding Cryptographic Primitives but any primary data type (numbers, text, datetimes, lists, maps) may be encoded in a composable way" (CESR spec > Abstract Domain representations, L11). Reviewers who model CESR as "a signature envelope" miss that it is a general primary-datatype encoding.

#### CESR is not naive Base64 {#04-not-naive-base64}

CESR is not naive Base64. Standard Base64 pads each individual conversion to a multiple of 4 characters, which yields only "one-way composability" — primitives are separable but not losslessly round-trippable en masse (CESR spec > Text Code Size, L252; L95; L139). Convert a concatenation of raw binary values through naive Base64 and bits from two adjacent primitives can land in a single text character (L184), destroying the boundaries. CESR therefore forbids the `=` pad character entirely "because all CESR-encoded Primitives are composable" (CESR spec > Concrete Domain representations, L93). If a proposal reaches for `=`, it has already lost composability.

#### The encoding is an external interop contract {#04-interop-contract}

The encoding is an external interop contract, not an implementation detail. Compliance is normative: "All compliant encoded Primitives MUST be Composable. All compliant encoded Primitives MUST be self-framing" (CESR spec > Composability, L5); "All compliant implementations MUST support the transformations between all three domains" (CESR spec > Transformations, L31). keripy is a reference implementation whose intent layer is exogenous — the spec itself. "A change that passes keripy's own tests but diverges from the spec/wire format is a defect, because it silently breaks interop" (00-lens.md, claim 5).

The design aesthetic is minimally-sufficient strength, no waste: "there is minimally sufficient cryptographic strength and more cryptographic strength just wastes computation and bandwidth" (CESR spec > Compact fixed-size codes, L446). 128 bits of entropy is the accepted floor; the compact tables deliberately exclude weak suites (CESR spec > Annex A > Code table entry policy, L783). And the format is text-first for humans, binary-only for compactness: "A primary design goal of CESR is to select an encoding approach that provides high usability, readability, or human friendliness in the 'T' domain... The 'B' domain's purpose is merely to provide convenient compactness at scale" (CESR spec > Stable Framing Codes, L202).

CESR was developed for KERI ("CESR was developed for the KERI protocol," CESR spec > SAID, L1180) and is the encoding substrate beneath KERI, ACDC, and TSP. But the composability contract is protocol-agnostic; the genus/version mechanism ([section 8](#04-genus-version) below) is exactly what lets one encoding serve many protocols.

---

## 2. The three domains and the six transformations {#04-three-domains}

CESR defines three representations of any primitive (CESR spec > Abstract Domain representations, L11):

- Text domain 'T' — streamable Base64 text.
- Binary domain 'B' — streamable binary.
- Raw domain 'R' — non-streamable binary, represented as a two-tuple `(code, raw)`: the text derivation code plus the unqualified raw bytes. Cryptographic operations happen here: "The actual use of Cryptographic Primitives happens in the 'R' domain using the raw binary element of the `(code, raw)` pair" (L11).

Composability is a property of T and B only; R is the special domain where the math is applied but not streamed. There are six transformations, one per ordered pair — `T(B)`, `B(T)`, `T(R)`, `R(T)`, `B(R)`, `R(B)` — and full circuits are possible, e.g. `R -> T(R) -> T -> B(T) -> B -> R(B) -> R` (CESR spec > Transformations between Domains, L17-31, L40).

The interop payoff is precise and load-bearing: `T(B)` is naive Base64 encode and `B(T)` is naive Base64 decode, so "CESR Primitives are compatible with existing Base64 (RFC-4648) tooling"; only R↔T and R↔B need new code (CESR spec > Text Code Size, L266). This is what lets a JSON-embedded CESR value be handled by ordinary Base64 libraries. The reference implementation makes this literal [code]: a primitive is `composable` iff `len(qb64b) % 4 == 0 and len(qb2) % 3 == 0 and encodeB64(qb2) == qb64b and decodeB64(qb64b) == qb2` (keripy core/coring.py, L1239-1247 @`b8f60166b`). That method is the composability contract, executable.

---

## 3. Composability — the core invariant and the 24-bit backbone {#04-composability}

### Definition (well-established) {#04-composability-definition}

"An encoding has Composability when any set of Self-Framing concatenated Primitives expressed in either the Text domain or Binary domain may be converted as a group to the other Domain and back again without loss" (CESR spec > Composability, L5). Formally, `T(B)` and `B(T)` are jointly concatenation-composable iff `T(cat(b[k])) = cat(T(b[k]))` and `B(cat(t[k])) = cat(B(t[k]))` for all k — "the transformation of a set (as a whole) of concatenated Primitives is equal to the concatenation of the set of individually transformed Primitives" (CESR spec > Concatenation composability property, L70-73). The invariant is total: "Each and every Primitive or Count Code group of primitives MUST satisfy the Concatenation Composability property" (L73).

#### Self-framing makes de-concatenation possible {#04-self-framing}

Self-framing is the mechanism that makes de-concatenation possible. A parser reads the first character (T) or byte (B), indexes a lookup table, and thereby learns exactly how many remaining characters/bytes belong to this primitive: "The self-framing property of the primitives enables de-concatenation" (L87); "This makes the Primitive self-framing" (CESR spec > Examples of pre-padding, L358). There are no delimiters and no ambiguity — the type code carries the length. keripy enforces this at parse dispatch [code]: `_exfil` reads `first = qb64b[:1]  # extract first char code selector`, and routes on it — a leading `-` is a count code, `_` is an op code, anything else indexes the `Hards` table (keripy core/coring.py, L1350-1362 @`b8f60166b`).

### 3.1 The 24-bit alignment rule (the arithmetic backbone) {#04-alignment}

#### Invariant: 24-bit alignment {#04-alignment-invariant}

"all Primitives MUST be aligned on 24-bit boundaries to satisfy the Composability property" (CESR spec > Conversions, L198). 24 = LCM(6, 8) — the least common multiple of Base64's 6 bits per character and a byte's 8 bits (L196). This single fact forces:

- every B-domain primitive length to be an integer multiple of 3 bytes (a triplet);
- every T-domain primitive length to be an integer multiple of 4 Base64 characters (a quadlet) (L198).

The pad-size formula is `ps = (3 - (N mod 3)) mod 3`, where `N` is the raw length in bytes (CESR spec > Text Code Size, L264). The double modulo is not a stylistic flourish; it maps `0->0, 1->2, 2->1`, and "simplifying" it breaks triplet alignment (30-invariants.md, A4). The number of leading pre-pad zero bytes equals the number of trailing pad characters for the same N (L260). Pad size then selects code size: pad 0 -> code length `4M`, pad 1 -> `4M+1`, pad 2 -> `4M+2` (CESR spec > Example of pad size computation, L276-280).

The reference implementation carries this arithmetic verbatim in `Matter._infil` [code]: for fixed-size primitives `ps = (3 - ((rs + ls) % 3)) % 3`, guarded by a raise when `ps != (cs % 4)`, above a comment reading "Assumes ls in (0,1,2) and cs % 4 != 3, fs % 4 == 0. Sizes table test must ensure these properties." (keripy core/coring.py, L1284-1290 @`b8f60166b`). `Matter._rawSize` recovers raw length as `(((fs - cs) * 3 // 4) - ls)`, under the comment "assumes .Sizes only has valid entries, cs % 4 != 3, and fs % 4 == 0" (keripy core/coring.py, L866-867 @`b8f60166b`). The order of operations in that expression is load-bearing — the multiply-and-floor must precede the lead-byte subtraction, and reordering desyncs — but note that the warning is the knowledge base's, not the source's: "Order of ops matters (`*3//4` before `- ls`)" is keripy-knowledge 30-invariants.md, A5 @`9489ac9bd` (L43-44), and no such comment exists in `coring.py` at `b8f60166b` or at `3a8e01aec`. Earlier revisions of this chapter attributed it to a keripy code comment; that attribution is corrected here, 2026-09-15, and the underlying arithmetic claim is unaffected because the expression itself is verbatim in the source. These are the invariants A1-A5: `fs % 4 == 0`, `cs % 4 != 3`, `(ls + rs) % 3 == 0`, `ls ∈ {0,1,2}`, and the raw-length equality (30-invariants.md > A @`9489ac9bd`).

### 3.2 Mid-padding — a deliberate "never do it the other way" {#04-mid-padding}

Two ways exist to reach 24-bit alignment: (1) post-pad trailing `=` characters, as naive Base64 does; or (2) pre-pad leading zero bytes to the raw before conversion ("lead bytes"). CESR chose (2): "all CESR primitives MUST employ mid-padding as defined" (CESR spec > Code characters and lead bytes, L234). The term "lead bytes" is used deliberately instead of "pad" to avoid confusion, and the count of lead bytes (pre-conversion) equals the count of pad characters (post-conversion) (L226). The consequence is that any zero padding lands in the middle of the primitive — after the type code, before the value — which keeps the value right-aligned and readable (CESR spec > Stable value encoding, L214). keripy's `_infil` implements exactly this [code]: `encodeB64(bytes([0] * (ps + ls)) + raw)[ps:]` — prepend `ps + ls` zero bytes, encode, then skip the first `ps` characters so that when the full code is prepended the total length is `fs` with the pad bits sitting as zeros in the interior (keripy core/coring.py, L1301 @`b8f60166b`).

#### Reviewer takeaway {#04-mid-padding-takeaway}

The padding-and-alignment math is the most fragile surface in the entire stack. Because CESR is self-framing (read code -> look up length -> read bytes), a parser that predates a miscomputed size does not throw — it silently mis-frames the next primitive and desyncs the rest of the stream. keripy-knowledge names this section "the Falcon-critical layer" (30-invariants.md > A, L29 @`9489ac9bd`) and states the failure mode directly: "Get the sizing math wrong and a parser that predates your code desyncs the entire stream — silently, because CESR is self-framing" (30-invariants.md > A, L31-32), with the double-modulo called out by itself — a "simplification" there "breaks triplet alignment" (30-invariants.md, A4, L43). Correction, 2026-09-15: earlier revisions of this chapter ran those two into a single quoted string, "breaks triplet/quadlet alignment and desyncs parsers silently", which appears nowhere in the source; the composite is cut and the two real sentences stand in its place. Any PR touching `Matter.Sizes`, `_infil`, `_rawSize`, or `composable` is touching an external contract, not internal code.

---

## 4. Stable framing codes — the usability doctrine {#04-stable-framing}

Two stability invariants govern how a type code behaves as the value changes.

### Stable type coding (invariant) {#04-stable-type-coding}

"The type portion of all compliant prepended Framing Codes MUST be stable in the Text domain" — "the leading characters that determine the type do not change when any other portion of the primitive changes" (CESR spec > Stable type encoding, L202-206). The type comes first, consumes a fixed integral number of T-domain characters (L210), and never shares information bits with the length or value in any single T-domain character. Stability is imposed on T, not B, and the choice is deliberate: binary parsers handle bit-fields and shifts trivially, but text parsers only see whole characters, "another reason to impose a stability constraint on the 'T' domain type coding instead of the 'B' domain" (L208).

#### Stable value coding (invariant) {#04-stable-value-coding}

"the value portion of any primitive MUST be right aligned" (CESR spec > Stable value encoding, L216). This makes small numbers legible — decimal `0, 1, 2` map to Base64 `A, B, C` (L214).

#### Each code table is keyed by the first character {#04-first-character-tables}

"Each code table MUST be uniquely indicated by the first character of the type code in the 'T' domain" (CESR spec > Multiple code table approach, L240). There is one integrated parse-and-convert table: read the type selector, and you know how to parse and convert the rest (L238). keripy realizes this [code] with the `Hards`/`Bards` dictionaries of hard-code sizes keyed by the T-domain and B-domain selector respectively (20-crosswalk.md @`9489ac9bd`; keripy core/coring.py, L1350-1355 @`b8f60166b`).

## 5. The multiple-code-table design and crypto agility {#04-code-tables}

### 5.1 Why multiple tables {#04-why-multiple-tables}

A single one-size-fits-all table would either waste characters on popular codes or run out of room for rare future ones. CESR resolves this with multiple tables, each optimized differently (CESR spec > Multiple code table approach, L238). The "sweet spots" are the two cryptographic common cases: 32-byte raw (pad 1 -> a 1-character code) and 64-byte raw (pad 2 -> a 2-character code) — EdDSA/ECDSA keys, 256-bit digests, 512-bit signatures (CESR spec > Compact fixed-size codes, L450-474). The optimized 1- and 2-character tables target these so the most common primitives carry the least framing overhead.

### 5.2 Code table selectors {#04-table-selectors}

Of the 64 Base64 characters, only 12 are needed as table selectors, leaving 52 for single-character type codes in the default table — 13 tables total (CESR spec > Code table selectors, L476-487):

- `-` = Count Code table selector (MUST).
- `_` = Op Code table selector (MUST, reserved/TBD).
- `[A-Z, a-z]` = single-character type codes (default table, 52 codes, pad size 1).
- `[0-9]` = selectors for the other 10 tables.
- "The first character of any Primitive MUST be either a selector or a 1-character code type" (L484).

### 5.3 How a new algorithm claims an unused slot without desyncing old parsers {#04-unused-slot-agility}

This is the crypto-agility mechanism, and it is the reason the encoding survives algorithm turnover. The derivation/type code encodes the crypto suite, and adding a new suite means adding a new entry (a previously-unused code point) in a table. Because framing is purely a function of the code -> length lookup, a parser that does not recognize the new code still frames the stream correctly for every primitive it does know — "The CESR derivation code enables cryptographic digest algorithm agility... Each serialization may use a different cryptographic digest algorithm as indicated by its derivation code. This provides interoperable future-proofing" (CESR spec > SAID, L1180). The primer states the operational rule as three steps a non-upgraded parser follows regardless: "Read Code -> Lookup Length -> Read Bytes" (keri-primer.md > 4.2, via raw/05 L155).

The load-bearing assumption here is subtle and worth flagging: an old parser frames the stream correctly only if the new code's sizing entry does not collide with, and does not alter, the size interpretation of any code the old parser already knows. Agility is "read code, look up length" — but the old parser looks the length up in its own table. A new fixed-size code in a table region the old parser treats as variable-size (or vice versa) would desync. This is why the compact-table entry policy is disciplined (CESR spec > Annex A > Code table entry policy, L783: first-needed-first-entered, ≥128-bit strength required) and why the reference implementation's shadow-table rule exists ([section 5.5](#04-shadow-tables)).

### 5.4 Backward-compatibility semantics of adding codes {#04-backward-compatibility}

The spec is explicit and asymmetric (CESR spec > Protocol genus/version codes, L618-622). All three quotes below were re-verified verbatim at `main` `bad6edd84` in this pass and their line hints are unmoved — this is the most-reused passage in the corpus, underwriting the crypto-agility claim in keri-doctrine.md, and it is stable [spec]:

- "Any addition of a new code to the code table is backward-breaking in at least one direction... New implementations with the new codes can accept streams from old implementations, but old ones will break if they receive the new ones" (L618).
- Major change = "a code's meaning changes" -> increment MAJOR version -> breaks both directions (L620).
- Minor change = "a code is added to a table" -> increment MINOR -> breaks only new-sender->old-receiver; a new receiver still handles old streams (L622).

There is deliberately far more minor room than major (4096 minor per major), because additive extension is the common case and meaning-change is meant to be rare. This is the honest, unglamorous truth an adversarial reviewer should hold: crypto agility is not "any parser can read anything." It is "a new algorithm is a minor version bump that old parsers can detect and reject cleanly, and new parsers can accept both." Old-receiver + new-code = a controlled, detectable break, not a silent misread — provided the sizing math is correct.

### 5.5 The reference-implementation trap: shadow tables {#04-shadow-tables}

Ground truth from keripy adds a critical operational caveat the spec does not spell out. A digest/key/signature code does not live in only one table. Registering a new code in `MatterCodex` + `Matter.Sizes` alone makes it round-trip as a primitive but leaves it invisible to SAID derivation and prefix validation — it "fails late and silently" (31-landmines.md, landmine L5, ~L83 @`9489ac9bd`). A correct addition must also touch `Saider.Digests`, `Serder.Digests`, and the relevant `*Dex` sets (`PreDex`, `DigDex`, `SmallVrzDex`/`LargeVrzDex`). The source says so itself, in a comment this pass re-anchored: "# When add new to DigCodes update Saider.Digests and Serder.Digests class attr" (keripy core/coring.py, L444 @`b8f60166b`) [code] — it was cited at keripy coring.py, L460 in earlier revisions of this chapter, and the line has moved. As of the 2.0-dev line this extends to `BodyUniversalCodex` (`BUDex`) plus `Counter.BUCodes` for CESR-native body framing (31-landmines.md, landmine L5; raw/08 section A9, both @`9489ac9bd`). keripy-knowledge calls getting the code-table entry and sizing math exactly right "the highest-risk surface in the flagship" (00-lens.md, claim 8, L81 @`9489ac9bd`).

#### Keep the discipline; drop the urgency {#04-shadow-tables-urgency}

The knowledge base writes this rule as advice about work in flight — "The Falcon PR must touch every shadow table" — and the corpus has repeated that framing. It is no longer accurate, and correcting it is a supersession worth recording. Superseded 2026-09-15: at keripy `b8f60166b` there is no Falcon PR and no post-quantum code of any kind. A repo-wide case-insensitive search of `src/keri` for FN-DSA, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, Dilithium, Falcon, SPHINCS, Kyber and ML-KEM returns only the `falcon` web framework, and the single hit inside `src/keri/core/` is a docstring line about "the Falcon compile route utility method" (keripy core/routing.py, L574) [code]. The knowledge base is candid about why: its own plan defers the work outright — "**Prereq:** resolve the two conflicting Falcon spec docs first" (PLAN.md > 7 effort table, L170 @`9489ac9bd`) — and its open-decisions section asks which of two in-repo Falcon designs is canonical, one specifying fixed-size signatures with `b`/`c`/`d`/`e` and one specifying variable-size signatures with digest-AIDs (PLAN.md > 9, ~L189-190). So nothing is blocked, because nothing has been written. The shadow-table rule remains exactly right as forward-looking advice for whoever eventually writes it, and that is how this chapter uses it; a reviewer should not read it as describing a PR that is close to landing.

### 5.6 Two allocation rules that turn taste into normative constraint [spec-next] {#04-allocation-rules}

The forward branch adds two rules about where a code may be placed, and they are doctrine rather than table bookkeeping. Both live in the entry-policy section at `v1.1` `65fd7518b` (CESR spec > Code table entry policy, L785-787) and have no counterpart on `main` at `bad6edd84`.

#### The compact tables are a scarce resource {#04-compact-tables-scarce}

The compact tables are a scarce resource, and scarcity is now an allocation rule. "The one- and two-character code tables are a scarce resource" (L785) — 52 codes in the one-character table, 64 in the two-character, against 262,144 in each four-character table. The admission test the branch derives from that is relative overhead, not importance: entries in the compact tables "MUST be reserved for Primitives whose raw size is small enough that a longer code would materially increase the size of the encoded Primitive" (L785). Post-quantum primitives fail that test by a wide margin, so the branch states the exclusion normatively: "Post-quantum codes MUST therefore be placed in the four-character fixed tables given by the `1`, `2`, and `3` selectors" (L785), the sentence continuing "and MUST NOT consume entries in the one- or two-character tables." This converts the [section 1](#04-what-cesr-is) design aesthetic — minimally-sufficient strength, no waste — into a hard constraint on the namespace itself, and it is why the compact-code assignments this chapter once carried are now forbidden rather than merely superseded ([section 5.7](#04-pq-in-practice)).

#### Which four-character table: arithmetic, not design {#04-four-char-table-arithmetic}

Which four-character table a code lands in is arithmetic, not design. "Which of the three four-character fixed tables a given Primitive occupies is not a matter of choice. It is determined by the raw size of the Primitive modulo 3" (L787), because the encoding must align on a 24-bit boundary: raw size ≡ 0 mod 3 takes no lead bytes and selector `1`; ≡ 2 mod 3 takes one lead byte and selector `2`; ≡ 1 mod 3 takes two lead bytes and selector `3`. This is [section 3.1](#04-alignment)'s alignment rule resurfacing as a table-assignment constraint, and the corollary is a live outsider-tell worth stating on its own: a selector encodes lead-byte alignment, not algorithm semantics. The spec draws it out itself — "the Primitives belonging to a single algorithm are commonly distributed across more than one table" (L787), the example being that an Ed25519 verification key uses the one-character `D` while an Ed25519 signature uses the two-character `0B`. A reviewer who infers an algorithm grouping, a security level, or a family relationship from a selector is reading length arithmetic as if it were taxonomy.

A third rule in the same section is narrower but shows the same temper. Parameter-set admission is deliberately restrictive on an ecosystem-scrutiny argument: "Admitting every variant of an algorithm invites the use of variants that have received little implementation scrutiny" (L791), the sentence ending "which weakens rather than strengthens the security of the ecosystem." Of the twelve SLH-DSA parameter sets FIPS 205 defines, only the six `s` sets get entries; the `f` fast-signing variants are excluded because they trade signature size for signing speed, which the branch calls "the wrong trade for a protocol whose signatures are transmitted and archived far more often than they are generated" (L791). That last is the spec's reasoning about KERI's traffic shape, and the corpus repeats it as reasoning — it is plausible for an event stream and much less obviously true for a constrained high-frequency signer.

#### The editor's reasons for fixed codes in the large tables {#04-allocation-rationale}

The allocation rules have a stated rationale outside the spec text, in the pull request that added the post-quantum table, and it is [proposal]: an editor's comment, not specification text. Answering a proposal to give signatures variable-length codes, Sam Smith ruled that the saving was illusory, because a fixed code is chosen by raw size modulo 3: "So at worst case there is never more than 2 bytes of overhead no matter the length of the primitive." (CESR spec GitHub > #165, comment of 2026-03-18, R-017, https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification/pull/165#issuecomment-4085555336). The placement rule above comes from the same comment — "Since PQ codes are so large, there is no reason to consume the limited code space from the compact code tables." — and so does a reason the spec does not give: a fixed code doubles as the dispatch key, so instead of inspecting the payload's size to choose a library call, "we use the fixed code itself as the dispatch". The normative weight still sits in the `v1.1` MUST and MUST NOT quoted earlier in this section; the comment explains them.

#### Too much agility is itself a defect {#04-goldilocks-agility}

The same thread carries a counterweight to the crypto-agility thesis this chapter otherwise argues: "There is a saying in crypto. Too much agility is a bad thing. There is a goldilocks amount of agility." (CESR spec GitHub > #165, comment of 2026-03-19, R-018, https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification/pull/165#issuecomment-4086516133) [proposal]. He applied it to Falcon, preferring only the fixed-length signatures, because squeezing out the last bytes "opens the vulnerability for timing attacks and makes downstream uses of the signatures more difficult". The `v1.1` text agrees with him on both counts: every post-quantum signature code is fixed-size ([section 5.7](#04-pq-in-practice)), and parameter-set admission is restrictive for the reason quoted above. Agility here means the ability to add a well-scrutinized algorithm at an unused code point. It is not a license to admit every variant, and a reviewer who argues that CESR should encode every parameter set of every scheme is arguing against the editor's stated position, not extending it.

#### A code names an encoding, never a use {#04-encoding-not-usage}

The corollary drawn above for selectors holds for codes too, and the editor states it as a rule: "The CESR code defines the encoding not the usage semantics." (CESR spec GitHub > #165, comment of 2026-03-19, R-019, https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification/pull/165#issuecomment-4087093269) [proposal]. The one exception he names is "the non-trans versus trans codes for public keys as AIDs", made to keep witness key management simple. The principle reached `v1.1` as the refusal of a code for a digest of a public key, quoted in [section 11](#04-said) [spec-next]: a digest is encoded by its algorithm, and the context in which it appears says whether it is a SAID, an AID, a pre-rotation commitment or something else. A proposal for a code that means "this digest is used as X" is the mixing of concerns that rule forbids.

### 5.7 Post-quantum agility in practice — what is actually where {#04-pq-in-practice}

#### Retraction first {#04-pq-retraction}

Retraction first, because this passage was the worst-supported material in the corpus. Earlier revisions of this chapter stated specific FN-DSA code assignments as normative: pubkeys `1AAQ` (FN-DSA-512) and a one-character code for FN-DSA-1024 at 2392 qb64; signatures `1AAR` and a one-character code at 1708; seeds `c` and `d` at 44 each; a compact AID formed by digesting the pubkey — all cited to "§Post-Quantum Security, L1514". Every one of those citations came from commit `d35125e61`, which is reachable from no ref in the CESR repository. It is a dangling object from an abandoned PR branch, surviving in one local clone and due to vanish on the next `git gc`; `git branch -a --contains` and `git for-each-ref --contains` both return nothing for it, and it is an ancestor of neither branch tip. The text was never on the standardizing line at any nameable commit. Under the corpus's own rule that a quote which cannot be found at its pinned commit is cut rather than reworded, the whole passage is cut, not re-anchored (raw/02 section 13b). The general lesson is worth more than the codes: a pin that resolves is not a pin that is citable, and `git rev-parse` will happily succeed on an object no reader can fetch.

#### Nothing on the standardizing line {#04-pq-main-empty}

On the standardizing line there is nothing to replace it with. At `main` `bad6edd84`, CESR has zero post-quantum codes. An exhaustive search of spec/spec-body.md at that commit for FN-DSA, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, ML-KEM, FIPS, `1AAQ` and `1AAR` returns no hits at all; "Falcon" occurs exactly once, in the older entry-policy paragraph, as a candidate — "Falcon appears to be among the leading candidates with open-source code already available" (CESR spec > Code table entry policy, L783). The fixed four-character table ends at `1AAN` (with `1AAO`/`1AAP` consumed by the variable-size group), the one-character table ends at `a`, and the two-character table ends at `0S`. Everything CESR says about post-quantum on the standardizing line is the pre-rotation hash firewall of [section 11](#04-said) — a way of deferring exposure, not a post-quantum primitive. A reader who took the old passage at its word would have believed `main` carried codes it has never carried.

#### The real work is [spec-next] {#04-pq-forward-branch}

The real work is [spec-next] and it is substantial. At `v1.1` `65fd7518b` the master code table gains roughly 33 post-quantum primitives across the four-character `1`, `2` and `3` tables, covering three NIST signature schemes: FN-DSA (FIPS 206), ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). The branch opens the subsection by naming the limit of the firewall rather than by announcing codes — "Hiding pre-rotated keys behind digests, as described above, protects the next key pair but does not protect the currently exposed one" (CESR spec > Post-Quantum Cryptographic Primitives, L1553) — and is explicit that the two are stacked: "The two mechanisms are complementary, not alternatives; pre-rotation continues to provide defense in depth for whichever signature scheme is in use" (L1553). Every code encodes a fixed raw size, including FN-DSA's, whose native encoding is variable: "Every post-quantum signature code defined in this specification encodes a signature of fixed raw size" (L1555). The first of the three reasons given for rejecting a variable-length encoding is [section 3](#04-composability)'s self-framing property defended by name — "A variable-length encoding obliges the parser to consult a length field rather than the code alone" (L1555) — and the third is hedged by the spec itself and must stay hedged: "Signature length in the variable-length format has also been examined as a possible side channel, although the significance of that finding is contested" (L1555).

#### The four compact assignments are retired {#04-pq-compact-retired}

The four compact assignments are retired, and their code points are now forbidden. `b`, `c`, `d` and `e` are unassigned on both branches — the one-character table ends at `a` (blinding factor) at `bad6edd84` and equally at `65fd7518b`. They existed only in the unreachable `d35125e61`, and the forward branch did not merely fail to adopt them: [section 5.6](#04-allocation-rules)'s placement rule makes a post-quantum code in the one-character table a MUST NOT. Their contents moved into the `2` table, with different sizes, because a four-character code plus one lead byte changes the arithmetic: `b` FN-DSA-1024 verification key → `2AAA` at 2396 qb64 (not 2392); `e` FN-DSA-1024 signature → `2AAB` at 1712 (not 1708); `c` seed of an FN-DSA-512 private key → `2AAC` at 48 (not 44); `d` seed of an FN-DSA-1024 private key → `2AAD` at 48 (not 44). Only `1AAQ` (FN-DSA-512 verification key, 1200 qb64) and `1AAR` (FN-DSA-512 signature, 892) survive at identical sizes, and [section 5.6](#04-allocation-rules) explains exactly why: 897 and 666 are both ≡ 0 mod 3, so they need no lead bytes and stay in the `1` table (`v1.1` L1021-1022, L1036-1039).

#### No shipped implementation carries the table {#04-pq-unimplemented}

No shipped implementation carries this table, and that is the month's cleanest cross-implementation finding. keripy at `b8f60166b` has none [code] — see [section 5.5](#04-shadow-tables) for the search. Upstream signify-ts at `ffba8406e` has none [code]: a search of `WebOfTrust/signify-ts` `src` for ML-DSA, FN-DSA, SLH-DSA, Dilithium, Falcon, SPHINCS and Kyber returns nothing. The only implementation anywhere is an unmerged branch on a personal fork — `feat/cesr-pq-codes` on `dhh1128/signify-ts`, where at `4ed767b49` `Matter.Sizes` carries all 33 rows, e.g. `'1AAR': new Sizage(4, 0, 892, 0), // FN-DSA-512 signature, 666 B` (signify-ts fork src/keri/core/matter.ts, L174). That is [proposal], not [code], and it must not be promoted: no implementation anyone else runs behaves this way. The earlier framing available to this corpus — that the reference implementation and the TypeScript client disagree about the post-quantum code table — does not survive checking. The three implementations agree, in that none of them have it. That is a much less exciting finding about interop and a considerably more honest one.

#### The fork as evidence for the central claim {#04-pq-fork-evidence}

The fork is nonetheless the best evidence this chapter has ever had for its own central claim, and the evidence comes from outside keripy [proposal]. In the same fork's stream parser, sizing is arithmetic on the code and never on the value: `probePrimitive` selects a table by class, looks up the hard code — `const sizage = sizes.get(head.slice(0, hs));` (signify-ts fork src/keri/core/parsing.ts, L256 @`4ed767b49`) — and returns the table's full size as the length without ever decoding the payload; group sizing has the same shape, `const innerEnd = innerStart + count * 4; // self-framing: count is quadlets` (signify-ts fork parsing.ts, L385). The consequence is the crypto-agility thesis demonstrated rather than asserted: the 33 post-quantum rows required no parser change at all. The commit does not touch `parsing.ts`, and a 21 KB SLH-DSA signature frames correctly the moment the table knows its size. A second, independently maintained implementation arriving at the same property is stronger support for [section 5.3](#04-unused-slot-agility) than keripy's own code can be, because keripy is the implementation the spec was written alongside.

#### Two negatives that are findings, not absences {#04-pq-negatives}

There is no ML-KEM code on either branch, and the deferral is deliberate rather than accidental: "ML-KEM is a key-encapsulation mechanism rather than a signature scheme; codes for it are not defined here and are left to a later version" (CESR spec v1.1 > Code table entry policy, L789). So CESR as pinned has no post-quantum key-encapsulation primitive at all — every post-quantum code in the table is a signature, a public verification key, or a private-key seed. Any claim that CESR supports post-quantum encryption is wrong at both pins. And there is no post-quantum indexed signature code on either branch: the indexed table at `v1.1` `65fd7518b` (L1109-1131) still holds only Ed25519, secp256k1 and Ed448 forms plus their big variants, and the same table stands at `main`. The consequence is concrete and belongs in the risk list rather than in a footnote — see [section 12](#04-interop-risks). The branch flags it itself, as open issue 171, alongside an issue for SQIsign and other on-ramp candidates (issue 170). The older placeholder marking post-quantum operations as open — issue #14, at L559 on both branches — was not closed by any of this work.

#### Status: a revert is proposed and pending {#04-pq-revert}

Status, added 2026-10-03: a revert of all of the above is proposed and pending. Pull request trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification#178 (https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification/pull/178), opened 2026-09-22 by Kor Dwarshuis from branch `revert-165-pq`, would undo the PR that added these primitives; its single commit `487fab701` is titled "Revert "Add post-quantum signature primitives (FN-DSA, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA)"" and touches only spec/spec-body.md, with 70 lines removed and one added (`git show --stat 487fab7`). The PR body is one line — "Reverts trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification#165" — and states no rationale. As of 2026-10-03 it is open, unmerged and unreviewed, and `v1.1` is unchanged at `65fd7518b`, so every [spec-next] marker in this section and in [section 5.6](#04-allocation-rules) stands as written. What changes is the hedge: the post-quantum table is not merely unmerged into `main`, it is contested on its own branch, and nothing read this month says why. A reader should not treat its eventual normative status as the default outcome, and should not read the revert as a technical rejection either, since no reason has been given.

#### What a reviewer should carry away {#04-pq-takeaway}

Treat the mechanism — a new entry in a four-character table, a minor version bump, disciplined sizing, shadow tables updated — as settled and demonstrated. Treat the codes as [spec-next]: real text at a real commit on a branch that is divergent from `main`, unmerged, and unimplemented by anything shipped. The gap between those two statements is the honest position, and it is wider than the previous revision of this chapter implied in both directions — the mechanism is better evidenced than before, and the assignments are further from normative.

## 6. Sizing math and the table taxonomy {#04-sizing-taxonomy}

There are two major raw-primitive kinds, fixed-length and variable-length, plus count-code, genus/version, opcode, and context-specific tables (CESR spec > Table types, L493-499).

### 6.1 Fixed-length raw-size tables (CESR spec, L503-531) {#04-fixed-size-tables}

- 1-char table (`[A-Z, a-z]`) — 52 codes, pad size 1 — the 32-byte sweet spot.
- 2-char table (selector `0`) — 64 codes, pad size 2 — the 64-byte sweet spot.
- Large fixed (selectors `1`/`2`/`3` = 0/1/2 lead bytes) — 4-char codes, 3 type characters -> `64**3 = 262,144` codes each. The selector "implicitly encodes the number of lead bytes." This is the headroom [section 5.6](#04-allocation-rules) now reserves post-quantum codes to, and on `v1.1` `65fd7518b` the `3` table is populated with a cryptographic suite for the first time — it was structurally defined but empty of crypto before [spec-next].

### 6.2 Variable-length raw-size tables (CESR spec, L533-577) {#04-variable-size-tables}

Size is measured in quadlets (4 T-chars) / triplets (3 B-bytes) — the 24-bit unit. T count = size × 4 chars; B count = size × 3 bytes.

- Small variable (selectors `4`/`5`/`6` = 0/1/2 lead) — 4-char code = selector + 1 type + 2 size chars. 64 types; size up to `64**2 - 1 = 4095` quadlets = 16,380 chars / 12,285 bytes.
- Large variable (selectors `7`/`8`/`9` = 0/1/2 lead) — 8-char code = selector + 3 type + 4 size chars. `262,144` types; size up to `64**4 - 1 = 16,777,215` quadlets = 67,108,860 chars / 50,331,645 bytes. The first 62 entries mirror the small-variable types so a value can use the shorter 4-char code when it is small.

### 6.3 Parse-part vocabulary (CESR spec, L718-778) {#04-parse-parts}

The parser flow is: first-char selector -> hard size (`hs`) -> extract hard chars -> index the parse-size table -> get remaining sizes -> extract/convert. The same table works in the B domain (each size counted in sextets, not chars) (L720). The part labels are worth memorizing because they appear throughout keripy: `hs` hard size, `ss` soft size, `os` other size, `ms` main size (`ss - os`), `cs` code size (`hs + ss`), `vs` value size, `fs` full size (`hs + ss + vs`), `ls` lead size, `ps` pad size, `rs` raw size, `bs` binary size (`ls + rs`) (L765-778). In keripy these live in `Sizage = namedtuple("Sizage", "hs ss xs fs ls")` and `Matter.Sizes` (keripy core/coring.py, L660 @`b8f60166b`; 20-crosswalk.md @`9489ac9bd`) [code]. A code with `fs is None` is variable-sized (`SmallVrzDex`/`LargeVrzDex`); a fixed code has an integer `fs` and satisfies `fs % 4 == 0` (keripy core/coring.py, L864, 882, 970 @`b8f60166b`).

#### Special-value codes {#04-special-value-codes}

Some fixed-size codes carry their value inside the code's soft/size part (compact tags and versions); the raw part MAY be empty (CESR spec, L660). keripy models this as `_special`: a code is special when `fs is not None and ss > 0` (keripy core/coring.py, L910-918 @`b8f60166b`; invariant A6, special soft implies fixed size, 30-invariants.md @`9489ac9bd`).

## 7. Count / group framing codes (grouping and pipelining) {#04-count-codes}

### Count codes count quadlets, never primitives {#04-count-quadlets}

Count Codes (a.k.a. Group Codes) count quadlets/triplets in a group — never primitives. "always counts the number of quadlets/triplets in the group not the number of primitives" (CESR spec > Count Code tables, L591). This is a recurring correction: reviewers reach for "number of items," but the count is in 24-bit units precisely so the group can be skipped without parsing its contents. Count codes enable pipelining (multiplex/demultiplex), core-affinity offloading, and hierarchical group-of-groups composition (CESR spec > Count or Group Framing Codes, L362; CESR spec > Composability, L7).

A count code is itself a composable primitive with no raw value, only its text code; pad size is always 0, and its length is a multiple of 4 chars / 3 bytes (L364, L591). keripy encodes this as invariant A7: for counters `hs + ss == fs` always — count codes carry no padding, and the soft encodes the quadlet/triplet count via `intToB64` (30-invariants.md, A7 @`9489ac9bd`; keripy core/counting.py, Counter).

#### Domain-invariant count (invariant) {#04-domain-invariant-count}

Because the count is in quadlets/triplets (both 24 bits), "the count value is invariant between 'T' and 'B' Domains... MUST be the number of Quadlets in the 'T' domain and the number of Triplets in the 'B' domain" (L581). This lets a parser "extract the number of characters/bytes in a group from the Stream without parsing the group's contents; it is therefore pipeline-able" (L583). "Each element in content of a Count Code group MUST be aligned on a 24-bit boundary. Thus the only elements allowed in the contents of a Count Code group are other primitives or groups" (L591).

Nested selectors: the first selector is always `-`. The second character being a letter `[A-Z, a-z]` means a single-char count code (52 total); a numeral, `-`, or `_` selects a secondary table (L594). The small count table is `-` + type letter + 2 size chars = 4 chars, counting 0-4095 (CESR spec > Small Count Code table, L599). The large count table is `--` + 1 type + 5 size chars = 8 chars, 64 types, counting 0 to `64**5 - 1 = 1,073,741,823` — groups up to ~4.29e9 chars / 3.22e9 bytes (CESR spec > Large Count Code table, L605).

In keripy these are the attachment doctrine. In the v1 codex at `80f77b73b`: `-A` ControllerIdxSigs, `-B` WitnessIdxSigs, `-C` NonTransReceiptCouples, `-E` FirstSeenReplayCouples, `-F` TransIdxSigGroups, `-G` SealSourceCouples (the anchoring couple), `-H` TransLastIdxSigGroups, `-I` SealSourceTriples, `-L` PathedMaterialCouples, `-Z` ESSRPayloadGroup — everything quadlet-aligned (keripy core/counting.py, L56-76 @`80f77b73b`; raw/09 section 8, corrected 2026-10-03) [code]. Superseded 2026-10-03: this list previously read "`-D`/`-N` TransReceiptIdxSigGroups", stamped `b8f60166b`. That entry no longer exists in keripy: `-D` was removed from the v1 table and v2 `-N` was given a different meaning, so the codex now runs `-A`, `-B`, `-C`, then `-E` with no `-D` at all ([section 7.1](#04-receipts-retired)). Corrected 2026-09-15: earlier revisions named `-L` "PathedMaterialQuadlets", which is no symbol in the source; the `Vrsn_1_0` codex defines `PathedMaterialCouples: str = '-L'` and the word "Quadlet" comes from its trailing comment (keripy core/counting.py, L65 @`b8f60166b`). The counter codes differ across `Vrsn_1_0` and `Vrsn_2_0` (`CounterCodex_1_0`/`_2_0`), which is exactly why the genus/version code ([section 8](#04-genus-version)) has to precede them.

### 7.1 2026-09: keripy retires transferable receipts as a wire type and reuses v2 `-N` — ahead of the spec {#04-receipts-retired}

All keripy claims in this subsection are [code] at `80f77b73b` and rest on raw/09 section 8b; the commits are Sam Smith's, merged in keripy PR #1683, beginning with `9762d6bb4` "retire use of TransReceiptIdxSigGroups group code".

#### Transferable receipts are no longer a wire type {#04-receipts-not-wire-type}

Transferable receipts are no longer a distinct wire type. `TransReceiptIdxSigGroups` is gone from both versions of keripy's counter tables. The v1 size table keeps it only as a comment, `#'-D': Cizage(hs=2, ss=2, fs=4),` (keripy core/counting.py, L618), so a v1 stream carrying a `-D` group has nothing to size it against; raw/09 did not run a parse to see the exact failure, and neither did this chapter. What replaced it is the group that already existed for controller signatures: a transferable endorsement now travels as `TransIdxSigGroups`, `-F` in v1 and `-X` in v2 (keripy core/counting.py, L60, L248), whose signer simply is not the event's controller. The parser routes it to the old receipt handler — `if exts['tsgs']:  # tsgs  TransIdxSigGroups (was trqs)` (keripy core/parsing.py, L1412) — and that handler's docstring calls each group "an endorsement from a transferable AID that is not the controller. Maybe a watcher." (keripy core/eventing.py, L4874–4875). The doctrinal shift is small but real: in keripy, "transferable receipt" is now a role a signature group plays, not a code a parser dispatches on.

#### Removing v1 -D contradicts no spec text {#04-v1-d-removal}

Removing v1 `-D` contradicts no spec text. The CESR specification defines a count-code table only for v2 — its sole master table is "Master code table for genus/version `-_AAACAA` (KERI/ACDC protocol stack Version 2.00)" (CESR spec, L872 @`bad6edd84`; L880 @`65fd7518b`) — and neither branch has a v1 count-code table. That is a negative result, not a conflict. The v2 `-D` is untouched on both sides: the spec's "Datagram Stream Segment up to 4,095 quadlets/triplets" (L840 @`bad6edd84`) matches keripy's `DatagramSegmentGroup: str = '-D'` (keripy core/counting.py, L208; raw/09 section 8b).

#### v2 -N is a spec-implementation divergence {#04-v2-n-divergence}

v2 `-N` is now a spec↔implementation divergence, and the implementation moved first. keripy reassigned the code: `NonceSealSingles: str = '-N'  # Nonce Seal Single(s), nonce as sealed data, nonce or dig.` (keripy core/counting.py, L228), backed by a new `SealNonce` structure whose field is "nd = nonce or digest qb64 as data" (keripy core/structing.py, L73–76). Both CESR branches still define `-N##` as "Transferable identifier receipt quadruples pre+snu+dig+sig up to 4,095 quadlets/triplets" (CESR spec, L915 @`bad6edd84` [spec]; the same row at L923 @`65fd7518b` — tier corrected 2026-10-03 (verification): previously marked [spec-next], but the row is on `main` too, so it is [spec] on both branches, not forward-branch-only text), and `v1.1` has no nonce-seal row at all. So the same two characters now mean different things to the reference implementation and to the text it is supposed to implement. A spec-following v2 parser handed a keripy `-N` group would try to read receipt quadruples, and the reverse misreading is equally available. This is a [code]-versus-[spec] finding, and the chapter states it as one: it does not say which side is right, only that they disagree at these pins and that the spec has not caught up.

The reassignment has a recorded origin. In June 2026 Sam Smith noted that the old code was dead — "TransReceiptQuadruples does not appear to actually be used anywhere" — and proposed either re-forming `-N` around indexed signature groups for watcher receipts, "so that BADA-RUN can be used for watched events from watchers that have transferable AIDs", or simply: "Or we can decide to delete the group." (keripy GitHub > #1450, issue body of 2026-06-23, R-009, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/issues/1450) [proposal]. PR #1683 then removed the receipt group and gave `-N` to nonce seals. Whether `NonceSealSingles` is meant to serve the watcher-receipt case was not established: #1683's code was read for the codex changes above, not for that purpose.

#### The divergence is latent {#04-v2-n-latent}

The divergence is latent rather than live at `80f77b73b`, and that boundary matters. `NonceSealSingles` is defined but not wired into CESR-native serialization or parsing: it is absent from `SealCodex_2_0` (keripy core/counting.py, L392–405), absent from `Serder.ClanCodes` (keripy core/serdering.py, L342–348), and has no `Parser.Methods` entry (raw/09, section 8b and section 10 item 8). The only exercise is in tests that put the seal in JSON event bodies, which does not touch the CESR-native path. ~~So keripy as pinned does not emit a `-N` group on the wire; the conflict is in the code table, waiting for the first producer.~~ Narrowed 2026-10-03 (verification): the negative result covers event-body serialization and stream parsing, not attachment emission. keripy's v2 `messagize` accepts any bond whose clan is in `AClanDom` (keripy core/eventing.py, L1851), `AClanDom` includes `SealNonce` (keripy core/structing.py, L396), and each clan group is framed by `Structor.enclose` using the `ClanCodens` map that sends `SealNonce` to `NonceSealSingles` (keripy core/eventing.py, L1859–1860; keripy core/structing.py, L468, L646–652). So, read from the code and not run, keripy appears able to emit a `-N` attachment group today if a caller passes a `SealNonce` bond — one its own `Parser` has no handler for. No `src/keri` caller was found doing so at `80f77b73b`, so no keripy code path is known to put `-N` on the wire; the producer exists as a library capability, not as wired behavior [code]. Whether a `SealNonce` in a CESR-native `ixn` would fail at `Serder.ClanCodes` was not tested.

#### Typed-digest seals may carry a nonce {#04-typed-digest-nonce}

A milder version of the same pattern: typed-digest seals may now carry a nonce. keripy's `SealKind` second element changed from a digest to "d = digest or nonce using custom derivation given by type field (Noncer)" (keripy core/structing.py, L69), and the TDCS parser now extracts with `klas=Noncer` (keripy core/parsing.py, L2198). `Noncer` accepts every digest code plus `Salt_128`, `Salt_256` and an empty value (keripy core/coring.py, L470–487). The spec's `-W` row still reads "Typed digest seal couples `type+dig`" (L933 @`bad6edd84`; L941 @`65fd7518b`). This one does not reassign a count code, and every value `Noncer` admits is a self-framing primitive, so stream framing survives. Whether a spec-following parser that expects a digest code would accept a salt code in that slot was not tested, and a verifier that assumes the second element of a `-W` couple is a content digest, and tries to match it against some content, is now wrong about keripy's output.

## 8. The protocol genus/version code — versioning the tables themselves {#04-genus-version}

This is the piece outsiders most often miss: there is a code whose job is not to carry data or count anything, but to switch which code tables the parser uses. "A protocol genus and version code itself MUST NOT provide a count of the following Quadlets or triplets but MUST modify the protocol genus and Version of all the following Count Codes" (CESR spec > Protocol genus/version table, L609).

### Format `-_GGGVVV` {#04-genus-version-format}

Format `-_GGGVVV` (8 chars): `-_` selector, `GGG` = 3-char genus (`262,144` possible genera), `VVV` = version where the first `V` is major and the last two are minor. `CAA` = 2.00, `CAQ` = 2.16; up to 64 majors × 4096 minors (CESR spec > Protocol genus/version codes, L615). The KERI/ACDC genus codes are `-_AAABAA` (v1.00) and `-_AAACAA` (v2.00) (L865-866).

#### Purpose is twofold {#04-genus-version-purpose}

Purpose is twofold (L611): (1) it lets one CESR encoding serve different protocols/stacks, each with its own code tables; (2) it versions the tables for a given protocol. "The only table that all protocols MUST share (i.e., has identical values) is the protocol genus and version table" — all small/large count tables must share the universal count codes, but everything else MAY vary by protocol.

#### Scope/override rule (invariant) {#04-genus-version-override}

A genus/version code applies to the following count codes at top level until another genus/version code appears, or inside a special enclosing count-code group. Only three universal overrideable enclosing count codes permit an embedded genus/version override (L609). And the override fires only in the right position: "the parser MUST only treat the genus/version count code, especially as an override, when it appears as the first count code within the framed material of an overrideable universal count code. Otherwise, there MUST be no special override meaning" (CESR spec > Universal genus/version override, L816). Inside a list (universal but non-overrideable), a genus/version code as the first element has no override semantics (L818). keripy carries the genus/version awareness in `GenusCodex`/`GenDex` mapping genera to code tables (keripy core/counting.py, L24-40 @`b8f60166b`; raw/09 section 8) [code].

#### Reviewer takeaway {#04-genus-version-takeaway}

The genus/version code is the crypto-agility and multi-protocol mechanism made explicit at the table level, above the per-code mechanism of [section 5](#04-code-tables). A new protocol or a table revision is not a new magic byte scattered through the stream — it is a single genus/version primitive whose scope is well-defined and whose override positions are tightly constrained. Ambiguity here is a downgrade/confusion surface, which is why the override position is normatively pinned.

### A message's version is permanent; its attachments follow the parser {#04-attachment-version}

The genus/version code versions a stream's count codes, and the editor has ruled on how that interacts with the version of the message the codes are attached to [proposal]. A signed key event keeps its version forever: "Key event messages, because they are signed and must be verifiable indefinitely, can't be upgraded." Its attachments do not inherit that version: "there should be no reason that attachments can't be version 2 even when the message is V1, except when talking to a V1-only parser." (keripy GitHub > #1519, comment of 2026-07-23, R-002, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1519#issuecomment-5060786324). The comment answered a review that had endorsed taking each replayed event's attachment genus from that event's own protocol version; Sam ruled against it as a default, so the receiving parser, not the message, selects the attachment version. The migration consequence is stated as bluntly: "there is no backward-compatible path for new v2 key event messages", because "The signatures won't verify on a v1 conversion of the message." A v1-only parser is therefore a dead end rather than a slower lane, and the same comment says "The v2 parser can handle both v1 and v2 messages and attachments." That is the editor's account of intent. Whether a given deployment runs a v2 parser is a [code] or [practice] question this chapter did not check.

#### v2 attaches messages instead of embedding them {#04-attach-not-embed}

v1 exchange messages carry other messages embedded in their bodies, and the editor rules that this does not survive v2's four serialization kinds: "This embedding requires that embedded messages share the same serialization of the embedding message. Which breaks down for v2 with 4 serialization types." His fix: "So the fix in version two is not to embed but to attach nested substreams that have the otherwise embedded message." (keripy GitHub > #1441, comment of 2026-06-22, R-022, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1441#issuecomment-4772533040) [proposal]. keripy reflects the first half [code]: `specialExchange`, the constructor that embeds, defaults to `version=Vrsn_1_0` and `kind=Kinds.json` (keripy peer/exchanging.py, specialExchange, L801-815 @`80f77b73b`). The comment describes the attaching side as work in progress in June 2026, and this chapter did not check whether keripy's parser handles nested message substreams at `80f77b73b`. For a reviewer, a v2 design that embeds one message's serialization inside another's body is reaching for a v1 construct. The v2 shape is an attached substream, consistent with [section 10](#04-interleaving-rule)'s rule that a non-native serialization nested inside a CESR group is wrapped as a primitive in a special count code.
