## 9. Version strings — framing the interleaved non-native serializations {#04-version-strings}

CESR must interleave with three non-native serializations, and here the framing device is not a count code but a Version String.

### Three interleaved non-CESR serializations {#04-interleaved-serializations}

A CESR parser MUST support three interleaved non-CESR serializations: JSON, CBOR, MGPK (CESR spec > Performant resynchronization, L388). For those, the framing device is a Version String as the first field, label `v` (lowercase) — the regex target that yields serialization type and total size (CESR spec > Version String field, L1123, L1125).

#### v2 format `PPPPMmmGggKKKKBBBB.` {#04-v2-version-string}

v2 format `PPPPMmmGggKKKKBBBB.` — 19 chars, five parts (L1131): `PPPP` protocol (`KERI`, `ACDC`), `Mmm` protocol major/minor (base-64 numeric), `Ggg` CESR genus-table version, `KKKK` serialization kind (`JSON`|`CBOR`|`MGPK`|`CESR`), `BBBB` total length in Base64 (inclusive), then a `.` terminator. Max size `64**4 = 16,777,216` chars; larger payloads chain via SAIDs (L1150). The terminator's purpose is forward-compatibility: it lets a future version change the version-string size while keeping the field regex-extractable (L1152). Note the subtlety flagged in the spec: `Mmm`/`Ggg`/`BBBB` are "base 64 numerical notation" — "a number expressed as a base 64 number, not a string encoded in Base64", positionally weighted with `A`=0 and `_`=63 (L1146). Mis-reading that is a parsing bug.

#### v1 legacy `PPPPvvKKKKllllll_` {#04-v1-version-string}

v1 legacy `PPPPvvKKKKllllll_` — 17 chars: `vv` two-char hex major/minor, `llllll` length in lowercase hex, `_` terminator. v2 implementations MUST support v1 to verify 1.XX events (CESR spec > Legacy Version 1.XX string field format, L1156-1174).

keripy makes all of this concrete. The regexes are `VER2FULLSPAN = 19` / `VER1FULLSPAN = 17`, with `VEREX2` matching `[A-Z]{4}` protocol + version + `[A-Z]{4}` kind + size + `.` terminator, and `VEREX = VEREX2 | VEREX1` compiled into `Rever` (keripy kering.py, L39-61 @`b8f60166b`) [code]. The combined regex is why a single parser can sniff either version — it tries v2 first, falls back to v1.

#### CESR-native field maps carry no version string {#04-native-maps-no-version}

CESR-native field maps carry no embedded version string. They use `-G##`/`--G#####` count codes for map-ness and size; the unique start bits ([section 10](#04-cold-start)) mean no regex version string is needed. A native map instead has a protocol version field (protocol + version, not size/kind). In memory an implementation may inject a placeholder `v` with kind `CESR` so re-serialization knows to emit native CESR, but "there is no normative indication that the in-memory object was deserialized from a CESR native field map" (L1148). This is a real gotcha for round-trip fidelity across implementations.

---

## 10. Streaming, cold start, and the eight tritets {#04-cold-start}

### The cold-start problem {#04-cold-start-problem}

After a cold start, a parser looks for framing info; ambiguity leads to confusion and a forced re-cold-start (TCP: close/reopen; UDP: ack/nack). "Good cold start re-synchronization is essential to robust performant Stream processing" — the goal is to resync by skipping to the next well-defined boundary, not by flushing buffers (CESR spec > Cold start Stream parsing problem, L380-384).

The solution is a BOM-analogue on the first three bits of the first byte. The start bits for text-CESR, binary-CESR, JSON, CBOR, and MGPK "MUST be mutually distinct" (CESR spec > Performant resynchronization, L390), giving a UTF-BOM-like ability to tell text vs binary domain from the first tritet. The eight cases (CESR spec > Top-level Stream Starting Tritets, L411-420):

- `0b000` — Annotated 'T' domain (whitespace LF/CR/tab all start `000`)
- `0b001` — CESR 'T' Count Code — char `-`
- `0b010` — CESR 'T' Op Code — char `_`
- `0b011` — JSON — `{` (0x7b)
- `0b100` — MGPK FixMap
- `0b101` — CBOR Map (Major Type 5)
- `0b110` — MGPK Map16/Map32
- `0b111` — CESR 'B' domain Count Code or Op Code

The assignment is not arbitrary: JSON/CBOR/MGPK map objects consume tritets `011,100,101,110`, leaving `000,001,010,111` free; Base64 `-` (0x2d, tritet `001`) and `_` (0x5f, tritet `010`) fit the free T-domain slots, and their binary forms (positions 62/63) land at `0b111` to mark the B domain (L392-404). INVARIANT: "Each Stream MUST start (restart) with one of eight cases" (CESR spec > Stream parsing rules, L427).

The reference implementation is a near-verbatim mirror. `ColdCodex` enumerates exactly these eight: `AnB64=0o0, CtB64=0o1, OpB64=0o2, JSON=0o3, MGPK1=0o4, CBOR=0o5, MGPK2=0o6, CtOpB2=0o7`, and `sniff(ims)` computes `tritet = ims[0] >> 5` and dispatches to `msg`/`txt`/`bny`/`ano` status (keripy kering.py, L239-322 @`b8f60166b`; `ColdCodex` at L239, `sniff` at L287, the shift at L317) [code]. The docstring even carries the worked example built on `x = bytearray([0x2d, 0x5f])` (keripy kering.py, L263).

#### The parse formula {#04-parse-formula}

Examine the first tritet -> select one of the eight. If a count code, the rest of the code carries what is needed to parse the group. If JSON/CBOR/MGPK, "the mapping's first field MUST be a Version String" providing type and length for regex extraction (L438). The spec calls this "an extremely compact and elegant Stream parsing formula" (L442).

#### Interleaving rule (invariant) {#04-interleaving-rule}

Non-native serializations may be interleaved with native CESR only at the top level of a stream. "This is NOT true for non-native serializations nested inside CESR groups." When nested, "a non-native CESR serializations MUST be encoded as a CESR primitive and then enclosed in a special count code for non-native messages" (CESR spec > Interleaved non-CESR serializations, L374-376). Nesting raw JSON inside a count-code group without wrapping it is a wire defect.

### A failing message tells the sender nothing {#04-no-failure-oracle}

Resynchronization has a security counterpart in how a parser reports failure, and the editor has ruled on it [proposal]. keripy's top-level parse methods are designed to log and swallow exceptions rather than return them, because for a security protocol in a long-running, internet-facing service the best practice is "to not inform the caller why a given message sent to the service failed" (keripy GitHub > #1580, comment of 2026-08-07, R-021, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1580#issuecomment-5221176507). The reason is oracle resistance, and it includes a timing channel: a crash that forces a restart is itself "a strong signal that an uncaught exception was triggered". The rule he draws: "So the approach is to swallow and log all exceptions, not bubble them up." A caller that needs the exceptions, such as one pre-qualifying its own outgoing messages (the case in that thread), should get a separate wrapper that does not swallow them, not a more talkative main path. The description of keripy's design is Sam's; the parser code was not re-read for it. A reviewer who proposes granular error responses from a public-facing KERI parser is proposing to build the oracle this rule exists to deny.

---

## 11. SAID — the content-address that lives inside its own content {#04-said}

SAIDs are where CESR's encoding contract meets KERI's integrity model, and the interaction is load-bearing enough to restate here in wire terms (fuller treatment belongs to [chapter 05, section 2](#05-saids)).

A SAID (Self-Addressing Identifier) is "a special type of content-addressable identifier based on an encoded cryptographic digest that is self-referential" — embedded inside the very serialization it identifies (CESR spec > SAID, L1178). A naive content-address cannot be self-referential (putting a digest inside the thing you are digesting changes the digest), which is why SAID uses a dummy-fill derivation: copy the SAID out, replace the field with dummy `#` characters (ASCII 0x23, chosen because it is not a valid Base64 char) sized to the exact full digest length, compute the digest of the dummied serialization using the algorithm named by the code, CESR-encode it to the same total length, and compare (CESR spec > Generation and Verification Protocols, L1197-1199). Because the encoded digest is the same length as the dummy fill, the surrounding byte offsets never move — the wire framing is preserved. keripy implements this in `Saider._derive`/`verify` [code]: `sad[label] = clas.Dummy * Matter.Sizes[code].fs`, digest, inject back, and on verify re-derive and compare `qb64b`, failing closed on any exception (keripy core/coring.py, L3875-3982, dummy-fill at L3899; `Dummy = "#"  # dummy spaceholder char for said. Must not be a valid Base64 char`, keripy core/coring.py, L3771, all @`b8f60166b`).

Two points matter for the wire contract specifically:

- A SAID MUST be a CESR primitive with a prepended derivation code (L1180, L1190) — so digest agility ([section 5](#04-code-tables)) applies to content addresses directly. Change the digest algorithm, change the code, keep the framing. The `v1.1` branch pushes this same separation one step further and refuses a code for "digest of a post-quantum public key" precisely because such a code "would mix the semantics of a Primitive's use with the semantics of its cryptographic algorithm" (CESR spec v1.1 > Post-Quantum Cryptographic Primitives, L1559 @`65fd7518b`) [spec-next] — the derivation code names the algorithm, and context names the role.
- Field ordering is insertion order, not lexicographic. "The crucial consideration in SAID generation is reproducibility. This requires the ordering and sizing of fields in the serialization to be fixed" (L1240), and "The natural canonical ordering for such mappings is insertion order" (CESR spec > Order-Preserving Data Structures, L1244). This is a pointed rejection of JCS-style lexicographic canonicalization: lexicographic ordering "appears un-natural" and "often results in oddly-labeled fields that are so named merely to ensure that the lexicographic ordering matches a given logical ordering" (L1246). Modern languages preserve insertion order natively — Python 3.6+ `dict`, Ruby 1.9+ `Hash`, JavaScript ES6 `Map` and ES11 `.stringify` — so "there is no need for any canonical serialization but natural insertion order" (L1250). An outsider who assumes KERI canonicalizes like JOSE/JWS is wrong at the wire level, and a re-ordering "cleanup" silently changes every SAID.

---

## 12. Why the encoding is an external interop contract — and the highest-risk surfaces {#04-interop-risks}

The through-line of this section is that CESR is a contract with other implementations, and keripy's tests do not test that contract — they test keripy. keria, signify-ts, and any conforming stack must agree byte-for-byte on: code-table entries and sizing, field names and order, SAID derivation, version strings, and count codes. "a change that passes keripy's own tests but diverges from the spec/wire format is a defect, because it silently breaks interop. CESR code-table entries and sizing, field names and order, SAID derivation, version strings, and count codes are external contracts" (00-lens.md, claim 5, L54-57 @`9489ac9bd`). Corrected 2026-09-15: earlier revisions dropped the "and" before "count codes" and capitalized the opening word, so the string could not be found in the source; the verbatim text is restored and the line hint re-anchored. That claim file carries its own caveat and it is worth passing on: 00-lens.md is marked "STATUS: DRAFT — needs Daniel's endorsement" with its endorsement checklist unticked at `9489ac9bd`, so the eight lens claims are one contributor's distillation of primary sources rather than a ratified statement. Where a claim below leans on a lens claim, the canonical source it cites is the stronger footing.

The ranked list of desync/downgrade surfaces an adversarial reviewer should probe first:

1. Sizing arithmetic in the primitive tables (`Matter.Sizes`, `_infil`, `_rawSize`, `composable`). The double-modulo pad formula, the `cs % 4 != 3` and `fs % 4 == 0` invariants, and the `*3//4`-before-`-ls` order of operations. A wrong entry desyncs every downstream primitive silently because the format is self-framing. keripy-knowledge calls this "the highest-risk surface in the flagship" (00-lens.md, claim 8, L81; 30-invariants.md > A, both @`9489ac9bd`; keripy core/coring.py, L856-1310 @`b8f60166b`).
2. Shadow-table completeness when adding a code. Registering only in `MatterCodex` + `Sizes` round-trips as a primitive but is invisible to SAID/prefix validation and fails late/silently. Must also touch `Saider.Digests`, `Serder.Digests`, the `*Dex` sets, and (2.0) `BUDex`/`Counter.BUCodes` (31-landmines.md, landmine L5 @`9489ac9bd`; the in-source reminder at keripy core/coring.py, L444 @`b8f60166b`). This is the surface a post-quantum code addition will land on whenever one is written — see [section 5.5](#04-shadow-tables) on why that is still hypothetical.
3. The genus/version override position. The override fires only as the first count code inside an overrideable universal count code; anywhere else it has no special meaning (CESR spec > Universal genus/version override, L816-818). A parser that honors it elsewhere, or a producer that emits it in the wrong position, creates a table-selection confusion — a downgrade vector.
4. Version-string parsing, base-64-number vs base64-string. `Mmm`/`Ggg`/`BBBB` are positionally-weighted base-64 numbers, not Base64-encoded strings (CESR spec > Version String field, L1146); the `.`/`_` terminators and the 19-vs-17 span disambiguate v2 from v1 (keripy kering.py, L39-61 @`b8f60166b`). A lenient or wrong regex reads the wrong length and mis-frames the message.
5. Cold-start tritet handling. All eight starting cases must be distinguished on the first three bits; a parser that mishandles the annotated (`000`) or B-domain (`111`) case, or that does not treat interleaving as top-level-only, cannot resynchronize (CESR spec, L411-427; keripy kering.py, L239-322 @`b8f60166b`).
6. Additive-code direction asymmetry (downgrade honesty). A new code is a minor bump: new receivers accept old streams, old receivers break cleanly on the new code — a detectable rejection, not a silent misread (CESR spec > Protocol genus/version codes, L618-622, re-verified verbatim and unmoved at `bad6edd84` this pass). A design that tries to make old parsers silently accept an unknown new code is smuggling a downgrade; the correct behavior is a clean version-gated reject.
7. No post-quantum signature can appear in any indexed group. There is no post-quantum indexed signature code on either branch: the indexed table at `v1.1` `65fd7518b` (L1109-1131) carries only Ed25519, secp256k1 and Ed448 forms plus their big variants, and `main` `bad6edd84` is the same. KERI's indexed signature groups — `-K` controller, `-L` witness, `-X`/`-Y` transferable — therefore have no code that can carry an FN-DSA, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA signature, so as pinned, a post-quantum signature cannot participate in a multisig or a witness receipt at all; only the single-key, single-signature path works. The spec flags this itself as open issue 171. This is ranked here rather than filed under "in flux" deliberately: it is a concrete interop limit with a known boundary, not a speculative one, and it is the constraint most likely to surprise someone designing a post-quantum migration for a thresholded KERI deployment.
8. Indexed-signature code switch at index ≥ 63. A group with more than 63 keys switches the `Siger` encoding (`Ed25519_Crt_Sig` -> `Ed25519_Big_Crt_Sig`); consumers that do not handle the "big" indexed codes will reject (31-landmines.md, landmine L14 @`9489ac9bd`). A latent interop cliff for large multisig. Note the pin: this was verified at keripy `60ab9e08d` and has not been re-tested at `b8f60166b`.
9. A count code with two meanings: v2 `-N`. Added 2026-10-03. keripy at `80f77b73b` defines `-N` as `NonceSealSingles` (keripy core/counting.py, L228) while both CESR branches define it as transferable receipt quadruples (CESR spec, L915 @`bad6edd84`, L923 @`65fd7518b`) — see [section 7.1](#04-receipts-retired). Because CESR is self-framing, a group whose code means different things to producer and consumer is parsed confidently and wrongly, not rejected. (uncited — flagged by verification 2026-10-03: no parser was run on such a group, and a spec parser reading nonce singles as `pre+snu+dig+sig` quadruples may instead reject on a code-type mismatch in the prefix or signature slot; treat "not rejected" as unverified.) It is latent at this pin, since no keripy code path is known to emit `-N` and keripy's parser has no `-N` handler [code] — narrowed 2026-10-03 (verification): previously "keripy wires `-N` into no CESR-native serializer or parser"; v2 `messagize` would frame a `SealNonce` bond as `-N` if handed one ([section 7.1](#04-receipts-retired)) — and it becomes live the moment either side emits it. This is the clearest instance this chapter has of the [section 1](#04-what-cesr-is) point that keripy's tests cannot catch a wire defect: ~~keripy is internally consistent here, and the inconsistency is with the spec~~ the main inconsistency is with the spec, and keripy is not wholly consistent with itself either, since its v2 attachment emitter can frame a group its own parser cannot read.
10. Sequence numbers are hex strings, and an implementation got that wrong until 2026-09-16. Added 2026-10-03. signify-ts built the source-seal `Seqner` in `messagize` from `new Seqner({ sn: parseInt(seal[1].s) })` (signify-ts src/keri/core/eventing.ts, L432 @`ffba8406e`), reading the hex `s` field as decimal — wrong from sequence number `0xa` upward. At `5a174b545` it reads `new Seqner({ snh: seal[1].s }).qb64b` (signify-ts eventing.ts, L430), the hex constructor (signify-ts#417; raw/10 section 11c) [code]. The resulting attachment would have been well-framed while carrying the wrong sequence number, so nothing at the framing layer could flag it (an inference from the code, not a run). The lesson for a reviewer is the same as item 9 from the other side: a value that is syntactically valid CESR can still be semantically wrong, and nothing in the type system caught this one.
11. The Ed448 seed code is a byte short, and the defect is acknowledged and unfixed. Added 2026-10-15. Both branches define `K` as "Seed of Ed448 private key" with a one-character code and 76 text characters (CESR spec, L961 @`bad6edd84`; L969 @`65fd7518b`), which by the arithmetic of [section 3.1](#04-alignment) holds 56 raw bytes. Issue trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification#175, opened 2026-09-01 by Daniel Hardman, reports that an Ed448 private key is 57 bytes, and the editor checked and accepted the premise: "The cryptography library has the raw size of both private and public keys at 57 bytes" (CESR spec GitHub > #175, comment of 2026-09-01, R-020, https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification/issues/175#issuecomment-5497714395) [proposal]. He wanted it fixed first — "So I would rather fix the ed448 before putting in the PQC codes" (same thread, https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification/issues/175#issuecomment-5496520050) — and that order did not happen: the post-quantum codes are on `v1.1` and `K` is unchanged on both branches. His remedy is a test rather than an argument: "We should actually implement 448 with unit test in keripy so we know that the codes are right." (https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-cesr-specification/issues/175#issuecomment-5496535050). The issue was open on 2026-10-14. A 57-byte value has pad size 0 and cannot take a one-character code at all ([section 3.1](#04-alignment)), so the repair is a new four-character code, not a resize of `K`. Until then a standard 57-byte Ed448 private key cannot be carried under `K`, and an implementation that puts one there is truncating it or storing something else.

### Well-established versus contested {#04-established-vs-contested}

Well-established and enforced in both spec and code: composability, the 24-bit alignment math, mid-padding, stable framing, count-codes-count-quadlets, the genus/version format and scope, the version-string formats, and the eight-tritet cold start. Uncertain or in-flux: the Op Code table is explicitly reserved/TBD (`_` selector, CESR L628, L948) — a whole stream-processing capability is gestured at but unspecified; and several large-variable/context tables are structurally defined but not exhaustively populated (raw/02 section Gaps). Superseded 2026-09-15: an earlier revision of this paragraph described the post-quantum code assignments as "being introduced in successive updates" with an open issue. That quoted phrase came from the unreachable `d35125e61` and appears on neither branch; it is cut ([section 5.7](#04-pq-in-practice)). The accurate statement is branch-dependent — no post-quantum code of any kind on `main` `bad6edd84`, and FN-DSA, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA populated with ML-KEM explicitly deferred on `v1.1` `65fd7518b`. The open issue is real and survives the retraction: `::: issue` "[Post-quantum cryptographic operations]", issue #14, sits at L559 on both branches unchanged, so the `v1.1` work did not close it. Minor source typos noted but non-doctrinal, both still present at `bad6edd84`: the `6A` table text says "pad size of 0" while the same paragraph ends with 2 lead bytes (L553), and a `-S#####` large count code is missing a leading `-` (L926) — both read as source typos, not design intent (raw/02 section Gaps).

#### The load-bearing assumption {#04-load-bearing-assumption}

The crypto-agility guarantee ("old parsers frame the stream correctly around a code they do not know") holds only because sizing is a pure function of the code and because a new code occupies a genuinely unused slot whose size-class the old parser does not otherwise depend on. It is not an unconditional "any parser reads any stream" promise; it is "a disciplined additive extension that old parsers reject cleanly and new parsers accept," resting entirely on the sizing math being exactly right (CESR spec > Protocol genus/version codes, L618-622; 00-lens.md, claim 8 @`9489ac9bd`). That single dependency is why the sizing tables sit at the top of the risk list. The strongest evidence the corpus now has that the assumption holds in practice is the one described in [section 5.7](#04-pq-in-practice): a second, independently maintained implementation sizes primitives by table lookup on the code alone, and adding 33 post-quantum rows to it required no parser change whatever [proposal].

---

## 13. Summary for the adversarial reviewer {#04-reviewer-summary}

CESR earns its complexity. Every construct maps to a concrete requirement: composability -> lossless en-masse T<->B conversion; 24-bit alignment -> the LCM of Base64 and byte widths; mid-padding -> readable right-aligned values with no `=`; stable framing -> parseability by whole-character text parsers; count codes -> pipelining without content parsing; genus/version codes -> multi-protocol and table versioning; version strings -> framing the three interleaved non-native serializations; the eight tritets -> deterministic cold-start resynchronization; derivation codes -> crypto agility. The corrections to outsider priors are sharp and defensible: it is not naive Base64 (no `=`, true two-way composability), not lexicographically canonicalized (insertion order, a deliberate rejection of JCS), not a place to nest raw JSON inside groups (top-level interleaving only), not a system where "more crypto strength" is better (128-bit floor, weak suites excluded), and — the newest of these tells — not a scheme where a table selector carries algorithm meaning, since a selector encodes lead-byte alignment and nothing else ([section 5.6](#04-allocation-rules)). The one place a reviewer should push hardest is the sizing math and its shadow tables, because that is where a well-intentioned "simplification" desyncs the entire network silently while keripy's own tests stay green — the definition of a wire-interop defect (30-invariants.md > A; 00-lens.md, claim 5, both @`9489ac9bd`).

One closing calibration, because this chapter's post-quantum material was rebuilt from the ground up this month and a reader is entitled to know how the position moved. The mechanism of crypto agility is better evidenced than it has ever been: a second implementation, maintained independently of keripy, frames 33 unfamiliar post-quantum primitives correctly without a line of parser change, which is the thesis demonstrated rather than argued. The codes are further from normative than this chapter previously implied: they are [spec-next] text on a divergent branch, a revert of them from that branch has been open and unreviewed since 2026-09-22 ([section 5.7](#04-pq-in-practice)), they are implemented nowhere that ships, four of them were withdrawn from the compact tables and are now forbidden there by a MUST NOT, there is no post-quantum key-encapsulation primitive at all, and no post-quantum signature can enter a multisig or a witness receipt. Both movements came from the same discipline — checking that a pin is reachable, and cutting what cannot be verified rather than rewording it into something that can.

# 05 — ACDC and Verifiable Data {#05-acdc}

## Thesis {#05-thesis}

An Authentic Chained Data Container (ACDC) is not a "credential format" in the W3C-VC or SD-JWT sense; it is a fragment of a globally distributed, cryptographically self-addressed property graph whose every node commits to its own content by a SAID, whose edges are typed and operator-bearing, and whose authority is bound not to a signing key but to an issuer's evolving key state anchored in a KEL or TEL. This chapter sets out the machinery that makes that claim precise: SAIDs and the single canonical "most compact form" digest algorithm; the mutually exclusive attribute (`a`) and aggregate (`A`) sections and the partial-vs-selective disclosure split they encode; the edge section and the unary/m-ary operator families that turn a bag of credentials into a reasoned graph of authority; the Ricardian-contract rule section; the graduated-disclosure ladder from compact through metadata, partial, nested-partial, selective, and full disclosure; contractually-protected disclosure (chain-link confidentiality and contingent disclosure); TEL-based registries and the observer/registrar split that refuses phone-home revocation; the IPEX exchange state machine; and the applied corpus (SEDI, GCD, vLEI, the Dossier) that shows what real schemas actually enforce. Throughout, the reference implementation (`keripy`) is treated as ground truth against the spec's prose, and where the two diverge — most sharply in the edge-operator family — that gap is stated plainly rather than papered over.

Adversarial reviewers should carry one framing into every section: ACDC's design goal is not data privacy per se but "the more general goal of protection from the unpermissioned exploitation of data" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Mechanisms, L1659). Privacy mechanisms are means, not ends. A critique that measures ACDC against a pure-privacy or pure-ZK yardstick is measuring the wrong thing.

## Status {#05-status}

Markers are carried where the tier is load-bearing, which in this chapter means the edge-operator family above all, because that is where the four sources genuinely disagree and where a reviewer is most likely to be misled by whichever one they happened to read.

## 1. What an ACDC fundamentally is {#05-what-an-acdc-is}

An ACDC is modeled abstractly as an ordered nested field map (`key:value`), serializable in JSON, CBOR, MGPK, or CESR, in which every field map MUST contain a SAID field — making each map a SAD (Self-Addressed Data structure): "One important feature of the fields maps used by ACDC is that they all MUST include a field with a SAID" (ACDC spec > ACDC Message Fields, L2982). The container carries no top-level type field, because "the Schema, `s`, field itself is the type field" (ACDC spec > Type-is-schema, L182); this is the recurring "type-is-schema" principle, whose corollary is that "type information is metadata, not data" (L182). Insertion-ordered field maps MUST be used for canonical serialization — never lexicographic (ACDC spec > Ordered Nested Field Maps, L10) — which is the design's direct answer to the JSON-canonicalization and JSON-LD term-redefinition fragilities that let a signed VC's meaning shift without breaking its signature (papers `keri-primer.md` > 4.1 The engineering bottleneck: text vs. binary, citing W3C vc-data-integrity issue #272).

A set of ACDCs "as nodes connected by edges forms a labeled property graph," each node "universally uniquely identified by the SAID of its ACDC," yielding "securely attributed fragments of a globally distributed property graph... a global verifiable knowledge graph that crosses trust domains" (ACDC spec > ACDCs as secure graph fragments, L1060-1068). No shared or trusted relationship between controllers and verifiers is required (ACDC spec > AID Fields, L95). In Hardman's own framing, ACDC is "not just a format — they're a *methodology* for creating verifiable evidence" (papers `x509-prob.md`), and the container is "not a mutable document; it is a crystallized fact" (papers `keri-primer.md` > 3.2 SAIDs).

### Top-level field order (MUST) {#05-field-order}

The top-level field order is `[v, t, d, u, i, rd, s, a, A, e, r]` (ACDC spec > Field Ordering, L32); the required fields are `[v, d, i, s]` (ACDC spec > Required Fields, L36). The hardest structural invariant: an ACDC MUST NOT have both a non-empty `a` and a non-empty `A` value (L106, L110) — attribute and aggregate sections are mutually exclusive.

#### Field label restrictions {#05-field-label-restrictions}

[spec-next] Field labels are about to become constrained, and the constraint is backward-incompatible. A `### Field Label Restrictions` section exists in `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` and nowhere in `main` @`f0bd097de`. Two rules: "A field label in an ACDC MUST NOT, therefore, contain the character `-`" (ACDC spec > Field Label Restrictions, L63 @`2362e48a1`), because the compact CESR serialization of a disclosure path replaces the `/` delimiter with `-` and the result must stay pure Base64; and a lone underscore is reserved, since "The label `_` MUST therefore be reserved as a virtual path component denoting that hop" across an edge (L65), narrowly — "Only that label is forbidden; `_` MAY appear within a longer label, such as `first_name`." The restrictions do not reach the Schema Section's labels, which come from the JSON Schema vocabulary and are never path-descended (L69). A reviewer should register the migration gap rather than the rule. Any already-issued ACDC carrying a label with a hyphen, or a lone `_`, becomes non-conforming the moment `v1.1` lands; `v1.1` argues the cost is low — most languages disallow `-` in an attribute name anyway — and says nothing whatever about migrating the ACDCs that are already in the world. That silence is the open question, not the rule itself.

These restrictions exist to serve the disclosure-path construct, `dp`, which is not an ACDC field at all: "The `dp` field is not an ACDC field. It appears in the messages that negotiate a disclosure, not in the ACDCs that are disclosed" ([spec-next], ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths, L1813 @`2362e48a1`). It is a negotiation construct living in IPEX `exn` messages, and [chapter 08, section 4](#08-disclosure-paths) owns it. Nothing in this chapter should be read as putting `dp` in a container.

## 2. SAIDs and SAIDification {#05-saids}

A SAID is "a special type of cryptographic digest of its encapsulating field map (block)" (ACDC spec > SAID Fields, L77). Its load-bearing property is commitment equivalence: "A digital signature on a SAID makes a verifiable cryptographic non-repudiable commitment that is equivalent to a commitment on the full serialization of the associated block from which the SAID was derived" (L81), requiring collision resistance and ~128-bit strength. Because a SAID may itself digest a block containing further SAIDs, the commitment is hierarchical — a single top-level commitment binds an entire tree.

The derivation mechanism is the dummy-fill-then-digest algorithm, and the reference implementation is the ground truth here. `Saider._derive` (keripy `core/coring.py`, `Saider._derive`, L4058-4096): copy the `sad`, fill the id field with the dummy character `#` to the exact full size of the digest (`sad[label] = Dummy * Matter.Sizes[code].fs`, keripy `core/coring.py`, L4085; the dummy "must not be a valid Base64 char", keripy `core/coring.py`, L3949), recompute the version-string size over the dummied serialization if versioned, digest the serialization, then inject the result back into the field. Verification (keripy `core/coring.py`, `Saider.verify`, L4117-4160) re-derives with dummy fill and compares `qb64b`; any exception returns `False` — fail-closed. So the SAID is "a tamper-evident commitment to exact serialized content at exact size"; change any non-ignored byte and verification fails. This is exactly the "44 `#` chars for Base64 256-bit, hash, overwrite" story in the papers (papers `keri-primer.md` > 3.2 SAIDs), made mechanical.

Two subtleties matter for reviewers. First, there MUST be one and only one unambiguous way to compute the SAID of a compactifiable section: the most compact form SAID, computed by depth-first search — SAID the expanded leaves, compact them, ascend computing enclosing-block SAIDs up to the trunk (ACDC spec > Most compact form SAID, L130-151). keripy invariant J3 states this at the credential layer: "An ACDC SAID is computed over its most-compact form, not its uncompacted serialization, so the SAID is stable across compaction/disclosure" (keripy-knowledge `30-invariants.md` > J3; keripy `vc/proving.py`). This stability is what makes graduated disclosure verifiable: "enables verification of portions of a set of nested compactifiable subblocks against their SAIDs without requiring that the whole tree be exposed. This is essential to Graduated Disclosure" (ACDC spec > Most compact form SAID, L136).

Second, the schema SAID uses the field label `$id`, not `d` — a repurposed JSON Schema keyword whose value MUST be the bare schema SAID, not a URI (ACDC spec > Schema ID Field Label, L186-210). In the applied corpus this was stated as a hard rule: "`$id` is a SAID." and "Never invent or hand-patch a SAID." (bakobo/schema `KNOWLEDGE_TRANSFER.md` > Hard facts about ACDC schemas (respect these), L88-90 @`cfcbdcc7a`). Re-cited 2026-10-15. The earlier quote joined three fragments with ellipses and an ASCII arrow the source does not have, and carried no pin. The file was deleted from bakobo/schema at `42674785b` (2026-10-09, "Remove references to private repositories"), so the quote resolves at the pin and not at the current head.

### The UUID field as a blinding factor {#05-uuid-blinding}

The UUID `u` field is a blinding factor, not decoration. Without it, "an adversary may be able to reconstruct the block contents merely from the SAID... and the Schema... using a rainbow or dictionary attack," because the power set of schema-allowed field values may be far smaller than the digest strength (ACDC spec > UUID Fields, L89). Sufficient entropy in `u` "ensures that the cardinality of the power set allowed by the schema is at least as great as the entropy of the SAID digest algorithm." This is the crisp correction of a common outsider assumption: compactness is not privacy. A public (no-`u`) compact ACDC is still rainbow-attackable — "It only provides compactness, not privacy" (ACDC spec > Targeted Public-attribute, L501). The presence or absence of `u` at top level is precisely what separates a public ACDC (no `u`) from a private one (`u` with entropy), and an empty `u` marks the metadata variant (ACDC spec > ACDC Variants, L120-174).

#### A naming change that is a naming change {#05-uuid-renamed-ue}

`v1.1` renames the field throughout: `### Universally Unique Identifier (UUID) Fields` on `main` becomes `### Unique Entropy (UE) Fields`, the field tables retitle `u` from "UUID" to "UE", and the same substitution runs through the Edge, Edge-group and Rule sections. The two paragraphs of substance — the rainbow/dictionary attack over the power set of schema-allowed values, `u` as blinding factor, a top-level `u` blinding the whole ACDC — are word-for-word identical on both branches once the term is swapped. This is recorded as terminology and deliberately not as doctrine: nothing above changes, and a reviewer who reads the rename as a change of meaning has read a change that is not there. The name is nonetheless worth knowing, because a `v1.1`-era reader searching for "UUID" will find nothing. This chapter keeps saying UUID, because the quotes it cites are from `main` and say UUID; a citation to `v1.1` says UE.

## 3. Static, immutable schema {#05-static-schema}

Schemas MUST be completely self-contained and statically fixed: "dynamic Schema references or dynamic Schema generation mechanisms MUST NOT be used" (ACDC spec > Static Schema, L194). The spec names two attacks this prevents. The schema revocation attack: an attacker who can mutate a dynamic schema resource makes validation fail on every ACDC using it, "effectively revok[ing] all the ACDCs that use that dynamic Schema reference" (L196). The semantic malleability attack (a transaction-malleability variant): an attacker "shift[s] the semantics of the dynamic Schema" so the ACDC still validates but downstream behavior changes (L198). Prevention: "all Schemas MUST be static, i.e., Schemas MUST be SADs and therefore verifiable against their SAIDs" (L200). The `$schema` dialect URI "is simply an identifier"; dereferencing it for validation code "would be an attack vector" — the Validator MUST control the tooling dialect (JSON Schema 2020-12) (ACDC spec > Schema dialect, L226). This is the ACDC answer to the JSON-LD `@context` link-rot and term-redefinition problems (papers `acdc-vc-diff.md` > Loss 6: Schema Stability).

A composable schema uses `oneOf` to bundle compact and expanded variants: "a verifiable bundle of metadata (composed) about content that can then be verifiably unbundled (decomposed) later. The Issuer makes a single verifiable commitment to the bundle" (L246). The Validator uses the composed base schema before disclosure and the decomposed schema (compact option removed) after, to force full disclosure. Two schema "versions" coexist and must not be confused: the `$id` SAID is "the normative determiner" used in validation; the semver `version` field is "informative" and is NOT used in validation (ACDC spec > Schema Versioning, L230). Availability is orthogonal to security: "Unavailable does not mean insecure or unverifiable. ACDCs MUST be verifiable when available" (ACDC spec > Schema Availability, L242).

## 4. Attribute section `a` vs aggregate section `A` {#05-attribute-vs-aggregate}

The two disclosable payload sections encode two different disclosure mechanisms, and choosing between them is the single most consequential schema-design decision.

The attribute section `a` is a labeled field map. Reserved nested labels are `d, u, i, dt` (ACDC spec > Attribute Section, L260). Its presence-of-`i` distinguishes Targeted (an Issuee AID is present — "a provably controllable identifier that is the Target," making the ACDC usable as a Verifiable Credential, L312) from Untargeted ("issued 'to whom it may concern'", verifiable authorship only, no counterparty, no delegation, L330). Crucially the Issuee `i` sits nested in `a`, not at top level, so it is "partially disclosable / correlatable only after Chain-Link Confidentiality [is] accepted" (L316). Because field labels are public (they live in the schema), the attribute section supports partial disclosure — each nested block carries its own `d` + `u`, and a withheld block travels as its bare SAID (bakobo/schema `docs/choosing-attribute-vs-aggregate.md`).

The aggregate section `A` (capital) is categorically different: "its compact value is an aggregate / AGID (Aggregate ID), NOT a SAID" (ACDC spec > Aggregate Section, L661). It is an ordered array of blinded blocks, each with its own `d` + `u`; "the block labels live *inside* each block, so they're blinded; array position is arbitrary" (bakobo/schema `docs/choosing-attribute-vs-aggregate.md`). This gives selective disclosure: field labels and positions are hidden, so `anyOf` ordering "is not correlated to the actual order" and cannot leak information by position (ACDC spec > Aggregate Section, L694). The AGID is computed as `AGID = H(C(a_i for i in {0..N}))`: the zeroth list element is dummied with `#` chars, the remaining N elements are block SAIDs, the list is serialized and digested (Blake3-256), and the digest replaces the dummy (L712-747). Its security rests on "sufficient cryptographic entropy of the blinding factors, collision resistance of the digests, and unforgeability of the non-repudiable digital commitments," and the digest-of-ordered-concatenation is "not subject to a birthday attack" (L688, L728). An inclusion proof discloses the detailed block at index j, the full list, the compact ACDC, and the issuance seal; the Disclosee recomputes the block, checks membership, recomputes the AGID, and confirms the KEL seal (L734-750).

### The deciding question {#05-deciding-question}

[practice] The deciding question, from the applied corpus, is exact: "Does hiding the field labels or positions buy you anything?" (bakobo/schema `docs/choosing-attribute-vs-aggregate.md`). The aggregate provides label/position blinding, valuable in exactly two cases — the presence/identity of a field is itself sensitive, or the field set is variable/homogeneous. Otherwise the aggregate is "pure cost, because you lose label-based pathing": graduated-disclosure negotiation (apply/offer path lists via keripy's `Pather`) "wants to name a field as `a/residenceState`. In an aggregate you can't." One further caveat worth quoting: "Attribute-form partial disclosure forces the issuee (`a.i`) and the `a`-section metadata to be revealed on any disclosure; an aggregate can disclose one element with no issuee." (bakobo/schema `docs/choosing-attribute-vs-aggregate.md` > Caveats worth remembering, L65-66 @`cfcbdcc7a`). That caveat is true of the mechanism and, at keripy `80f77b73b`, not true of a registry-backed credential presented through keripy's IPEX — see [section 4.1](#05-age-credential).

~~SEDI's `sedi-age` is the aggregate done right — a homogeneous boolean vector `ageOver13/16/18/21/55/65` with element 0 as the AGID, "exactly the ISO mDL `age_over_NN` model... a poor man's sparse Merkle tree" that satisfies a statutory "prove a minimum age without disclosing age or birth date" duty (`sedi-age/index.md`).~~ Superseded 2026-10-03. That was Bakobo's own profile, now archived as `sedi-age-3.0.0/`. The current `sedi-age` is Sam Smith's Age schema from keripy's SEDI fixtures, "reproduced byte for byte" (bakobo/schema `sedi-age/index.md`, L3 @`cfcbdcc7a`): an issuee block, issued and expiration date blocks, and "blinded boolean blocks for thresholds 13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 21, 40, 62, 65, 67 and 70" (same). It is still the aggregate's natural case — a homogeneous vector disclosed in subset — and Sam reached the attribute-versus-aggregate choice independently. The "poor man's sparse Merkle tree" framing survives only in Bakobo's decision record, and the statutory duty now lives in the governance artifact: a verifier "MUST honor the holder's selective disclosure -- including proof of a minimum age without the birth date" (bakobo/schema `sedi-id/rules.json`, `dataMinimization`, L3). Whether the mechanism actually delivers that is the subject of [section 4.1](#05-age-credential).

The distinction from partial disclosure is subtle and load-bearing: a partially-disclosed block, when fully disclosed, "exposes, at the very least, the labels of other fields in its enclosing block," whereas a selectively-disclosed block "does not expose any information about other yet-to-be-exposed fields, including their labels" (L2733). Selective disclosure is "separating a 'stew' of 'ingredients' into its constituent ingredients without correlating them via the stew."

#### Same issuer or different issuers {#05-same-or-different-issuers}

[proposal] Sam gives the rule for when information belongs in separate credentials, and it turns on who issues it: "If two pieces of information have different issuers then they must be in different ACDCs and then a blindable edge enables graduated disclosure." and "If the two pieces of information have the same issuer then a blindable sub black in the attribute section is all that is needed." ([keripy conversations > discussion #1550](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1550#discussioncomment-17909785), comment of 2026-08-05, R-034; "sub black" is his slip for "sub block"). Read with the deciding question above, it orders the choice: the issuer decides whether to split, and only then does label or position hiding decide between `a` and `A`. The same comment rules out an edge back from a far node to a near node that already points to it, "(not a DAG not possible with SAID calculation)", because each node's SAID would have to be known before the other's.

#### Where the aggregate's guarantee stops {#05-aggregate-guarantee-limit}

[spec] And there the guarantee stops, by the spec's own account. The worked selective-disclosure example added to `main`'s annex states the residue without hedging: "The verifier does still learn how many elements the section has and which were withheld — the count and positions are structural, not blinded" (ACDC spec > Graduated Disclosure, L5051-5053), and "only the withheld values themselves are protected." The mechanism blinds values and labels, not cardinality and shape. That matters for exactly the schemas the aggregate is good for: an age vector leaks how many thresholds exist and which of them were withheld (eleven thresholds in Sam's current Age schema, six in the Bakobo profile this sentence was first written against), and a schema whose element count varies per holder leaks a per-holder fingerprint before any value is disclosed. A design whose privacy argument depends on the verifier not knowing how many claims are in the set needs a different mechanism — a DAG of separately-issued ACDCs, per the chaining argument at L2739 — not a bigger aggregate.

### 4.1 The age credential, the reference implementation, and two findings (added 2026-10-03) {#05-age-credential}

The age credential is where the aggregate's design case meets running code, and at keripy `80f77b73b` the two do not agree. Both findings below are recorded in `raw/11` section 1 and section 9 items 1 and 8 with the full chain of citations, and both carry the same boundary: no test in keripy at `80f77b73b` presents an Age credential — `test_ipex_sedi.py` does not import `AgeSchema` at all (keripy `tests/sedi/test_ipex_sedi.py`, L39-50) — so nothing in keripy exercises either collision. They are findings from reading the code paths, not from running them. Both also sit under [section 5.1](#05-verifying-ground-truth)'s scoping caveat: the IPEX path in question is `acdc/ipexing.py`, which keripy's own CLI does not call.

#### Finding 1: no selective Age presentation through IPEX grant {#05-age-finding-grant}

[code] Finding 1: an Age credential cannot be presented selectively through keripy's IPEX grant. The chain has four links. Sam's Age schema requires a top-level `rd` (keripy `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`, L1180), and the fixture issues Age into the state agent's registry (`regid=sueRids[4]`, L4397), so every conforming Age is registry-backed. keripy represents a withheld aggregate element as its SAID string (keripy `core/mapping.py`, `Aggor.disclose`, L1899-1900), which is the shape of the Age schema's withheld arm. For a registry-backed ACDC, `_presentationRegistries` refuses any aggregate entry after the AGID that is not a mapping — "Every inspected aggregate entry must be a mapping." (keripy `acdc/ipexing.py`, `_presentationRegistries`, L1458-1460) — and the code gives the reason: "A verifier cannot distinguish an omitted requirement from an undisclosed one using only its digest." (L1414-1415). That refusal fails the node, and the node fails the grant (`_verifyPresentationAuthGraph` returns `None` at L1508-1512, and the grant handler returns `False` on it at L610-617). So a holder who wants to prove over-21 through this path must disclose every element, including over-40 and over-62, which brackets the age into a band. The rule is not arbitrary: it exists so a hidden element cannot conceal a presentation-registry declaration (see [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md)). But it collides with the age credential's central use case, and it contradicts three statements in the applied corpus — the page's "The holder can disclose the over-21 block without disclosing a birth date" (bakobo/schema `sedi-age/index.md`, L3, true of the birth date but not of the other thresholds), bakobo's `prove-over-21` example, which "discloses only its issuee and over-21 blocks" (bakobo/schema `sedi-age/index.md`, L5), and the design doc's "an aggregate can disclose one element with no issuee" ([section 4](#05-attribute-vs-aggregate)). The schema bakobo validates and the protocol keripy enforces disagree. `raw/11` section 9 item 8 sketches possible resolutions; none is proposed anywhere read, and this chapter does not choose one.

#### Finding 2: the aggregate issuee is read from a fixed position {#05-age-finding-issuee}

[code] Finding 2: keripy reads an aggregate's issuee from one fixed position, and the schema does not fix it. The library resolves an aggregate ACDC's issuee "for aggregative ACDC .sad["A"][1]['i']" (keripy `core/serdering.py`, L2830), inside a bare `except` that returns `None` (L2837-2844). Sam's Age schema has no `prefixItems`, `minItems` or `contains` on `A` (keripy `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`, L1204-1493), so nothing requires the issuee block to sit at index 1 or to be disclosed. An Age whose element 1 is withheld or misplaced therefore reads to keripy as untargeted. Bakobo's decision record had already named the consequence from the schema side — the shape "lets a holder withhold element 1 and present a targeted credential as an untargeted affidavit" (bakobo/schema `this.i` > `@lkfnoess`, L2144-2147 @`cfcbdcc7a`) — and sequenced the fix upstream-first. What closes the hole on the IPEX path at this pin is Finding 1: a rule that forbids withholding any element also forbids withholding element 1. The hole is closed by also closing selective disclosure, which is not a fix either finding can live with for long.

#### The issuee position is intended, not specified {#05-age-issuee-intended}

[proposal] Added 2026-10-15. Sam has said which way Finding 2's gap should close: "The issuee in an ACDC with Agg section (selectively disclosable) is the "i" field in the second (index 1) attribute block." and "This could/should be better clarified in the spec." ([keripy conversations > PR #1505](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1505#issuecomment-4981932724), comment of 2026-07-15, R-025). Neither ACDC branch states the rule. Both place an issuee block at index 1 in their aggregate example and note that "the value of the `i` field is the Issuee of the ACDC" (ACDC spec > Aggregate Section > Composed Schema for selectively disclosable Aggregate section > JSON Serialization, L914, L930; `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` L925, L941), but an example is not a requirement. So keripy's fixed read of `A[1].i` implements the editor's stated intent, and Finding 2 is a gap between that intent and the specification and schema rather than an open design question. On this chapter's reading, a schema that wants the read to be safe has to pin element 1 itself until the specification does. A companion ruling says the date has no such position: "there is no preferred index to place the dt" ([keripy conversations > issue #1679](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/issues/1679#issuecomment-5671060930), comment of 2026-09-14, R-025).

#### Sam's sparse-Merkle-tree proposal {#05-age-smt-proposal}

[proposal] Sam's mechanism of record for age is something else again. Discussion [#1098](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1098) proposes a static sparse-Merkle-tree predicate rather than a vector of booleans. It opens on staleness — "a static a priori issuance of a given proof of age could become invalid as the individual's age changes." The construction: "The issued ACDC includes an attribute that is the Root of the SMT," with one leaf per date on which a predicate is true, and "A proof-of-age is given by an inclusion proof of a given predicate leaf in the SMT." Leaves are salted from a secret shared at issuance, so "only 2nd parties to a disclosure can construct a valid query of the SMT." Its case against zero-knowledge predicates is detectability, not cost: "ZKPs are not a viable solution to the proof-of-age problem with KERI/ACDC-based proof-of-age entitlements," because with unlinkable ZKPs "the Issuer of the credential is unable, by virtue of that unlinkability, to detect that a credential has been fraudulently issued," and on the holder's side, "Likewise, the key compromise of an Issuee (Holder) can be made detectable using a presentation registry. Which would also be defeated by an unlinkable ZKP." The verdict: "a static SMT predicate proof preserves KERI's security properties, whereas a dynamic ZKP predicate proof defeats them." The discussion is candid about its own limit — "age-range predicate proofs provide only weak protection when used in isolation" — and reframes the problem: "In this light, birthdate privacy is relieving the symptom, not curing the disease," the disease being birthdates used as shared-secret authenticators. This is the same contracts-plus-detection posture as [section 8](#05-contractual-disclosure), applied to a cryptographic choice, and it is Sam's assessment in a design discussion, not a surveyed result. Provenance caution: the body was last edited 2026-09-26, and without its edit history the presentation-registry sentence is evidence of his position at that date, not of when he first held it (`raw/16` section 1a).

#### Fixture versus proposal {#05-age-fixture-vs-proposal}

The fixture and the proposal differ in kind, and nothing read says which is the plan. This comparison is interpretive. The fixture's booleans are point-in-time — "Over21 True if age>=21 else False" (keripy `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`, L1385) is false for a twenty-year-old and stays false after the birthday — which is exactly the staleness #1098 opens by naming; the fixture's remedy is its expiration-date block, which means reissuance. #1098's leaves are dated predicates and stay correct for life. Whether the fixture is an interim stand-in for the SMT, a deliberate alternative, or a demo convenience is not stated anywhere this pass read.

## 5. Edges, chaining, and the operator families {#05-edges}

Edges connect ACDCs into a DAG: the near node is the enclosing ACDC, the far node is the ACDC referenced by `n` (a SAID) (ACDC spec > Edge Section, L1172). Reserved edge labels are `[d, u, n, s, o, w]` in fixed order (L1149). An edge's `s` field is an additional constraint — the far node MUST validate against both its own schema and the edge's `s` (L1176) — which is what the vLEI ladder uses to const-pin each hop (see [section 11](#05-applied-patterns)). This is a genuine capability W3C VCs lack: RDF "cannot attach properties to edges directly," forcing reification/"triple bloat," whereas ACDC edges are first-class property-graph objects carrying native `w`/`o`/`s`/`n` (papers `acdc-vc-diff.md` > Loss 3: Edge Weights and Conditional Logic).

### The edge schema constraint is enforced {#05-edge-schema-enforced}

[code] The `s` constraint is enforced, and the semantics the code chose are "satisfy", not "equal". `processCredential` — not `verifyChain` — checks an edge's declared far-node schema on a stated reading of the spec: the edge `s` "is a schema the far node must" "*satisfy*, not a SAID that must equal the far node's own schema" SAID (keripy `vdr/verifying.py`, `processCredential`, L196-197 @`80f77b73b`, the code citing Sam Smith and keripy issue #1534). A direct SAID match short-circuits, since the far node already validated against its own schema; where the edge declares a different schema the far node is validated against it, and failure raises `MissingChainError`. A schema not yet cached escrows and cues a query rather than failing, so transient unavailability is distinguished from a real violation (the whole block is L195-230 @`80f77b73b`; the per-branch hints L211-218 and L219-227 are as of `b8f60166b`). This landed between `60ab9e08d` and `b8f60166b` and is unchanged at `80f77b73b`. It means the vLEI const-pinning pattern of [section 11](#05-applied-patterns) has a verifier behind it rather than only a schema convention — and it changes what an unpinned edge schema means, which matters now that one schema family has stopped pinning ([section 11](#05-applied-patterns), telco).

#### The m-ary operators {#05-m-ary-operators}

The m-ary operators (on edge-groups, via `o`): `AND` (default; group valid iff all members valid), `OR` (one member valid), `NAND`, `NOR`, `AVG` (arithmetic average of a member property), `WAVG` (weighted average using `w`) (ACDC spec > Edge Section, L1099-1116). Default when `o` is missing is `AND`; validity logic is EGF-dependent. The table is identical on both spec branches. [code] Two of the six are implemented, a prose-to-code movement first recorded at `b8f60166b`: `EdgeGroupOps = ("AND", "OR")` (keripy `acdc/ipexing.py`, `EdgeGroupOps`, L45), defaulting to `AND` (`groupOp = group.get("o", "AND")`, L870) and reduced at L903 as `return any(results) if groupOp == "OR" else all(results)`, with an empty group treated as malformed (L899-900) — quotes and hints as of `b8f60166b`. By `80f77b73b` 913 lines of the file had changed (+729/−184, `git diff --numstat b8f60166b 80f77b73b`; corrected 2026-10-03 by verification from "grew by 913 lines") and the m-ary AND/OR reduction (now L1020-1053) is unchanged in substance (`raw/09` section 7b). `NAND`, `NOR`, `AVG` and `WAVG` still have no code path anywhere. So "m-ary edge-group operators are read but unused" — the corpus's standing formulation, from keripy landmine L16 — is no longer accurate as written; the accurate replacement is that the two boolean group operators evaluate and the four others do not exist in the implementation. Read the scoping caveat in [section 5.1](#05-verifying-ground-truth) before leaning on this: the module it lives in is not wired into keripy's own CLI.

#### The unary operators {#05-unary-operators}

The unary operators (on individual edges, via `o`) are the family reviewers most need to understand, because the gloss and the enforced behavior diverge:

| Op | Spec gloss | Default | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| `I2I` | Issuer-To-Issuee: this ACDC's Issuer AID MUST be the Issuee AID of the far node | Yes (targeted far node) | [spec] |
| `NI2I` | Not-Issuer-To-Issuee: no such requirement | Yes (untargeted far node) | [spec] |
| `DI2I` | Delegated-Issuer-To-Issuee: this Issuer MUST be the Issuee AID or a delegated AID of the Issuee | No | [spec] |
| `NOT` | logical NOT — inverts far node validity | No | [spec] |
| `E1E` | IssueE-To-IssueE: "The Issuee AID of this ACDC MUST be the Issuee AID of the node this Edge points to" | No | [spec-next] (and [code]; proposed in [proposal] #1515) |

#### E1E, the fifth unary operator {#05-e1e}

The family is no longer four, and the fifth member is not a variation on the first four. `E1E` appears in `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` (ACDC spec > Edge, L1206 @`2362e48a1`) and occurs zero times in `main` @`f0bd097de`; it is [spec-next] and must not be quoted as normative. What makes it worth a reviewer's attention is that it constrains a different thing than its siblings do: "This is an identity relation on the two ACDCs' Issuees and places no constraint on either ACDC's Issuer" (L1206). `I2I` and `DI2I` are delegative — they bind this ACDC's Issuer to the far node's Issuee — whereas `E1E` binds the two Issuees to each other and leaves both Issuers free. Both ends must therefore be Targeted: "both the ACDC in which the Edge resides and the node to which the Edge points MUST be Targeted ACDCs (each MUST have an Issuee), and the Edge is valid when, and only when, those two Issuee AIDs are equal" (L1223). The motivating case is same-subject, different-issuer — a core identity credential and a separate entitlement credential issued to the same Issuee by different Issuers, where "`E1E` binds them as being about the same subject, a relationship the delegative `I2I` Operator cannot express" (L1223), because `I2I` would instead demand that the entitlement's Issuer be the identity credential's Issuee. That is exactly the shape [section 5.2](#05-same-holder-binding)'s SEDI material used to work around by binding at presentation rather than by edge, and now binds by edge. `E1E` is never a default.

#### Where `E1E` came from, now cited directly {#05-e1e-origin}

The proposal is Sam Smith's, in keripy discussion [#1515](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1515), New Unary Edge Operators to Support SEDI (opened 2026-07-17): "E1E which means near side IssueE AID must equal far side IssueE AID." [proposal]. The opening post proposed a larger family — `I1I`, `I1E`, `E1I`, a "3" equivalence class, and `DI1I` — and Sam narrowed it in discussion to `E1E` alone: "The only concrete use case we have is for E1E, and we want to avoid it falling into the unknown operator trap." (keripy discussion #1515, comment of 2026-07-18). So `E1E` is a discussion proposal that keripy implemented and `v1.1` defines; `raw/09` reads the sequence as implementation-led (`[proposal]` → `[code]` → `[spec-next]`), and nothing read contradicts that, though this chapter has not dated the `v1.1` commit that added it. (Discussion quotes keep Sam's wording as written.)

#### `I1I` and `DI1I`, proposed 2026-10-01 {#05-i1i-di1i}

[proposal] Two more operators were proposed on 2026-10-01, and nothing implements them. In a #1515 comment headed "Concrete Use Case in SEDI for I1I and DI1I operators", Sam argues that a SEDI leaf credential's edge to Core should assert issuer identity as well as issuee identity: "the leaf edge to the core is both E1E and I1I  that is issuee is issuee and issuer is issuer." When `I1I` fails, "an alternate edge providing the chain of authority for the issuer is required," and `DI1I` is the delegated variant: "if the delegation edge for the core is DI2I then the for leaf to core edge should have DI1I instead of I1I." Neither appears in either keripy operator table or anywhere in `src/keri` at `80f77b73b`; the words occur only in comments in `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py` (L32-33, L67-68), as design notes in a test file (`raw/09` section 10 item 7). Until one does, an edge carrying `o: "I1I"` is silently dropped to the default operator by `vdr/verifying.py` and rejected as malformed by `acdc/ipexing.py` — [section 5.1](#05-verifying-ground-truth)'s disagreement, in a case that is about to matter. This chapter's reading, not the discussion's: `DI1I` would inherit `DI2I`'s problem, since it is defined against a delegation that no keripy code path evaluates ([section 5.1](#05-verifying-ground-truth)). One sentence in that comment also says "I2I" where its context seems to call for "I1I"; `raw/09` section 11 item 8 records it as a probable slip and does not correct it, and neither does this chapter.

The spec's default inference: a targeted far node appends `I2I`, an untargeted far node appends `NI2I`; on a conflict list "the latest Operator... in the list takes precedence" (L1186). A chain of I2I-linked targeted ACDCs "can be used to provide a chain-of-authority... a delegation chain for authorization" (L1203). The gate that triggers the default differs between the branches, and both forms are given here rather than one overwriting the other. On `main` @`f0bd097de` L1197 it fires when `o` "is missing or empty or is present but does not include any of the `I2I`, `NI2I` or `DI2I` Operators"; on `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` L1209 the same sentence reads "any of the `I2I`, `NI2I`, `DI2I`, or `E1E` Operators". The defaults themselves — `I2I` for targeted, `NI2I` for untargeted — are unchanged on both branches. The practical difference is narrow, real, and this chapter's own reading rather than anything either branch states: an edge whose only operator is `E1E` suppresses the default under `v1.1`'s gate and would not under `main`'s, so an implementation that accepts `E1E` while leaving `main`'s gate in place would silently append a delegative `I2I` alongside it and reject exactly the same-subject/different-issuer case `E1E` exists to permit. keripy, as it happens, behaves like the `v1.1` gate — see [section 5.1](#05-verifying-ground-truth) — which is a coherence worth noting and not a licence to read `v1.1` as settled.

#### The empty-operator default is to change in v1.1 {#05-default-change-v1-1}

[proposal] Added 2026-10-15. The default described above has been decided against, and no text has changed yet. ACDC issue [#205](https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-acdc-specification/issues/205) proposes that an empty operator list default to `NI2I`, and Sam recorded the outcome of a maintainer call: "The change of default is to land in v1.1 of the ACDC spec." and "the v1.1 code must have a version switch that changes the default for v1.1 ACDCs but not for prior versions of the ACDC protocol." ([ACDC spec conversations > issue #205](https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-acdc-specification/issues/205#issuecomment-5268897690), comment of 2026-08-12, R-030). The switch is there because "most of the vLEIs in the wild depend on the default to `I2I`" (same). Neither branch carries the change: `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` L1209-1213 still appends `I2I` for a targeted far node, and keripy at `80f77b73b` still infers `I2I` in `vdr/verifying.py` ([section 5.1](#05-silent-default)). Issue #205 was open when it was fetched on 2026-10-14 (`raw/21` T-05). If the change lands as decided, an operator-less edge to a targeted far node will mean issuer-to-issuee in an ACDC before v1.1 and nothing at all in a v1.1 ACDC, so a validator will have to read the ACDC's version before it can read the edge. That consequence is this chapter's reading, not the comment's.

#### How far `DI2I` reaches {#05-di2i-depth}

[proposal] Added 2026-10-15. The specification says `DI2I` admits "any delegated AIDs of the Issuee of the node to which the Edge points" (ACDC spec > Edge Section, L1209; the same on `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` L1221), and says nothing about depth. Sam's ruling on that silence reversed within three days. On 2026-07-30 he agreed that "the safe choice is to limit DI2I to one layer children not all the way down." ([keripy conversations > PR #1564](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1564#issuecomment-5137135970), comment of 2026-07-30, R-015). On 2026-08-02 he wrote "After some thought, I am revising my previous comments.", under the heading "DI2I is a permission that enables AID Delegation All the Way Down", and put the safety elsewhere: "This is how we are safe, not by interpreting the `DI2I` operator as only being for children not grandchildren." ([keripy conversations > PR #1564](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1564#issuecomment-5158683549), comment of 2026-08-02, R-015). Depth is limited by the delegated AIDs' inception-time configuration traits, `DND` and `DID`, which [chapter 03, section 8](#03-config-traits) covers. He also said the text must change: "the spec language needs to include the qualification that the a delegated AID in the context of `DI2I` is any layer of delegation." (same). Neither branch carries that qualification, so a reader of the specification alone is likely to implement the narrower reading he proposed and then withdrew. The implementation status in [section 5.1](#05-di2i-not-fail-closed) is unchanged: keripy at `80f77b73b` evaluates `DI2I` at no depth at all, and PR #1564, which implements the any-depth reading, was open at the 2026-10-14 fetch (`raw/21` R-015).

### 5.1 verifying.py ground truth — gloss versus enforced behavior {#05-verifying-ground-truth}

This is where an adversarial reviewer earns their keep, and where the reference implementation must be cited against the prose. It is also where this chapter was most wrong at its previous pin, so the correction comes first.

#### Superseded 2026-09-15 {#05-superseded-60ab9e08}

This chapter previously said, at keripy `60ab9e08d`, that only three operators are recognized, that `DI2I` is not implemented and will crash if exercised (`NotImplementedError`, keripy `vdr/verifying.py`, L368), that m-ary group operators are read but unused, and that DAG acyclicity is unvalidated. At `b8f60166b` the first is false, the second is right in substance and wrong in mechanism, the third is false, and the fourth is confirmed still true. The distinction between "wrong in substance" and "wrong in mechanism" is worth drawing rather than collapsing, because the substance is what the chapter's argument needs: the claim that delegated-issuer-to-issuee has no machine behavior in the reference implementation is exactly as true as it ever was, and only the shape of the failure changed. A reviewer who read the old formulation and expects an unhandled `NotImplementedError` to fall out of a `DI2I` edge will now see a `ValidationError` instead, and will conclude wrongly that the operator has been implemented. It has not.

`Verifier.verifyChain(nodeSaid, op, issuer, issuee=None)` in keripy `vdr/verifying.py` is what actually enforces edge semantics, and the picture is mixed rather than uniformly thin. Re-anchored 2026-10-03 at `80f77b73b`. The file was re-read whole at the new pin; it changed by 17 lines, all comments, and every behavioral claim below still holds (`raw/09` section 6c). Line hints below are at `80f77b73b` where `raw/09` or `raw/11` records the new position, and are otherwise marked as `b8f60166b` hints. One quoted comment changed, and the `E1E` paragraph records it.

#### Five operators are recognized {#05-five-operators-recognized}

Five operators are recognized, not three: `UnaryOps = ('I2I', 'NI2I', 'DI2I', 'E1E', 'NOT')` (keripy `vdr/verifying.py`, `UnaryOps`, L43; `acdc/ipexing.py` carries the same set as `UnaryEdgeOps`, L44). The code says plainly why the unimplemented ones are on the list at all: "DI2I and NOT are recognized but unimplemented: they are listed so they fail closed diagnosably instead of being dropped and silently defaulting" (L38-39 @`b8f60166b`; the comment starts at L38 @`80f77b73b`). That is a design decision a reviewer should recognize as correct and should not let anyone "simplify" away — dropping an unknown token from the list hands the edge to the default-inference rule, which is the silent-weakening failure this listing exists to prevent.

#### Lists, and conflict resolution over the delegative subset {#05-delegative-subset}

`o` may be a list, and conflict resolution runs over the delegative subset only. `DelegativeOps = ('I2I', 'NI2I', 'DI2I')` (L49) names the operators that each constrain "the near ACDC's issuer relative to the far node's issuee, so they are mutually exclusive" (L44-45 @`b8f60166b`); the latest of those wins (L436), which is the code's reading of the spec's latest-takes-precedence rule at L1186. `E1E` is outside that subset and therefore composes rather than overriding: "E1E constrains the near issuee instead, so it does not conflict with them and composes (AND)" (L428-429 @`b8f60166b`; L431 @`80f77b73b`). Tokens outside `UnaryOps` are dropped from the list (L435) — hold onto that, it reappears below as a real inconsistency.

#### The silent default survives {#05-silent-default}

When nothing recognized survives, the operator is still silently inferred: `op = 'I2I' if creder.iseaid is not None else 'NI2I'` (L443), applied only when the list is absent, empty, or wholly unrecognized. The predicate moved from `'i' in creder.attrib` to `.iseaid`, which also resolves an aggregate (`acg`) far node's issuee at `.sad["A"][1]["i"]`. So the silent default survives and now sees aggregate credentials too; the "explicit operator" story remains softer than the prose suggests. Note that the aggregate case reads the issuee from one fixed position, which [section 4.1](#05-age-credential) Finding 2 shows the Age schema does not guarantee.

#### I2I is plain string equality {#05-i2i-equality}

I2I is still enforced as plain AID string equality: `if op == 'I2I' and issuer != farIssuee: return None` (L481). That is the entirety of the I2I check. The multi-hop "chain of authority" remains an emergent property of the recursive edge walk, not of any operator that re-derives delegated authority — unchanged across all three pins, and the single most durable finding in this section. The point has been put to Sam in #1515 (Daniel Hardman, 2026-07-18: the deployed I2I "is computed as that equality and nothing more"), and his reply did not dispute the mechanism; on whether a second equality operator with a different meaning is needed, "The short answer is I don't know yet for sure.  Its something to be sussed out." (keripy discussion #1515, 2026-07-18).

#### E1E is enforced {#05-e1e-enforced}

`E1E` is enforced, and it is enforced in code before it appears in any standardizing text: `farIssuee = creder.iseaid` then `if farIssuee is None or issuee is None or issuee != farIssuee: return None`, under the rule that "the issuee AID of the near ACDC (the one carrying this edge) MUST equal the issuee AID of the far node" (full sentence quoted at `b8f60166b` L455-456; its "MUST equal the issuee AID of the far node" is at L459 @`80f77b73b`, where the `E1E` branch is L457-466, under the heading comment "Identity relation (discussion #1515)"). The code's own comment names the motivating case in this corpus's vocabulary: "Unlike the delegative I2I, this says nothing about the issuer, so the common SEDI case -- both credentials issued by a third party to the same subject" is "valid (and is exactly what I2I rejects)" (L462). The tier bookkeeping is delicate, and the code comment is not the source for it. `E1E` is [proposal] in origin (#1515, [section 5](#05-edges) above), [code] here, and [spec-next] on the specification's own text — `raw/03` reads it as a table row in `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` and absent from `main` @`f0bd097de`. It is not [spec]. Do not cite `v1.1` as evidence that it is standard.

~~keripy hedges in a comment that "E1E is a keripy extension not yet in the spec's normative operator table" (L40) — accurate about `main` and stale about `v1.1`.~~ Superseded 2026-10-03. At `80f77b73b` that comment instead reads "E1E is normative on the spec's v1.1 branch (kswg-acdc-specification#197)" and says `E1E` is "absent from the 1.0 text currently under ToIP ratification" (keripy `vdr/verifying.py`, L40-41 @`80f77b73b`). The new comment agrees with `raw/03`'s spec read, but it is not independent evidence of it: it landed in commit `d9ba3d9da` (2026-09-11, "Comments and docstrings only; no behavior change."), authored by Daniel Hardman, the corpus's own author. The `[spec-next]` marker rests on the spec text, not on this comment, and should be cited that way.

#### DI2I and NOT fail closed {#05-di2i-not-fail-closed}

`DI2I` and `NOT` fail closed, deliberately and diagnosably. `if 'NOT' in ops:` raises `ValidationError` (L449); `if op == 'DI2I':` raises `ValidationError` carrying "DI2I validation is not implemented" (L453-455). The choice of exception is the load-bearing part, and the code explains it: a `MissingChainError` would escrow, and "escrowing would promise a retry that can never succeed" (L445 @`b8f60166b`). `acdc/ipexing.py` rejects both too, by returning an unsatisfied edge (keripy `acdc/ipexing.py`, L926-927 @`80f77b73b`); a repo-wide search finds no third site. A reviewer must not accept either branch being "simplified" into a `MissingChainError` or into a silent skip. Every prose description of delegated-issuer-to-issuee edge behavior — including the Dossier reference's operators table (`operators-ref`) — remains a gloss with no machine behind it. Sam's own account of why `DI2I` is in the spec, in #1515, is a QVI horizontally scaling its signing hosts: "This came up in discussions with QVIs in the context of the EBA pilot, so we put it in the spec.  But the EBA backed out", and "That use case has yet been implemented by anyone AFAIK." (keripy discussion #1515, 2026-07-18) — his assessment, not a survey.

#### NI2I is a deliberate no-op {#05-ni2i-no-op}

NI2I skips the issuer/issuee binding entirely; it only requires that the node credential exists and is in issued state — a non-authority reference. It is a no-op binding check by construction, not an unimplemented one, and the distinction matters when counting what is enforced.

#### Chain revocation propagates {#05-chain-revocation}

Chain revocation propagates: a revoked far node raises `RevokedChainError` (keripy `vdr/verifying.py`, L178-180 @`b8f60166b`) — but note the root credential is still saved even when revoked (see [section 9](#05-registries)).

#### A second implementation, and its scoping caveat {#05-second-implementation}

A second implementation exists, and the scoping caveat on it is not a footnote. keripy now carries two IPEX/edge evaluators: `vdr/verifying.py`, which the CLI actually runs, and the new `acdc/ipexing.py`, which is where the m-ary group operators, the closed-DAG walk, and per-node issuer-auth proof live. `acdc.ipexing.loadHandlers` has no caller anywhere in `src/keri` at `b8f60166b`, re-checked and still true at `80f77b73b` (`loadHandlers` is now L2149-2167; a search for `ipexing` and for imports of `acdc.loadHandlers` finds only the `acdc/__init__.py` re-export and the module's own docstring); the module is exported and exercised by tests, but keripy's own commands still load the V1 handler from `vc/protocoling.py`. Every [code] claim sourced to `ipexing.py` — including the `AND`/`OR` implementation cited in [section 5](#05-edges) above — is therefore a claim about code that exists and is tested in the reference implementation, not about behavior any shipped keripy command performs. Do not upgrade it past that, and do not let a design review treat it as deployed.

#### The two modules disagree on three axes {#05-module-disagreement}

The two modules disagree about edge operators, and the disagreement is exactly the kind of seam this chapter exists to surface. At `b8f60166b` this chapter recorded one axis of disagreement. Widened 2026-10-03: at `80f77b73b` there are three (`raw/09` section 7e, section 9, section 11 item 1; [chapter 08, section 5](#08-edges) and its [section 13](#08-ground-truth) ground-truth matrix carry the detail, and [chapter 07, section 10.5](#07-edge-operators) the shibboleth). In brief:

- Unrecognized tokens. `vdr/verifying.py` drops them and falls through to the default if nothing recognized remains (L435); `acdc/ipexing.py` treats any unrecognized element as malformed and fails closed — `if any(operator not in UnaryEdgeOps for operator in recognizedOps): return None` (keripy `acdc/ipexing.py`, L921-922 @`80f77b73b`), where `None` means malformed and malformed always fails.
