- Conflicting delegative operators in a list. `vdr/verifying.py` resolves them latest-wins (L436); `acdc/ipexing.py` deleted its delegative subset and conjoins every listed operator, so `["I2I", "NI2I"]` is `NI2I` to one module and `I2I` to the other.
- An absent `o`. `vdr/verifying.py` infers `I2I` or `NI2I` (L443); `acdc/ipexing.py` applies no relation check at all (L910-911).

The second and third axes matter more than the first, because they give two different answers for edges a conformant issuer may legitimately write. The same edge can pass credential processing and fail IPEX grant verification, or the reverse. The SEDI fixtures use `["E1E", "NI2I"]`, which both modules evaluate identically, so keripy's tests do not exercise the divergence. Neither file acknowledges the other, and neither branch of the specification says what a validator should do with an operator it does not recognize. Silently substituting a default for an operator you failed to parse remains the weaker behavior, and it is still the one in the module that actually ships.

#### DAG acyclicity is unchecked {#05-dag-acyclicity}

The DAG acyclicity gap survives, and is now a confirmed finding rather than an untested assumption. `_walkGraph` (keripy `acdc/ipexing.py`, `_walkGraph`, L627-719 @`b8f60166b`; L780-872, with the `seen`-set BFS at L808-820, @`80f77b73b`) is a breadth-first walk with a `seen` set, so a cycle among disclosed nodes terminates the walk instead of triggering a rejection — the set is a termination guard, not a validity check, and no code path reports a cycle. `vdr/verifying.py`'s edge walk does not recurse at all; `verifyChain` resolves one hop. A repo-wide search for `acyclic` and `cycle` in `src/keri` at `b8f60166b` returns only unrelated scheduler docstrings. So the corpus's standing claim that edge/provenance DAG acyclicity is unvalidated (keripy landmine L17, twin #1040) is confirmed still true at `b8f60166b`, and re-tested and still true at `80f77b73b`, where the same search finds only scheduler docstrings, an import-cycle comment, and a database-key "diamond graph" docstring, none of them a check (`raw/09` section 10) — which is a stronger statement than leaving it unexamined, and the right way to carry a negative across a refresh. A reviewer evaluating an edge-heavy design should still assume nothing rejects a cyclic provenance graph, and should ask what the proposal does when one arrives.

The general posture to carry out of this section has narrowed rather than reversed. It is no longer true that the operator gloss is uniformly specified intent with no deployed enforcement: `I2I` and `E1E` are enforced, `NI2I` is a deliberate no-op, the edge `s` constraint is enforced, and the two boolean group operators evaluate in a module nothing calls yet. What remains true is that `DI2I` and `NOT` have no behavior, four of the six m-ary operators have no behavior, acyclicity is unchecked, a missing operator is silently inferred by one module and unchecked by the other, two modules disagree on three axes, and the two operators proposed on 2026-10-01 exist only in a discussion. That is still the most consequential prose-versus-machine divergence in the ACDC layer — it is just a more interesting one than it was a month ago. (Restated 2026-10-03 at `80f77b73b`; the 2026-09-15 version said "two modules disagree about unrecognized ones".)

### 5.2 The same-holder binding pattern {#05-same-holder-binding}

~~The applied corpus supplies the sharpest doctrinal statement of what I2I means in practice: "I2I holds only when the issuer of this presentation is the issuee of the credential the edge points to... it is what distinguishes 'Alice presenting *her own* credentials' from 'two credentials that merely share an AID,' which anyone could assemble" (`sedi-present-age-portrait/index.md`).~~ Superseded wording, 2026-10-03: that passage is no longer anywhere in bakobo/schema at `cfcbdcc7a` (it was read in July at an unrecorded commit). [practice] The doctrine survives in shorter form — "`I2I` requires the presenter to be the issuee of both source credentials." (bakobo/schema `sedi-present-age-portrait/index.md`, L5) — and the schema pins it: "Edge operator: I2I asserts the issuer of this presentation is the issuee of the far node (same holder)", with `"const": "I2I"` (bakobo/schema `sedi-present-age-portrait.schema.json`, L152-153). In a holder-issued presentation the holder is the issuer and is the issuee of both source credentials, so I2I edges to both are the same-holder proof, and a non-I2I operator is rejected. The far schema is now Sam's Core.

~~The corollary is a chaining trap worth internalizing: "don't force an edge whose operator semantics you can't actually satisfy; bind at presentation instead." `sedi-age` deliberately carries no edge to `sedi-id`, because an I2I edge would hold only if the holder self-issued the age attestation (`sedi-age/index.md`).~~ Superseded 2026-10-03: the age credential now carries the edge. The page that said so is gone; the reasoning survives in Bakobo's decision record, annotated "SUPERSEDED IN PART". Age now has a required edge to Core: "Its required `coreIdentity` edge links to Core with `E1E` and `NI2I`." (bakobo/schema `sedi-age/index.md`, L3 @`cfcbdcc7a`), and Sam's fixture builds it that way, with `"o": ["E1E", "NI2I"]` on Guy's Age edge to Guy's Core (keripy `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`, L4360 @`80f77b73b`; fixture evidence, not library behavior). The old lesson was half right. Its first half holds — an `I2I` edge here would be wrong, because the state, not the holder, issues Age. Its second half, "bind at presentation instead", was a workaround for a missing operator. The lesson that replaces it: choose the operator that states the relation you mean — issuer-to-issuee, issuee-to-issuee, or none — rather than dropping the edge. The presentation-time binding is kept alongside, not replaced: "this adds an issuance-time identity relation, it does not replace the presentation-time one." (bakobo/schema `this.i` > `@lkfnoess`, L2130-2131). And the module docstring in Sam's fixture gives the reason for edging leaves to Core at all: "Edges allow revocation without continuing reissuance. This better balances power.", with the advantage that "all leaves are revoked when core is revoked" and the cost that "all leaves must be reissued if core is reissued" (keripy `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`, L15, L20, L38) — working notes, `[proposal]`-grade statements of intent in a test file.

#### The tier caution survives {#05-e1e-tier-caution}

The tier caution survives the movement. Two state-issued credentials about the same subject cannot be bound by any operator in `main`'s table: `I2I` demands the wrong thing, `NI2I` demands nothing, and `DI2I` has no implementation. `E1E` asks the question the SEDI case needs asked, and the spec author's own fixtures now use it. But it is still [spec-next] on the spec side and [code] in one implementation, so a schema that requires `E1E` today — as Sam's Age fixture and bakobo's `sedi-guardian` `citizen` edge both do (narrowed 2026-10-03 by verification: Sam's Age schema does not require `E1E` — its `coreIdentity.o` is an unconstrained string array, keripy `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`, L1520-1527 @`80f77b73b` — so only his fixture uses it; bakobo's `citizen` edge does pin it, bakobo/schema `sedi-guardian.schema.json`, L284, L317 @`cfcbdcc7a`) — is building on a forward branch. That is a reasonable bet with the spec's author on the other side of it, and still a bet. The `NI2I` beside it is not decoration, on this chapter's reading: under `main`'s default gate ([section 5](#05-edges)) an edge whose only operator is `E1E` would acquire a delegative `I2I`, and an explicit `NI2I` states "issuer unconstrained" on either branch, so `["E1E", "NI2I"]` means "same issuee, issuer unconstrained" to every reader. Both keripy modules evaluate that list identically.

#### Standing edges as a correlation point {#05-standing-edges}

[proposal] Added 2026-10-15. An edge that a credential always carries, such as a leaf's edge to Core, is a correlation point whatever its operator: two verifiers who receive different leaves can join on the far node's SAID. Daniel Hardman raised this on #1515, and Sam agreed and answered it two ways. Bulk issuance partitions the edges: "With bulk issuance, each presentation context consisting of discloser and disclosee gets its own set of SEDI credentials and standing edges." ([keripy conversations > discussion #1515](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1515#discussioncomment-17681089), comment of 2026-07-18, R-066). And "an edge can also be blinded, which means that disclosure of the edge itself can be held back" until the disclosee has agreed not to exploit it ([keripy conversations > discussion #1515](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1515#discussioncomment-17682012), comment of 2026-07-18, R-066). The two are independent and can be combined. Bulk issuance is covered under [section 9](#05-bulk-issuance).

## 6. Rules and Ricardian contracts {#05-rules}

The rule section `r` is a Ricardian Contract (RC): "both human and machine-readable and referenceable by a cryptographic digest," with the section's top-level SAID `d` providing the digest that "supports the bow-tie model of RC" (ACDC spec > Rule Section, L1239). Rules are terminal (MUST have a legal `l` field); rule-groups are intermediate and may nest; reserved labels are `[d, u, l]` and a Rule MUST NOT have other fields (L1265-1300). A rule with both `d` and high-entropy `u` is private — protected "from discovery via a rainbow table attack merely from its SAID and subschema" (L1313). The spec's worked examples are `warrantyDisclaimer`/`liabilityDisclaimer` and a `permittedUse` clause ("MAY only use this ACDC for non-commercial purposes", L1512).

[practice] The applied GCD corpus turns the rule section into a governance surface with five required disclaimers, each quotable doctrine: `noRoleSemanticsWithoutGfw` ("the role field has no enforceable semantics unless the gfw field is also defined"), `issuerNotResponsibleOutsideConstraints`, `noConstraintOutsideConstraints` ("enforceable constraints exist only inside the constraints container, or in the role field when gfw is defined." … "an unrecognized key inside the constraints container MUST be treated as fail-closed."), `useStdIfPossible`, and `onlyDelegateHeldAuthority` ("Issuers agree to only delegate authority that they reasonably believe they hold.") (bakobo/schema `gcd/rules.json`, L3-7 @`cfcbdcc7a`; the earlier text of this sentence elided the `role`/`gfw` exception, which is part of the clause). The `gfw` field names a supplemental rules block and carries a hard verifier obligation: a verifier "MUST NOT impute a delegator's approval of delegated authority to a delegate without understanding and enforcing the rules of these extra rules." (bakobo/schema `gcd.schema.json`, `a.gfw`, L79), and "The act of issuing or receiving a GCD credential constitutes binding acceptance of the rules." (bakobo/schema `gcd/index.md` > Governance Framework, L116). ~~This binding-by-participation pattern recurs verbatim in the SEDI governance framework's chain-link-confidentiality clause.~~ Corrected 2026-10-03: the pattern recurs, but not verbatim — SEDI states it in its own words, "Issuing or accepting a SEDI credential is binding acceptance of its referenced revision." (bakobo/schema `sedi-id/index.md` > Governance, L159), and Provenant's newer telco pages do the same (public-schema `brand-owner/index.md`, L79 @`95a07e544`).

### Rules are not machine-enforced {#05-rules-not-enforced}

Load-bearing caveat for reviewers: rules are disclosure and accountability, and in keripy the disclosure/rule layer is largely not machine-enforced by the credential `Verifier`. The keripy crosswalk flags this explicitly: "disclosure rules not enforced in `Verifier`" (keripy-knowledge `20-crosswalk.md`). A rule clause is a commitment a human or an application-layer policy engine must honor; it is not a predicate the reference verifier evaluates. GCD's own doctrine embraces this: "Duties are disclosure and accountability -- a stranger-verifier does not gate on them -- so they live here in r, not in a.constraints." (bakobo/schema `gcd.schema.json`, `r.duties`, L526 @`cfcbdcc7a`; quote corrected to the source wording 2026-10-03). As of GCD 3.1.0 the same division reaches inside `constraints` itself — see [section 11](#05-applied-patterns).

## 7. The graduated-disclosure ladder {#05-graduated-disclosure}

"Graduated Disclosure" is recursive least disclosure: "disclose enough to enable more disclosure, which in turn may enable even more disclosure" (ACDC spec > Graduated Disclosure, L1747). (Note the deliberate vocabulary choice: "selective disclosure" is avoided as a top-level term because it "has a long and unpleasant history in financial regulation," per papers `sdjwt-acdc.md` > 1. Similarities.) The ladder's rungs (L1749-1774):

1. Compact Disclosure — a SAID commitment via `oneOf` compact/full; compactness only, not privacy.
2. Metadata Disclosure — the metadata ACDC (empty `u`) lets a Discloser commit to metadata (Issuer, Schema, Edges, Rules) of a yet-to-be-disclosed private ACDC "without providing any point of correlation to the actual top-level SAID." Critically, "When metadata ACDC is disclosed, only Discloser commitments attach, NOT Issuer commitments" — so the Issuer's commitments do not become a correlation point until after the Disclosee agrees to the Rules (ACDC spec > Metadata ACDC, L168-172).
3. Partial Disclosure — SAID + salty nonce; SAID + schema is not enough to discover content.
4. Nested Partial Disclosure — each nested block carries its own `d` + `u`, with per-level `oneOf`, so branches disclose at different nesting depths (L633).
5. Full Disclosure — no hiding.
6. Selective Disclosure — `anyOf` + `oneOf`, order-independent, membership via the SAID set (the aggregate mechanism of [section 4](#05-attribute-vs-aggregate)).
7. Bulk-issued Instance Disclosure — many non-correlatable instances (see [section 9](#05-bulk-issuance)).

"All the Graduated Disclosure mechanisms MAY be used in combination" (L1775). The keripy reference `tests/acdc/test_clc_disclosure.py` is the executable exemplar cited by the SEDI corpus (bakobo/schema `sedi-id/index.md`, L167-168 @`cfcbdcc7a`; the citation moved off `sedi-present-age-portrait/index.md`, and the test itself has not been re-read). keripy's SEDI IPEX tests now carry their own worked graduated disclosure — Residence disclosed as state only, then county and postcode, with both compacted forms asserted to keep the issued SAID (keripy `tests/sedi/test_ipex_sedi.py`, L1494-1496 @`80f77b73b`).

### Worked examples in the standardizing branch {#05-ladder-worked-examples}

[spec] The ladder now has worked examples in the standardizing branch, and their framing is the useful part. A Graduated Disclosure subsection in `main`'s annex (@`f0bd097de`, L4988-5098) presents two flows explicitly as "how an issuer *plans* for disclosure by the way it structures the credential, and how a holder *performs* disclosure at presentation while a verifier checks it" (L4991-4993). That split — planning at issuance, performance at presentation — is the thing most outsiders miss, because in the SD-JWT and BBS+ worlds disclosure is a runtime capability of the signature scheme rather than a schema-design decision made months earlier. In ACDC the issuer's structural choices fix what can ever be disclosed separately, which is why [section 4](#05-attribute-vs-aggregate)'s attribute-versus-aggregate question is consequential and irreversible. The first flow walks selective disclosure via an aggregate section: every attribute gets its own element with its own `u` and `d`, the AGID is element 0, the holder "discloses only the chosen elements as full blocks and leaves the rest as their bare SAIDs" (L5031-5032), and the verifier "recomputes the AGID over the mix of disclosed blocks and undisclosed SAIDs and confirms it still equals the committed AGID" (L5048-5049) — with the count-and-position leak recorded in [section 4](#05-attribute-vs-aggregate). The second walks partial disclosure via compaction, and states the invariant that makes the whole ladder coherent: "Because the top-level SAID is computed over the most compact form, it is identical whether the credential is held compact or expanded" (L5058-5060), so "Every disclosure level... verifies to the same top-level SAID, so what the credential commits to never changes as disclosure progresses" (L5095-5098). It also shows the chain-link-confidentiality ordering concretely rather than abstractly: "Under Chain-Link Confidentiality the rule (terms-of-use) section is disclosed first — so a potential Disclosee can agree to the terms" (L5078-5080) while the attribute section is still a bare SAID. These examples are new to this chapter but not new to `main` — they may read as forward-branch material and are not; they are substantively identical on `v1.1` apart from the UUID-to-UE substitution of [section 2](#05-saids).

An important disambiguation for reviewers who arrive from the Merkle-tree / transparency-log world: ACDC graduated disclosure and Merkle Tree Certificate inclusion proofs share hash vocabulary but discharge different obligations. ACDC's proof obligation is semantic — "that a particular view corresponds to a specific underlying claim" — motivated by correlation-minimization; MTC's is historical/membership — "is this object a member of a committed set" — motivated by efficiency. "A Merkle inclusion proof establishes placement in a history. A SAID establishes identity of content" (papers `acdc-and-mtc.md` > 3.2 Trees, structure, and meaning). They are orthogonal, not competitive.

## 8. Contractually-protected disclosure {#05-contractual-disclosure}

Two mechanisms attach obligations to disclosed data (ACDC spec, L1783-1792):

### Chain-Link Confidentiality (CLC) {#05-chain-link-confidentiality}

In Chain-Link Confidentiality the offer is a partial disclosure of metadata plus terms; full disclosure follows only after the Disclosee agrees — "permissioned disclosure" in which "the disclosed data has 'strings attached.'" CLC chains Disclosees (distinct from the edge-chaining of ACDCs): "each Disclosee... in turn, is the Discloser to the next," and terms-of-use MUST propagate, imposing "conditions and limitations on the further disclosure and/or use." The SEDI governance framework operationalizes this as the `chainLinkConfidentiality` rule: the verifier MUST NOT "assimilate, aggregate, correlate, sell, or otherwise combine disclosed attributes... for any purpose beyond the disclosed purpose," and "This binds each downstream recipient reached through the edge section of a presentation." (bakobo/schema `sedi-id/rules.json`, L3 @`cfcbdcc7a`). At `cfcbdcc7a` the named clauses are carried as text inside a single `l` string, because "Sam's r object permits only d and l" (bakobo/schema `this.i` > `@2vqmhxai`, L2235). Sam's own fixtures go further: every rule section in them is empty, `{"d": "", "l": ""}` saidified (keripy `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`, e.g. L4381-4393 @`80f77b73b`), so the chain-link-confidentiality language is Bakobo's profile, not the spec author's.

#### Contingent Disclosure {#05-contingent-disclosure}

Contingent Disclosure is an obligation in the Rules to disclose when a contingency is met (e.g. breach); the responsible party may be the Discloser or an escrow agent, and the rule references a private ACDC. This enables latent accountability: "Recourse via Full Disclosure of PII is latent... but never realized until the conditions of the contingency is satisfied," limiting PII exposure to a "just-in-time, need-to-know basis" (L1792).

The doctrine that governs when to reach for expensive cryptographic unlinkability instead is blunt: cryptographically-provable correlation resistance is unlinkability, but "this is a weak form... as it does not prevent statistical correlation from contextual information." "There is no cryptographic mechanism that precludes statistical correlation among a set of colluding Verifiers" (ACDC spec > Bulk-issued, L2785). Consequently, advanced cryptographic unlinkability can be "an exercise in diminishing returns" without contractually-protected disclosure. This is a deliberate, load-bearing design position: ACDC leans on contracts-plus-detection where a ZK-maximalist would spend cryptography.

## 9. Registries and TELs {#05-registries}

A TEL (Transaction Event Log) is "a hash-chained data structure of sealed transaction events" tracking an ACDC's issuance/revocation/transfer state; TEL events are sealed/anchored in a KEL via seals (a seal is an event SAID, optionally plus sequence number). Because they are anchored to a KEL, TELs are "also securely attributable to the KEL's controller" (ACDC spec > TEL Overview, L1918). The persistence property is central: "the verifiability of transaction events in the TEL persists in spite of changes to Key States in the sealing KEL" (L1920). TEL events need not themselves be signed — "the digest in the seal in the KEL is cryptographically equivalent to signing the transaction event itself" (L1946).

### The registry-dependent issuance lifecycle {#05-registry-lifecycle}

[spec] The spec now walks the whole registry-dependent lifecycle end to end, filling a gap its earlier examples left. The Registry-Dependent Issuance Lifecycle section (`main` @`f0bd097de`, L4852-4986) opens by naming the gap: "The examples above reference each issuer's registry by its identifier (for example `regAmy`) as though it already existed" (L4854-4856). The five steps are `rip` → `acm` → `bup` → verify → revoke, with Amy a school issuing to Bob a student. Two of them carry doctrine a reviewer can use directly. The registry inception is derived, not chosen — "The registry identifier is the SAID of this event, so it is *derived* from the event rather than chosen" — and it is deliberately contentless: "The inception commits to no credential state: it is a vacuous placeholder that reveals nothing about what will later be issued" (L4865-4867). The same self-derivation applies one layer down at issuance: "Because the SAID is derived from the credential's content, it is not known in advance; it is produced by issuance, not assumed" (L4890-4892), which is the mechanical refutation of every design that wants to mint a credential identifier before the credential exists. The `bup` then carries a blinded state block `{d, u, td, ts}` blinded by a nonce derived from a salt Amy shares with Bob and the update's sequence number, and "Only the blinded block's SAID travels in the `bup`; neither the credential SAID nor the word `issued` appears" (L4917-4918). Revocation is a second `bup` whose nonce is independent of the first, so a verifier that once confirmed `issued` "cannot later read the `revoked` state by watching the registry: it would need the salt" (L4979-4981).

#### The lifecycle's own boundary {#05-lifecycle-boundary}

The example states its own boundary, and the boundary is the quotable part. "The registry *events* remain public and chained (the `rd` and prior links are in the clear); it is the state *content* each event commits to that is protected" (L4981-4983), and therefore: "This is confidentiality of registry state, not anonymity of the credential — issuer, registry, and issuance chronology remain linkable, which is the intended, auditable trade-off" (L4983-4985). A reviewer who reads blindable state as an anonymity mechanism is reading past the spec's own disclaimer. Note also what the lifecycle is not: it is Issuer-controlled end to end — Amy incepts the registry, Amy issues, Amy appends every update, and Bob's only role is holding the shared salt. There is no Issuee-controlled registry anywhere in it, on either branch, which is the load-bearing negative for [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md).

Terminology a reviewer should keep straight: ACDCs generically are Verifiable Containers; as entitlements they are Verifiable Credentials; a VCR (Verifiable Credential Registry) is a type of TEL, which is a form of VDR (Verifiable Data Registry); a TEL tracking issuance/revocation is a Revocation Registry (ACDC spec, L1948). keripy's `Tever`/`Tevery` implement this, with registry-inception `vcp` and issue/revoke events `iss`/`rev` (backerless) or `bis`/`brv` (backer) (keripy `vdr/eventing.py`).

The anti-phone-home stance is a deliberate rejection of OCSP/CRL. A Registrar (under the Issuer) maintains and publishes the registry; an Observer (under one or more Validators) caches the registry so Validators "validate the state... without exposing a point of validation (PoV)." "It can mask the usage of a given ACDC from the Issuer." Observer-to-Registrar sync happens on state changes, NOT at the point of validation, which "protects against forced validator-to-issuer correlation of ACDC usage, i.e., no forced phone home validation" (ACDC spec > TEL Registrars and TEL Observers, L1693). Race conditions on rare state changes are handled by "timed grace periods on revocations" (L1695). In Hardman's framing, "A registry consulted at verification time is a phone-home in disguise" (papers `sda.md` > 7. Open loop, not closed); the corollary invariant is that "verification must succeed from the credential and key-state alone, and any registry or log is an issuance-time and audit-time convenience, never a verification-time dependency."

#### Registrar and Observer as a governance split {#05-registrar-observer-governance}

The split is a governance decision, not a caching optimization — a point the spec never makes but Sam states directly. At KERIcon 2026 he presented Registrar/Observer as a deliberate replay of the witness/watcher structure one layer up: "notice that this models the witness watcher governance structure. So, we learned a lesson. We shouldn't have shared governance. So, we have witnesses that are controlled by controllers, watchers that are controlled by verifiers. We split the verification between two places. We do the same thing with ACDCs" (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, The Digital Identity Tradespace, 16:48; `raw/14`). The Observer's remit is correspondingly thin — "All our observer is doing is it's keeping track of the registry state" (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, The Digital Identity Tradespace, 32:13) — and it is layered on, not substituted for, KEL assurance: asked why Observers and watchers must be separate components, "they have different purposes... They depend on watchers, but they aren't watchers" (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, State of the KERI Suite, 52:25). The cleanest one-line distinction in the corpus is from the same Q&A: "watchers watch the KEL... looking for duplicity in your KEL. Observers are watching the state of issuances that are anchored to the KEL... it's a TEL observer." (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, State of the KERI Suite, 52:00). Caution on provenance: these are hand-edited auto-captions, `[architect]` in substance but not verbatim in wording — see `raw/14` section 0 before quoting any of it to Sam or into a spec issue.

#### The split's proposed third leg {#05-proposed-third-leg}

The split has a proposed third leg. Registrar (Issuer-controlled) and Observer (verifier-controlled) leave the Holder as the one party to a transaction running no state infrastructure of its own. A presentation registry — an Issuee-controlled blindable state registry that a `grant` must be anchored in — closes that, giving the Issuee the same detect-and-recover capability the Issuer already has against impersonation. It is pre-normative and unimplemented; see [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md), and note that its origin document calls it an Issuee usage registry (keripy #1095).

#### Bulk updates as a privacy requirement {#05-bulk-updates}

Bulk updates are a privacy requirement, not a performance one. The spec mentions "optimized batch synchronization" in a performance register (L1695); the talks make batching load-bearing. "if you update it instantly, then the observer could correlate a change to some registries and not others. But if all the registries, 100% of them update at the same clock time... then there's [synchronization] in the time of update" (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, The Digital Identity Tradespace, 32:48), generalized to a design law in the same talk: "if you want to make it so that it's not statistically correlatable, you have to do it in a bulk or herd privacy protected way." (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, The Digital Identity Tradespace, 33:14). The batch window closes correlation in both directions — backward from a point of validation to the state change that preceded it, forward from a state change to the validations that follow. The residual weakness is named by Sam himself, and a reviewer should quote it rather than overclaim: "if an observer is malicious and the issuer is malicious, they can collude... but there's no phone home here. The issuer can't force an observer... There's no technical thing that makes it impossible in this, but what it does is it means that there's no easy way for them to do it" (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, The Digital Identity Tradespace, 34:46). The claim is that collusion is unforced, out-of-band and legally repressible — the same technical-plus-legal posture as the rest of the ACDC privacy story ([chapter 06, section 4](#06-layered-privacy), the three-party exploitation model), not a cryptographic impossibility.

#### Usage registries {#05-usage-registries}

Usage registries are where presenter-side compromise detection actually lives, and they are the thing most often misattributed to Observers. Observers cache state; they detect nothing. Detection of a presenter's key compromise comes from a second registry controlled by the issuee, in which every presentation is anchored: "if somebody steals my private keys as a presenter, I know that they stole them because the only way that they can gain access is to anchor it in my registry that I control" (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, The Future of KERI, 13:39). The verifier then checks two registries, the issuer's and the presenter's, "so that both the issuer and the user can detect if either one has been compromised and the verifier knows it." (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, The Future of KERI, 15:15). It is opt-in and it costs ephemerality — "Makes the presentation less ephemeral" (KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, The Future of KERI, 13:28) — and it is the mirror of the issuer-side anti-forgery story at L1687-1689, applied at the other end of the presentation. Tier this carefully: it is talk-only. The sole trace in the specification is the `rd` field description listing registry kinds as "Issuance and/or revocation, transfer, retraction, or usage registry" (ACDC spec > Top-Level Fields, L48); there is no usage-registry section, and Sam's own framing of it is a novelty claim ("a new thing that nobody else does", KERIConf26 caption, Sam Smith, The Digital Identity Tradespace, 14:38).

#### Implementation status of Registrar and Observer {#05-registrar-observer-status}

Implementation status (2026-09-01): neither component exists. `keri-foundation/observer` and `keri-foundation/registrar` are public placeholder repos holding a LICENSE and a one-line README; `src/keri/acdc/registraring.py` in keripy is a docstring-only stub Sam created 2026-07-02, and keripy has no observer module at all. What is implemented is the layer beneath — the blindable `bup` update event and `BlindState` structures (keripy `core/structing.py`; keripy `acdc/messaging.py`, `blindate()`) and the `RegBaser`/`WebRegBaser` registry stores. Nothing anywhere specifies the Observer wire protocol, how a validator discovers or pools Observers, or how the batch-window-versus-revocation-latency trade should be set. A reviewer should treat Registrar/Observer as architecturally committed and operationally unbuilt, and should not accept "the Observer handles that" as an answer to a live design question.

#### Binding ACDC state to issuer key state {#05-key-state-binding}

Binding ACDC state to issuer key state is the core anti-forgery doctrine, and it is where ACDC most sharply corrects the W3C-VC/SD-JWT prior. ACDCs are "not directly signed by the Issuer... bound to the Issuer's Key State... and the Issuer's Key State is signed. This enables the Key State of the Issuer to change independently of the ACDC state" (ACDC spec > Binding to Key State, L1673). The explicit anti-pattern: in "other verifiable credential schemes, where the credentials are signed directly... a key rotation forces all the credentials signed with a given set of keys to be revoked; otherwise, a key compromise would enable the compromiser to issue... forged [credentials]" (L1675). This is the retrograde attack defense (papers `was.md`): a bare signature "provides no assurance that the private key was used to sign the message at that time" (NIST SP 800-102, via papers `keri-primer.md` > 3.3 Anchored vs. paired signatures), so ACDC uses anchored rather than paired signatures — validity is judged against issuer key state "AS OF its KEL anchor's sequence position, not current key state or wall-clock" (keripy invariant H1, keripy-knowledge `30-invariants.md` > H1; enforced in `Tever.verifyAnchor`).

#### The Dossier specification on anchoring {#05-dossier-anchoring}

[spec] A second standardizing specification now says this in its own words, and it is the better citation to hand an outsider. The Dossier specification at `main` @`b9227753c` (2026-08-25) swept its whole text to distinguish anchoring from signing, adding a normative section titled "How a Dossier Is Issued: Anchoring, Not Attached Signatures" that opens with a flat denial — "A dossier is not a signed document. The issuer does not compute a signature over the dossier ACDC and attach that signature to it as proof of authenticity" (Dossier spec > How a Dossier Is Issued: Anchoring, Not Attached Signatures, L13-14) — and locates the signature precisely: "The signature exists on the anchoring key event, not on the dossier" (L27-28). It reaches the verifier as an obligation: "A verifier MUST NOT treat an attached signature as equivalent to an anchor when evaluating a dossier as of any referenceTime other than the present" (L77-79). What makes this the citation of choice is not that it is stronger but that it is a correction — a working spec author found the signing/anchoring conflation dangerous enough to sweep an entire document for it and define three terms to stop it recurring — and that it argues from key rotation rather than from ACDC internals, which is the argument an arrival from the VC world can follow.

#### Two refinements {#05-anchoring-refinements}

Two refinements guard against reading that too absolutely, and a reviewer should carry both. First, the partition is drawn on lifespan, not on artifact kind. The spec partitions its own artifacts explicitly: "key events are signed, and so are the short-lived transactional objects described under *Dossiers and Derivative References*. Dossiers, endorsements, and other ACDCs are anchored." A token "is one of the few artifacts in this specification that genuinely bears an attached signature... it can afford one because its lifetime is measured in seconds and it is never expected to outlive a key rotation" (L473). Second, an attached signature is explicitly permitted in the ephemeral case: a dossier that lives only for one interaction and will never be verified after the issuer's next rotation MAY be authenticated by an attached signature, at the stated price that it "ceases to be verifiable once the signing key is no longer part of the current key state" and that the issuer's commitment "becomes repudiable in practice." So the shibboleth "ACDCs are never signed" overstates the case. The accurate form — and the one a reviewer should use, because it survives the obvious counterexample — is that nothing expected to outlive a key rotation is authenticated by an attached signature.

#### Recon hypothesis: anchors not re-verified on presentation {#05-verifyanchor-hypothesis}

A serious caveat, flagged as a keripy recon hypothesis (L15, HIGH severity, medium confidence). The credential `Verifier.processCredential` checks registry existence, TEL state, freshness, schema, and chain edges, but recon "found no call to `Tever.verifyAnchor`" in that path — anchor validation appears to happen only when a TEL event is ingested by `Tevery`, "not when a credential + proof is verified." If confirmed, "a credential presented with a forged `(seqner, saider)` proof could pass schema + TEL-state checks without the anchor being confirmed against the issuer's actual KEL at that sn — undermining invariant H1" (keripy-knowledge `31-landmines.md` > L15). A reviewer relying on anchor-time-of-signing verification must confirm the ingest path actually ran `verifyAnchor` on the events in question; do not assume the credential-verification call re-checks it.

#### Revocation is a state, not a deletion {#05-revocation-state}

Revocation is a state, not a deletion. The keripy verifier explicitly saves a revoked credential rather than raising: "Log this and continue instead of the previous exception so we save a revoked credential" (keripy `vdr/verifying.py`, L129-132). State is queried from the TEL (`vcState`), not from a central revocation list. This is the direct machine-level contradiction of the "revocation = CRL/blocklist" mindset.

#### Blindable state (BLID) {#05-blindable-state}

Blindable state (BLID) extends registries to private/blinded state: a blinded attribute block `[d, u, td, ts]` whose SAID is computed over a fixed-field concatenation, derived from an Issuer+Discloser shared salt via HD derivation keyed by sequence number, so "an observer cannot correlate state to event updates" (ACDC spec > Blinded State Disclosure, L2043-2135). The Discloser recovers state by brute-forcing the small combination space of possible `td` x `ts` until the BLID matches (only ~6 combinations in the revocation example, L2288). Placeholder decorrelation (publishing empty state before any real ACDC exists) and continued blind updates after revocation "decorrelate the time of revocation" (L2324). Herd privacy can be strengthened with Sparse Merkle Trees amalgamating all seals into one KEL root, giving `O(log N)` inclusion proofs where "a given seal in the KEL... no longer provides a point of correlation to any other transaction event" (L2914).

#### `upd` is deprecated and still specified {#05-upd-deprecated}

[proposal] Added 2026-10-15. The registry's non-blindable update event is on its way out. Sam, 2026-07-30: "We have discussed without disagreement of deprecating the `upd` event so only the `rip` and `bup` remain.", for the reason that "a blindable update can be unblinded by merely attaching the unblinded attribute block." ([keripy conversations > discussion #1566](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1566#discussioncomment-17846317), comment of 2026-07-30, R-036). And on 2026-08-11: "We are going to drop support for `upd` in v1.1" ([keripy conversations > PR #1612](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1612#issuecomment-5259378594), comment of 2026-08-11, R-036). The specification has not followed. `v1.1` still defines `upd` as a "non-blindable transaction event state update" (ACDC spec > Registry Message Types and Fields, L2161 @`2362e48a1`) and gives its field order under Update event fields (L2192-2194), as `main` does. [code] keripy is split: the V2 registry processor says "The v2 ACDC TEL only supports registry inception and blind updates" (keripy `acdc/regeventing.py`, L121 @`80f77b73b`), while `acdc/messaging.py` still builds an `upd` (`update`, L78-104 @`80f77b73b`). An implementer reading `v1.1` alone will build an event its editor has deprecated.

#### Registry transfer, approved and unspecified {#05-registry-transfer}

[proposal] Added 2026-10-15. Sam first proposed transferring a registry on 2026-04-23, as an `rxr` event: "New message that enables transfer of control of registry to a different delegatee.", under the principle that "when the ACDC of the delegatee is revoked, authority over any down stream ACDC state reverts to the delegator (State)." ([keripy conversations > discussion #1082](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1082#discussioncomment-16688843), comment of 2026-04-23, edited 2026-04-26, R-037). On 2026-07-30 the event was renamed: "The second planned change is to add a transfer `xfr` event", moving control "from the issuer AID defined in the `rip` to a new controller issuer defined in the `xfr`", and "This event must doubly anchored." ([keripy conversations > discussion #1566](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1566#discussioncomment-17846317), comment of 2026-07-30, R-037). The next day: "I already discussed `xfr` with the community and got approval. so was planning to add it to ACDC v1.1." ([keripy conversations > discussion #1566](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1566#discussioncomment-17856451), comment of 2026-07-31, R-037). Neither ACDC branch has `xfr` or `rxr`, and keripy at `80f77b73b` has neither (`raw/21` R-037, T-04). The comment does not say which two logs the double anchor is in. Until the event is specified, the Registrar model above assumes that the issuer that incepted a registry controls it for life.

#### TEL anchors follow first-seen {#05-tel-anchor-first-seen}

[proposal] Added 2026-10-15. Sam ruled that a TEL event's anchor follows the KEL's first-seen rule: "anchoring TEL events should follow the idempotent first seen rule used for KEL events.", so that a new anchor "does not clobber a previously verified anchor" ([keripy conversations > PR #1612](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1612#issuecomment-5373529636), comment of 2026-08-21, R-038). [code] keripy does something close to that and different from it. `putAnchor` keeps "the earliest verified sealing event for this TEL event": it refuses a new anchor unless its sealing sequence number is lower than the stored one, and then writes it with `pin`, which replaces the stored anchor (keripy `acdc/registering.py`, `putAnchor`, L58-64 @`80f77b73b`). So keripy keeps the anchor earliest in the KEL, and Sam's rule keeps the anchor verified first. They pick different anchors for a TEL event sealed twice in one KEL when the later seal is verified first; whether that case arises in practice has not been tested (`raw/21` T-08). The first-seen rule for KELs is in [chapter 03, section 10](#03-recovery-rotation).

### Bulk issuance {#05-bulk-issuance}

Bulk issuance gives a holder many copies of one credential, each issued to a different AID, so that presentations in different contexts cannot be joined through the credential. The specification describes it in its annex (ACDC spec > Annex > Bulk-issued Private ACDCs, L2765; `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` L2966). Sam's rulings in the 2026 SEDI work fill several gaps in that text, and one of them has reached the standardizing line. Added 2026-10-15.

#### What landed: one salt, the `k.` path, qb64, Blake3-256 {#05-bulk-landed}

[spec] The derivation of each member's blinding factor `v_k` from the set's single shared salt is now pinned on both branches. Its path "is therefore `k.`, that is, the textual representation of the index `k`" (ACDC spec > Annex > Bulk-issued Private ACDCs > Basic Bulk Issuance Procedure, L2811; `v1.1` L3012). The concatenation operators "operate on the fully qualified CESR (qb64 text) representations of their operands", and "unless a different algorithm is negotiated out of band, H is Blake3-256" (L2818). These follow Sam's review of ACDC PR #200, which starts from "there is only one shared secret salt" ([ACDC spec conversations > PR #200](https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-acdc-specification/pull/200#issuecomment-5063392427), comment of 2026-07-23, R-043). The [spec] carries the caveat of the next subsection.

#### Normative status: to leave the annex in v1.1 {#05-bulk-normative-status}

[proposal] Every MUST in the bulk-issuance material, including the ones just cited, sits under `## Annex` on both branches (`main` L2697, `v1.1` L2898), and neither branch says whether its annex binds. Sam: "For the v1.1 spec I would think we will want to move Bulk issuance from the annex so as to be normative." and "But yes lets make the language normative." ([ACDC spec conversations > PR #204](https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-acdc-specification/pull/204#issuecomment-5273991502), comment of 2026-08-12, R-045). At `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` the section has not moved. Until it does, cite bulk-issuance rules as standardizing-line text in an annex whose force neither branch declares.

#### Independent registries: pre-created, not derived {#05-bulk-independent-registries}

[proposal] The specification's Independent Registry Bulk-Issued ACDCs section (`main` L2897, `v1.1` L3098) does not say how registries come into being for a bulk set, and Sam distinguishes two ways. In the first, registries are pre-created by `rip` events with a salty-nonce `u` and no ACDC attached, and "This enables the Issuer to fully decorrelate the registry state updates from any data in the ACDC." The cost is that the issuer must give the holder an indexed list of registry SAIDs, because "The `rd` field value is not derivable from the salt with a path." ([keripy conversations > PR #1576](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1576#issuecomment-5195334135), comment of 2026-08-05, R-040). In the second, the `rip`'s `u` is derived from the bulk salt at issuance, which "does not provide the third party decorrelation" (same). SEDI has chosen the first: "for SEDI the use case the State has confirmed they want is the decorrelatable registrities" (same; "registrities" is his slip). A week later he doubted the second deserves text at all: "I wonder if there is any point in even specifying the second case." ([keripy conversations > PR #1576](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1576#issuecomment-5273063343), comment of 2026-08-12, R-040). ACDC PR #204, which would specify the distinction, was open at the 2026-10-14 fetch. The 2026-08-05 comment also sketches herd privacy for pre-created registries, with figures that illustrate rather than require: millions of unassigned registries anchored at once, then updates padded with vacuous ones, because "The State would only update registries in bulk." (same, R-041). That is the mechanism behind [Bulk updates as a privacy requirement](#05-bulk-updates) above.

#### The registry blinding salt: path unsettled {#05-bulk-blinding-salt}

[proposal] For the registries of a bulk set, Sam proposes that "the blinding factor for each registry could be HDKey-derived from the same shared secret salt used for bulk issuance", so that one salt is exchanged instead of one per registry ([keripy conversations > PR #1576](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1576#issuecomment-5273063343), comment of 2026-08-12, R-044). The derivation path is not settled. Daniel Hardman's text in ACDC PR #204 uses `k.s`; Sam asked "Do we need the "k.s," or isn't "k." sufficient to disambiguate?" and in the same review offered `k|` ([ACDC spec conversations > PR #204](https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-acdc-specification/pull/204#pullrequestreview-4922214480), review of 2026-08-13, R-044). Treat all three as provisional.

#### Revocation is universal across the set {#05-bulk-revocation}

[proposal] A bulk set is revoked as a whole: "An issuer when it revokes authority revokes it universally. In a bulk issued set this means that all members of the set MUST be revoked." ([keripy conversations > discussion #1574](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1574#discussioncomment-17938568), comment of 2026-08-07, R-042). The ruling answers a proposal to revoke one copy because it was compromised at one verifier. Sam's correction is that a copy is not what gets compromised, a key is, and "if the keys get compromised then the keystate is changed not the ACDC state." (same). The holder rotates the affected AID, and the other AIDs in the set are untouched. The exception is the salt: if the set's AIDs were derived from one private salt and that salt is compromised, "the whole set has to be abandoned." (same). The same comment separates the issuer's registry, which tracks ACDC state, from a presentation registry, which "is not tracking ACDC state, but is merely logging presentations" ([chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md)). Per-copy revocation treats a copy as a bearer token; Sam's reply opens by asking whether the proposal is "conflating ZKP proofs with KERI/ACDC anchored proofs."

## 10. IPEX — the issuance and presentation exchange {#05-ipex}

The ACDC spec's IPEX section is explicitly non-normative (ACDC spec, L1795), but the framing is doctrine: "all exchanges (both issuance and presentation) MAY be modeled as the disclosure of information by a Discloser to a Disclosee. The difference between exchange types is the information disclosed, not the mechanism" (L1797). IPEX rides routed KERI `exn` messages, with routes:

| Route | By | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `apply` | Disclosee | initiate; defines wanted disclosure (schema, label list, aggregate elements, signature) |
| `offer` | Discloser | initiate; proposes acceptable disclosure (Metadata ACDC or SAID, partial disclosure, signature) |
| `agree` | Disclosee | accepts the offer |
| `grant` | Discloser | initiate; discloses the agreed content (Full or Selective Disclosure ACDC, signature) |
| `admit` | Disclosee | confirms receipt |
| `spurn` | either | rejects apply/offer/agree~~/grant~~ (corrected 2026-10-15, below) |

Corrected 2026-10-15. This table said that `spurn` rejects a `grant`, and the struck-through entry is kept so the change is visible. Neither ACDC branch's route table has that row: `spurn` appears three times, and the rows read "rejects `apply`", "rejects `offer`" and "rejects `agree`" (ACDC spec > Issuance and Presentation Exchange (IPEX) > IPEX Protocol Messages, L1812-1816; `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` L2005-2009). The specification is silent on spurning a grant. [code] keripy's V2 module goes further than the specification in one direction only: it allows a spurn of a flow-starting grant and refuses a spurn of a grant that answers an earlier message, which follows Sam's ruling that "an unsolicited grant i.e using a xip message should be spurnable." ([keripy conversations > issue #1628](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/issues/1628#issuecomment-5349282926), comment of 2026-08-19, R-051). [Chapter 08, section 6](#08-spurn-grant) carries the code citations and the corrected account of that rule.

The keripy implementation is a strict state machine, not a message log, and this is where prose and code agree cleanly. `Ipexage(apply, offer, agree, grant, admit, spurn)` with a legal-predecessor table `PreviousRoutes` (keripy `vc/protocoling.py`, `PreviousRoutes`, L17-23): `offer` <- `apply`; `agree` <- `offer`; `grant` <- `agree`; `admit` <- `grant`; `spurn` <- any of the four. `IpexHandler.verify` enforces it: `apply` may only start an exchange (empty prior `p`); `offer`/`grant` may start or must reference a legal predecessor; `admit`/`agree`/`spurn` may never start; and there is no double-response — "reject if a response to that prior already exists" (keripy `vc/protocoling.py`, `IpexHandler.verify`, L60-113). Unmatched routes fail closed. This corrects the outsider assumption that "peer disclosure messages get logged like credentials / like a VC exchange endpoint" — out-of-order or duplicate-response messages are rejected, not merged (`raw/09` section 4).

The commitment mechanics that make IPEX safe across variants: a commitment (signature or KEL-anchored seal) to any variant commits to the shared top-level section fields of all variants, because each section value is SAD-or-SAID. "A signature on any variant MAY be used to verify the Issuer's commitment to any other variant... on a top-level section-by-section basis." The variants form a hash tree, and "A commitment to the top-level SAID of the compact version... is equivalent to a commitment to the hash tree root," so the Issuer MUST provide a signature or seal on the SAID of the most compact form variant (ACDC spec > Issuer Commitment Rules, L1843). Mutual anchoring — issuer logs "I issued," holder logs "I accepted" — "prevents spam (you can't force a credential into someone's wallet) and provides non-repudiation of receipt" (papers `keri-primer.md` > 3.1 Issuance model).

### Bespoke and disclosure-specific ACDCs {#05-bespoke-acdcs}

A Discloser may issue its own ACDC referencing another via an edge, naming the Disclosee as Issuee, to attach context-specific obligations and enable "rich presentation" (combining attributes from multiple edge-referenced ACDCs) "without requiring any new tooling" (ACDC spec, L1860). The SEDI corpus refines this. ~~"'Bespoke' describes an *issuance pattern*... not a credential *type* — so there is no useful generic 'bespoke' schema. What is reusable is a named verification pattern," and "The club's accepted shape and the holder's issued presentation are one schema viewed from two sides" (`sedi-present-age-portrait/index.md`).~~ Re-cited 2026-10-03: that wording is no longer on the page; the doctrine stands in Bakobo's decision record, where "Bespoke" "names an ISSUANCE PATTERN, not a credential TYPE" and "the club's accepted-shape and the holder's issued presentation conform to that ONE schema viewed from two sides" (bakobo/schema `this.i` > `@sdp3wk`, L1950-1960 @`cfcbdcc7a`). The page itself now says the presentation "is a named presentation pattern, not a Sam Smith schema." (bakobo/schema `sedi-present-age-portrait/index.md`, L3). One reversal belongs here: the presentation, once deliberately unregistered so it would not be logged, now requires `rd` — the holder's presentation registry, which Sam's Core names in `a.rd` as the "Issuee Presentation Registry SAID" (same page, L5). The argument for that belongs to [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md); this chapter records only that the schema reversed.

## 11. Real-world credential patterns and what schemas enforce {#05-applied-patterns}

### vLEI {#05-vlei}

vLEI is the production proof point (ISO 17442-3, finalized Oct 2024): GLEIF -> Qualified vLEI Issuers -> legal entities -> role credentials -> individuals, each hop a SAID-linked, schema-pinned edge. "A verifier receiving an employee's credential can traverse the chain back to GLEIF without consulting a trust registry. The entire graph is self-certifying" (papers `acdc-vc-diff.md` > Real-World Validation). [practice] Concretely, the Legal Entity vLEI carries edge `qvi` -> the QVI credential with `s` const-pinned to the QVI schema, and the ECR Authorization vLEI carries edge `le` -> the LE vLEI with `s` const-pinned to the LE schema SAID (public-schema `vLEI/acdc/legal-entity-vLEI-credential.json`, L99, and `ecr-authorization-vlei-credential.json`, L114, re-verified @`95a07e544`; the `vLEI/` tree is unchanged since `8db57eb75`). The chaining "eliminates the need for trust registries" whose rise "is proof that this conceptual gap needs plugging" (papers `x509-prob.md`).

#### Telco schemas stopped pinning far-node schemas {#05-telco-unpinned}

[practice] One schema family stopped pinning far-node schemas, and that is not the same as weakening the graph. Between public-schema `8db57eb75` and `95a07e544`, Provenant removed the SAID-valued `const` from the edge `s` fields of its telco credentials — commit `2c8e834e2`, "remove the const schema SAID constraints from the vvp-dossier schema" — so that the `tnalloc` edge's `s` is now only `"SAID of TN allocation schema"` with `"type": "string"` (public-schema `vvp-dossier/vvp-dossier.schema.json`, L180), and no edge in the current telco schemas carries a SAID-valued `const`. The intent is written down for one edge: tn-alloc's `issuer` edge is "Intentionally generic — does not constrain the schema of the identity credential." (public-schema `tn-alloc/index.md` > Edge structure, L51). Read together with [section 5](#05-edges)'s `[code]` paragraph, what moved is who restricts the edge schema, not whether it is checked: keripy still validates the far node against whatever `s` the issued edge carries, and what the schema no longer does is restrict which `s` an issuer may write, which leaves that to verifier policy. That reading is interpretive; neither repo states the reason. It runs opposite to the vLEI ladder and to bakobo's SEDI presentations, which still pin.

#### SEDI {#05-sedi}

[practice] SEDI (Self/State-Endorsed Digital Identity) applies KERI's root-of-trust to civil identity: "The state endorses an identity; it does not create one." — withdraw the endorsement and the identity persists, "because the holder, not the state, holds the key." (bakobo/schema `sedi-id/index.md` > Purpose, L15-17 @`cfcbdcc7a`). The family was rebuilt between this chapter's passes, so read what follows as current state with its history marked. At `cfcbdcc7a` the state-issued credentials are Sam Smith's own — IAR, Core, Residence and Age, pinned to his keripy test module at `80f77b73b` (bakobo/schema `README.md` > Status, L65) — and `sedi-id` is "Superseded for new issuance" while it "remains resolvable for existing credentials" (bakobo/schema `sedi-id/index.md`, L3). The presentation, guardian, ward and authorization schemas "are Bakobo profiles for the November SEDI Summit; they are not Sam's schemas or statements of Utah policy." (bakobo/schema `README.md` > Status, L65). Nothing in the active family contradicts the founding inversion: "The state issues Core to the citizen." (bakobo/schema `sedi-core/index.md`, L3).

~~Schema enforces minimalism: exactly four attributes (name, birth date, image, Utah residence).~~ Superseded 2026-10-03 for the active family. That was `sedi-id`, and it is still on that historical page. Sam's Core does not hold to four: its required blocks include given, middle and family name, name suffix, birth date, facial image proof, legal presence status, issued and expiration dates, and a bare boolean `primary` (bakobo/schema `sedi-core.schema.json`, `a.required`, L67-81) — and `primary` is not a blinded block, so it cannot be withheld while `a` is expanded (keripy `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`, L587 @`80f77b73b`). Residence left Core and is its own credential, every block of which has a compact arm. So the decomposition principle survives one level up: residence is split from identity at the credential level, still because "a single residence block would force over-disclosure on every verifier who only needs jurisdiction." (bakobo/schema `sedi-id/index.md`, L70-71, historical but still the clearest statement). The image is still a commitment rather than a locator — Core's image block is "Facial Image Proof Value as SAID of typed media block" (bakobo/schema `sedi-core.schema.json`, L293) — and the old reasoning for that stands on the `sedi-id` page: a download URL is "phone-home by another name" and an availability chokepoint. Whether Core's `legalPresenceStatus` is an endorsed attribute rests on relayed correspondence and contradicts the governance artifact's `noOverAssertion` clause; `raw/11` section 9 item 3 holds that tension, and this chapter does not resolve it.

#### The Utah delegation chain {#05-utah-delegation-chain}

The Utah "delegation chain" is a chain of credentials, not KERI delegation. Sam's fixture heads it "Create State's three level delegation chain AIDs" / "Root AID -> Org Unit (division/department/program) -> Issuing Agent" (keripy `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`, L3165-3166 @`80f77b73b`), but every one of those AIDs is made with plain `incept`, not `delcept`; a search of the file for `delcept`, `dip` and `delpre` finds nothing. The chain is ACDCs: the root issues an Organizational Unit credential, the unit issues an Issuing Agent credential whose `orgUnit` edge is `"o": "I2I"` (L3598-3605), and the agent issues each citizen's Core with a `utahAgent` edge, also `I2I`, to its Agent credential (L3997-4004). Leaves — Residence, Age — reach the chain only through their `coreIdentity` edge to Core. A reviewer who reads "delegation" here as KEL delegation, with its cooperative `dip`/`ixn` binding and superseding recovery, has read a different mechanism. This is fixture evidence of the spec author's intended design, and it is the same move GCD made below: authority evidenced by chained credentials, with KEL delegation optional. The fixture also defines a "SEDI AID Replace Schema" (L200) that names an obsolete AID and its replacement — AID replacement by credential, for a holder who has lost control of an identifier, which KERI rotation does not cover; the fixture does not say when it is used rather than rotation.

~~`sedi-guardian` enforces the anti-impersonation invariant: the guardian holds the credential and the ward is named only by a `subject` edge — "Collapsing the two (guardian-as-subject) is the classic impersonation/commingling failure the whole field warns against" — and it is registry-bound (`ri` mandatory) because guardianship "terminates dynamically... a verifier MUST check current status, not just the signature and dates."~~ Superseded 2026-10-03. Version 3.0.0 "names the guardian as its issuee (`a.i`) and the ward by AID in the separately disclosable `a.ward` block", and "There is no guardian-to-ward edge." (bakobo/schema `sedi-guardian/index.md`, L3); the reason given is that "This avoids a cyclic pair of edges and allows the ward identity to be withheld independently." (bakobo/schema `this.i` > `@6ge27cya`, L2254-2255). The quoted "classic impersonation/commingling failure" sentence is absent from the whole tree at `cfcbdcc7a`. The invariant itself survives in the schema — `a.i` is "Issuee = the GUARDIAN's AID (holder != subject)" (bakobo/schema `sedi-guardian.schema.json`, L81) — and so does registry binding, now in the v2 envelope: `rd` is "MANDATORY; guardianship terminates dynamically" (same, L43). The link back runs from the ward: Sam's Core carries an optional `guardians` edge group, but in his fixture it is schema-only — its operators are unconstrained strings, and no ward Core is issued at `80f77b73b` — so "a verifier must hold the group to `AND` or `OR` and each member to the guardianship schema and `NI2I`" (bakobo/schema `sedi-core/index.md`, L3).

#### GCD {#05-gcd}

[practice] GCD (Generalized Cooperative Delegation) is the applied delegation model, at version 3.1.0 on bakobo/schema `cfcbdcc7a`. ~~The delegation relationship itself is "not embodied in a credential" but in the cooperative two-way AID binding (delegate inception + delegator interaction).~~ Superseded 2026-10-03: that wording is still on public-schema's GCD page, but Bakobo removed it in GCD 2.0.1. KERI cooperative delegation is now "the exemplar these credentials were named for" (bakobo/schema `gcd/index.md` > Purpose, L7), "But it is not a precondition." (L9, where the source sets it in bold): "A GCD credential is a standard targeted ACDC; its authorization and constraint mechanics do not depend on the issuee being KEL-anchored to the issuer." (L9). The decision record states the precision that keeps this from weakening GCD — what is decoupled is delegated authority, which GCD documents, from the cooperative-delegation KEL binding, "a stronger, optional fact"; dip+ixn "is now the EXEMPLAR, not the gate" (bakobo/schema `this.i` > `@n8wq3d`, L258-263). What survives intact is GCD's job: "Whichever binding is used, it only proves the *state* of the delegation relationship and defines how it is controlled." (bakobo/schema `gcd/index.md`, L11), and GCD says what actions are expected and what constrains them.

Two further changes matter to a reviewer. `rd` is required from GCD 3.0, overriding the spec's default on purpose: "the ACDC spec makes `rd` optional for correlation minimization, but a GCD is authority evidence, so secure discovery of its revocation registry wins here." (bakobo/schema `gcd/index.md` > Schema, L37-40). And the `constraints` container no longer enforces fail-closed in the schema. ~~Its `constraints` container is fail-closed (`additionalProperties: false`; an unrecognized key MUST deny), while its descriptive `facet` container is open/forward-compatible — "the open-vs-closed choice tracks descriptive-vs-gating."~~ Superseded 2026-10-03: as of 3.1.0 the container is `"additionalProperties": true` (bakobo/schema `gcd.schema.json`, L130), so that custom constraints named by a governance framework can be expressed at all. The deny-unknown rule is unchanged, but it moved from the schema to the verifier: "This container remains FAIL-CLOSED, but the obligation runs to the verifier, not to schema validation" (L128), and "Validating against this schema is not an authorization decision" (bakobo/schema `gcd/index.md` > Custom constraints, L102). The descriptive-versus-gating distinction now lives in the verifier obligation and the `noConstraintOutsideConstraints` clause ([section 6](#05-rules)), not in `additionalProperties`. The accepted cost is stated: "a verifier that gates on schema validation ALONE loses a free backstop" (bakobo/schema `this.i` > `@vy7qoj`, L360-361). This is the general shape the applied corpus keeps arriving at — the schema checks shape, the verifier decides — and it is the same move as the telco edge schemas above. The `acts` grid crosses five effects (observe/create/modify/preserve/destroy) with six state-kinds (info/record/commitment/authority/resource/relationship): "the two axes of one coordinate, neither meaningful alone." A consequence reviewers must note: "these credentials do not support graduated disclosure. All constraints must be disclosed every time a verifier is evaluating delegated authority" — because within a field values are ORed and across fields ANDed, so partial disclosure would silently loosen the gate (bakobo/schema `gcd/index.md`, L86). This is the general rule: authority/legal credentials are disclosed whole; identity/attribute credentials support graduated disclosure. Qualified 2026-10-03: `sedi-guardian` 3.0.0, an authority credential, now carries its ward as "Ward AID in an individually disclosable block" (bakobo/schema `sedi-guardian.schema.json`, L101), so the guardian can withhold whose guardian it is — the rule bends where the subject's identity is itself the sensitive datum.

#### The Dossier {#05-dossier}

The Dossier is itself a valid ACDC used as a curated bundle of evidence: "The primary payload of a dossier is not a set of direct claims, but rather a graph of references to external evidence." ~~What the issuer's signature attests is composition/integrity, "NOT veracity."~~ Superseded 2026-09-15 at Dossier `main` @`b9227753c`: the veracity half stands, the signature half does not, because there is no issuer signature on a dossier at all. What attests composition is the issuer's anchor: "The issuer of a dossier is the entity that curates the collection of evidence and attests to its composition by anchoring the container" (Dossier spec > The Role of the Issuer, L83), while the veracity boundary is unchanged — "The issuer does not necessarily attest to the veracity of the claims within the evidence, but rather to the integrity and composition of the collection itself" (same). See [section 9](#05-registries) for the general doctrine this is an instance of, and for the two refinements that keep it from being overstated. This encodes the authenticity-vs-veracity distinction — authenticity is mechanizable, veracity "inherently require[s] subjective assessments of reputation" (papers `authenticity-vs-veracity.md`). The Dossier adds joint-issuance threshold operators (`MxN`, `RMxN`, `MxQ`, `RMxQ`) in an edge-group's `o`, weighted so Endorsed slots sum to >= unity — "the same fractionally weighted threshold KERI uses for key-event signing thresholds (`kt`)." Its key contrast with group multisig: joint issuance "relies on logic within the ACDC layer," letting members "anchor their endorsements of a dossier at different times and via different channels, each in their own KEL, without immediate impact on a shared one" — a wording the same 2026-08-25 sweep sharpened rather than weakened, since members are not adding signatures to a shared object at all but each writing to a log they alone control. Validity is thereby decoupled from synchronous key-event coordination. The sweep had a wire-format consequence a reviewer must not file as editorial: rewriting the two normative schemas' prose descriptions in anchoring rather than signing terms changed their SAIDs — the base dossier schema from `ECpZgR2Y…` to `EKuLzS_oN_mIao5og1NOujtF2QMXloiMCZP7xuAR5tY7`, and the endorsement schema from `EAfn0gRM…` to `ECRjgun8t3cay_YBiVxEY-qXKCz37oUrvE5GvmySwxCh`. Because a dossier schema is identified as one by an `allOf` `$ref` naming the base schema's SAID, and because a joint-issuance slot names the endorsement schema by SAID in its `s` field, any schema or slot still naming an old SAID no longer resolves. This chapter never quoted either value, so nothing here was stale; anything built against the pre-August schemas is. Foreign material (W3C VC, ISO mDL, PDFs, X.509) is bridged via a Foreign Artifact wrapper ACDC, never referenced directly — "Direct reference to non-ACDC material without a wrapper is NOT RECOMMENDED." The FAA corpus makes the trust stance explicit: a bridge issuer's `art_posture` and `rev_latency` fields let "verifiers to treat the FAA as a proxy for the foreign credential, assuming they trust the FAA issuer" — trust in a bridge is "explicit and issuer-scoped, not systemic."

#### A deployed dossier schema's evidence rule {#05-deployed-dossier-schema}

[practice] A deployed dossier schema states the evidence rule outright (added 2026-10-03). Provenant's revised dossier base at public-schema `95a07e544` (`dossier-base/dossier-base.schema.json`, `$id` `EHxI61CGs7FRuStz8P6QWJyMK4u2bGH1LQqIXsA4bT7q`) puts the division of labour between sections in its top-level description: "A dossier SHOULD NOT include an issuee; all evidence MUST be carried in e, never in a." (public-schema `dossier-base/dossier-base.schema.json`, L5), with `a` as metadata that "MUST NOT carry primary evidence." (L54). Type membership is structural, as in the specification: "A schema S IS-A dossier iff S's top-level allOf array contains a $ref to this schema's SAID, or recursively to another schema that IS-A dossier." (L5). It also states a reissuance doctrine for evolving evidence — "When phase transitions, a new dossier version SHOULD be issued." (L127) — so a dossier is a point-in-time artifact, not a live document. Two cautions. Its base-schema SAID is not the Dossier specification's (`EKuLzS_…`, above), and bakobo/schema still publishes an older base (`EFf_1u…`), so three dossier bases are now in circulation; this chapter's comparison of the values is its own, and whether either schema repo intends to track the specification exactly was not checked (`raw/11` section 9 item 9). And Provenant's one derived dossier, `vvp-dossier` 2.0.0, inherits that base while still requiring the v1 `ri` where the base offers `rd`.

#### The negative corpus {#05-negative-corpus}

[practice] The negative corpus (what real schemas reject in CI) is the clearest statement of schema teeth, re-checked against directory listings at bakobo/schema `cfcbdcc7a` (fixture bodies not opened): GCD rejects a missing `rd`, `terminatingEvents` without a `validUntil` backstop, and two-sided braces in `acts`; the historical `sedi-id` rejects a block missing its blinding nonce, a missing issuee, or an image missing its digest; `sedi-present-age-portrait` rejects a non-I2I edge operator and a presentation missing `rd`. Two entries reversed, and both reversals are doctrine. ~~GCD rejects an unknown key inside `constraints` (fail-closed)~~ — that fixture was deleted at 3.1.0, because "an unknown key inside `constraints` is now *valid*" (bakobo/schema `gcd/index.md`, L143-144), and fail-closed moved to the verifier as above. ~~`sedi-present-age-portrait` rejects a registry-bound (`rd`) presentation~~ — inverted to `missing-rd`, with the presentation-registry reversal ([section 10](#05-ipex)). These rejections are where schema stops being documentation and becomes enforcement; the two reversals are where a schema author decided enforcement belonged somewhere else.

## 12. What ACDC corrects, and what remains uncertain {#05-corrections-and-uncertainty}

### Where ACDC corrects outsider priors {#05-outsider-priors}

ACDC explicitly corrects these outsider priors (well-established, spec-grounded): direct-signing of credentials (rejected — forces mass revocation on rotation, L1675); phone-home revocation via OCSP/CRL (rejected via Observer/Registrar split, L1693); dynamic/URL-dereferenced schemas (rejected — schema-revocation and semantic-malleability attacks, L194); treating compact form as private (a public compact ACDC is still rainbow-attackable, L501); bundled multi-claim credentials (refactorable into a graph of separately-disclosable chained ACDCs, "obviating the need for Selective Disclosure," L2739); centralized namespace registries (unnecessary — content-address plus content-addressable schema is the namespace, L2936); over-investing in cryptographic unlinkability ("diminishing returns" without contractually-protected disclosure, L2785); and privacy-as-end-goal (reframed to exploitation-protection, L1659).

#### Where the ground truth is softer than the prose {#05-softer-ground-truth}

Where the ground truth is softer than the prose, restated at keripy `b8f60166b` (2026-09-14), which moved several of these. ~~"The DI2I operator is unimplemented (`NotImplementedError`); m-ary edge-group operators and DAG acyclicity are read but not enforced; all re-confirmed as of `60ab9e08`."~~ Superseded 2026-09-15; [section 5.1](#05-verifying-ground-truth) holds the detail and the reasons. At the new pin: `DI2I` and `NOT` are still unimplemented but now fail closed by design with a `ValidationError` rather than crashing, which is a better failure and not an implementation; four of the six m-ary edge-group operators still have no code path, while `AND` and `OR` do, in a module nothing in `src/keri` calls; DAG acyclicity is confirmed still unchecked, `_walkGraph`'s `seen` set being a termination guard rather than a validity check; a missing edge operator is still silently inferred; two modules disagree about what to do with an operator they do not recognize; and disclosure and rule clauses remain commitments for application-layer or human enforcement rather than predicates the reference verifier evaluates. Moving the other way, the edge `s` constraint is now enforced and `E1E` is implemented ahead of the standardizing branch.

#### Re-checked 2026-10-03 {#05-rechecked-2026-10-03}

Re-checked 2026-10-03 at `80f77b73b`. Every item in the paragraph above still holds at the new pin, with two widenings and one addition ([section 5.1](#05-verifying-ground-truth), [section 4.1](#05-age-credential)). The module disagreement grew from one axis to three — unrecognized tokens, conflicting delegative operators in a list, and an absent operator — and the silent default now applies in one module while the other checks nothing. The operator family has two more proposed members, `I1I` and `DI1I` ([proposal], #1515, 2026-10-01), with no code. And the age credential, the aggregate section's showcase, cannot be presented selectively through keripy's IPEX grant, because a registry-backed aggregate must disclose every element; keripy also reads an aggregate's issuee from a position the schema leaves free. No keripy test presents an Age credential, so both are findings from reading code paths, not from running them.

#### Not re-examined: the verifyAnchor hypothesis {#05-verifyanchor-not-reexamined}

One item on the old list was not re-examined this pass and must not be read as re-confirmed. The recon hypothesis that the credential `Verifier` may not re-run `verifyAnchor` on presentation, potentially undermining the anchor-position (retrograde) defense (landmine L15, HIGH severity, medium confidence, [section 9](#05-registries) above), still stands at the older `60ab9e08d` pin; the 2026-09-15 keripy pass read `vdr/verifying.py` in full but recorded no finding on it, and this chapter under-claims rather than assuming it survived unchanged. Treat it as an open question at an older commit, not as a fact at the new one.

None of these are protocol defects — they are implementation-maturity gaps on the keripy 2.1-dev line (`__version__ = '2.1.0-dev1'` at `b8f60166b`, unchanged at `80f77b73b`; the corpus's older material was tagged against 2.0.0-dev6, and nothing here is a release). The honest posture is Hardman's own: ACDC's constraints today "are constraints of *youth*, not of *architecture*" (papers `wtbo.md` > 6. The Transition Problem: A Comparison of Trajectories). A reviewer who conflates the two — who reads an unimplemented operator as a design flaw, or an unenforced rule as a broken guarantee — is making the category error the whole corpus is built to prevent. The month's movement is evidence for that posture rather than against it: the gaps that closed closed because someone implemented them, not because the design changed. One item added on 2026-10-03 may be an exception, and it should be carried as one: the age-credential collision of [section 4.1](#05-age-credential) is two deliberate rules meeting — hide nothing that could conceal a presentation-registry declaration, and disclose one threshold without the others — and resolving it may take a design decision about where such a declaration may live, not just more code. Which kind of gap it is has not been settled by anyone read here.

# 06 — Governance, Ecosystems and Interop {#06-governance}

## Thesis {#06-thesis}

KERI draws a hard line between two kinds of trust decision, and everything in this chapter follows from where that line is drawn. On one side is cryptographic verification — signatures, SAIDs, hash-chain consistency, anchor-position validity — which is universal, mechanical, observer-independent, and answerable by anyone, anywhere, at any time, with no authority in the loop. On the other side is ecosystem-defined behavior — what a credential means, which edge operator makes a chain valid, whether an issuer is fit to issue, what a recipient may do with disclosed data — which is inescapably semantic, contextual, and human- or policy-governed. An Ecosystem Governance Framework (EGF) lives entirely on the second side; it never adjudicates the first. This is the structural fact that lets KERI claim decentralization honestly: because Layer-1 verification depends on no governance body, no EGF, no registry, and no browser-vendor root program, the only thing an ecosystem's governance can do is publish rules that opt-in participants cryptographically bind themselves to — it cannot become a new root of trust or a new choke point.
