The corollaries occupy the rest of the chapter: who (if anyone) arbitrates ecosystem behavior; how SEDI applies the "endorse-not-issue" inversion to civil identity; why correlation-resistance and a duty of data loyalty are layered properties that KERI-core does not and cannot promise (they live in the ACDC/disclosure/governance strata); how semantics cross trust domains without a global namespace authority; what versioning and migration actually cost; how four independent implementations stay byte-compatible; and how KERI scores against SD-JWT/OIDC4VC on a decentralization scorecard — with the honest caveats about where KERI's advantage is architecture and where it is merely youth.

Adversarial reviewers should carry one framing throughout: a critique that faults KERI for "not preventing correlation" or "still needing governance" is usually attacking the wrong layer. KERI-core promises key-state continuity and duplicity-evidence, not unlinkability and not semantic agreement. The interesting questions are whether the layering is clean, whether the governance seam is defensible, and whether the migration story survives contact with four codebases.

## Status {#06-status}

Most of this chapter argues from specification text and from the applied corpus, and where it does the source is named inline. [Section 6](#06-versioning-migration) and [section 7](#06-implementation-compat) are where the marker ordering does the most work, because that is where the chapter's crypto-agility and interop arguments live and where the difference between a specification branch, a standardizing branch and a shipped implementation decides what may be claimed.

The distinction between the standardizing line [spec] and the `v1.1` forward branch [spec-next] carries almost the whole post-quantum argument of [section 6](#06-versioning-migration). Nothing marked [spec-next] may be promoted on the expectation that it will merge forward, because the branches are divergent; the CESR spec and KERI spec entries under [Sources](#06-sources) give the detail.

An unmerged branch on a personal fork is not [code], however real its code, because [code] means an implementation anyone runs behaves this way; [section 7](#06-pq-parity-test) turns on that line and marks such material explicitly.

## 1. What an EGF is, and the two-layer verification split {#06-egf-two-layer}

The load-bearing distinction is stated most cleanly in the Dossier specification's verification doctrine: verification is a two-layer process. Layer 1 is cryptographic validation — "confirming anchors, SAIDs, and KEL consistency" — and "The first layer, cryptographic validation, is universal and defined by this specification." Layer 2 is semantic validation, which "is necessarily application-specific and requires context-dependent business logic" (Dossier spec > Dossier Data Model (Normative) > Base JSON-Schema Definition, L127 @b9227753c). The spec's own illustration is exact: a generic verifier "can verify that an edge labeled 'lunarPropertyDeed' is cryptographically linked, but it cannot know what that means or how to process it." And "This separation allows the dossier format to be a universal building block for evidence aggregation". Corrected 2026-10-15: this paragraph previously quoted Layer 1 as ~~"confirming signatures, SAIDs, and KEL consistency"~~, wording the Dossier specification replaced at `b97c2f2` (2026-08-25, "Distinguish anchoring from signing throughout the spec"), an ancestor of the chapter's own pin; and two other phrases it presented as quotations, "universal, defined by this spec" and "is what makes the dossier a universal building block for evidence aggregation", are not verbatim at the pin. The first change is doctrinal rather than cosmetic: a dossier carries no issuer signature, so what Layer 1 confirms is anchoring (raw/04 section 1A). An EGF is the artifact that supplies Layer-2 rules for a given ecosystem: what schemas are blessed, what an issuer must do to be trusted, what validity means for a particular chain of authority, what obligations attach to disclosed data.

That the Layer-2 rules are genuinely outside the cryptographic core is visible throughout the ACDC spec, which repeatedly defers behavior to the EGF rather than defining it. The m-ary edge operators (`AND`, `OR`, `NAND`, `NOR`, `AVG`, `WAVG`) define provenance-chain validity, but "validity logic is EGF-dependent" (ACDC spec > Edge Section, L1112-1116). Schema availability constraints "may [be] impose[d]" by the EGF (ACDC spec > Schema Availability, L242). Extensibility is "permission-less... no shared governance... completely decentralized and zero-trust," and a registry of ACDC types collapses to "merely Schema discovery or schema blessing for a given context or ecosystem" (ACDC spec > Extensibility, L2934-2936). The recurring pattern is that the cryptographic machinery is fixed and universal while meaning and fitness are pushed out to a per-ecosystem governance layer that the core neither knows nor needs.

### The authenticity/veracity axis {#06-authenticity-veracity}

The authenticity/veracity axis is the theoretical spine of this split. Hardman's framing makes it precise: authenticity is "the truthfulness of an imputed origin"; veracity is "the truthfulness of claimed facts in content"; the two "must be analyzed primarily as orthogonal" (authenticity-vs-veracity.md > Formal definitions). The key doctrine is mechanizability: "Judgments about authenticity can — if managed very carefully — be reduced to an objective mathematical computation, whereas judgments about veracity inherently require subjective assessments of reputation" (authenticity-vs-veracity.md > Independence). Layer 1 verifies authenticity; Layer 2 (governance, reputation, human judgment) adjudicates veracity and fitness. The applied corpus states the same boundary at the level of a single credential: an ACDC validation "can prove that an issuer remains committed to a citation — but only the interaction context... plus governance, plus possible validation external to the world of ACDCs" establishes what proposition is actually true (bakobo/schema citation/index.md > Semantic precision, L39 @cfcbdcc7a). This is a clean statement of what cryptographic verification does and does not prove, and it is why an EGF is never optional in a real deployment even though it is invisible to the crypto.

#### A governance hook bound by SAID {#06-governance-hook}

The governance hook is cryptographically bound, not merely referenced. In the applied schemas the EGF is reachable by SAID: GCD (Generalized Cooperative Delegation) credentials carry a `gfw` field described as "A SAID that identifies a governance framework that adds richer semantics to the role field and any custom constraints present in this credential," and when it is defined "a verifier MUST NOT impute a delegator's approval of delegated authority to a delegate without understanding and enforcing the rules" (bakobo/schema gcd/gcd.schema.json, a.gfw.description, L79 @cfcbdcc7a; GCD 3.1.0). Corrected 2026-10-03: this sentence previously quoted the field as "is a SAID naming a supplemental rules block," which is not in the schema at either fork's pin; the meaning survives in the schema's next sentence, that the SAID "identifies a JSON rules block that supplements the generic rules in the rules block." Crucially, "The act of issuing or receiving a GCD credential constitutes binding acceptance of the rules" (bakobo/schema gcd/index.md > Governance Framework, L116 @cfcbdcc7a; public-schema gcd/index.md > Governance Framework, L54 @95a07e544). ~~a formulation that recurs verbatim across org-vet, citation, and SEDI~~ Superseded 2026-10-03: the sentence is no longer uniform across the corpus. In bakobo it survives verbatim in `gcd/index.md` and in the archived `org-vet-1.0.0/` and `citation-1.0.0/` pages; current `org-vet` 2.0.0 replaces it with four named Ricardian clauses ([section 2](#06-arbitration)), and SEDI says it in its own words — "Issuing or accepting a SEDI credential is binding acceptance of its referenced revision" (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md > Governance, L159). In public-schema `org-vet/` is deleted, and the newer telco pages adopt the idea in fresh wording: "The act of issuing or accepting this credential constitutes binding acceptance of those rules" (public-schema brand-owner/index.md > Rules and governance, L79). The doctrine is unchanged; what changed is that it is now restated per credential family rather than copied, which is the more honest shape for it. The Ricardian-contract rule section (`r`) is the general mechanism: rules are "both human and machine-readable and referenceable by a cryptographic digest," supporting the bow-tie model of Ricardian Contracts (ACDC spec > Rule Section, L1239). So an EGF's terms are not a URL a verifier optionally consults; they are a SAID-committed contract whose acceptance is entailed by participation. This is how governance binds without becoming a phone-home dependency or an external authority.

## 2. Who arbitrates ecosystem-defined behavior {#06-arbitration}

The sharpest way to see KERI's governance position is by contrast with the arbiter it rejects. In the X.509/CT world, "the ultimate arbiter of CA trustworthiness is a handful of browser vendors" (wtbo.md > 1. The Identity Problem: Administrative Trust and Its Limits); the root programs of Google, Mozilla, and Apple have "immediate, global effect... no formal appeals process. No government, no standards body, and no external adjudicator sits above them" (wtbo.md > Notes, note [b]). The load-bearing distinction is between enforcement and observation: "A browser vendor that distrusts a CA is making an enforcement decision — exercising judgment with immediate global consequences... A KERI watcher that detects duplicity is making an observation — surfacing cryptographic evidence that the relying party confirms independently" (wtbo.md > 4. KERI's Architecture: A Different Root of Trust). A watcher "cannot unilaterally 'distrust' an identifier the way a browser root program can distrust a CA. The worst a dishonest watcher can do is stay silent about duplicity it has seen" (wtbo.md > 4. KERI's Architecture: A Different Root of Trust). The architectural claim is that KERI has no Layer-1 arbiter at all — verification "bottoms out in mathematics," not in administrators (wtbo.md > 3. Common Ground: What CT and KERI Share).

So who arbitrates Layer-2? The answer is deliberately plural and opt-in. The Dossier model "operates on a decentralized root of trust. A verifier does not rely on a single authority but makes explicit trust decisions about a plurality of evidence issuers" (Dossier spec > Security Considerations > Verifier Trust and Root of Trust Management). In a compositional dossier "trust is derived from the leaf nodes (the authorities), not merely from the dossier issuer" — the LEI issuer for legal identity, the carrier/regulator for number authority, the trademark steward for brand (Dossier spec > Use Cases and Architectural Patterns > Verifiable Voice Protocol (VVP): The Compositional Dossier). There is no single body that certifies fitness across the ecosystem; each verifier composes trust from the specific authorities relevant to the specific claim, and the EGF for that vertical publishes the rules by which those authorities are judged. The flagship example is GLEIF's Ecosystem Governance Framework for the vLEI, developed with ToIP (keri.one resource directory; raw/13 section 7), where the arbitration structure is itself a KERI credential chain — GLEIF blesses Qualified vLEI Issuers, who vet legal entities, who authorize roles — and "A verifier receiving an employee's credential can traverse the chain back to GLEIF without consulting a trust registry. The entire graph is self-certifying" (acdc-vc-diff.md > Real-World Validation). The ladder's schema pins were re-verified at public-schema `95a07e544`, where the `vLEI/` tree is unchanged since the fork point. keri.one's resources page, re-read 2026-10-03, still lists the vLEI EGF, and its adoption block now also carries "Utah SEDI Identity Proofing" and verifiable-voice items such as "OVC Goes Live with Microsoft" — link titles, not doctrine, but corroboration that the site's own adoption story has widened from vLEI to SEDI and verifiable voice (raw/13 section 11).

This is the direct corrective to the outsider prior that "decentralized identity needs a trust registry." KERI's position is that trust registries "are a band aid; they just move the centralization back to a different level of the architecture... immature and fragmented... primarily address governance for issuers, not issuees," and that ACDC chaining "eliminates the need for trust registries" (x509-prob.md). The rise of trust registries in the W3C-VC world is read as "proof that this conceptual gap needs plugging" — the gap being that a VC captures only the immediate issuer→holder edge and lets the broader chain of authority "become implicit" (acdc-vc-diff.md > What Makes a Credential Format Lossy? > Loss 1: The Trust Chain). The EGF plus edge-chaining fills that gap without a registry, because the fitness rules travel as SAID-committed governance and the authority chain travels as verifiable edges.

One nuance an adversarial reviewer must hold: the assurance level a verifier demands is its own threshold, not an ecosystem-imposed hierarchy. The org-vet schema models Level of Assurance as "a positive number, where larger numbers map to higher levels of assurance," so that "verifiers... decide what level of assurance will satisfy them, and accept any credential having an LoA >= their threshhold" (bakobo/schema org-vet/index.md > Levels of assurance, L14 @cfcbdcc7a; `org-vet` 2.0.0; the misspelling is the source's, restored 2026-10-03). LoA-3 ("gold") is defined in KERI-native primitives — a ceremony proving "no MITM between any two members of the signing committee," at least one external observer, and "enough witnesses to reliably detect and recover from duplicity" — mapping to the GLEIF Legal-Entity vLEI (bakobo/schema org-vet/index.md > Levels of assurance, L20). This is a reframing of CA "high assurance" in duplicity-detection terms rather than administrative vetting, and it keeps arbitration on the verifier's side of the transaction rather than a central authority's.

Two additions from the 2026-10-03 re-anchor sharpen that reading, and one complicates the citation. `org-vet` 2.0.0 adds Ricardian clauses that say outright what the LoA is not: `loaIsTheIssuersProcedure` holds that the LoA "states which procedures the issuer carried out — not a guarantee about the organization," and `assuranceIsPointInTime` "requires a verifier to check the registry rather than treat an unexpired credential as current" (bakobo/schema org-vet/index.md > Governance framework, L30 @cfcbdcc7a). Both push judgment further onto the verifier, which is the direction this section argues. The complication is that "org-vet" no longer names one credential. public-schema deleted `org-vet/` at `95a07e544` and renamed its sibling `ovc-org-vet` to `org-identity`, which keeps the LoA table nearly word for word but reframes the credential as one that "connects different identifiers for the same organization" and governs it with citation-style rules rather than the Ricardian clauses (public-schema org-identity/index.md > Purpose, L5; public-schema org-identity/index.md > Rules and governance, L76-80). Every LoA citation in this chapter is to bakobo's `org-vet`; a reader following it into public-schema will find a different credential.

### Recipient-side arbitration of OOBI bootstrap {#06-oobi-mfa-arbitration}

The KERI specification added a second instance of recipient-side arbitration this cycle, and its boundary is stated more carefully than most. The out-of-band-authentication section now carries a worked pattern: the same AID published at two or more `/.well-known/oobi/{aid}` locations "hosted on independently controlled namespaces" — the example given is a domain the controller administers and a third-party platform where the controller has an account — with each URL "delivered to the recipient through a channel whose compromise is independent of the others." [spec] (KERI spec > OOBI with MFA, L2838 @fbdd4a615) Acceptance is thresholded on agreement: the recipient resolves each URL, compares the returned target URLs, and treats the introduction as acceptable "only when a configured threshold of namespaces returns a consistent OOBI for the same AID," so that an adversary "must therefore compromise multiple independent namespaces to influence the bootstrap decision rather than only one." The threshold is the recipient's configuration, not the controller's declaration — the exact inverse of the witness threshold of accountable duplicity, which the controller declares in its own inception event. Arbitration over whether to bootstrap at all sits with the party bearing the risk.

The limit on that pattern is stated by the specification itself and must travel with any citation of it. "This pattern does not change the trust model of an OOBI"; the AID binding produced by resolution "is still cryptographically verified through KERI in the usual way," and "the multi-factor arrangement governs only whether the recipient is willing to bootstrap from the OOBIs at all." [spec] (KERI spec > OOBI with MFA, L2838) So agreement across independently controlled namespaces is evidence about willingness, never about authenticity. A reading that treats N-of-M well-known agreement as strengthening the AID binding is wrong on the spec's own terms, and is exactly the confusion this chapter's Layer-1/Layer-2 split exists to prevent: the crypto is unchanged, and what the arrangement governs is a policy decision the recipient was always free to make. The configuration side of this pattern, and the finding that the implementations checked this cycle do not implement it, are in [section 6](#06-bootstrap-buckets).

### EGFs define the exchange shapes {#06-egf-shapes}

The editor puts one more thing on the governance side of the line, the shape of a presentation exchange [proposal]. "In my experience totally free-form credential exchanges are largely impractical." Enterprises and regulators define acceptable credential graphs in advance through their EGFs, "So predefined shapes will be the norm." (keripy GitHub > #1542, comment of 2026-07-30, R-055, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1542#discussioncomment-17842586). He is candid that the specification does not yet say so: "The current spec is very unrestrictive. This is because hardening means having an opinion, and I didn't have a strong opinion." The same reasoning puts leak prevention in an EGF-driven workflow rather than in schemas. Asked whether exchange messages should carry schemas to stop an apply asking for too much or an offer leaking too much, he answered that "Schemas are not rich enough by design to handle all those", and that "using contructors that limit what gets put there for sensitive message that want to avoid inadvertent leakage is an easy fix" (keripy GitHub > #1532, comment of 2026-07-22, R-063, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/issues/1532#issuecomment-5052264212). The next day he generalized it: "There is no universal set of rules." (https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/issues/1532#issuecomment-5058749739). This is the two-layer split applied to IPEX itself. The protocol fixes how an exchange is authenticated and chained; what an exchange may ask for and disclose at each stage is a Layer-2 rule that an EGF writes and tooling enforces by construction. A reviewer who expects the protocol to guarantee a leak-free apply is asking Layer 1 for a Layer-2 property.

## 3. SEDI: state-endorsed, not state-issued {#06-sedi}

SEDI (State-Endorsed Digital Identity) is the cleanest application of KERI's root-of-trust doctrine to civil identity, and it is worth dwelling on because it makes the governance boundary concrete against the most centralizing prior of all — the state. Its founding premise "inverts the usual state-ID relationship: identity is 'innate to the individual's existence and independent of the state... fundamental and inalienable' (§63A-20-101(1)). The state endorses an identity; it does not create one" (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md > Purpose, L13-15 @cfcbdcc7a, quoting Utah Code). The mechanics enforce the inversion: the issuer field names the State, "but the subject is bound by the holder's own personal digital identifier (a KERI AID) — withdraw the endorsement and the identity persists, because the holder, not the state, holds the key" (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md). This is exactly the KERI worldview — key-holder is controller, root of trust is the identifier's own key-event history (keripy-knowledge 00-lens.md > The load-bearing claims, claim 1) — applied to a domain where the reflexive assumption is that the government owns the identity.

### The SEDI family as of 2026-10-03 {#06-sedi-family-now}

The paragraph above quotes `sedi-id`, which is still on the page at bakobo `cfcbdcc7a` but is "Superseded for new issuance" and "remains resolvable for existing credentials" (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md, L3). The state-issued credentials are now Sam Smith's own — IAR, Core, Residence and Age — pinned to his keripy test module at `80f77b73b`, while the presentation, guardian and authorization schemas "are Bakobo profiles for the November SEDI Summit; they are not Sam's schemas or statements of Utah policy" (bakobo/schema README.md > Status, L65). Bakobo's stated reason for the switch: "calling it Sam-compatible would mislead issuers" (bakobo/schema this.i, `@epnvr5oq`, L2217-2218). The inversion survives the switch — "The state issues Core to the citizen." (bakobo/schema sedi-core/index.md, L3), to the citizen's own AID — so the founding doctrine of this section is unchanged. What changed is detail this chapter had built on, and the next three paragraphs mark each point.

#### An authority chain of credentials, not delegation {#06-sedi-authority-chain}

The state's authority chain is a credential chain, not KERI delegation — and that is the governance seam working as [section 1](#06-egf-two-layer) describes. keripy's SEDI fixtures at `80f77b73b` head the state's hierarchy "Create State's three level delegation chain AIDs" and "Root AID -> Org Unit (division/department/program) -> Issuing Agent" (keripy tests/sedi/test_sedi.py, L3165-3166 @80f77b73b), but every one of those AIDs is created with a plain `incept`, and a search of the module for `delcept`, `dip` and `delpre` finds nothing (raw/11 section 4). The chain is ACDCs: the root issues an Organizational Unit credential, the unit issues an Issuing Agent credential whose `orgUnit` edge is `I2I`, and the agent issues each citizen's Core with a `utahAgent` edge, also `I2I` (keripy tests/sedi/test_sedi.py, L3519, L3598-3605, L3997-4004). This is a fixture — the spec author's intended shape, not library behaviour — but it is the same move GCD 2.0.1 made when it decoupled "delegated AUTHORITY" from the "KERI COOPERATIVE-DELEGATION KEL binding", which it now treats as "a stronger, optional fact" (bakobo/schema this.i, `@n8wq3d`, L258-260). The consequence for this chapter: a reviewer who reads "delegation chain" in SEDI as KEL delegation will look for `dip` events and find none, and should instead be walking edges. Authority here is evidenced by chained, revocable credentials whose fitness rules a governance layer supplies, exactly the Layer-2 pattern of [section 1](#06-egf-two-layer).

#### Minimization by schema, superseded {#06-sedi-minimization}

~~SEDI also demonstrates governance-by-schema rather than governance-by-policy-document. The statute permits endorsing "exactly four attributes — name, birth date, image, and Utah residence address," and the schema "carries those four and nothing more; everything richer... is a separate credential that chains to this one" (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md > Purpose).~~ Superseded in the active family, 2026-10-03. Those sentences are still on the historical `sedi-id` page (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md > Purpose, L20-22 @cfcbdcc7a), but the active Core does not hold to four attributes: its required blocks are given, middle, family and suffix names, birth date, facial image proof, legal presence status, issued and expiration dates, and a boolean `primary` (bakobo/schema sedi-core/sedi-core.schema.json, a.required, L67-81), while residence has left Core for its own credential. So "minimization enforced by a four-attribute schema" is no longer a description of what Utah will issue; it is a description of a design Bakobo proposed and has retired. The decomposition principle survives one level up, at the credential boundary: Residence is its own credential, and inside it every attribute block has a compact arm, so "a holder can reveal one block, such as county, while withholding the others" (bakobo/schema sedi-residence/index.md, L3 @cfcbdcc7a). The historical argument for decomposition is still the best statement of why, and it holds for any schema that keeps attributes in one credential: because a block discloses atomically, "a single residence block would force over-disclosure on every verifier who only needs jurisdiction, making the statute's minimization duty... un-satisfiable at the schema level" (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md > The attributes > Name and residence are decomposed — deliberately, L70-71). The privacy teeth are in the data structure. This is the schema layer doing what the governance layer specifies, and it is a template for how an EGF's rules become mechanically enforceable rather than merely aspirational.

#### Duty of data loyalty {#06-data-loyalty}

Duty of data loyalty enters through SEDI's governance framework, `sedi-id/rules.json`, ~~referenced by SAID from every SEDI credential's `r` block (SAID `EA5O9z0TB932sm8kJIVdAIpwLpEWRWC5--VNS5r69frn`)~~. Corrected 2026-10-03: that SAID is now the archived revision at `sedi-id-2.0.0/rules.json`, which "remains resolvable under SAID" for credentials that carry it (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md > Governance, L157-158). The current artifact is a single `l` string carrying the former named clauses as text (`d` `EG8X1nQFCrQ4Rg8BjfE0-BIuKSo1TVbwqymQ3Wuam6VW`), because "Sam's r object permits only d and l" (bakobo/schema this.i, `@2vqmhxai`, L2235), and it is referenced from new SEDI examples — not from every SEDI credential. Sam's own fixture credentials at keripy `80f77b73b` carry a rule section of `{"d": "", "l": ""}` saidified, so the state-issued credentials as their author wrote them carry no legal language at all (raw/11 section 4). The data-loyalty duty therefore binds only where an issuer chooses to reference Bakobo's artifact; it is a profile, not a property of SEDI-as-specified. The clauses, each grounded in Utah Code, codify a fiduciary posture toward disclosed data: `chainLinkConfidentiality` (a verifier MUST NOT "assimilate, aggregate, correlate, sell, or otherwise combine disclosed attributes... for any purpose beyond the disclosed purpose," and "this binds each downstream recipient reached through the edge section of a presentation"); `dataMinimization`; `noSurveillance` (no using a presentation "to enable monitoring, surveillance, profiling, tracking, or persistent correlation"); `respectRevocation`; `safeHarbor` (accepting the presentation elects the statutory safe harbor, and breach forfeits it and is evidence); and `noOverAssertion`, with `purposeLimitation`, `dutyOfLoyalty`, `acceptGuardianPresentation` and `consentAndNotice` also present (bakobo/schema sedi-id/rules.json, L3 @cfcbdcc7a). "Issuing or accepting a SEDI credential is binding acceptance of its referenced revision" (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md > Governance, L159; corrected 2026-10-03 from "binding acceptance of it", which predates the archiving of revisions). Data loyalty is thus a contractual and governance property — a duty a recipient owes because acceptance bound it to the rules — not a cryptographic guarantee. This is the essential point for the next section: the correlation-resistance a SEDI holder enjoys is assembled from a disclosure mechanism (selective disclosure of `sedi-age`), a governance duty (chain-link confidentiality, no-surveillance), and a deployment choice ~~(un-registered one-time presentations)~~, none of which is provided by KERI-core. Two of those three legs moved on 2026-10-03, and [section 4](#06-layered-privacy) carries the detail. The deployment choice reversed: Bakobo's presentation schemas now require `rd`, the holder's own presentation registry, a decision that "REVERSES the "rd disallowed, unregistered, not logged" clause" and answers the correlation worry by keeping the registry "the holder's own, so "logged" means logged in the holder's KEL and nowhere a third party watches" (bakobo/schema this.i, `@lm37js6k`, L1987, L1993-1994). And the disclosure leg does not hold in the reference implementation: keripy at `80f77b73b` will not grant a registry-backed Age credential with any element withheld, so selective disclosure of a single age threshold is not available through keripy IPEX today [code] ([section 4](#06-layers-not-composing)).

#### An open governance tension {#06-sedi-governance-tension}

One governance tension is open, and it is a governance artifact disagreeing with a credential. The `noOverAssertion` clause says "the state endorses only name, birth date, image, and Utah residence address (63A-20-301(2)(f))" (bakobo/schema sedi-id/rules.json, L3), while the active Core carries `legalPresenceStatus` as an endorsed attribute on the strength of "an email to Daniel Hardman on 2026-09-23" from Sam Smith (bakobo/schema sedi-core/index.md, L5). That email is relayed correspondence with the weight of a first-hand report, usable for status and intent and not as a written source. So the rules file a SEDI verifier binds itself to and the schema the state issues under disagree about what the state endorses, and nothing citable settles which is right. It is a small instance of a general hazard this chapter's split predicts: when Layer-2 rules and Layer-2 schemas are maintained as separate artifacts, nothing mechanical keeps them consistent.

#### The author's proposed architecture and the custody of children {#06-sedi-architecture}

Two further positions from the specification's author bear on SEDI's governance, and both are proposals for a state program, not Utah policy [proposal]. For issuance: "the proposed architecture for SEDI is the the IAL3 identity assurance process issues a SEDI management ACDC", and "The SEDI management ACDC is only used in one context and that is to request bulk issued SEDI credentials", with the wallet following "a simple rule of don't reuse a bulk issued aid unless its with the same disclosee" (keripy GitHub > #1532, comment of 2026-07-23, R-047, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/issues/1532#issuecomment-5061387439). That is the decorrelation argument of [section 4](#06-decorrelation) turned into an issuance design: the identity-proofed credential stays home, and each disclosee gets its own bulk-issued set. For children, custody comes first: "So if the State issued a SEDI to the Baby they are issuing it to an AID controlled by the parents not the Baby." (keripy GitHub > #1550, discussion body of 2026-07-28, R-072, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1550), in a body that calls its diagrams "notional arrangements for discussion" not reflecting any Utah policy. On a parent's control over a minor's social-media access, he lists five key-management arrangements between parent and child and observes that the one requiring no key-management trick, a platform that accepts the authorization only from the parent's AID, works under all of them and is "the minimally sufficient means for the parent to have control over the childs access to social media" (keripy GitHub > #1573, comment of 2026-08-07, R-071, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1573#discussioncomment-17935861). The governance consequence he draws is the one this chapter should carry: "policy may reach down to the key management layer of the Issuee (citizen) not merely the Issuer (State)" (https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1573#discussioncomment-17935891). He calls that unprecedented and leaves the emancipation ceremony at adulthood open.

## 4. Correlation-resistance and data loyalty as layered properties {#06-layered-privacy}

This is the section where KERI most sharply corrects a common misreading, so it must be stated flatly: KERI-core does not promise unlinkability, and cannot. The core is a decentralized key-state continuity and duplicity-evidence mechanism. Unlinkability, correlation-minimization, and the duty of data loyalty are properties of higher layers — the ACDC disclosure machinery, the governance/contractual layer, and deployment discipline — composed on top of a substrate that is itself indifferent to them. An adversarial reviewer who expects the KERI whitepaper's key-management guarantees to include privately-verifiable, correlation-free presentation has confused the layers.

The ACDC spec is explicit that even at its own layer the primary goal is not privacy: "the primary design goal is not data privacy protection per se but the more general goal of protection from the unpermissioned exploitation of data. Privacy mechanisms are means, not ends" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Mechanisms, L1659). And it is equally explicit about the ceiling of cryptographic unlinkability. Cryptographically-provable correlation resistance is termed unlinkability, but "this is a weak form... as it does not prevent statistical correlation from contextual information." "Contextual linkability may defeat cryptographic unlinkability," and "there is no cryptographic mechanism that precludes statistical correlation among a set of colluding Verifiers" (ACDC spec > Bulk-issued, L2785). The blunt conclusion is that advanced cryptographic unlinkability can be "an exercise in diminishing returns" without contractually-protected disclosure. This is a spec that refuses to oversell its own privacy layer.

The layering is best seen by enumerating what each stratum contributes.

### The disclosure layer (ACDC) {#06-disclosure-layer}

This layer contributes the graduated-disclosure ladder — compact, metadata, partial, nested-partial, selective, full, and bulk-issued-instance disclosure — plus the private/metadata ACDC variants whose blinding UUID (`u`) forecloses rainbow reconstruction of contents from a SAID (ACDC spec > UUID Fields, L89-91). This layer provides technical correlation minimization: selective disclosure of a single blinded aggregate element "with no issuee" (bakobo/schema docs/choosing-attribute-vs-aggregate.md > Caveats worth remembering), bulk-issued private ACDCs generating a fresh SAID per usage context (ACDC spec > Bulk-issued, L2767), and herd privacy via sparse Merkle trees so that "a given seal in the KEL... no longer provides a point of correlation to any other transaction event" (ACDC spec > Bulk-issued, L2914-2924). This yields "3rd party unlinkability" (ACDC spec > Bulk-issued, L2854).

#### The governance/contractual layer (EGF, rules) {#06-contractual-layer}

This layer contributes Contractually Protected Disclosure — chain-link confidentiality and contingent disclosure — where "the disclosed data has 'strings attached'" and terms-of-use MUST propagate to each downstream Disclosee, who "in turn, is the Discloser to the next" (ACDC spec > Contractually Protected Disclosure, L1783-1792). This is the source of "2nd party unlinkability via contractual disincentives to link" (ACDC spec > Bulk-issued, L2854), and it is precisely the SEDI data-loyalty duty of [section 3](#06-data-loyalty). It is a legal/governance control, not a cryptographic one; the spec is honest that where "Chain-link Confidentiality does not sufficiently deter provable correlation due to unpermissioned malicious collusion," you must fall back to stronger technical measures (Independent-AID or Independent-Registry bulk-issued ACDCs) "at storage/compute cost" (ACDC spec > Bulk-issued, L2887-2911).

#### An agree binds; an admit removes the easy defense {#06-agree-binds}

The editor has ruled on where in an IPEX exchange the contractual binding happens, and the ruling puts the weight of this layer on one message [proposal]. "An agree is legally binding not sending an admit does not convey backing out." The admit amends nothing; it closes off a defense: "The admit is a corner case that enables easy enforcement by removing plausible deniablity." (keripy GitHub > #1505, comment of 2026-07-17, R-049, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1505#issuecomment-4997904242). Without an admit, a disclosee who agreed to confidentiality can claim the grant never arrived; to give it a reason to admit, "The grantor gets an escape clause unless the admitter verifiably admits." He ties the mechanism to the statutory duty of [section 3](#06-data-loyalty) in one line, "So CLC and DDL are mutually reinforcing": chain-link confidentiality binds by contract, the duty of data loyalty applies however the recipient came by the data, and a recipient that wants the safe harbor has a reason to supply the admission itself. A companion comment explains why the sequence works without a settlement party: "anchoring the tail also anchors the whole transation including the head", because the messages of one exchange are hash-chained, and "Multiple anchors are not meant to anchor multiple transactions but as continencies for the transaction to proceed" — contingencies, each party's commitment anchored before the other proceeds (keripy GitHub > #1505, comment of 2026-07-16, R-050, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1505#issuecomment-4996894599). [Chapter 08, section 10](#08-anchoring) owns the anchoring mechanics. What belongs here is that the contractual layer's enforceability is designed into the message sequence, not left to a registry or to a court's reconstruction of what was received. This is the editor's account of intent, and the ACDC specification's text was not checked for it here.

#### The deployment layer {#06-deployment-layer}

This layer contributes per-facet AIDs so that "Cecilia as chief executive at Acme" and her other facets are "uncorrelatable identifiers for one person" (sda.md > 6. Who is acting); frequent rotation of a citation-signing AID independent of the long-lived issuer AID; and pools of AIDs for herd privacy (Dossier spec > Privacy Considerations; raw/04 section 8). Origin's applied doctrine makes this a hard rule: "Each facet of an identity really should have its own AID... a separate AID each time a person is granted a new Origin role... security and trust never cross-contaminate" (origin-platform docs/managing-aliases.md > Solution > 1. AIDs, L91 @cb758b1b5; re-verified 2026-10-03) [practice], correcting the surveillance-economy anti-pattern where "most of us are terribly over-identified" (origin-platform docs/managing-aliases.md > The need for boundaries, L53 @cb758b1b5). This is Provenant client documentation — one deployment's stated practice, not KERI doctrine — and the chapter cites it only for that.

#### Two correct layers that do not compose {#06-layers-not-composing}

A finding from the reference implementation qualifies the disclosure layer, and it is the sharpest correction in this refresh. The layering above assumes that the disclosure layer's selective disclosure is actually available when the governance layer is in force. For SEDI's age credential at keripy `80f77b73b` it is not. Sam's Age schema requires a top-level `rd`, so every conforming Age is registry-backed; keripy represents a withheld aggregate element as its SAID string; and for a registry-backed ACDC, keripy's presentation-registry extraction returns `None` whenever any aggregate element after the AGID is withheld — the code comment reads "Every inspected aggregate entry must be a mapping." — and `None` fails the node (keripy src/keri/acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._presentationRegistries, L1458 @80f77b73b; raw/11 section 9 item 8) [code]. The reason is stated in the docstring and is a sound one: "A verifier cannot distinguish an omitted requirement from an undisclosed one using only its digest" (keripy src/keri/acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._presentationRegistries, L1414-1415 @80f77b73b) [code], so a withheld element might be hiding a presentation-registry declaration the verifier is obliged to check. The consequence is that a holder proving over-21 through keripy IPEX must also disclose every other threshold block, which brackets the age to a band. No test at that commit presents an Age, so nothing exercises the collision; and the module that enforces the rule, `acdc/ipexing.py`, has no caller in `src/keri` at that commit — its `loadHandlers` is re-exported by `acdc/__init__.py` and called nowhere, while keripy's own commands load the V1 handler from `vc/protocoling.py` — so the [code] here is code that exists and is tested in the reference implementation, not behaviour of any shipped keripy command (boundary added 2026-10-03 by verification; see [chapter 05, section 5.1](#05-verifying-ground-truth)); and Bakobo's schema gallery still validates an example, `sedi-age/examples/prove-over-21.json`, that "discloses only its issuee and over-21 blocks" (bakobo/schema sedi-age/index.md, L5 @cfcbdcc7a). The lesson for this section is structural rather than about age: two layers can each be correct and still not compose. A presentation-registry rule that protects detectability at the protocol layer silently withdrew selective disclosure at the disclosure layer, and nobody owned the seam. Whether it is resolved in the schema, in keripy, or by making Age registry-less is open and is Sam's to decide; [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md) owns the presentation-registry argument itself.

#### The three-party exploitation model {#06-three-party-model}

The three-party exploitation model frames why all three layers exist: 1st party is the data subject/Discloser, 2nd party the intended Disclosee, 3rd party any non-intended Observer, and "any use of 1st party data by a 3rd party is likewise, by definition, exploitive" (ACDC spec > Data Privacy, L1712-1726). Third-party protection is encryption (out of scope, deferred to SPAC/TSP); second-party protection is contractual (data loyalty); and correlation-minimization across contexts is technical. The no-forced-phone-home property belongs to the disclosure layer and is a genuine architectural correction of OCSP/CRL: the Observer/Registrar split means Observer-to-Registrar sync happens on state changes, not at the Point of Validation, so there is "no forced phone home validation" and no forced Validator-to-Issuer correlation of ACDC usage (ACDC spec > TEL Registrars and TEL Observers, L1693). Contrast OCSP, which "requires the client to query a central responder for every validation, creating a privacy leak (the CA knows every site you visit)" (wtbo.md > 2. Certificate Transparency: Progress and Its Limits). Hardman's `sda.md` paper generalizes the rejection: "A registry consulted at verification time is a phone-home in disguise" (sda.md > 7. Open loop, not closed; corrected 2026-10-03 — this sentence previously attributed the paper to Origin, which it is not). The SEDI portrait is committed by digest with bytes holder-carried because a download locator "is phone-home by another name §301(3)/§701, and creates an availability chokepoint" (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md > The attributes > Image: committed by digest, bytes holder-carried, L89-91 @cfcbdcc7a). Corrected 2026-10-03: this sentence previously quoted the page as saying "a resolvable URL in a credential is 'phone-home' surveillance and an availability single-point-of-failure," which is not on the page at the pin; the meaning is the same. The active Core keeps the mechanism, describing its image block as "Facial Image Proof Value as SAID of typed media block" (bakobo/schema sedi-core/sedi-core.schema.json, L293) — a commitment, not a locator.

The synthesis: correlation-resistance is a stack, and the honest KERI claim is that the stack composes cleanly — the disclosure layer minimizes technical correlators, the governance layer imposes loyalty duties on the parties the technical layer cannot reach, and deployment discipline (facet-granular AIDs, ~~un-logged presentations~~ presentations logged only where no third party watches — revised 2026-10-03 after SEDI's presentation schemas moved to holder-owned registries, [section 3](#06-data-loyalty)) closes the remaining gaps. The keripy finding above is the standing caution on "composes cleanly": it is a claim each pair of layers has to earn at each pin, not one the architecture grants. What KERI-core supplies is the substrate that makes each of those layers possible and verifiable — SAIDs that blind, AIDs that are cheap and disposable, anchored seals that reveal no PII, TELs that need not phone home — not unlinkability itself. A reviewer should test the seams (does the disclosure layer actually blind labels as claimed? does the governance duty actually bind downstream? does the deployment actually rotate?), not fault the base layer for a property it never claimed.

### Decorrelation, not uncorrelatability {#06-decorrelation}

The editor states the goal of this stack more sharply than the specification does [proposal]. Unlinkability of shared identifiers is not uncorrelatability of the person, because real presentation contexts leak, and for anyone not living off grid correlation is eventually achievable: "So the viable goal can not be uncorrelatability it must be decorrelation." (keripy GitHub > #1515, comment of 2026-07-18, R-065, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1515#discussioncomment-17682212). Decorrelation in his usage means correlatable information that is not exploited in correlated form, which is what contractually protected disclosure is for. That reframes bulk issuance rather than abandoning it: despite its "eventual defeat by a super correlator (an AI)", one reason to use it "is that partitioning identifier sets makes enforcement easier." An identifier set confined to one vendor context turns its appearance anywhere else into evidence of a breach of data loyalty, so the technical layer serves the governance layer's enforcement rather than standing in for it.

The same thread answers a standing-edge worry: two entitlements that each carry a standing edge to one stable core credential let two verifiers join on its SAID. His answer has two parts: "With bulk issuance, each presentation context consisting of discloser and disclosee gets its own set of SEDI credentials and standing edges." (keripy GitHub > #1515, comment of 2026-07-18, R-066, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1515#discussioncomment-17681089), and "an edge can also be blinded, which means that disclosure of the edge itself can be held back" until the disclosee has agreed not to exploit it (https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1515#discussioncomment-17682012). Both are layer-composition claims of the kind [section 4](#06-layers-not-composing) says must be earned at each pin, and this chapter did not check whether any implementation issues a bulk set with per-context standing edges.

#### Participation is not correlation {#06-participation-not-correlation}

One correlator the stack does not try to hide is the identifier an exchange is conducted under, and the editor treats its exposure as the price of a binding contract: "Proof of participation is not the same as correlation." (keripy GitHub > #1542, comment of 2026-07-23, R-054, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1542#discussioncomment-17755467) [proposal]. An authenticated negotiation needs a pair of AIDs, contract law needs "a clear intent to engage in legal relations", and graduated disclosure governs only what the presented ACDCs reveal. A critique that faults IPEX for exposing the negotiating AID is asking the contractual layer to work without parties.

## 5. Cross-ecosystem semantics: meaning across trust domains {#06-cross-ecosystem-semantics}

An ACDC is "a fragment of a globally distributed property graph" whose nodes are "securely attributed fragments... a global verifiable knowledge graph that crosses trust domains" (ACDC spec > ACDCs as secure graph fragments, L1060-1068), and "No shared or trusted relationship between the Controllers and Verifiers is REQUIRED" (ACDC spec > AID Fields, L95). The question is how meaning — not just authenticity — crosses a trust-domain boundary when there is no shared authority to define it.

KERI's first answer is type-is-schema: "no top-level field types exist in an ACDC... the Schema, `s`, field itself is the type field," and "type information is metadata, not data" (ACDC spec > Type-is-schema, L182). Because schemas are content-addressed (the `$id` is a bare SAID, not a URI, and must be static/SAIDified, ACDC spec > Schema ID Field Label, L186-210), the namespace is the content-address. This is the direct correction of the centralized-namespace prior: "no need for centralized permissioned name-space Registries to resolve name-space collisions" — the universal content-address plus content-addressable schema is the namespace, and a type registry reduces to "Schema discovery or schema blessing for a given context or ecosystem" (ACDC spec > Extensibility, L2936). Schemas "do not require standardization — just publication and consensus on use within an ecosystem," in pointed contrast to SD-JWT's reliance on IANA registration (sdjwt-acdc.md > 2. Differences > 2.7 Standards path); and because a schema is referenced "by its cryptographic content, not its location," there is "no link that can rot" (acdc-vc-diff.md > What Makes a Credential Format Lossy? > Loss 6: Schema Stability) — the answer to JSON-LD `@context` link-rot and term-redefinition, where "the meaning of a signed credential can be altered without invalidating the signature" (keri-primer.md > 4. CESR > 4.1 The engineering bottleneck: text vs. binary, citing W3C vc-data-integrity issue #272).

But content-addressing a schema fixes identity of meaning, not agreement on meaning across ecosystems. Two ecosystems that mint different schema SAIDs for "residence" have two different types, and no amount of cryptography reconciles them. The applied corpus is honest about this and shows the actual technique: semantic interop, not field-name interop. SEDI's historical `sedi-id` design says to "align the component *semantics* with 18013-5 so a bridge crosswalk is mechanical, but keep the statute's vocabulary" — `residence`, not ISO mDL's `resident` — so the interop is achieved by making the meaning of decomposed components match the mDL model while the field labels stay statute-native (bakobo/schema sedi-id/index.md > The attributes > Name and residence are decomposed — deliberately, L79-82 @cfcbdcc7a). Corrected 2026-10-03: the earlier quotation, "component semantics with ISO 18013-5 mDL but keep[s] the statute's vocabulary ('residence' not 'resident')," was a compression presented as verbatim. The example has also aged: Sam's active Core uses its own labels (`givenName`, `familyName`, `birthDate`), which is part of what Bakobo meant when it said its `sedi-id` "differs in field placement" from Sam's (bakobo/schema this.i, `@epnvr5oq`, L2217). The principle — semantic interop is a governance act, field names are not — is untouched by which labels won. Cross-ecosystem semantic agreement is a governance/standards act (align to mDL, align to ISO 6709 for geo, ISO 3166 for jurisdiction), not a protocol act. The edge `s`-constraint is the machinery that lets an ecosystem pin which foreign schema a chained node must satisfy: the vLEI ladder const-pins each hop's schema SAID (QVI→LE→AUTH→role), so a chain that crosses issuer trust-domains still carries a machine-checkable declaration of what each far node must be (public-schema vLEI/acdc/legal-entity-vLEI-credential.json, L99, and ecr-authorization-vlei-credential.json, L114 @95a07e544, re-verified 2026-10-03; ACDC spec > Edge Section, L1176).

### Two coherent choices on far-schema pinning {#06-far-schema-pinning}

The same fork now shows the opposite choice, and both are coherent. Between `8db57eb75` and `95a07e544` Provenant removed far-schema pinning from its telco credentials: at the newer pin the `tnalloc` edge's `s` is described only as "SAID of TN allocation schema" with `"type": "string"` (public-schema vvp-dossier/vvp-dossier.schema.json, L180), and no edge in `org-identity`, `brand-owner`, `tn-alloc`, `a2p-campaign`, `vvp-dossier` or `dossier-base` at that pin carries a SAID-valued `const` (raw/11 section 2). One page states the intent: the `issuer` edge is "Intentionally generic — does not constrain the schema of the identity credential" (public-schema tn-alloc/index.md > Edge structure, L51). This does not weaken the graph, because keripy's verifier treats an edge's `s` as a schema the far node must satisfy and validates the far node against it (keripy src/keri/vdr/verifying.py, Verifier.processCredential, L196-197, L208-228 @80f77b73b) [code]; what it changes is who decides which far schemas are acceptable. The vLEI ladder puts that decision in the schema, so every issuer is bound by it; the telco family moves it to verifier policy. That is the cross-domain question of this section answered two ways inside one organization's corpus, and the choice between them is exactly the kind an EGF should make explicitly rather than inherit from whichever schema template was copied. Neither repository states its reason, so the reading here is interpretive.

#### Bridge, do not adopt {#06-bridge-dont-adopt}

When meaning must cross into a foreign ecosystem entirely — W3C VC, ISO mDL, X.509, SD-JWT, AnonCreds, signed PDFs — KERI's stance is bridge, don't adopt. A designated bridging party verifies the foreign credential per its native rules, then issues a Foreign Artifact ACDC (FAA) or bridge-wrapper attesting "I... successfully verified the attached foreign credential on date X according to policy Y" (Dossier spec > Incorporating Evidence > Referencing Non-ACDC Evidence > Bridging from Foreign Credential Ecosystems; bakobo/schema faa/index.md). This "transforms the problem of verifying a foreign format into the problem of trusting the attestation of the bridging party" (Dossier spec > Incorporating Evidence > Referencing Non-ACDC Evidence > Bridging from Foreign Credential Ecosystems), and the trust is explicit and issuer-scoped, never systemic: an FAA's `art_posture` records whether the issuer merely recorded a digest, witnessed the artifact, or verified its integrity, and `rev_latency` records whether and how fast it mirrors the foreign credential's revocation, where a non-zero value "allows verifiers to treat the FAA as a proxy for the foreign credential, assuming they trust the FAA issuer" (bakobo/schema faa/index.md > What belongs in this credential, L30-31 @cfcbdcc7a). Trust in a bridge is therefore explicit and issuer-scoped, never systemic. Corrected 2026-10-03: that last sentence was previously presented as a quotation from `faa/index.md`; it is a summary, found in neither fork, and is now written as one. Two caveats are called out: trust depends on the bridging party's reputation/policies, and "the revocation lifecycles of the original foreign credential and of the bridge wrapper are decoupled unless a specific governance framework explicitly links them" (Dossier spec > Incorporating Evidence > Referencing Non-ACDC Evidence > Bridging from Foreign Credential Ecosystems). This is the interop corollary of the lossless/lossy doctrine: keep the lossless ACDC authoritative and treat foreign VCs ~~"as derivative artifacts wrapped/bridged, not as native roots of trust" (acdc-vc-diff.md)~~. Cut 2026-10-03 (verification): that quotation is not in `acdc-vc-diff.md` at papers `68a5e2f76`, and the wording is `raw/04`'s own summary. The "keep the lossless ACDC authoritative" half rests on that paper's lossless-original/lossy-derivative argument; the "not native roots of trust" half is now unsupported. The bridge direction matters for a second reason: "AIDs can be transformed to DIDs, but the opposite transformation is typically impossible" (sdjwt-acdc.md > 2. Differences > 2.2 Identifiers).

The uncontested part: content-addressed static schemas eliminate the namespace-collision and link-rot problems and make type-identity cryptographic. The load-bearing assumption a reviewer should flag: semantic agreement across ecosystems remains a human/governance achievement, exactly as the authenticity/veracity split predicts — the protocol guarantees you are looking at schema `E...`, not that your ecosystem and mine mean the same thing by it.

## 6. Versioning and migration cost {#06-versioning-migration}

Versioning in the KERI stack is layered like everything else, and each layer has its own compatibility rules.

### The wire/encoding layer (CESR) {#06-wire-layer-versioning}

The wire/encoding layer (CESR) versions the code tables themselves through a protocol genus/version code, `-_GGGVVV`, which "MUST NOT provide a count... but MUST modify the protocol genus and Version of all the following Count Codes" (CESR spec > Protocol genus/version table, L609). Genus lets one CESR serve multiple protocols each with their own tables; version lets a protocol evolve its tables (`CAA` = 2.00, `-_AAABAA` = KERI/ACDC v1.00, `-_AAACAA` = v2.00; CESR spec, L615, L865-866). The backward-compatibility semantics are stated as a normative asymmetry: "Any addition of a new code to the code table is backward-breaking in at least one direction... New implementations with the new codes can accept streams from old implementations, but old ones will break if they receive the new ones" (CESR spec > Protocol genus/version codes, L618). A minor bump = "a code is added to a table" (breaks only new-sender→old-receiver); a major bump = "a code's meaning changes" (breaks both directions) — with far more minor room than major (4096 minor per major) deliberately (L620-622). This is the same mechanism as crypto agility: a new algorithm "enters by claiming an unused CESR code-table slot; non-upgraded parsers still frame the stream correctly (read code → look up length → read bytes)" (keripy-knowledge 00-lens.md > The load-bearing claims, claim 8; CESR spec > SAID, L1180). Every CESR fragment quoted in this paragraph was re-read at `main` `bad6edd84` this cycle and is [spec], unmoved and verbatim; the knowledge-base gloss on agility is a distillation of those same sources rather than a source in its own right, and carries the scope stated in its entry under [Sources](#06-sources). The asymmetry claim is the load-bearing one, and the six paragraphs that follow rest on it.

#### The withdrawn FN-DSA illustration {#06-fn-dsa-withdrawn}

A correction, and it is a cut rather than a re-anchoring. Until this refresh the paragraph above ended by saying that post-quantum FN-DSA (Falcon) primitives were being introduced "in successive updates" as exactly such additive minor entries, cited to the CESR specification's Annex A and to its post-quantum section. That claim is withdrawn. The quoted string exists at neither CESR branch head. It was mined from commit `d35125e61`, which is reachable from no ref in the CESR repository — a dangling object from an abandoned pull-request branch, surviving only in one local clone and destined to vanish on any garbage collection. A pin that resolves is not a pin that is citable: `git rev-parse` succeeds on any object still in a local store, and only a reachability check answers whether a reader can get there. What the withdrawn sentence used to support was the concreteness of the agility argument — it was this chapter's only worked instance of a named algorithm claiming named slots. The abstract mechanism it illustrated is untouched and was re-verified word for word this cycle. What follows replaces the illustration with one that can be cited, and the replacement turns out to carry more weight than what it replaces.

#### Post-quantum on the standardizing line {#06-pq-standardizing}

What the standardizing line says about post-quantum is older than the corpus had recorded, not newer. At `bad6edd84` the code-table entry policy still reads that "there is the expectation that the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) soon will approve standardized post-quantum resistant cryptographic operations," and names Falcon exactly once, as a candidate: "Falcon appears to be among the leading candidates with open-source code already available." [spec] (CESR spec > Code table entry policy, L783) NIST published FIPS 203, 204 and 205 in August 2024, so the branch the community is standardizing is anticipating an approval that has already happened. And it carries zero post-quantum codes of any kind: an exhaustive search at the commit for FN-DSA, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, ML-KEM, FIPS, `1AAQ` and `1AAR` returns nothing beyond that single occurrence of "Falcon"; the fixed four-character table ends at `1AAN`, the one-character table ends at `a`, and the two-character table ends at `0S`. Any claim that CESR-as-standardized has post-quantum primitives is wrong, and was wrong in this chapter until now.

#### Post-quantum on the forward branch {#06-pq-forward}

The real post-quantum work is on the forward branch, and read as governance rather than as wire mechanics it is the more interesting half. CESR `v1.1` at `65fd7518b` defines roughly thirty-three post-quantum primitives — FN-DSA under FIPS 206, ML-DSA under FIPS 204, SLH-DSA under FIPS 205 — across the four-character `1`, `2` and `3` fixed tables, all [spec-next] and none of it normative today. [Chapter 04, section 5.7](#04-pq-in-practice) owns the wire mechanics of those rows. What belongs here is that they arrive under two new normative rules that are themselves versioning-governance doctrine, because they change how a code point gets allocated at all.

The first rule makes the compact code space a governed resource rather than a first-come-first-served one. "The one- and two-character code tables are a scarce resource" [spec-next] (CESR spec > Code table entry policy, L785 @65fd7518b) — fifty-two codes in the one-character table, sixty-four in the two-character, against 262,144 per four-character table — and admission now turns on relative overhead rather than on importance: entries there "MUST be reserved for Primitives whose raw size is small enough that a longer code would materially increase the size of the encoded Primitive." The consequence is a prohibition, not a preference: "Post-quantum codes MUST therefore be placed in the four-character fixed tables given by the `1`, `2`, and `3` selectors, and MUST NOT consume entries in the one- or two-character tables." [spec-next] (CESR spec > Code table entry policy, L785) The policy already on `main` is a quality filter — at least 128 bits of cryptographic strength, best-of-class operations only. The `v1.1` policy adds a scarcity filter on top of it, and that is a different kind of rule: it governs who may spend a shared namespace, not who is good enough to enter it. This is the first time the CESR code space is administered rather than merely populated, and it is a versioning-governance change dressed as an encoding detail.

The second rule removes discretion from table selection entirely. "Which of the three four-character fixed tables a given Primitive occupies is not a matter of choice. It is determined by the raw size of the Primitive modulo 3" [spec-next] (CESR spec > Code table entry policy, L787 @65fd7518b), because the encoding must align on a 24-bit boundary: a raw size that is a multiple of three needs no lead bytes and takes the `1` selector, congruent to two needs one lead byte and takes `2`, congruent to one needs two lead bytes and takes `3`. The specification draws out the consequence itself — the primitives belonging to one algorithm are commonly spread across more than one table, just as an Ed25519 verification key uses the one-character code `D` while an Ed25519 signature uses the two-character code `0B` — so a reader who infers an algorithm family from a selector is reading the wrong thing. The governance point is that this converts what could have been a committee decision into arithmetic. There is nothing to negotiate about placement, so placement cannot become a venue for anyone's preference. Taken together the two rules run the chapter's thesis in the opposite direction from [section 1](#06-egf-two-layer): where meaning is pushed out to a governance layer, allocation is pushed back into mechanism, and the residue of genuine policy is confined to a single admission question about relative overhead.

#### The message layer {#06-message-layer-versioning}

The message layer carries a version string as its first field. v2 format `PPPPMmmGggKKKKBBBB.` encodes protocol, protocol version, CESR genus version, serialization kind, and size (CESR spec > Version String, L1131). The critical backward-compat rule: "Compliant Version 2.XX implementations MUST support the old Version 1.XX Version String format to properly verify field maps created with 1.XX format events" [spec] (CESR spec > Legacy Version 1.XX, L1158 @bad6edd84; KERI spec, L273), and the `.` terminator exists specifically to let future versions change the version-string size while preserving regex extractability (L1152). So the stack is designed for old-format ingestion by new code, not the reverse — a deliberate one-way compatibility gradient.

The editor has stated one migration rule for exchanges that bears on governance directly: "Its only with v2 exchange messages that we plan to anchor exchanges. We really don't want to be anchoring v1 exchanges." (keripy GitHub > #1492, comment of 2026-07-27, R-057, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1492#issuecomment-5093267019) [proposal]. Anchored IPEX, and with it the contractual sequence of [section 4](#06-agree-binds), is therefore a v2-only capability. An ecosystem whose agents run a keripy line without V2 IPEX, as KERIA's `keri==1.2.14` pin does ([section 7](#06-keripy-lines)), cannot have it without upgrading.

#### The schema layer {#06-schema-layer-versioning}

The schema layer distinguishes two "versions" that MUST NOT be confused: the `$id` SAID is "the normative determiner," "cryptographically verifiable," and used in validation; the semver `version` field is "informative" and NOT used in validation, though any content change forces a new SAID and SHOULD also bump `version` (ACDC spec > Schema Versioning, L230-234). The applied corpus operationalizes this: "$id is a SAID... Edit content → the SAID changes → registry.json and any credential referencing the old SAID must be updated. Never invent or hand-patch a SAID" (bakobo/schema KNOWLEDGE_TRANSFER.md > Hard facts about ACDC schemas (respect these), L88-90 @cfcbdcc7a), and `registry.json` is "the crawl-free index of released schemas (SAID → path)" (bakobo/schema KNOWLEDGE_TRANSFER.md, L91-92). A schema evolution is therefore a new content-addressed object. This chapter used to add that forward-compatibility across schema versions is handled at the edge layer, where an edge's `s`-constraint ~~"enables forward-compatibility constraints without adding each minor version to `oneOf`" and "enables self-deprecating old schemas" (ACDC spec > Edge Section, L1176-1182)~~. Cut 2026-10-03 (verification): neither phrase is in the ACDC spec at `f0bd097de` or `2362e48a1`, and both were compressions presented as verbatim. The edge-layer forward-compatibility claim is unsupported until re-cited.

#### The Dossier schema-SAID recompute {#06-dossier-said-recompute}

The Dossier specification supplied a clean worked instance of that cost this cycle, and it is the sharpest illustration the corpus has. At `b9227753c` both of the specification's normative schema SAIDs changed: the base dossier schema from `ECpZgR2Ybj2QCfFZrnNQUqhbLnZuMl5cjL2MtgDaxMbY` to `EKuLzS_oN_mIao5og1NOujtF2QMXloiMCZP7xuAR5tY7`, and the endorsement schema from `EAfn0gRMUnp6d1hyE5qJCN86kBFBp80JwMdm0BqiC1B0` to `ECRjgun8t3cay_YBiVxEY-qXKCz37oUrvE5GvmySwxCh`. [spec] (Dossier spec schemas/dossier-base.json and schemas/endorsement.json, $id, L3 @b9227753c) The commit that caused it was titled "Correct signing language in the schemas and recompute their SAIDs" — the schemas' prose descriptions were rewritten to speak of anchoring rather than signing, which is as editorial a change as a specification ever makes. Under content-addressed schemas it is not editorial; it is a wire-format change. The base schema's own IS-A rule is the reason: "A schema S IS-A dossier iff S's top-level allOf array contains a $ref to this schema's SAID, or recursively to another schema that IS-A dossier" (Dossier spec schemas/dossier-base.json, description, L5), and a `$ref` naming the old SAID no longer resolves to anything. Every derived schema in the wild must be re-pointed and re-SAIDified, and every credential referencing one of those is affected in turn.

This is the price of the property [section 5](#06-cross-ecosystem-semantics) praises. Content-addressing gives type-identity that no registry can equivocate about and no link can rot out from under, and the same mechanism means there is no such thing as a correction too small to break a reference. A semver-style "informative" version field exists precisely so that humans can tell a prose fix from a semantic one, but "The `version` field value is not used in the JSON Schema validation against the ACDC" (ACDC spec > Schema Versioning, L230 @f0bd097de), so nothing mechanical can act on that distinction. Cut 2026-10-03 (verification): this sentence previously quoted the field as one that ~~"is NOT used in validation"~~, which is not verbatim at `f0bd097de`; the claim stands on the sentence now quoted. The honest statement of the trade is that KERI moves the cost of schema evolution from ambiguity to coordination: you never wonder which version of a schema a credential meant, and you always have to re-point every reference when the bytes move. A reviewer weighing the migration claims below should hold this example next to them, because it is a case where the architecture's own virtue generated the breaking change.

#### Three dossier bases {#06-three-dossier-bases}

The applied corpus shows what the coordination cost looks like when nobody pays it. Provenant revised its own dossier base this cycle: at public-schema `95a07e544` it moved from `dossier-base/dossier-base.json` (`$id` `EFf_1uI94VBDwHH7yEkyWUq3jtWy1HXCvG5YYY1DNWfW`) to `dossier-base/dossier-base.schema.json` (`$id` `EHxI61CGs7FRuStz8P6QWJyMK4u2bGH1LQqIXsA4bT7q`, L3), renamed `assemble_dt` to `assembly_dt` and `class` to `cls`, and adopted the same IS-A rule quoted above (L5), plus a division of labour it states as "all evidence MUST be carried in e, never in a" (L5). bakobo/schema at `cfcbdcc7a` still publishes the old base, `EFf_1u…` with `assemble_dt` (bakobo/schema dossier-base/dossier-base.json, L3, L65). Neither public base matches the Dossier specification's own base SAID quoted in the previous paragraph, and whether either is meant to track the specification was not checked (raw/11 section 9 item 9). So three published "dossier base" schemas now exist, each internally consistent and each a different type under content-addressing, and a derived schema that IS-A one of them IS-NOT-A the other two. There is a smaller seam inside public-schema too: its one derived dossier, `vvp-dossier` 2.0.0, inherits the new base by `$ref` while still requiring the ACDC v1 `ri` where the base offers v2 `rd` (public-schema vvp-dossier/vvp-dossier.schema.json, L7-11, L19, L37-38). None of this is a defect in the architecture; it is the architecture reporting, precisely and without ambiguity, that three parties have not coordinated. That is the honest form of the trade stated above — content-addressing does not prevent divergence, it makes divergence impossible to miss.

#### The Well-Known OOBI repath {#06-well-known-oobi}

The bootstrap layer produced a smaller migration this cycle, and it is instructive for a different reason: the trust model did not move at all, only the plumbing. The Well-Known OOBI was repathed. Where the specification previously described an OOBI returned from a `GET` to an RFC5785 well-known URL at `/.well-known/keri/oobi/{aid}`, it now reads "An OOBI MAY be returned as the result of an HTTP `GET` request to a well-known URI [RFC8615] using the registered `oobi` suffix," with the example path `/.well-known/oobi/{aid}`. [spec] (KERI spec > Well-Known OOBI, L2693 and L2698 @fbdd4a615) Three things changed at once: the `keri/` path segment is gone, the normative reference moved from RFC5785 to RFC8615 — the bibliography's new entry 42 notes that RFC8615 "Obsoletes RFC5785," while RFC5785 itself was kept as entry 34 rather than removed — and the permissive `may` became a normative `MAY`. An implementer who built against the old path is now non-conformant. Four rules are also new rather than restated: the AID in the path "MAY identify any KERI role"; "the request is unauthenticated and the response is untrusted at the transport layer," so "any returned material MUST be verified in-band before use, as with any other OOBI"; hosts provisioning the suffix "SHOULD make responses reachable over both `http` and `https`"; and the media type "is determined by its CESR-compatible serialization." [spec] (KERI spec > Well-Known OOBI, L2713) The governance-relevant part is the second of those, and it is a restatement, not a discovery: it is the same untrusted-bootstrap stance the specification already took at L2629 and L2633, now written where an implementer of the well-known endpoint will actually read it. So this is a conformance change for implementers and a non-change for the trust model — which is the correct shape for a change at this layer, and worth noting because it is easy to mistake a repath for a policy shift.

#### Bootstrap Configuration buckets {#06-bootstrap-buckets}

Alongside it a Bootstrap Configuration section was added, defining three named buckets for pre-configured OOBIs. `iurls` are introduction OOBIs whose target AID "identifies a KERI role such as a controller, witness, watcher, juror, judge, or registrar," with a catch-all rule that "An OOBI of unspecified purpose is an `iurls` entry." `durls` are data OOBIs resolving "to SAID-addressed data rather than to a KERI AID, for example an ACDC schema referenced by a `sad` URI," whose integrity "is verified by re-deriving the SAID of the returned bytes and comparing it to the SAID embedded in the URI." `wurls` are "a list of singular well-known OOBI URLs designated by the operator for use as factors in an out-of-band multi-factor authentication arrangement" — the OOBA configuration of [section 2](#06-oobi-mfa-arbitration) — with two constraints that matter: "Each entry is one URL, not a MOOBI," so the multiplicity lives across entries and never inside one, and a consumer may keep `wurls` in a store separate from the others "so that the additional trust assumptions of an OOBA arrangement do not leak into the general endpoint cache." [spec] (KERI spec > Bootstrap Configuration, L2851-2855 @fbdd4a615) The specification's own hedge should travel with every citation of this section: these buckets "are a deployment convention and SHOULD NOT be treated as distinct wire forms," since "every entry is an OOBI in one of the forms defined above" (L2851), and "the on-disk schema, file format, and merge semantics of a configuration file are out of scope" (L2857). There is no configuration format to conform to; only bucket semantics.

#### Unconfirmed convergence on the buckets {#06-bucket-convergence}

And here the section makes an empirical claim that this refresh could not confirm. Its opening sentence is descriptive rather than prescriptive — "Implementations have converged on three named buckets that classify pre-configured OOBIs by their intended use" [spec] (KERI spec > Bootstrap Configuration, L2851) — so the specification presents itself as ratifying deployed practice. The two implementations checked this cycle do not support that. KERIA at `7e685edaa` reads `iurls` and `durls`, both settable from the environment and merged into each agent's configuration at startup, and contains no `wurls` anywhere in `src/keria`. [code] signify-ts at `ffba8406e` has no bootstrap-bucket implementation at all: its single occurrence of `iurls` is a type declaration in `src/types/keria-api-schema.ts`, which is generated from KERIA's OpenAPI specification and is a reflection of the server's configuration shape rather than any client behavior. [code] Neither reads `wurls`; neither serves a `/.well-known/` route of any kind. Enumerating every `add_route` call in KERIA at that commit — forty-one routes across `agenting.py`, `aiding.py` and `credentialing.py` — turns up no well-known endpoint; KERIA's OOBI surface is `/oobis`, `/oobis/{alias}` and `/identifiers/{name}/oobis`, and its `WellKnown` class is a contact annotation recording well-known URLs observed for a contact, not an endpoint served. [code] So the repath is a live conformance question for keripy and for witness hosts, and moot for KERIA; and "implementations have converged" is, on the evidence available here, a claim about a convergence that at least two of the four implementations have not joined. This is not a defect in the specification — ratifying a convention in advance of universal adoption is ordinary standards practice — but the corpus should record it as a finding rather than repeat the sentence as though it were verified. Whether keripy implements the buckets was not checked this cycle and is an open question, not a negative result.

#### Migration cost against X.509 {#06-migration-cost}

Migration cost is where KERI stakes its most aggressive comparative claim, and it is worth stating carefully because it is both strong and honestly hedged. The argument is that the fair comparison between KERI and X.509 is not deployed-today capability but migration cost: PKI's post-quantum transition is "mandatory, global, and expensive... a global re-rooting," whereas KERI's PQ migration is "one rotation per identifier, made unilaterally... not a global re-rooting," so "early KERI adopters are not accumulating architectural debt" (wtbo.md > 6. The Transition Problem: A Comparison of Trajectories). The grounding is that pre-rotation already hides the next key behind a hash, so a controller can "rotate to stronger quantum-safe functions over time" and remain "computationally infeasible indefinitely" (KERI spec > Pre-rotation, L1680), and that integrating a NIST-finalist PQ algorithm into keripy "took only a couple of hours" (kspqs.md, personal communication, Sam Smith, Oct 7 2025). The quantum posture is "hybrid ECC+PQ multisig plus the hash-hidden next key" (keripy-knowledge 00-lens.md > The load-bearing claims, claim 8). This is a real architectural advantage — unilateral per-identifier migration versus coordinated global ceremony.

#### Two bounds on the migration argument {#06-migration-bounds}

Two things bound that argument, and they were not stated sharply enough before this refresh. The first is a sourcing bound: the "couple of hours" figure is a first-hand report of a conversation, not a written or reviewable artifact.
