A report of that class is usable for status and intent — that the work was attempted, that it is not abandoned — and not as evidence about effort, design or scope, and it certainly cannot be reconciled against anything. The second bound is that whatever was integrated did not land: keripy at `b8f60166b` contains no post-quantum codes at all, and a case-insensitive search of `src/keri/core` at that commit for FN-DSA, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, Dilithium, SPHINCS, Kyber and ML-KEM returns nothing. [code] So the single quantitative data point behind the migration-cost claim describes an exercise no reader can inspect, on code that is not in the reference implementation. The architectural argument — one unilateral rotation per identifier against a coordinated global re-rooting — stands on the pre-rotation mechanism and does not need that figure; the figure should stop being carried as though it corroborated the implementation half. The honest counterweight (below) is that the implementation cost of getting a new code-table entry exactly right is nontrivial and error-prone, and that it remains a forward-looking cost rather than one anybody has yet paid.

#### Scope of the knowledge-base evidence {#06-kb-scope}

Before the counterweight, its scope, because the scope is now most of the story. The account below comes from a private, unpublished contributor knowledge base pinned at `9489ac9bd`, whose own code baseline is keripy `60ab9e08d` — 493 commits behind `b8f60166b` — and which declares itself a description of `2.0.0-dev6` against keripy's current `2.1.0-dev1`. Every landmine and invariant cited here therefore describes a superseded dev line. They stand as discipline: a reviewer touching this code should assume each hazard is still there until they have looked. They do not stand as statements about keripy today, and none of them was re-tested at the current pin. The knowledge base's own banner claim that all twenty landmines still hold was verified at `60ab9e08d` and has at least one known counterexample since, so each item below is stated individually rather than under that claim's cover. One further correction of framing: the knowledge base writes these entries as advice about work in flight — "The Falcon PR must touch every shadow table" — and that framing is out of date in the strongest possible way. Nothing is blocked, because nothing has been written. The knowledge base is candid about why: its own open decisions ask which of two conflicting in-repo Falcon design documents is canonical — fixed-size signatures with compact codes and no digest-derived AIDs, against variable-size signatures with digest AIDs — and its plan defers the post-quantum work entirely behind "resolve the two conflicting Falcon spec docs first" (keripy-knowledge PLAN.md > 7. Phase plan with recommended effort, and 9. Decisions to confirm at approval (not now), @9489ac9bd). A chapter that named a winner there would be inventing an answer no source has. What survives intact is the discipline; what does not is the urgency.

With that scope attached, the knowledge base is the best available account of the implementation cost, and it is sobering. Adding a single new primitive code is "the highest-risk surface in the flagship" because a code lives in multiple shadow tables: registering only in `MatterCodex` + `Matter.Sizes` is not enough; digest codes must also update `Saider.Digests` and `Serder.Digests`, and the relevant `*Dex` sets (`PreDex`, `DigDex`, `SmallVrzDex`/`LargeVrzDex`), plus in 2.0 the `BodyUniversalCodex` (`BUDex`) and `Counter.BUCodes` — "Registering only in MatterCodex + Matter.Sizes is not enough and fails late/silently" (keripy-knowledge 31-landmines.md > L5; keripy-knowledge 30-invariants.md > A. CESR wire-format & sizing, A9). The sizing arithmetic is unforgiving: fixed codes need `fs % 4 == 0`, variable codes `(ls + rs) % 3 == 0`, lead size `ls = (3 - (rize % 3)) % 3` where "the double-modulo is intentional (0→0, 1→2, 2→1). A 'simplification' here breaks triplet alignment" (keripy-knowledge 30-invariants.md > A. CESR wire-format & sizing, A1-A5), and "Get the sizing math wrong and a parser that predates your code desyncs the entire stream — silently, because CESR is self-framing" (keripy-knowledge 30-invariants.md > A. CESR wire-format & sizing, introduction). Pre-rotation verification can even go "permissive on a digest-code mismatch," silently excluding a mismatched `ondex` from threshold satisfaction rather than failing closed, and "New digest codes (Falcon/PQ) widen this surface" (keripy-knowledge 31-landmines.md > L6). Two further migration hazards live in storage: `Komer` records "have no schema versioning → adding a field breaks old stores" and "Any new field on a persisted record needs a migration" (keripy-knowledge 31-landmines.md > L18), and pre-1.2.0 DB key formats crash format-assuming iterators so "escrow contents [are treated] as discardable across migrations" (keripy-knowledge 31-landmines.md > L2; keripy-knowledge 30-invariants.md > I. Storage / DB, I4). The lesson for a reviewer: KERI's protocol-level migration story (unilateral rotation, additive codes) is genuinely cheaper than PKI's, but the implementation-level migration surface is a minefield the reference codebase navigates with explicit shadow-table discipline, and a naive change "passes keripy's own tests but diverges from the spec/wire format" — which "is a defect, because it silently breaks interop" (keripy-knowledge 00-lens.md > The load-bearing claims, claim 5).

#### A dead freshness guard {#06-dead-freshness-guard}

One observation about the tooling around that discipline, because this chapter is where ecosystem maturity is assessed and it is a real data point. The knowledge base ships a freshness ritual and tells its readers to run it "at the start of any KB-using session or before a PR." That guard is dead. Its `freshness.sh` defaults to a repository path that no longer exists, and the session registry that selects between the 2.0 and 1.x knowledge bases points at two more paths that no longer exist — all three were invalidated when the repositories moved, and the script now errors out rather than reporting anything. Nothing told anyone. That is the mechanism by which a knowledge base whose entire value proposition is currency could fall 493 commits behind in silence, and it is the same failure mode [section 7](#06-implementation-compat) identifies on the interop surface: a rule or a check that lives in one place, with nothing watching whether it still runs, drifts without announcing itself. The general lesson is worth stating plainly, because it applies well past this one script — when a document asserts that a mechanism is active, the mechanism has to travel by the same route the document does, or the document becomes a confident lie the moment the environment moves. A quiet guard and a working one look identical from outside, and only one of them is good news.

## 7. Backward compatibility across keripy, keria, and signify-ts {#06-implementation-compat}

The interop surface is not one implementation but at least four that must agree byte-for-byte: keripy (the Python reference), KERIA (the cloud agent), signify-ts (the TypeScript edge signer), and SignifyPy. The governing doctrine is that "keripy's 'intent layer' is exogenous: the CESR / KERI / ACDC specifications" (keripy-knowledge 00-lens.md > The load-bearing claims, claim 5) — the spec is the external contract, and "CESR code-table entries and sizing, field names and order, SAID derivation, version strings, count codes are external contracts." This inverts the usual "reference implementation is the truth" assumption: passing keripy's tests is not sufficient; the wire format is.

The KERIA/Signify split is itself an interop architecture with a two-AID delegation spine: the Client AID (edge, delegator) and the Agent AID (cloud, delegated `dip` with `di` = Client AID), where "unencrypted private key material never leaves the client" and the agent holds only encrypted blobs it cannot decrypt (KERIA docs/protocol.md > Key Generate Methods; signify-ts README.md). Externally the agent is "just another KERI node relaying edge-signed CESR" — the Signify split is "an internal implementation detail invisible to verifiers" (KERIA README.md > Message Router). This matters for compatibility because it means the external wire contract (CESR-over-HTTP on the KERI Protocol interface, port 3902) is the same normal KERI contract every implementation speaks, while the internal admin contract (SKRAP, the Signify/KERIA Request Authentication Protocol) is a private surface between edge and cloud.

Three compatibility surfaces are load-bearing and each has documented parity hazards.

### HTTP message-signature construction {#06-http-signature-parity}

HTTP message-signature construction is "the highest-risk interop surface" — the signed byte string `ser` must be assembled identically in TS and Python or auth breaks silently. Default signed fields must match (`@method`, `@path`, `signify-resource`, `signify-timestamp`), but the two default lists are in different order between `authing.ts` (`@method` first) and `authing.py` (`Signify-Resource` first); order agreement is enforced by the emitted `Signature-Input` header, not the constant, "Still, this asymmetry is a landmine" (raw/10 > 7a. HTTP message-signature construction). Timestamp format even differs cosmetically (signify-ts writes `000+00:00` where keripy writes ISO `Z`), and both must parse each other's format.

#### Key-derivation determinism {#06-key-derivation-parity}

The passcode-to-key path must be byte-identical across edge implementations. The `bran` construction (`Salt_128 '0A' + 'A' + passcode[0:21]`), the Argon2 stretching, and the salty path must match, or "the edge and any other edge impl derive different keys from the same passcode" (raw/10 > 7c. Key derivation must be deterministic & identical). keripy's `SaltyCreator` must produce identical output to signify-ts `SaltyCreator` for the same salt/tier/path. The salty-path landmine (missing delimiter → seed collisions → recovery break) is an active cross-impl bug, confirmed as twin #928 (keripy-knowledge 31-landmines.md > L10).

#### Event, threshold and serialization parity {#06-event-parity}

The CHANGELOG parity fixes prove these are live constraints — `rotate` defaulting to next (not current) threshold (#208), correct `adds`/`cuts` (#359), string/hex `s` parsing, `ondex` computed from the prior establishment event not the proposed one (#378), and a `rotated=true` flag on signing, "matching KERIpy `BaseHab.sign` behaviour" (signify-ts CHANGELOG.md > 0.4.0). Rotation-ilk switching (`drt` when delegated) and default rotation thresholds (`max(1, ceil(count/2))` in hex) must match keripy exactly (raw/10 > 7d. Event/threshold semantics parity). A fresh instance landed this cycle and is the best kind of evidence that the hazard is live. signify-ts's `messagize` built a source-seal sequence number with `new Seqner({ sn: parseInt(seal[1].s) })` (signify-ts src/keri/core/eventing.ts, messagize, L432 @ffba8406e), which reads KERI's hex `s` as decimal and is wrong from sequence number `0xa` upward; at `5a174b545` it reads `new Seqner({ snh: seal[1].s }).qb64b` (signify-ts src/keri/core/eventing.ts, messagize, L430 @5a174b545), the hex constructor [code]. The invariant that both implementations treat `s` as hex was broken in shipped client code until 2026-09-16, and nothing in the type system caught it — which is what "maintained by vigilance" means in practice.

#### Four implementations on different keripy lines {#06-keripy-lines}

The four implementations are not on one keripy line, and a reader of this chapter has to carry that. KERIA's dependency tightened this cycle from a range to an exact pin, `"keri==1.2.14",` (KERIA pyproject.toml, L30 @928ce26a4; it read `"keri>=1.2.13,<1.3",` at `7e685edaa`) [code]. keripy `main` is on the `2.1.0-dev` line, where this cycle's work landed — IPEX V2, `E1E` enforcement, presentation-registry checks — and none of it is in a `keri==1.2.14` dependency (raw/10 section 11a). So a claim that "keripy does X" at a `main` commit is not evidence that a KERIA deployment does X; where KERIA matches keripy `main`, it did so by reimplementing the behaviour in its own code, and that is independent evidence rather than inheritance. For the parity question this cuts both ways. It means the interop surface is not four implementations of one specification at one moment but a 1.2.x server, a 2.1-dev reference, and two clients that must speak to whichever they meet. And it means the [section 4](#06-layers-not-composing) finding about Age credentials is a statement about keripy `main` and says nothing yet about what a KERIA-hosted holder can present.

The formal compatibility contract for the admin API is machine-enforced: signify-ts "generates its request/response types directly from KERIA's OpenAPI (`npm run generate:types`)," so "KERIA's specing.py/spec.yaml is the source of truth for the admin API contract; the TS client is a downstream consumer" (raw/10 > 7e. Types are generated FROM the KERIA OpenAPI spec). But the deepest layer — the CESR matter/counter/indexer code tables — is not generated; it is independently reimplemented in each language, "the deepest interop layer (the qb64 derivation-code tables must be identical across all four impls)" (raw/10 > Gaps / not covered). This is the same shadow-table hazard of [section 6](#06-kb-scope) seen from the interop side: a code added to keripy's tables but not to signify-ts's tables (or added with different sizing) is an invisible break.

#### The post-quantum table as a parity test {#06-pq-parity-test}

This cycle produced the best test that hazard has ever been given, and the result is the strongest interop evidence in this chapter. The `v1.1` post-quantum table of [section 6](#06-pq-forward) is roughly thirty-three new rows across three code tables — exactly the class of change the paragraph above says is most likely to drift. The finding is that no shipped implementation carries it. keripy at `b8f60166b` has no post-quantum codes; a search of `src/keri/core` for every scheme name returns nothing. [code] Upstream signify-ts at `ffba8406e` has none either; a search of `src` for the same terms returns no match. [code] CESR `main` at `bad6edd84` defines none to carry. [spec] The only implementation of those rows is an unmerged branch on a personal fork, and it is marked here as what it is: not [code], because [code] means an implementation anyone runs behaves this way, and no one runs a branch that exists on one fork.

The right reading of that is not the one it first invites. An earlier framing of this finding — that the reference implementation and the TypeScript client disagree about the post-quantum code table — does not survive checking. They agree, in that neither has it. What exists is a fork branch ahead of both, and a specification branch ahead of the standardizing line. That is a far less dramatic finding about interop and a far more honest one, and it is the outcome the layering predicts: nothing shipped, so nothing drifted. The hand-maintained code tables are the seam most likely to drift, and the seam has not drifted, because the change that would have stressed it has not been taken up by anyone obliged to keep parity. A reviewer should hold this as evidence of discipline preserved by inaction, which is weaker than discipline preserved by process and should not be dressed up as the latter. The real test arrives when the `v1.1` codes reach `main` and four implementations must add thirty-three rows each, with sizing arithmetic that fails late and silently when it is wrong.

#### Evidence from the fork branch {#06-fork-evidence}

The fork branch does supply one genuinely positive piece of evidence, and it is the best the corpus has for its own agility thesis. An implementation written independently of keripy confirms that primitive sizing is a pure function of the code, never of the value: its parser selects a table by primitive class, looks up the hard code, and returns the table's declared full size as the element's length, and group framing is the same shape — the count is in quadlets, so the frame is known before any content is read. The payload is never decoded before its length is decided. The consequence is the one the agility argument has always asserted and never demonstrated: the thirty-three post-quantum rows required no parser change at all. The commit that added them touches the sizing table and a test file, and does not touch the parser; a 21-kilobyte SLH-DSA signature frames correctly the moment the table knows its size. That is the "read code → look up length → read bytes" claim of [section 6](#06-wire-layer-versioning) holding under an implementation that did not inherit keripy's assumptions, which is exactly where a designed-in property either holds or breaks. Mark the evidence honestly: it is [proposal], because code on an unmerged fork is a proposal made in code, and it is evidence about the encoding design, not about the ecosystem's readiness to adopt it. Changed 2026-10-15: this sentence previously called the evidence "[code]-adjacent at best", a marker outside the legend; the tier it describes is [proposal].

The honest reviewer's takeaway: backward compatibility across the stack is maintained by convention and vigilance (spec-as-contract, generated types where possible, CHANGELOG parity notes) rather than by a single shared codebase, and the two independent message-signature implementations plus the hand-maintained code tables are the surfaces most likely to drift. Two findings from this cycle should be read alongside that. The code-table seam was not stressed, because the change that would have stressed it exists only on a specification branch and a fork, so parity here is an absence of divergence rather than a demonstration of process. And on the bootstrap surface, where the KERI specification records that "implementations have converged" on three configuration buckets, neither KERIA nor signify-ts reads `wurls` and neither serves a `/.well-known/` route at all ([section 6](#06-bucket-convergence)) — so at least one place where the specification describes convergence, the implementations have not converged. The vigilance model works when someone is watching a given seam. Nothing in the architecture says who is watching which.

## 8. Decentralization scorecard: KERI versus SD-JWT / OIDC4VC {#06-scorecard}

The following scorecard contrasts KERI/ACDC with the SD-JWT / OIDC4VC family (SD-JWT VCs presented under OpenID4VP/OID4VCI, which build on JWT/OAuth/OIDC). A methodological caveat first, because an adversarial reviewer must weigh the source: the SD-JWT column is grounded in Hardman's comparison papers, which are KERI-partisan advocacy. The technical claims in it (JWT tokens verified only against current key state; `kid` points at a key not an identifier; standalone envelopes pushing toward issuer registries) are checkable against the SD-JWT and JWT specifications and are accurate as stated; the evaluative framing ("re-centralizes," "drift") is argumentative. Treat the ratings as a structured argument, not a neutral benchmark.

| Principle | KERI / ACDC | SD-JWT / OIDC4VC | Source grounding |
|---|---|---|---|
| Root of trust | Self-certifying identifier; "bottoms out in mathematics" | Administrative — issuer key trusted via registry/CA; bottoms out in administrators | wtbo.md > 3. Common Ground: What CT and KERI Share; x509-prob.md |
| Holder key rotation | Survives; identifier constant across rotation (transferable AID) | Solved by issue-to-identifier indirection where DID method allows | keri-primer.md > 2.1 Autonomic identifiers; sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.3 Signing mechanism |
| Issuer key rotation | Credential validity binds to issuer key state at anchor position, survives rotation | `kid` binds to a key; "key rotation invalidates historical signatures" | ACDC spec > Binding to Key State, L1673-1675; sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.3 Signing mechanism |
| Historical / point-in-time verification | Yes — anchored signatures defeat retrograde attacks; validate against key state "as of" the anchor | No — "tokens are only designed to be evaluated against current key state" | keripy-knowledge 30-invariants.md > H. Anchored signatures, H1; was.md > Mitigation 3 (pyrrhic victory); sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.3 Signing mechanism |
| Trust-chain expression | Native typed, operator-bearing edges → verifiable DAG of authority | Captures only issuer→holder; broader chain "becomes implicit" | ACDC spec > Edge Section; acdc-vc-diff.md > Loss 1: The Trust Chain |
| Issuer-registry dependence | Eliminated by chaining; registry reduces to "schema blessing" | "SD-JWTs will need registries of trusted issuers... centralized, governed" | ACDC spec > Extensibility, L2936; sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.4 Chaining |
| Revocation privacy (phone-home) | Observer/Registrar split → "no forced phone home validation" | Inherits OCSP/status-list phone-home tendencies | ACDC spec > TEL Registrars and TEL Observers, L1693; wtbo.md > 2. Certificate Transparency: Progress and Its Limits |
| Correlation control | Layered: graduated/selective disclosure + CLC + per-facet AIDs (see [section 4](#06-layered-privacy)) | Selective disclosure at token level; weaker chain/registry-driven correlation | ACDC spec > Bulk-issued; sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.5 Serialization details |
| Crypto agility / PQ migration | Additive code-table slot + unilateral per-identifier rotation; no PQ primitive standardized yet ([section 6](#06-pq-standardizing)) | Tied to JWT/COSE alg negotiation; migration coordinated | CESR spec > SAID, L1180 [spec]; CESR spec > Code table entry policy, L785 [spec-next]; wtbo.md > 6. The Transition Problem: A Comparison of Trajectories |
| Jurisdiction independence | Chains to a global root, crosses borders (vLEI, VVP) | CA/ecosystem trust is jurisdiction-bound (SHAKEN not accepted EU/Asia) | acdc-vc-diff.md; keri-primer.md > 1.1 Fragility of centralized roots |
| Canonicalization robustness | Insertion-order field maps; SAID over exact bytes; no JCS/JSON-LD | JCS "brittle"; JSON-LD term-redefinition alters signed meaning | CESR spec > Order-Preserving, L1250; keri-primer.md > 4.1 The engineering bottleneck: text vs. binary |
| Offline / open-loop verification | Yes — "verify authority without consulting its issuer" | Token verification typically needs issuer metadata/keys reachable | sda.md > 7. Open loop, not closed; sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.3 Signing mechanism |
| Ultimate arbiter | None at Layer 1; plural, opt-in EGFs at Layer 2 | Registry governance + underlying CA/browser-vendor roots | wtbo.md > 1. The Identity Problem: Administrative Trust and Its Limits; wtbo.md > 4. KERI's Architecture: A Different Root of Trust; x509-prob.md |

The unifying "drift" thesis behind the scorecard is that "SD-JWT, W3C-VC, and most DID methods imported PKI/OAuth assumptions (issue-to-key thinking, current-key-state-only verification, standalone envelopes, trust registries, `@context` link-rot, three-party holder bias) and thereby re-created centralization one level up while losing time, trust-chain, and key-history fidelity" (raw/06 section 9). The complementary framing is lossless-versus-lossy: ACDC is the archival RAW format and W3C-VC / SD-JWT / ISO mDL are the lossy JPEG/MP3 distribution formats, so the recommended architecture keeps the lossless ACDC authoritative and generates the lossy format when a consumer needs it (acdc-vc-diff.md > Lossless vs. Lossy: A Choice That Matters).

## 9. Load-bearing assumptions and contested points {#06-assumptions}

An adversarial reviewer should hold the following as the flagged uncertainties of this chapter, separated from the well-established.

### Well-established {#06-well-established}

The two-layer split (cryptographic Layer 1 universal, semantic Layer 2 governance) is a coherent and repeatedly-stated architecture, not a rationalization (Dossier spec > Dossier Data Model (Normative) > Base JSON-Schema Definition, L127; ACDC spec > Extensibility). KERI-core genuinely does not promise unlinkability, and the ACDC spec is unusually honest that even its own privacy layer is defeatable by contextual/statistical correlation (ACDC spec > Bulk-issued, L2785). Content-addressed static schemas genuinely eliminate namespace-collision and link-rot (ACDC spec > Extensibility, L2936). The wire-versioning and crypto-agility mechanisms are concrete and specified, and the asymmetry they rest on was re-verified verbatim and unmoved at CESR `main` `bad6edd84` this cycle (CESR spec > Protocol genus/version codes, L618). The no-phone-home revocation property is real and mechanically enforced by the Observer/Registrar split.

#### Superseded this cycle, recorded rather than removed {#06-superseded-pq}

This chapter previously stated that post-quantum FN-DSA primitives were being introduced into CESR "in successive updates" as additive minor entries. That claim is withdrawn: its quote is at neither CESR branch head and was mined from an unreachable commit on an abandoned branch ([section 6](#06-fn-dsa-withdrawn)). It had been the chapter's only worked example of the crypto-agility mechanism operating on a named algorithm. What replaced it is stronger than what it replaced — a real, citable [spec-next] code table, arriving under two new allocation rules that are themselves governance doctrine — but the replacement is on a forward branch and the standardizing line still has no post-quantum primitive at all. A reader who took this chapter's word for it before this refresh believed CESR-as-standardized carried codes it has never carried, and the record of having believed that is part of what the correction is for.

#### Superseded on 2026-10-03, recorded in place {#06-superseded-sedi}

[Section 3](#06-sedi) had described SEDI as a four-attribute root credential whose governance framework every SEDI credential references by SAID, with correlation-resistance completed by un-registered presentations. All three have moved: the four-attribute `sedi-id` is superseded for new issuance by Sam Smith's IAR, Core, Residence and Age, Core requires names, birth date, facial image proof, legal presence status, issue and expiration dates and a `primary` flag rather than four attributes, the governance artifact is an optional Bakobo profile that Sam's own fixtures do not reference, and Bakobo's presentation schemas now require a holder-owned registry. [Section 1](#06-governance-hook) had said the "binding acceptance" sentence recurs verbatim across org-vet, citation and SEDI; it is now restated per family. Four quotations from the applied schema corpus — the GCD `gfw` description, the SEDI image-locator rationale, the SEDI mDL-alignment sentence and the FAA "issuer-scoped, not systemic" line — were not verbatim at either fork's pin and have been replaced with the source's words or rewritten as summary. And one attribution was wrong: `sda.md` is Hardman's paper, not Origin documentation.

#### Contested or assumption-laden {#06-contested}

(1) The "no arbiter" claim is a Layer-1 claim only; at Layer 2 an EGF like GLEIF's is an authority, and a reviewer may fairly argue that the ecosystem's dependence on GLEIF concentrates trust even if the cryptography does not — KERI's rebuttal is that this authority is opt-in, per-vertical, and cryptographically bound rather than globally imposed, but the concentration is real. (2) The migration-cost advantage is architecturally sound at the protocol level but partly offset by a treacherous implementation-level code-table surface (keripy-knowledge 31-landmines.md > L5, L6, L18; keripy-knowledge 30-invariants.md > A. CESR wire-format & sizing) — and both halves of the evidence for it are weaker than they look. The "couple of hours" figure is a single first-hand report of a conversation with the protocol's author (kspqs.md), usable for status and intent and not for effort or design, describing work that is not in keripy at `b8f60166b`. The landmines are knowledge-base observations at pin `9489ac9bd`, whose code baseline is 493 commits behind current keripy and a `2.0.0-dev6` line against `2.1.0-dev1`; they are discipline, not a description of the code as it stands, and the framing that a Falcon pull request is imminent is simply false — the work has not started, and the knowledge base's own plan blocks it on resolving two conflicting in-repo design documents ([section 6](#06-kb-scope)). (2a) A related and newly sharp point: KERI's post-quantum story is entirely [spec-next] plus one unmerged fork branch. The standardizing CESR line has zero post-quantum codes; no shipped implementation has any; the forward branch's codes cannot be cited as normative and may not merge in their current form, since the branches are divergent in both directions. The architectural agility claim survives all of that untouched — it is a claim about what adding a code costs, not about whether one has been added — but any statement that KERI has post-quantum support is wrong at every pin this chapter names. (2b) The Dossier schema-SAID recompute ([section 6](#06-dossier-said-recompute)) is the counterexample a reviewer should press on the migration argument: an editorial prose fix forced a wire-format break, because content-addressing admits no such thing as a change too small to move a reference. (3) Cross-ecosystem semantic agreement is explicitly a human/governance achievement, not a protocol guarantee; the protocol fixes type-identity, not meaning-agreement, and any claim of "semantic interop" is really "we both aligned to mDL." (4) Backward compatibility across the four implementations rests on convention and vigilance (spec-as-contract, generated admin types, CHANGELOG parity) rather than shared code, with the independent message-signature implementations and hand-maintained CESR tables as the drift-prone seams (raw/10 > 7. Cross-language / cross-implementation interop invariants (keripy ↔ KERIA ↔ signify-ts ↔ SignifyPy)). The one hard test available this cycle came out well but proves less than it appears to: keripy and upstream signify-ts agree about the post-quantum code table in that neither has it, and the standardizing CESR line defines nothing for them to carry, so the seam held by inaction rather than by process ([section 7](#06-pq-parity-test)). (4a) A second, smaller instance of the same pattern: the KERI specification's Bootstrap Configuration section says "Implementations have converged on three named buckets," and the two implementations checked at their current pins do not support that reading — KERIA reads `iurls` and `durls` but has no `wurls` at all, signify-ts has no bootstrap-bucket implementation, and neither serves a `/.well-known/` route in either the old or the new path shape ([section 6](#06-bucket-convergence)). A specification sentence in the descriptive mood is an empirical claim, and this one is unconfirmed at the pins this chapter can reach. (4b) The four implementations are not on one keripy line: KERIA pins `keri==1.2.14` at `928ce26a4` while keripy `main` is `2.1.0-dev`, so keripy-`main` evidence does not describe KERIA deployments, and signify-ts was still breaking the hex sequence-number invariant until a fix at `5a174b545` ([section 7](#06-keripy-lines)). (4c) Layers that are each correct can fail to compose. At keripy `80f77b73b` a registry-backed Age credential cannot be granted with any aggregate element withheld [code] (in `acdc/ipexing.py`, which no keripy command calls, and exercised by no test), so the presentation-registry rule withdraws the selective disclosure SEDI's privacy story leans on ([section 4](#06-layers-not-composing)); the schema Bakobo validates and the protocol keripy enforces disagree about the age credential's central use case, and which gives way is open. (4d) SEDI's governance artifact and its active credential disagree: `noOverAssertion` lists four endorsed attributes, Core endorses `legalPresenceStatus` on the strength of an uncitable email ([section 3](#06-sedi-governance-tension)). Separately, the authority chain that issues SEDI credentials is a credential chain built with plain `incept`, not KERI delegation, which a reviewer looking for `dip` events will misread. (4e) The applied schema corpus has forked: bakobo/schema `cfcbdcc7a` and public-schema `95a07e544` now publish different organization-vetting credentials (`org-vet` 2.0.0 against `org-identity`) and different dossier bases, neither matching the Dossier specification's base SAID, and inside public-schema the vLEI and telco families take opposite positions on far-schema pinning (see [section 2](#06-arbitration), [section 5](#06-far-schema-pinning) and [section 6](#06-three-dossier-bases)). Any citation of "the schema" for these must name the fork. (5) The scorecard's SD-JWT/OIDC4VC column is sourced from KERI-partisan comparison papers; its technical claims check out, its evaluative framing is advocacy. (6) The honest external gaps apply to the whole ecosystem story: KERI's formal literature "remains thin" (the strongest KAWA analysis is a non-peer-reviewed 2025 Master's thesis), and "legal and regulatory recognition... [is] still developing... constraints of youth, not of architecture" — X.509 has eIDAS legal standing KERI lacks, "a gap of legal recognition, not of technical capability" (wtbo.md > 5. Evaluating KERI: Real Tradeoffs, Honestly Stated; wtbo.md > 6. The Transition Problem: A Comparison of Trajectories; wtbo.md > Notes, note [c]). A governance-and-ecosystem critique that lands is one that targets these seams; one that faults KERI-core for lacking unlinkability, or faults the protocol for not achieving semantic agreement, is aiming at the wrong layer.

# 07 — Shibboleths and Anti-Patterns {#07-shibboleths}

## Thesis {#07-thesis}

Every technical community has shibboleths — framings that instantly mark a speaker as an insider or an outsider — and KERI's are unusually load-bearing, because the whole architecture is a deliberate, point-by-point correction of the priors that PKI, IAM, blockchain, and mainstream verifiable-credentials work install in the people who grew up on them. A reviewer who reasons from those priors will produce critiques that KERI's core contributors recognize instantly as category errors: criticizing a duplicity-evident system for not being duplicity-resistant, asking who the trusted authority is, wanting global consensus or finality, treating a witness as a CA, treating revocation as a blocklist, treating a credential as a signed envelope, or treating "decentralized" as a synonym for "on a ledger." This section is a catalog of those outsider-tells. For each, it states the generic framing the outsider brings, explains precisely why that framing is a category error in KERI's own terms, gives the KERI-correct reframing, and cites the source. It closes with the single most important habit an adversarial reviewer of this codebase can cultivate — the reflex to check what the code actually enforces before believing what the prose claims — because KERI's implementations contain real, documented gaps between the doctrine and the machine. The goal is inoculation: after this section, a reviewer should be able to hear their own PKI/blockchain/OAuth reflexes firing and catch them before they reach the page.

## Status {#07-status}

This chapter is about framings rather than about pins, so it carries markers only in the handful of places where a tier is load-bearing — where the correction to a shibboleth lives on one branch of a specification and not the other, or where the evidence is code rather than text. Two applications of the rule against upgrading a marker bite in this chapter: text that exists only on a `v1.1` branch is not [spec] however obviously it reads as a correction, and an unmerged branch on a personal fork is not [code].

---

## 1. How a shibboleth works here, and why it matters {#07-how-shibboleths-work}

A shibboleth is not merely jargon. It is a framing whose shape encodes an assumption. When an outsider says "how does KERI revoke a certificate," the words "certificate" and "revoke" smuggle in the entire X.509 model — an issued artifact with a validity window, a separate revocation list, a phone-home check — none of which exists in KERI. The question cannot be answered on its own terms; it must first be reframed, and the need to reframe it is the tell.

This matters for a review panel for two reasons. First, a critique built on a smuggled assumption is not just wrong, it is unfalsifiable from inside the outsider's model — the reviewer will keep finding "missing" features that were deliberately never there. The security-analysis corpus makes this the first rule of its analysis method: an analyst "MUST restate the claim verbatim... If you cannot do so, stop and ask," and must "name the objective function first," precisely because "outsider critiques smuggle in unstated invulnerability goals" (standard-analysis.md > 0). Second, KERI's own advocates are candid that some outsider critiques survive reframing — the observer/watcher infrastructure really is immature, the formal literature really is thin — so a reviewer who cannot separate the category errors from the genuine residuals will either dismiss KERI wholesale or swallow it wholesale, and both are failures of the same discipline (dg-c02-claude.md, sections 5-6; wtbo.md, sections 5-6).

The catalog below is organized by the outsider's home domain, because that is how the reflex fires. Each entry follows the same shape: the framing, why it is a category error, the reframing, all cited.

---

## 2. PKI / X.509 / CA tells {#07-pki-tells}

### 2.1 "Who is the trusted authority / who vouches for the identifier?" {#07-trusted-authority}

#### The framing {#07-trusted-authority-framing}

In PKI the root of trust is an administrator: a CA signs a certificate that asserts a binding between an identifier and a key, and relying parties trust the CA's operational process. The outsider reflexively asks who plays that role in KERI.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-trusted-authority-error}

KERI's foundational move is to eliminate the role, not to fill it. "The fundamental flaw... is the separation of the identifier from the cryptographic keys that control it"; in X.509 the binding is "merely an assertion — a digital certificate — signed by a third party," creating "a root of trust that is external to the identity itself" (keri-primer.md > 1). The KERI spec states the same flaw as a verifiability failure: the CA's certificate "is not made with the controlling keypairs of the identifier but made with keypairs controlled by the CA," giving "evidence of authenticity of the assignment... but not evidence of the veracity of the mapping" (KERI spec > Overcoming existing security overlay flaws, L81).

#### The reframing {#07-trusted-authority-reframing}

"The identifier is the root of trust" (keri-primer.md > 1.3). An AID is self-certifying — cryptographically derived from its own controlling keys — so its authenticity "can be verified without any external authority" by replaying its KEL (cr-ad-trust.md > 4). There is no authority to vouch for it because the mathematics vouches for it. Asking "who is the CA" is like asking who notarizes a hash: the question presumes an administrative layer the design deletes.

### 2.2 "The strength of the system is the rigor of the CA's vetting." {#07-ca-vetting}

#### The framing {#07-ca-vetting-framing}

PKI experts locate assurance in how carefully the issuer vets applicants. The reflex is to evaluate KERI by asking how rigorously its issuers vet.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-ca-vetting-error}

It targets the wrong locus of risk. "*Certificate authorities aren't the ones that choose or manage the keys in certs.* Holders of certs do that. It's the key management of *holders* that's the ubiquitous locus of the risk" (x509-prob.md > Governance). The CA vets an applicant once; thereafter the security of every certificate depends on the holder's opaque, unauditable key custody — the "missile silo" guarded by "one opaquely managed secret" (x509-prob.md > Governance). All the CA machinery "guarantees... is that someone provided a public key before the certificate was created" (x509-prob.md > Governance).

#### The reframing {#07-ca-vetting-reframing}

KERI moves assurance into observable key management: pre-rotation, weighted multisig, witnessing, and anchoring are all declared in the public KEL and are continuously verifiable. "KERI's real innovation in multisig is less about inventing and more about exposing: multisig is optional and infinitely variable, but defining and following policy about it is required" (keri-primer.md > 2.4). The right question is not "how good is the vetting" but "what does the key-state history actually show, and can I replay it myself."

### 2.3 "Renew the credential / rotate to a new certificate." {#07-renewal}

#### The framing {#07-renewal-framing}

Certificates expire and are renewed; a compromised key is handled by issuing a fresh, unrelated certificate.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-renewal-error}

It conflates identity with privilege. "Identity means *sameness*: the thing that holds constant across contexts" (wtbo.md > 1); "An organization incorporated in 1975 doesn't renew its identity every ninety days" (cr-ad-trust.md > 1). X.509's mandatory Validity field means "Evidence of identity expires by design, not by necessity" (cr-ad-trust.md > 1). Renewal, moreover, "proves less than it appears": it "demonstrates that a CA is willing to re-assert a binding, not that the underlying key was rotated, that the old key was retired, or that any meaningful change in key management occurred" (wtbo.md > 1). Re-issuing after compromise "is essentially the same as starting over by creating a brand-new independent mapping" (KERI spec, L83), with "no cryptographically Verifiable way to link the new... key(s) to the prior" (KERI spec, L83).

#### The reframing {#07-renewal-reframing}

A transferable AID persists across every key change: "The identifier string remains constant even as the keys change... Identity survives key rotation" (keri-primer.md > 2.1). Rotation is a linked event in the KEL, cryptographically chained to the prior state, not a fresh unrelated artifact. "Renewing an *identity* is a non-sequitur" (x509-prob.md > Lifespans). The dynamic thing that should expire — a privilege, a role grant — is carried by a separate ACDC, not by the identity itself.

### 2.4 "Pin the key / pin the certificate for continuity." {#07-pinning}

#### The framing {#07-pinning-framing}

To get continuity across a connection, pin the key you saw last time.

#### Why it is a category error / the tell {#07-pinning-error}

In 2026 Google Cloud advised customers not to pin certificates because pinning "will cause your application to break during routine certificate rotations" (x509-prob.md > Prerotation). That advice is itself the tell: "there is no cryptographic thread joining the old key to the new one, so a relying party that pinned the old key pinned nothing durable — the only continuity on offer is the CA's say-so" (x509-prob.md > Prerotation; wtbo.md > 1). The industry's own guidance concedes that X.509 continuity is administrative, not cryptographic.

#### The reframing {#07-pinning-reframing}

"Prerotation is exactly what would let a relying party commit to a durable cryptographic anchor *and* survive the rotation" (x509-prob.md > Prerotation). A relying party pins the AID — which is stable across all rotations — and follows the KEL forward; the durable anchor and rotation survival are the same fact. Notably, the fix here is to "trust *more* administrative anchors, not fewer" in PKI, versus KERI's single cryptographic anchor (wtbo.md > 1).

### 2.5 "Trust ultimately bottoms out somewhere administrative anyway." {#07-administrative-bottom}

#### The framing {#07-administrative-bottom-framing}

All trust chains end at some human authority; KERI just moves the humans around.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-administrative-bottom-error}

The claim is about where the chain bottoms out, and the answer is genuinely different in kind. "CT's chain of assurance bottoms out in administrators... KERI's bottoms out in mathematics: the self-certifying identifier derives from the initial public key, and the KEL's validity can be checked by anyone who replays its hash chain, without querying any authority" (wtbo.md > 3). This is not rhetorical: the KEL replay requires no trusted third party at any step.

#### The reframing {#07-administrative-bottom-reframing}

Trust bottoms out in the controller's custody of its own keys plus the soundness of the hash and signature primitives — assumptions A1 (cryptographic soundness) and the controller's key secrecy — and nothing else (background.md > 4.6). Governance and reputation still matter for veracity (see [section 9](#07-semantic-tells)), but the authenticity chain is closed cryptographically. A reviewer should insist on this distinction: KERI does not claim to abolish human judgment, only to remove it from the authentication path.

### 2.6 "Publishing the same AID at several well-knowns strengthens the AID binding." {#07-multiple-well-knowns}

#### The framing {#07-multiple-well-knowns-framing}

Corroboration across independent sources makes a binding stronger. This is the reflex behind multi-perspective domain validation, DNS CAA checks, and the ordinary advice to look a fingerprint up in a second place — and it fires hard on KERI's OOBA pattern, where a controller publishes the same AID at two or more `/.well-known/oobi/{aid}` URLs on independently controlled namespaces. The outsider reads agreement across the namespaces as evidence about the identifier.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-multiple-well-knowns-error}

The binding was never in the well-knowns to be strengthened. [spec] The KERI specification states the limit itself, and states it as a limit: "This pattern does not change the trust model of an OOBI", because "the AID binding produced by resolution is still cryptographically verified through KERI in the usual way", and "The multi-factor arrangement governs only whether the recipient is willing to bootstrap from the OOBIs at all" (KERI spec > OOBI with MFA, L2838 @`fbdd4a615`; present verbatim on `v1.1` too). This is the [section 2.5](#07-administrative-bottom) error in a new costume: administrative corroboration reasserting itself where a cryptographic anchor already closes the chain. An OOBI's worst case was never a false binding — "an OOBI may be part of a DDOS attack but not as part of a service endpoint cache poison attack" (KERI spec > OOBI Forwarding, L2831) — so agreement across namespaces cannot improve a property that resolution verifies unconditionally.

#### The reframing {#07-multiple-well-knowns-reframing}

OOBA is a willingness-to-bootstrap control, and the thing it multiplies is the attacker's cost of denying or flooding discovery, not the confidence in what discovery returns. The independence requirement makes this legible: it is required of the delivery channel and not merely of the namespace — "Each well-known OOBI URL is delivered to the recipient through a channel whose compromise is independent of the others" (L2838) — so two URLs in one email are one factor, which is a statement about channels, not about identifiers. The tell to catch is any sentence in which the count of well-knowns appears as an input to an authenticity judgment. Note also that the recipient's threshold has no encoding anywhere and no owner in the protocol, deliberately: the controller declares its witness threshold in its KEL because that threshold is about accountability, and declares nothing about `wurls` because this one is about the recipient's own willingness.

---

## 3. Revocation, CRL, OCSP, and phone-home tells {#07-revocation-tells}

### 3.1 "How does KERI revoke — where is the CRL / OCSP responder?" {#07-crl-ocsp}

#### The framing {#07-crl-ocsp-framing}

Revocation is a separate subsystem: a list you download (CRL) or an endpoint you query at verification time (OCSP).

#### Why it is a category error {#07-crl-ocsp-error}

There is no separate revocation layer to point at. Key state "lives in the KEL" and is "continuously current"; a revoked or abandoned identifier is signaled inside the log itself by rotating to a null next-key list (cr-ad-trust.md, sections 2 and 4; KERI spec, L340). Worse, the outsider's model is actively criticized: OCSP "requires the client to query a central responder for every validation, creating a privacy leak (the CA knows every site you visit)," and when the responder is offline browsers "fail open," so "The system is most vulnerable precisely when it is most needed" (keri-primer.md > 1.1; wtbo.md > 2). CRLs are "heavy, bandwidth-intensive... scale poorly" (keri-primer.md > 1.1).

#### The reframing {#07-crl-ocsp-reframing}

For key state, revocation is just the current head of the replayed KEL. For credential status, KERI uses a TEL (Transaction Event Log) whose state is anchored in the issuer's KEL, checked "without privacy leaks or 'fail open' risks" (cr-ad-trust.md > 3). The ground truth is even sharper than the prose: the reference verifier, on encountering a revoked credential, does not raise — it logs and continues so it can "save a revoked credential"; revocation is a TEL state transition (`Ilks.rev`/`brv`), queried from the TEL, not a delete or a blocklist (keripy vdr/verifying.py, L129-132; raw/09 section 4).

### 3.2 "A registry / status endpoint is consulted at verification time." {#07-status-endpoint}

#### The framing {#07-status-endpoint-framing}

Verification legitimately reaches out to an authority to confirm current status.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-status-endpoint-error}

Any verification-time callback reintroduces exactly the runtime trust dependency that end-verifiability exists to eliminate. "A registry consulted at verification time is a phone-home in disguise" (sda.md > 7). The ACDC spec builds the rejection into its architecture: the Observer/Registrar split lets a Validator check an ACDC's status "without exposing a point of validation (PoV)" and syncs on state changes rather than at presentation — "no forced phone home validation" (ACDC spec > TEL Registrars and Observers, L1693). This is a direct, named rejection of the OCSP/CRL model.

#### The reframing {#07-status-endpoint-reframing}

"Verification must succeed from the credential and key-state alone, and any registry or log is an issuance-time and audit-time convenience, never a verification-time dependency" (sda.md > 7). Applied design corroborates: a download URL in a credential is "phone-home by another name... and creates an availability chokepoint," which is why SEDI commits an image by digest and has the holder carry the bytes rather than linking to a resolvable location (sedi-id/index.md > Image). The tell to watch for in a deployment review is any credential field that resolves to a live endpoint at verification time.

### 3.3 "Certificate Transparency already solved this." {#07-certificate-transparency}

#### The framing {#07-certificate-transparency-framing}

Append-only public logs plus monitors give detection; KERI is reinventing CT.

#### Why it is a partial truth that becomes a category error {#07-certificate-transparency-error}

The corpus is explicit that CT and KERI share DNA — both are "fundamentally detection-oriented. Neither prevents a bad actor" (wtbo.md > 3), both use append-only hash-chained structures and signed receipts. But CT "is a detection mechanism, not a prevention mechanism; fraudulent certificates may be usable for a time" and, decisively, it "redistributes administrative trust rather than eliminating it" (keri-primer.md > 1.1; wtbo.md, abstract). The ultimate arbiter of CT remains "a handful of browser vendors" with "immediate, global effect... no formal appeals process" (wtbo.md > 1, Note [b]). "The result is not a decentralized trust hierarchy. It is a more elaborate one" (cr-ad-trust.md > 2).

#### The reframing {#07-certificate-transparency-reframing}

KERI keeps CT's detection orientation but changes what detection bottoms out in. "Unlike certificate transparency, KERI enables the detection of Duplicity in the Key state via nonrepudiable cryptographic proofs of Duplicity, not merely the detection of inconsistency... that MAY or MAY NOT be duplicitous" (KERI spec, L85). The witness/watcher split is the CT analogue (witnesses ≈ CT logs, watchers ≈ monitors), but a KERI watcher makes "an observation — surfacing cryptographic evidence," whereas a browser root program makes "an enforcement decision... with immediate global consequences" (wtbo.md > 4). Detection without re-centralized enforcement is the distinction; a reviewer who says "just use CT" has missed the re-centralization critique.

---

### 3.4 "Revoke just the compromised copy of a bulk-issued credential." {#07-bulk-copy-revocation}

#### The framing {#07-bulk-copy-revocation-framing}

A bulk-issued set gives each verifier its own copy, so a copy compromised at one verifier can be revoked while the copies presented elsewhere keep verifying, and that granularity is a feature.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-bulk-copy-revocation-error}

It conflates three different repairs. The specification's editor answered exactly this framing [proposal]: "An issuer when it revokes authority revokes it universally. In a bulk issued set this means that all members of the set MUST be revoked." What a holder can lose at one verifier is a key, not a credential, and "if the keys get compromised then the keystate is changed not the ACDC state" (keripy GitHub > #1574, comment of 2026-08-07, R-042, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1574#discussioncomment-17938568). The framing also confuses the two kinds of registry: an issuer registry tracks the credential's state, while "A presentation registry on the other hand is not tracking ACDC state, but is merely logging presentations". Per-copy revocation is the X.509 instinct, revoke the artifact that leaked, carried into a system where the artifact is not what leaked.

#### The reframing {#07-bulk-copy-revocation-reframing}

Three events, three remedies. Withdrawn authority: the issuer revokes every member of the set, and the registries' state moves in lock step even though vacuous updates keep their event histories uncorrelated. A compromised issuee key: that one AID rotates, and the other AIDs in the set are uninvolved. A compromised private salt from which the whole set's keys were derived: per the same comment, "the whole set has to be abandoned". The property that makes the middle case work, repairing either party's key state without touching the authority the credential grants, is the one [section 6.1](#07-signed-envelope) credits to anchoring over bare signatures. This is the editor's account in a discussion thread, not specification text; the bulk-issuance section of the ACDC specification was not checked for it here.

## 4. Blockchain / consensus / global-ordering tells {#07-blockchain-tells}

### 4.1 "You need a ledger / global consensus / total ordering." {#07-global-consensus}

#### The framing {#07-global-consensus-framing}

Decentralized identity needs a blockchain so that everyone agrees on one history.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-global-consensus-error}

Global total ordering across identifiers is an explicit non-goal (background.md > 1.3). The reasoning is precise: key events are "idempotent authorization operations as opposed to non-idempotent account balance decrement or increment operations. Total or global ordering may be critical for non-idempotency, whereas local ordering may be sufficient for idempotency" (KERI spec > KAWA insight, L1836). Because "the controller is the sole source of truth for the creation of any and all key events, it alone, is sufficient to order its own key events" (KERI spec, L1836). "KERI rejects the need for global consensus regarding identity. Instead, it uses microledgers called key event logs (KELs)" (keri-primer.md > 2). Del Giudice-background readers who "interpret 'not duplicity-resistant' as a criticism" are "Misunderstanding KERI as 'weaker than a blockchain' when it solves a different problem" (dg-c03-claude.md > 6).

#### The reframing {#07-global-consensus-reframing}

Each AID has its own microledger; "Event 5 for Identifier A must come after Event 4 for Identifier A, but it has no required ordering relative to Event 5 for Identifier B" (keri-primer.md > 2). This yields horizontal scaling, cross-jurisdiction ease, and decayed hacking incentives (a breach is scoped to one identifier). Where a ledger is ever used it is only a last-resort tiebreaker in the total-compromise case, requiring "minimal use of a distributed consensus ledger" (KERI spec, L1888). The reference implementation embodies this: recovery forks the KEL and keeps the disputed branch visible (keripy eventing.py, L3143-3149; raw/09 section 4) — the opposite of a single globally-agreed chain.

### 4.2 "Anchoring signatures in time sounds like a blockchain." {#07-anchoring-not-blockchain}

#### The framing {#07-anchoring-not-blockchain-framing}

To prove when a signature was made you need a total order, hence a chain.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-anchoring-not-blockchain-error}

The anchoring requirement is strictly weaker than a ledger. "We don't need to know the relative order of two signing events — only how any one event relates to its key state. That means no total ordering, and no cumbersome consensus algorithm... no permissioning problem, no big central *anything* in the sky, no scale or performance bottlenecks, and no regulatory problems with data locality, privacy, or erasure" (was.md > Solution). KERI implements it with "tiny, identifier-specific files called KELs... and TELs" that anchor the hashes of signed events (was.md > Solution).

#### The reframing {#07-anchoring-not-blockchain-reframing}

Anchoring establishes the position of a signature relative to its own identifier's key-state history, which is all that is needed to defeat the retrograde attack (see [section 11](#07-retrograde-attack)). "Sounds like blockchain" is a lazy tell precisely because it assumes the strong property (global order) when only the weak one (per-identifier order) is required.

### 4.3 "Immutability requires a chain." {#07-immutability}

#### The framing {#07-immutability-framing}

Tamper-evidence and immutability are blockchain properties.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-immutability-error}

A SAID gives tamper-evident content-addressing and immutability with no ledger and no consensus: "a SAID will verify if and only if its encompassing serialization has not been mutated, which makes the content immutable" (CESR spec > SAID, L1196). CESR is "a streaming format, not a chain" (raw/02 section 15).

#### The reframing {#07-immutability-reframing}

Immutability is a property of a cryptographic commitment, not of a distributed agreement protocol. "A Merkle inclusion proof establishes placement in a history. A SAID establishes identity of content" (acdc-and-mtc.md > 3.2) — different proof obligations, only one of which needs a chain.

### 4.4 "But then how do you honor the right to be forgotten?" {#07-right-to-be-forgotten}

#### The framing {#07-right-to-be-forgotten-framing}

A shared immutable ledger and GDPR erasure are fundamentally incompatible, so KERI must have the same problem.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-right-to-be-forgotten-error}

KERI's "non-intertwined trust bases" mean "a given identifier's data may be erased and truly forgotten" (keri.one homepage). Because KELs are per-identifier microledgers, "'forgetting' an identifier requires a hard fork of the entire chain" only on a blockchain; in KERI a user can delete "their specific Key Event Log... without disrupting the global ecosystem" (keri-primer.md > 3.5). And ACDC payloads are held off-chain: the KEL stores only anchors (hashes), so deleting the payload "leaves an irreversible hash; identity history intact, personal data removed" (keri-primer.md > 3.5).

#### The reframing {#07-right-to-be-forgotten-reframing}

RUN replaces CRUD: "there is no Delete. Instead of Delete, Peers Nullify" — but naive total erasure "exposes the data controller to a replay attack of erased data," so a nullified record is kept as an invalidity marker while its confidential payload is discarded (KERI spec > RUN off the CRUD, L2870, L2927). Erasure is a first-class outcome by construction, not a fatal contradiction.

---

## 5. OAuth / OIDC / SAML / IAM / perimeter / federation tells {#07-iam-tells}

### 5.1 "Authentication precedes authorization as one indivisible login." {#07-authn-before-authz}

#### The framing {#07-authn-before-authz-framing}

A user logs in once (auth), gets a session/token, and is thereafter authorized (authz) by presenting that token — the sentry-at-the-gate model.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-authn-before-authz-error}

This is "a natural consequence of a perimeter-oriented mindset... all the way back to... a sentry challenged someone approaching the gate" (ASAAU > Appendix). The perimeter re-challenge is satisfied merely by producing "a token that the sentry gave them," and internal challengers "don't do any deep checking of their own... because the token is too lossy to support deep checking anyway. The token is thus faster but less safe and far more opaque than verification at the perimeter" (OS > 1). The named technologies — "IAM, SAML, OAuth, OIDC, LDAP, AD, API keys — are mostly embodiments of perimeter security" (OS > 1).

#### The reframing {#07-authn-before-authz-reframing}

Zero-trust: "assume everything — outside OR inside the perimeter — is unsafe until proven otherwise" (OS > 1). Every request is independently signed and verified at every hop; there is no "trust after entry" (GOC > 2). Authentication and authorization are partially dissociated into Attribute-Based Authorization: "someone can receive permission if they can prove certain characteristics, even if a sentry does not (yet, or maybe ever) know who they are" (ASAAU > Appendix). The voting-booth example (prove citizenship, not identity) and the pharmacy example (any licensed doctor may browse; authenticate only when accountability attaches) show authz preceding auth.

### 5.2 "Use a bearer token / session / API key to call the service." {#07-bearer-tokens}

#### The framing {#07-bearer-tokens-framing}

Hold a bearer credential; possession is authorization.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-bearer-tokens-error}

A bearer token is "a signet ring handed out for an errand": "Possession of an API key... makes the holder indistinguishable from the account it belongs to, free to do anything that account can" (sda.md > 1). It is opaque, replayable, long-lived, and exfiltratable from the server. The applied doctrine is categorical: "We do not use sessions, cookies, tokens, JWTs, OAuth, OIDC, SAML, or any similar technologies to secure calls" (ASAAU, item 0; GOC > 2).

#### The reframing {#07-bearer-tokens-reframing}

Identity is an AID; proof is a fresh signature per request over the method, path, resource header, and a timestamp (RFC 9421 message signatures) (GOC > 2; raw/10 section 7a). "A stolen header set can't be replayed against a different method/path, and there is no long-lived secret to exfiltrate from the server" (raw/10 section 4). The signet-ring/errand distinction is the doctrine: "The key authorizes an act; the ring authorizes a person to stand in your place" — never hand over the ring for an errand (sda.md > 1).

#### The boundary {#07-bearer-tokens-boundary}

The boundary runs in both directions and must be stated whenever this row is used. The signature is better than a bearer token in two respects a token cannot match: the stolen header set is scoped to one method and path pair, and to one key state. It is not better in the respect an outsider will assume, because neither side of the channel enforces freshness, and on that one pair the captured request therefore replays indefinitely. [code] In KERIA at `7e685edaa`, `Signify-Timestamp` is folded into the signed byte string alongside every other covered field and is never parsed into a datetime — `fromIso8601` does not appear in `authing.py` at all, and the file's only two time calls are outbound stamps. The RFC-9421 `expires` and `nonce` params are appended to the signature-params string, so they are cryptographically bound, but `expires` is never compared to a clock and there is no replay cache: nothing in `src/keria` stores a seen nonce (raw/10 section 2). [code] signify-ts at `ffba8406e` is the same on the client half — `authing.ts` folds `input.expires` into the params string and never compares it, and its ESSR path checks only that a timestamp is present, which is a presence check and not a freshness check (raw/10 section 2). What the signature buys is therefore request integrity and origin authentication, not replay protection, and what retires a stolen header set is key rotation, not expiry. The fields needed to enforce freshness are present and signed, so enforcement would be a verifier change with no wire change — which is a reason not to read this as a design flaw, and not a reason to read "the fields exist" as "the protocol resists replay."

### 5.3 "The server is trusted infrastructure; the cloud holds my keys." {#07-custodial-cloud}

#### The framing {#07-custodial-cloud-framing}

A cloud agent, KMS, or HSM-as-a-service holds and uses your private keys and is the authority (custodial-wallet / cloud-KMS mental model).

#### Why it is a category error {#07-custodial-cloud-error}

In the KERIA/Signify architecture the cloud agent "never has access to the decryption keys" and holds "only the public keys and blake3 hash of the next keys" in cleartext (signify-ts README; raw/10 section 2). "Agents... don't have the secrets of the client" (keria README). The custodian is "a blind store + relay, not a signer." Inverting the usual asymmetry, the client authenticates the server: the agent signs every response, and the client rejects a response "from a different remote agent" or one whose signature fails (signify-ts clienting.ts, L240-255).

#### The reframing {#07-custodial-cloud-reframing}

"Signing at the edge": key generation and event signing happen on the client; the cloud does event storage (encrypted) and validation only (signify-ts README; raw/10 section 1). Externally the agent is "just another KERI node relaying edge-signed CESR" and "contributes no authority to the controller's events" (raw/10 section 4). A cloud agent adding authority is the CA/federation prior reasserting itself.

### 5.4 "Federation decentralizes." {#07-federation}

#### The framing {#07-federation-framing}

Centralization is cured by federating — a hierarchy of trust domains.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-federation-error}

KERI people see federation as compounding the disease, not curing it. Centralization "provides a locus for abuse, and creates silos. This is typically solved by aggressive federation (centralization hierarchies)," and "When you combine these 'solutions', you get the worst of all worlds, not the best" (OS > 1). Trust registries get the same verdict: "a band aid; they just move the centralization back to a different level of the architecture" (x509-prob.md).

#### The reframing {#07-federation-reframing}

Decentralization comes from self-certifying roots plus chaining, not from federated hierarchies. In the vLEI graph "A verifier receiving an employee's credential can traverse the chain back to GLEIF without consulting a trust registry. The entire graph is self-certifying" (acdc-vc-diff.md > Real-World Validation). Chaining "eliminates the need for trust registries" (x509-prob.md).

### 5.5 "Secure the pipe (VPN/TLS) and the data inside is safe." {#07-secure-pipe}

#### The framing {#07-secure-pipe-framing}

Transport-layer security (TLS/VPN) protects data end to end.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-secure-pipe-error}

"The walls of a pipe may be a secure perimeter, but every place where a pipe ends is a gap"; a realistic routed path has "at least 8" joints where "data is siphoned off, trust rules change, or trust input data changes while holding rules constant" (ASAAU > 3.6). This is not hypothetical: SSL-visibility appliances deliberately MITM TLS, and eIDAS reforms "appear to be planning legislation that allows the same attack to be carried out by national governments" (ASAAU > 3.6). And "Secure pipes protect data in motion, but not data at rest" (ASAAU > 3.6).

#### The reframing {#07-secure-pipe-reframing}

"Move Security with the Data, Not the Transport" (GOC > 8) — sign (and where needed encrypt) the payload itself, so authenticity travels with the data through every joint. This is message-level security (IETF MLS) and ToIP's Trust Spanning Protocol, not transport-level. The honest caveat, which a reviewer should preserve: KERI deployments still keep TLS for cheap defense-in-depth, but "do not expend massive effort guaranteeing that our secure pipes are perfectly leak-proof" (ASAAU > 3.6).

---

## 6. SD-JWT / W3C-VC / DID "decentralized" drift tells {#07-vc-drift-tells}

This family is the subtlest, because the outsiders here believe they are already doing decentralized identity. The KERI position is that SD-JWT, W3C-VC, and most DID methods imported PKI/OAuth assumptions and thereby re-created centralization one level up while losing fidelity.

### 6.1 "A credential is a signed envelope (paired signature)." {#07-signed-envelope}

#### The framing {#07-signed-envelope-framing}

A verifiable credential is data plus a `proof` block; the signature travels with the container because the format says so (W3C-VC `proof`, JWT bundle, X.509 `tbsCertificate` + `signature`).

#### Why it is a category error {#07-signed-envelope-error}

A paired signature binds to the container context and only to the current verification moment. ACDCs are not directly signed at all: they are "bound to the Issuer's Key State... and the Issuer's Key State is signed. This enables the Key State of the Issuer to change independently of the ACDC state" (ACDC spec > Binding to Key State, L1673). The explicit contrast: in schemes "where the credentials are signed directly... a key rotation forces all the credentials signed with a given set of keys to be revoked; otherwise, a key compromise would enable the compromiser to issue... forged [credentials]" (ACDC spec, L1675).

#### The reframing {#07-signed-envelope-reframing}

ACDCs use anchored signatures: a provable KEL association independent of container context. Validity is judged against "the issuer key state AS OF its KEL anchor's sequence position, not current key state or wall-clock" (keripy-knowledge invariant H1; keri-primer.md > 3.3). NIST SP 800-102 is the grounding: a signed message "provides no assurance that the private key was used to sign the message at that time" (keri-primer.md > 3.3). Anchoring removes that ambiguity without an external timestamp authority.

#### The citation to hand an outsider, and two guards on it {#07-signed-envelope-citation}

The Dossier specification swept its own text for this exact conflation and now states the correction more flatly than the ACDC spec does. [spec] "A dossier is not a signed document. The issuer does not compute a signature over the dossier ACDC and attach that signature to it as proof of authenticity" (Dossier spec > How a Dossier Is Issued: Anchoring, Not Attached Signatures, L13-14 @`b9227753c`); "The signature exists on the anchoring key event, not on the dossier. What binds the issuer to the dossier is the anchor: a commitment to the dossier's SAID" (L27-28). The schemas carry it too, which is the useful part for an implementer: an endorsement "is authenticated by anchoring... It is not signed and carries no attached signature" (Dossier spec schemas/endorsement.json, `description`, L5). It is the better citation for an outsider than the ACDC spec's Binding to Key State section because it argues from key rotation and log properties rather than from ACDC internals: an attached signature can be checked "only against the key that produced it, and nothing in the signature itself establishes when it was made" (L32-34), so "once that key is rotated or compromised, a verifier has no way to distinguish a signature made while the key was authoritative from one made afterward" (L34-36). Two guards, because a reviewer who arrives at this row from the slogan will over-read it. First, the partition is drawn on lifespan, not on artifact kind: the same spec says "key events are signed, and so are the short-lived transactional objects... Dossiers, endorsements, and other ACDCs are anchored" (L45-55), so "ACDCs are never signed" overstates the doctrine and misstates its reason. Second, an attached signature is explicitly permitted in the ephemeral case — a dossier that "lives only for the duration of a single interaction, and that will never be verified after the issuer's next key rotation, MAY be authenticated by an attached signature" (L59-62) — guarded by the sentence that makes the permission safe: "A verifier MUST NOT treat an attached signature as equivalent to an anchor when evaluating a dossier as of any referenceTime other than the present" (L77-79). The doctrine is about what survives a rotation, not about which bytes may carry a signature.

### 6.2 "DIDs already solved decentralized issuance." {#07-dids-solved-it}

#### The framing {#07-dids-solved-it-framing}

DIDs create indirection — issue to an identifier, not a key — so holder key rotation is handled; the problem is solved.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-dids-solved-it-error}

They solved half the problem. "Evidence is also *issued by* an identifier... If the issuer updates their identifier, old evidence is invalidated" — "This risk is poorly understood in SSI circles" (x509-prob.md > Much better alternatives). Worse, "*most DIDs, including crowd favorites like did:web, can only be resolved to the current key state*," so historical actions are unprovable unless the method supports `versionId`/`versionTime`, which most lack (was.md > Mitigation 3). An issuer key compromise then "invalidates all the evidence they have ever created" — "the driver's license bureau whose recover-from-breach plan required all current license holders to come back to the office" (was.md).

#### The reframing {#07-dids-solved-it-reframing}

A transferable AID resolves to key state at any point in time via KEL replay, so issuer-side rotation does not invalidate historical evidence. "AIDs can be transformed to DIDs, but the opposite transformation is typically impossible" (sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.2) — the AID is the richer, lossless form. This is the RAW-vs-JPEG doctrine: keep the lossless ACDC authoritative and generate a VC when an ecosystem needs one; "once you've chosen a lossy format as your primary evidence, you cannot reconstruct what you've lost" (acdc-vc-diff.md > Lossless vs. Lossy).

### 6.3 "SD-JWT gives you selective disclosure and issuer flexibility." {#07-sd-jwt}

#### The framing {#07-sd-jwt-framing}

SD-JWT is a standard, flexible, standalone token supporting selective disclosure and any identifier type.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-sd-jwt-error}

SD-JWTs are standalone envelopes, so they "will need registries of trusted issuers... centralized, governed, and managed for scale," which "reinforce[s] boundaries between verticals" (sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.4). They sign a key, not an identifier (`kid` points at the key), so "*tokens are only designed to be evaluated against current key state*. If keys change, all existing tokens become invalid" (sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.3). And `iat` is self-asserted (sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.3). Identifier flexibility, far from a virtue, "makes it much more difficult to predict or enforce security properties" (sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.2). "OAuth2 and OIDC and SD-JWTs use JWTs as tokens; they inherit the same limitation" (was.md > Mitigation 3).

#### The reframing {#07-sd-jwt-reframing}

ACDCs "prove the bona fides of issuers by chaining to other ACDCs" instead of registries (sdjwt-acdc.md > 2.4); they anchor to a rotating identifier's key state, not a static key; and they mandate AID issuers so security properties are predictable. Even the term is corrected: "selective disclosure" has "a long and unpleasant history in financial regulation, where it refers to... illegal behavior"; KERI prefers "graduated disclosure" (sdjwt-acdc.md > 1).

### 6.4 "Canonicalize the JSON (JCS / JSON-LD) so the signature is stable." {#07-json-canonicalization}

#### The framing {#07-json-canonicalization-framing}

To hash a credential, normalize its JSON with a canonicalization algorithm (JCS, or JSON-LD's URDNA2015).

#### Why it is a category error {#07-json-canonicalization-error}

`{"a":1,"b":2}` and `{"b":2,"a":1}` "are semantically identical but have different cryptographic hashes," and JCS "normalization logic is brittle" (keri-primer.md > 4.1). In JSON-LD "this fragility has led to 'term redefinition' vulnerabilities, where the meaning of a signed credential can be altered without invalidating the signature" (keri-primer.md > 4.1, citing W3C vc-data-integrity issue #272; acdc-vc-diff.md > Loss 6). And `@context` URLs "cause link rot" (acdc-vc-diff.md > Loss 6).

#### The reframing {#07-json-canonicalization-reframing}

KERI/ACDC canonicalization is insertion order — "The natural canonical ordering for such mappings is insertion order" — and lexicographic ordering is called "un-natural," forcing "oddly-labeled fields... merely to ensure that the lexicographic ordering matches a given logical ordering" (CESR spec > Order-Preserving Data Structures, L1250-1252). Schemas are referenced "by its cryptographic content, not its location" (a SAID), so "there is no link that can rot" (acdc-vc-diff.md > Loss 6). A reviewer who reaches for JCS is importing exactly the fragility KERI designed out.

### 6.5 "A self-referential identifier can't be cryptographically bound / a UUID is fine." {#07-uuid-identifiers}

#### The framing {#07-uuid-identifiers-framing}

A content identifier must live outside the content (you can't hash a thing that contains its own hash); a UUID is a perfectly good identifier.

#### Why it is a category error {#07-uuid-identifiers-error}

The SAID dummy-derivation transcends the "can't be self-referential" assumption: fill the id field with dummy characters, digest, then overwrite (CESR spec > Generation and Verification Protocols, L1200-1206). And an identifier that is self-referential but not cryptographically bound "is a security vulnerability" — "Anyone can place such an identifier inside some other serialization and claim that the other serialization is the correct serialization" (CESR spec > SAID discussion, L1194) — which is precisely the plain-`id`/UUID failure mode. "The problem with a UUID is that it has no relationship to the data" (keri-primer.md > 3.2).

#### The reframing {#07-uuid-identifiers-reframing}

A SAID is both self-referential and bound, so "An ACDC is not a mutable document; it is a crystallized fact" (keri-primer.md > 3.2). "An AID is a self-certifying identifier (SCID)," not a "domain name, which is rent-seeking text, or a UUID, which is arbitrary entropy" (keri-primer.md > 2.1).

---

## 7. "Security means invulnerability / prevention / finality" tells {#07-invulnerability-tells}
