# 08 — Presentation Architectures and the IPEX Disclosure Model {#08-presentation}

## Thesis {#08-thesis}

An ACDC presentation is not the disclosure of a credential. It is the disclosure of a directed acyclic graph of credentials, normalized so that the graph has exactly one source node — the origin — and negotiated by naming paths into that graph rather than by naming attributes. That single structural commitment is what lets ACDC absorb the other verifiable-credential architectures as special cases: a one-node DAG is a portable data lake, and a bespoke origin node with N edges is a credential soup that has been converted into something cryptographically rigid. Everything hard about ACDC presentation follows from a second observation, which the graph structure does not answer: a DAG commits to data, and a presentation must also establish who is presenting, right now, and with what authority. That is the authentication-factor problem, and it is where the current design is least settled — freshness (KRAM), multiple endorsement, anchoring (`ax`), tethering, and presentation registries are all answers to it, all proposed since late July, and none of them present in any specification branch today. This chapter separates the tiers rigorously, because the single most common error in this area is quoting a design discussion as though it were the spec — and the second most common, which this chapter itself committed in its previous draft, is quoting the forward branch of a specification as though it were the standardizing one.

## Status {#08-status}

### Staleness warning: read this before you rely on anything below {#08-staleness-warning}

This chapter covers the fastest-moving, least-settled area of the KERI/ACDC design space. Between 2026-07-25 and 2026-08-19 the presentation model was revised five times in public, twice in ways that superseded earlier proposals outright, and the pace has not slowed: in the two weeks from 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-15, keripy's V2 IPEX module more than doubled in size, `dp` arrived in code, and a design conflict raised on a discussion on 2026-09-01 was settled by an implementation within ten days. This chapter is a synthesis as of 2026-09-15, with a keripy-side refresh on 2026-10-03; it is our best current reading, not a stable reference.

#### What the 2026-10-03 pass changed, in one paragraph {#08-changes-2026-10-03}

keripy moved from `b8f60166b` to `80f77b73b` (2026-10-01), and the V2 IPEX module saw another 913 changed lines (729 insertions, 184 deletions, net +545; corrected 2026-10-03 (verification): previously "grew by another ~900 lines"). Grant anchoring now accepts any of three AIDs — sender, origin Issuee, origin Issuer — and a presentation-registry binding counts as one of them ([section 10](#08-anchoring)). The presentation-registry leg, which this chapter called "not implemented at all" two weeks ago, is now built on `grant` in the V2 module ([section 10](#08-anchoring); [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md) owns the detail). Multiply-endorsed grants are generated and their endorsements stored, but the verifier does not use the endorsement signatures to decide validity ([section 9](#08-multiple-endorsement)). Every disclosed node must now pass one of three issuer-authentication checks, where registry-less nodes used to pass automatically ([section 7](#08-authentication-factors)). The two edge-operator verifiers now disagree in three ways rather than one ([section 5](#08-edges)). Discussion #1515 has been read, and it proposes two further operators, `I1I` and `DI1I`, that no code implements ([section 5](#08-edges)). Two things did not move: `dp` is still negotiated and not enforced ([section 4](#08-disclosure-paths)), and the V2 handler still has no caller in `src/keri` ([section 6](#08-two-ipex)). This pass re-read keripy and #1515; it did not re-fetch the other tracked discussion bodies or either ACDC spec branch, whose pins and quotes below stand as of 2026-09-15.

#### What the 2026-10-15 content pass changed {#08-changes-2026-10-15}

This pass corrected one error and added Sam Smith's GitHub rulings from `raw/21`, a sweep of his comments from 2025-10-14 to 2026-10-14. The error was in [section 6](#08-two-ipex): this chapter said keripy's V2 module refuses to spurn a thread-opening grant, and the code does the opposite, refusing a spurn only of a grant that answers a prior message, which matches Sam's ruling on keripy #1628 ([section 6](#08-spurn-grant)). The rulings added are tiered [proposal], since a GitHub comment is a position, not specification text: the decision to change the empty-operator default to `NI2I` in ACDC v1.1 ([section 5](#08-default-change)), the meaning of an empty `dp` ([section 4](#08-empty-dp)), why disclosure requests are paths rather than schemas ([section 4](#08-why-paths)), predefined DAG shapes ([section 4](#08-predefined-shapes)), the purpose clause ([section 3](#08-purpose-clause)), the receiver AID ([section 7](#08-receiver-aid)), why the V1/V2 split is deliberate and v1 exchanges will not be anchored ([section 6](#08-split-deliberate)), the contractual logic of agree and admit and of tail anchoring ([section 10](#08-contract-logic)), the four tiers of IPEX ([section 10](#08-four-tiers)), and the origin `o` on an `offer` ([section 10](#08-offer-origin)). The spec branches and keripy were not otherwise re-read; pins below stand as stated.

#### This warning has already fired once {#08-warning-fired}

This warning has already fired once on this chapter. It was first drafted on 2026-08-25 against a version of #1627 whose only concrete proposal was a field-map form of `dp`/`o`/`ax`. Later the same day the author appended a list form to the same post, marked it "the preferred approach," and left the post date unchanged. Roughly half of [section 11](#08-dag-soup) had to be rewritten. Treat that as the expected case, not the exception.

#### Scanning for newer intel {#08-newer-intel}

Before you build an argument on it, scan for newer intel. In order of cost: WebOfTrust/keripy discussion [#1627](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1627) and its comment stream, which is where the architecture-level thinking lands and whose body was last edited 2026-09-11; then [#1613](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1613), which its author has revised in place at least six times without changing the post date — its body still carries the self-declared version string "v1.5 2026/08/18" while GitHub records an edit on 2026-09-02, so a reader trusting the in-body version dates that text two weeks early; then the comment streams of the open keripy and `kswg-acdc-specification` PRs listed in [Sources](#08-sources), where the settled answers to several questions below are recorded only as review comments.

Two specific traps. First, a discussion body is a moving target — cite the quote, not the line, and re-read before you rely. That warning is better satisfied on this pass than usual: all six tracked discussion bodies were re-fetched on 2026-09-15 and `refresh/snapshot-discussions.py --check` reported zero drift across all six snapshots, so the discussion quotes below rest on verified text rather than on a recollection of it. Second, normative status moved for a large block of this material, and it moved one tier rather than two: Disclosure Paths and the `dp` field were prose in a discussion in July and are now in the ACDC `v1.1` branch at `2362e48a1`, in a ~185-line section that declares itself normative. That makes them [spec-next], not [spec] — the standardizing line, `main` at `f0bd097de`, contains the string "Disclosure Paths" zero times. The 2026-09-02 draft of this chapter marked that whole block [spec]. That was wrong, and it is corrected throughout [section 2](#08-one-dag-one-origin) and [section 4](#08-disclosure-paths) below; if you are working from a copy dated before 2026-09-15, every `dp` claim in it is over-tiered by one.

#### How far from normative this chapter's material is {#08-distance-from-normative}

Further than its confidence suggests, and the distance is uneven enough that a single sentence would mislead. Nothing in the authentication half of the chapter — [section 7](#08-authentication-factors) through [section 10](#08-anchoring), covering freshness, multiple endorsement, tethering, anchoring and presentation registries — appears in any specification, on any branch. All of it is design discussion. The structural half — [section 2](#08-one-dag-one-origin) and [section 4](#08-disclosure-paths), the one-DAG-one-origin normalization and the whole `dp` disclosure-path apparatus — is in the ACDC `v1.1` branch only and has no text in the standardizing line, so it is new thinking that is likely rather than certain to fold into the next standard. What is genuinely normative today is a smaller set than a first reading suggests: the bespoke ACDC, four of the five unary edge operators, the m-ary operator family, the edge `s` constraint, and an IPEX route table in which disclosure is negotiated by naming attributes rather than paths. The reference implementation, meanwhile, has started to move faster than the standardizing line on several of these, which means [code] and [spec] now disagree in both directions at once. As of keripy `80f77b73b` (2026-10-01) that gap widened again: anchoring with its three-AID fallback, presentation-registry authentication of a `grant`, and stored non-sender endorsements all exist in the reference implementation's V2 IPEX module while appearing in no specification branch — and that module is still not what keripy's own CLI runs ([section 6](#08-two-ipex)). Treat the chapter as a map of a live argument, not as a conformance reference.

Every substantive claim below carries one of four markers. They are not decoration; they are the point of the chapter. The previous draft used three, collapsing a specification's two live branches into a single [spec]; the ACDC spec's branches have since diverged far enough that the collapse was doing real damage, so the fourth marker is now carried explicitly. Several of the [proposal] proposals below have already been superseded once. Note that [code] is frequently none of the other three — it is sometimes ahead of the spec, sometimes behind it, and occasionally at odds with both. It now also carries an internal split that [section 6](#08-two-ipex) makes explicit: some [code] claims describe code keripy's own CLI runs, and some describe code that exists and is tested but that nothing in `src/keri` calls. Where the tiers disagree, this chapter says so rather than reconciling them.

## 1. The four presentation architectures {#08-architectures}

The taxonomy is from discussion #1627, "ACDC Presentation Architectures" (SmithSamuelM, 2026-08-19). It is a framing document rather than a proposal for most of its length, and the framing is useful independent of whether one accepts its conclusions. [proposal]

### Portable Datalake {#08-portable-datalake}

One document, nested blocks, all attributes about one subject from one issuer; the holder discloses a subset at presentation time, often by checking boxes against an array. This is mDoc/mDL and mainstream W3C VC. Its advantage is simplicity. Its named disadvantages: it cannot express delegation or a delegation chain; everything must come from exactly one issuer, "Not one root-of-trust with a distributed set of hierarchically delegated Issuers, but one and only one Issuer"; the issuer must pull from every relevant database to issue it, so the architecture pushes issuers toward exactly the consolidated data lake that maximizes breach blast radius; and reissuance is forced at the periodicity of the most rapidly changing attribute in the document.

#### Credential Soup {#08-credential-soup}

Attributes drawn from several credentials, potentially several issuers and several issuees, assembled at presentation time. This was Sovrin's model. It permits issuer-side database partitioning and reissuance tuned to each attribute's dynamism. Its costs are that presentation negotiation becomes ambiguous (an attribute may be sourced from any of several credentials), that each distinct source needs its own fresh proof of control, that proving several issuee AIDs represent the same party needs a mechanism the soup does not supply, and that a soup "cannot support delegation in any normative secure way. At least not as a cryptographically verifiable data structure."

#### Verifiable DAG {#08-verifiable-dag}

ACDC's default. Edges carry properties, each node is separably authenticable, and each edge carries a cryptographic digest of the node it points to. The consequence: "A verifiable cryptographic commitment to the origin ACDC of that DAG is a verifiable commitment to every node in the DAG," giving the graph Merkle-tree-like properties. Typically only the issuer or issuee of the origin needs a fresh authentication factor. Delegation is native. Forgery "must be in totality, and not piecemeal," where a soup can be forged piecemeal. The costs are verification complexity and a reissuance cascade discussed in [section 12](#08-sedi-recipes).

#### DAG Soup {#08-dag-soup-architecture}

Several disconnected DAGs presented in one exchange, each with its own origin, requiring a multiply-endorsed grant. Most general, most complex, and the subject of #1627's only concrete proposal ([section 11](#08-dag-soup)).

#### The load-bearing claim of the taxonomy {#08-subsumption-claim}

The load-bearing claim of the taxonomy is that ACDC subsumes the other two: "the ACDC DAG, as a special case, can mimic either a portable data lake or a credential soup as needed." A single ACDC with a selectively disclosable aggregate section is a portable data lake. A bespoke origin ACDC with N edges is a credential soup that has been given a verifiable spine. This is well-supported by the normative structure in [section 2](#08-one-dag-one-origin) and [section 3](#08-bespoke-origin) and is, in this chapter's judgment, the strongest argument in #1627.

## 2. The normalized structure: one DAG, one origin {#08-one-dag-one-origin}

This is the structural commitment everything else rests on, and it is [spec-next] — present in the `v1.1` branch at `2362e48a1` and absent from the standardizing line, where the section that states it does not exist. The previous draft of this chapter marked it [spec]. That was an over-tiering, and it mattered: a reader who took "one DAG, one origin" as binding today would be treating an unadopted branch as conformance. The structure is well-argued and is the premise of everything from [section 4](#08-disclosure-paths) through [section 12](#08-sedi-recipes), but nothing obliges an implementer to honor it yet.

An ACDC is not a node; it is a graph fragment. "It consists of a near-side node and that node's outgoing Edges, which its Edge Section contains. An ACDC holds no Edges incoming to its own node, only outgoing ones; its incoming Edges belong to other fragments" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > DAG of ACDCs, L1817 @2362e48a1). A source node "has no incoming Edges. It MUST either have no Edges at all or only outgoing Edges" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > DAG of ACDCs, L1819 @2362e48a1). [spec-next]

The normalization is two sentences, and both are worth memorizing because the rest of the design quotes them constantly: "That DAG MUST have exactly one source node, called the origin node" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > DAG of ACDCs, L1821 @2362e48a1), and where the material to be conveyed is not already connected, "a DAG MUST be formed by issuing a bespoke ACDC whose node is the origin, with Edges chaining back to every other ACDC the exchange includes" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > DAG of ACDCs, L1823 @2362e48a1). The second gives the bespoke-ACDC construction of [section 3](#08-bespoke-origin) a structural job it did not have before, on top of its contractual one. The branch states plainly what the normalization is for: "This gives every exchange the same normalized structure, on which the `dp` field depends." [spec-next]

Two consequences an adversarial reviewer should hold onto.

First, the origin is a source, not a root of authority, and these run in opposite directions. Edges point near→far and carry a digest of the far node, so authority flows toward the origin from the far nodes, while commitment flows from the origin to everything reachable. #1627 uses "root of the DAG" for the far-side, deepest node — "if a given ACDC is the root of the DAG, and that ACDC's attributes change and it must be reissued, then every branch that sinks into the ACDC must be reissued" — which is the correct cascade direction but the opposite end of the graph from the origin. The terms "origin" and "root" name opposite ends here. Anyone reading #1627 alongside the spec should translate rather than assume.

Second, the DAG is well-ordered and therefore linearizable. Field maps inside an ACDC MUST be insertion-ordered — that part is [spec], on both branches — and arrays are ordered, and each Edge Section is an ordered field map, so "A well-ordered DAG with a single source node linearizes into a unique, reproducible order" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > DAG of ACDCs > Ordering, L1831 @2362e48a1). Breadth-first from the origin is the chosen order, "because in some applications, such as a dossier using joint issuance, the joint-issued ACDCs fall together in breadth-first order and scatter in depth-first." Depth-first would also be unique and reproducible; the choice is argued from readability rather than correctness. This reproducibility is what lets `dp` identify an ACDC by position rather than by SAID ([section 4](#08-disclosure-paths)), which is in turn what keeps a disclosure request from introducing correlators of its own. [spec-next]

One vocabulary trap the branch sets deliberately, and it will bite anyone reading [section 4](#08-disclosure-paths) quickly. "A DAG of ACDCs is therefore a graph of subgraphs, one subgraph per ACDC. So in what follows, node may mean a node of the DAG of ACDCs or a node of one ACDC's subgraph." The overload is intentional and is never disambiguated by a qualifier, so "node path" in [section 4](#08-disclosure-paths) means a node of the subgraph — a block within one ACDC — while "origin node" means a node of the DAG of ACDCs. [spec-next]

## 3. The bespoke origin ACDC {#08-bespoke-origin}

A bespoke (disclosure-specific) ACDC is issued by the Discloser, for one exchange, specifically to become the origin. It is [spec] and has been for some time: "A given Discloser issues its own bespoke ACDC referencing some other ACDC via an Edge. This means that the normal validation logic and tooling for a chained ACDC can be applied without complicating the presentation exchange logic" (ACDC spec > Disclosure-specific (Bespoke) Issued ACDCs, L1862 @f0bd097de; identical at L2063 @2362e48a1). The spec names the rich-presentation use directly: it "effectively enables a type of rich presentation or combined disclosure where multiple ACDCs MAY be referenced by edges in the bespoke ACDC... without requiring any new tooling."

Note the tier split running through this section. The bespoke construction itself is [spec] — it is in `main`, and was there before any of the current design conversation started. The structural job [section 2](#08-one-dag-one-origin) gives it, normalizing several unchained ACDCs into one DAG with a single origin, is [spec-next] and lives only in the forward branch. A reader who conflates them will think the whole origin-node apparatus is standardized because the bespoke ACDC is.

Its two standard jobs are to carry presentation-specific contractual terms in its rule section — the spec's worked example carries an anti-assimilation clause and a one-time-purpose clause (ACDC spec > Disclosure-specific (Bespoke) Issued ACDCs > Example of a Bespoke Issued ACDC, L2069-2114 @2362e48a1) — and to name the Disclosee as its Issuee, so that "Signing the agreement to the offer of that bespoke ACDC consummates a contract between the named Issuer and the named Issuee."

### A purpose clause belongs in the bespoke origin {#08-purpose-clause}

Asked whether an exchange message should carry a human-readable statement of purpose in its `m` field, Sam pointed at the bespoke origin's rule section instead: "The advantage of putting it in the DAG is that it gets all the security, perpetuality, etc of the DAG" (keripy discussion #1617, comment of 2026-08-13, R-064, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1617#discussioncomment-18006490). His hesitation is the design ethos, not the mechanism: "I am always worried when we do stuff like that , that we are not following the design ethos of minimally sufficient means." It is a stated preference, not a ruling for removal. Phil Feairheller replied that Locksmith and keripy's `kli` both use `m`; Sam asked whether it reaches the user and did not decide (same discussion, 2026-08-13 and 2026-08-14). [proposal]

### The bespoke origin as recipe {#08-recipe}

#1627 adds a third job and a name for it: the bespoke origin as recipe. [proposal] The argument is that a set of unchained ACDCs issued by one root-of-trust to one issuee — the SEDI shape, State → citizen — looks like a soup but is a degenerate one, since "All the ingredients came from the same cupboard." A bespoke origin with one edge per ingredient converts it into a DAG at presentation time. The origin "does not need to be anchored or use a registry, so it's simple... It merely needs to be signed and have attached signatures because it's a one-time use ACDC."

The interoperability move is the interesting part: the bespoke ACDC is one-time-use but its schema is not. "The schema of the bespoke ACDC, however, is not one-time use. It acts as a permanent recipe for the soup... an EGF can define the schema of the bespoke ACDC for all its seminal use cases." Since type-is-schema and the schema SAID is a cryptographic commitment, an EGF-published recipe schema gives tooling a fixed target without fixing the instances.

#### A correction that matters, because the sentence will be quoted {#08-recipe-correction}

#1627 justifies the edge operator on a recipe edge as follows: "the Issuer of the origin ACDC (recipe) is the Issuee of the ACDCs on the far side of each of its edges. Therefore, each edge from the recipe ACDC can use the I2I edge operator." That is right, and it is exactly the `I2I` relation ([section 5](#08-edges)). The restatement immediately following it — "the Issuer of the recipe is the citizen AID, and the Issuer of all the far node ACDCs is also the citizen AID" — is wrong: the far nodes are issued by the State and the citizen is their Issuee. The first sentence is the correct one; the second contradicts it and would, if implemented, describe a set of self-issued credentials.

## 4. Disclosure paths: the `dp` field {#08-disclosure-paths}

`dp` is how a disclosure is requested, and it is the month's flagship movement: after evolving through discussions #1542 → #1512 → #1549, it landed in the ACDC `v1.1` branch as a ~185-line section that declares its own normativity, and it landed in keripy as a validated wire field. Both movements are real and neither is as large as it sounds, for opposite reasons. On the spec side the tier is [spec-next] and stops there: `## Disclosure Paths` exists only on `v1.1` at `2362e48a1`, and the standardizing line at `f0bd097de` contains the phrase zero times, so there is no `main` text to upgrade it with. On the code side the tier is [code] for the wire shape only, and nothing validates a disclosure against the plan it negotiated — see the end of this section.

The section asserts its own status in its first sentence: "This section is normative. It defines the path syntax that designates the parts of an ACDC, or of a DAG of chained ACDCs" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths, L1811 @2362e48a1). That assertion is worth reading carefully rather than at face value, because the only place the branch binds `dp` to a wire format is the Disclosure Paths in `apply` and `offer` subsection, which sits inside the IPEX section that opens "This section is non-normative." The syntax is normative and its sole use is not — a seam in the branch itself, not an artifact of this chapter's reading, and it is carried as an open question in [section 14](#08-open-questions). [spec-next]

### Not an ACDC field {#08-dp-not-acdc-field}

It is not an ACDC field. This is the first of two shape facts that are easy to state wrongly, and the spec states it flatly: "The `dp` field is not an ACDC field. It appears in the messages that negotiate a disclosure, not in the ACDCs that are disclosed" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths, L1813 @2362e48a1). It is deliberately not added to the reserved-label table for that reason — unlike `_`, which is ([section 5](#08-edges)). An ACDC that carried a `dp` field would be making a category error: the disclosure plan belongs to the negotiation, and the negotiation is not what gets signed as evidence. This matters for [section 11](#08-dag-soup). [spec-next]

#### Shape {#08-dp-shape}

The value is "a list of tuples," each of which "represents one ACDC in the DAG that is the object of the exchange and is of the form `(ACDCSchemaSAID, PathPrefix, [paths])`", and "In a serialization that has no distinct tuple type, such as JSON, each tuple MUST be represented as a three-element array" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Disclosure Paths, `dp`, Field, L1881 @2362e48a1). The first element is the qb64 SAID of that ACDC's schema. The three-element form is the settled one; a two-element form appears in #1549's body and was superseded by its own comment stream on 2026-08-04. [spec-next]

#### Why a list and not a field map {#08-dp-why-list}

This is the design decision most directly at stake in [section 11](#08-dag-soup): "A list of tuples is used rather than a field map keyed by Schema SAID so that a Schema SAID MAY appear more than once. Two ACDCs of the same type, that is, of the same Schema SAID, MAY appear in one DAG, and a field map could not tell them apart" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Disclosure Paths, `dp`, Field, L1883 @2362e48a1). The branch's own worked example is such a case, with a research report and a project report sharing one schema. [spec-next]

#### Why paths and not schemas {#08-why-paths}

The reason a disclosure request is a path over a graph, rather than a schema describing the wanted subset, is Sam's layering argument, stated while `dp` was being designed: "So disclosure is reasoning about exposure. What parts to expose when. Not what those parts mean." (keripy PR #1505, comment of 2026-07-16, R-058, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1505#issuecomment-4992746261). Knowledge graphs reason about semantics, and in the same comment ACDC exists "to invert that layering", putting security and correlation resistance below the semantic layer, so schema stays type and nothing more. It is his design rationale, not specification text. [proposal]

#### Path syntax {#08-path-syntax}

"A path is a tuple of components," each a field label or, where the collection is an array, a zero-based integer offset. A path beginning with `/` is DAG-absolute, rooted at the origin's top level; one that does not is ACDC-relative. Edge traversal MUST be DAG-absolute and "MUST therefore begin with `/e`"; the hop across an edge to the far ACDC is written with the virtual component `_`, so `/e/reports/project/_/a/author` descends the origin's edge section to the `project` edge, hops, and lands on the far ACDC's `a/author` (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Path Syntax > Traversing Edges, L1845 @2362e48a1). The `n` field label is not a path component; "`_` stands for the traversal that `n` designates." Two hops nest the same way. Requirements bind the effective path — prefix and path taken together — not the entry alone. [spec-next]

#### Two delimiters, and the label restriction that pays for them {#08-label-restrictions}

Components are separated by `/` in the ordinary serialization "and when serialized compactly as a CESR primitive, by `-`". That choice forces two new rules, which `v1.1` states in a section that does not exist on `main` at all: a field label "MUST NOT, therefore, contain the character `-`", and since that leaves `_` as the only free Base64 character, "The label `_` MUST therefore be reserved as a virtual path component denoting that hop" and a field MUST NOT be labeled with a single `_`. Only the lone label is forbidden — `first_name` is fine — and the restriction does not reach schema-section labels, which no path descends into. This is backward-incompatible for any already-issued ACDC carrying such a label, and the branch argues the cost is low without saying anything about migrating; [section 14](#08-open-questions) carries that as an open question. [spec-next]

#### Node vs leaf: the hammer and the scalpel {#08-node-vs-leaf}

A path ending in `/` designates a whole node and "the full expansion of every branch beneath it", plus enough of the branch leading to it to validate the SAIDs along the way; a path ending in a non-empty component "designates a single leaf" and "requires no sibling branch" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Path Syntax > Node Paths and Leaf Paths, L1855-1861 @2362e48a1). The spec's own slogan is "The node form is a hammer, the leaf form a scalpel." `a/d/` and `a/` designate the same block, and the top-level `d/` therefore designates a whole ACDC. [spec-next]

#### Closures {#08-closures}

Closures are the semantics, and they depend on how the section blinds. "A disclosure path translates into a closure over the fields or array elements it implies," and "The disclosure designated by a set of paths is the union of their closures" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Path Syntax > Closures, L1865 @2362e48a1). In a partially disclosable section — Attribute, Edge, Rule — one SAID and one UUID cover the whole block, so a leaf path "closes over every simple field of that block. Its nested sub-blocks stay compacted as their SAIDs." That is why a leaf path into an edge yields the edge's `n` along with its siblings: it is exactly what verifying the edge against the far ACDC requires. In the selectively disclosable Aggregate Section each block carries its own `d` and `u`, so a leaf path there "closes over that block alone and tells nothing of any sibling." The schema section is always disclosed and needs no path; the rule section is usually but not necessarily disclosed, "MUST NOT be assumed fully disclosed," and must be designated when wanted. And the boundary that keeps this mechanism from being mistaken for a permissions system: "A closure states what a path discloses. It does not bound what the Disclosee may then do with what it holds." Unblinding an edge yields the far SAID and so enables a further request, but that request is a separate disclosure with a closure of its own. Chain-Link Confidentiality does that job; paths do not. [spec-next]

#### Prefix factoring {#08-prefix-factoring}

The prefix is the DAG-absolute route to the ACDC the tuple names; it "MUST be either the empty string or a DAG-absolute path that both begins and ends with the path delimiter." Effective path is prefix ⧺ entry with nothing inserted, and "An entry of a path list MUST NOT begin with the path delimiter," which makes the concatenation always well-formed (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Disclosure Paths, `dp`, Field > Path Prefix, L1889-1891 @2362e48a1) and holds equally of the compact `-` serialization. A prefix "MUST NOT reach past the top level of the ACDC it names." With a non-empty prefix, an empty entry `""` designates the whole named ACDC; with an empty prefix it designates nothing, and `d/` is the shortest way to say "the whole of this one." [spec-next]

#### Ordering, and when it stops being sufficient {#08-dp-ordering}

Elements MUST appear in breadth-first order and "The zeroth element MUST represent the origin node ACDC" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Disclosure Paths, `dp`, Field > Identifying Each Tuple's ACDC, L1899 @2362e48a1). Where prefixes are non-empty, position is not what identifies a tuple, and the list "MAY omit any ACDC from which nothing is requested." The ordering is required anyway, on the grounds that any party generating `dp` must linearize the DAG to walk it. The exception that forces explicit prefixes: where a schema makes an edge or edge-group optional, "a party that knows only the Schema cannot generate a total ordering… The ordering then has gaps. In that case the prefix of every element after the zeroth MUST be non-empty" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Disclosure Paths, `dp`, Field > Identifying Each Tuple's ACDC, L1911 @2362e48a1). Completeness follows the same split: with empty prefixes the list must hold one element per ACDC, an element requesting nothing carrying an empty path list; with non-empty prefixes it may omit such ACDCs entirely. [spec-next]

#### Placement: the second detail that is easy to state wrongly {#08-dp-placement}

"So where a `dp` field appears in an `apply` or `offer`, it MUST appear in that message's query section, `q`, and not in its attribute section, `a`" (ACDC spec > IPEX Protocol Messages > Disclosure Paths in `apply` and `offer`, L2015 @2362e48a1). The reasoning is the ReST analogy the `exn` message shape already encodes — the route `r` holds the path, `q` holds the query string, `a` holds the body, and "A request to disclose names which parts of which ACDCs are wanted. It is a query." `dp` appears in `apply` and `offer` only. It does not appear in a `grant`. (Qualified 2026-10-15: true of `v1.1`; keripy's head at `c102367ea` validates a `dp` on `agree` and `grant` too, see [the empty-`dp` ruling](#08-empty-dp).) Getting this backwards is not a stylistic error: `a` is where `ax` and the origin `o` are proposed to live ([section 10](#08-anchoring)), so a `dp` in `a` would collide with a different field family and would put a request in the slot reserved for what is being conveyed. [spec-next]

#### The route table {#08-route-table}

The route table changed with it, and this supersedes what the standardizing line says. At `main` @`f0bd097de` the `apply` row reads "Schema or its SAID, Attribute field label list, Aggregate element label list, signature on `apply` or its SAID" and the `offer` row reads "Metadata ACDC or its SAID, Schema or its SAID, partial disclosure, Aggregate element label list, signature on `offer` or its SAID" (ACDC spec > IPEX Protocol Messages, L1811-1813 @f0bd097de) — that is [spec], and it is the model in which a disclosure is negotiated by naming attributes. At `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` both label lists are replaced by `dp`: the `apply` row becomes "Disclosure Paths, `dp`, signature on `apply` or its SAID" and the `offer` row "Metadata ACDC or its SAID, Disclosure Paths, `dp`, partial disclosure, signature on `offer` or its SAID" (ACDC spec > IPEX Protocol Messages, L2004-2006 @2362e48a1) — [spec-next]. The `spurn`, `agree`, `grant` and `admit` rows are identical on both branches. Both rows are live, on different branches, and this chapter records both rather than replacing one with the other: the label-list form is what a conformant implementation of today's standard does, and the path form is what the forward branch expects. Anyone reading a single row without its branch will mis-state the protocol.

#### Solicited response {#08-solicited-response}

An empty list `[]` in an answering message means "the answering path list is the same as the one it answers"; where the answering list differs, or where the message is unsolicited, the value "MUST NOT be an empty list" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Disclosure Paths, `dp`, Field > Solicited Response, L1917 @2362e48a1). The IPEX subsection carries the same rule through for an `offer` answering an `apply`. [spec-next]

#### An empty `dp` with no prior: the editor and the code have moved past the branch {#08-empty-dp}

Added 2026-10-15. Sam ruled on 2026-10-01 that an empty list copies the prior plan and, with no prior, requests nothing: "An empty [] for dp field means ditto the prior dp field from the apply or offer not give me everything." And: "If there is no prior message then an empty [] means give me nothing. To get everything their must be a path." (keripy PR #1698, comment of 2026-10-01, R-052, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1698#issuecomment-5937132701). The second sentence contradicts the `v1.1` rule quoted above, under which an unsolicited message's `dp` "MUST NOT be an empty list"; the spec text follows Sam's own July wording in #1549, so the branch lags its editor. [proposal] keripy's upstream head implements the ruling. At `c102367ea` (2026-10-14, after this chapter's `80f77b73b` pin, read through the GitHub API) the `dp` check carries the comment "An empty plan inherits from a prior message and means no disclosure" and now runs on `agree` and `grant` as well as `apply` and `offer` (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L513-519 @c102367ea). That makes the sentence in [the placement subsection](#08-dp-placement) that `dp` "does not appear in a `grant`" correct about `v1.1` and stale about keripy's head, which validates a `dp` on a `grant`. [code] at `c102367ea` only (`raw/21` T-02).

#### Predefined DAG shapes are the norm {#08-predefined-shapes}

Added 2026-10-15. The `dp` machinery is general, and Sam expects it to be used narrowly: "In my experience totally free-form credential exchanges are largely impractical." And: "So predefined shapes will be the norm." (keripy discussion #1542, comment of 2026-07-30, R-055, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1542#discussioncomment-17842586). The same comment explains why the branch is permissive anyway: "The current spec is very unrestrictive. This is because hardening means having an opinion, and I didn't have a strong opinion." The shapes he means are EGF-defined, with constrained optionality, and the `v1.1` text carries half of it: "in practice the requester defines the shape of the DAG it will accept" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Disclosure Paths, `dp`, Field > Identifying Each Tuple's ACDC, L1903 @2362e48a1). An earlier comment in the thread adds a rule the branch does not carry: an `offer` whose origin schema differs from the `apply`'s "is functionally the same as if the Offerer spurned the apply and then initiated a new IPEX with an unsolicited offer", and "A valid IPEX can start on the Offerer side with an offer or a grant. It does not have to start with an apply." (keripy discussion #1542, comment of 2026-07-30, R-055, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1542#discussioncomment-17841472). Sam left open whether to harden that equivalence into a requirement. [proposal]

#### Aggregate-section pathing {#08-aggregate-pathing}

Aggregate-section pathing is the one genuinely special case. Blinded blocks are array elements whose offsets a Disclosee does not know, so a path MAY name a block by its uniquely labeled field: `A/over21` and `A/1/over21` designate the same closure. The shorthand designates the block, not the field, and closes over all of it. It cannot reach into nested sub-blocks — `A/over21/issued` "MUST be rejected when expanded" — on the grounds that partial disclosure inside selective disclosure is an anti-pattern, and "a Schema that calls for it is better rewritten as a DAG of ACDCs" (ACDC spec > Disclosure Paths > Special Cases > Aggregate Section Pathing, L1923-1931 @2362e48a1). The two forms cannot be confused, because a field label MUST NOT begin with a numeral. [spec-next]

#### Superseded 2026-09-15: `dp` is in keripy {#08-dp-in-keripy}

Superseded 2026-09-15 — `dp` is in keripy, and the previous draft's flat negative is wrong. This chapter said on 2026-09-02 that "keripy implements none of this," on the evidence that `grep` for `'dp'` across `src/keri/` returned nothing at `42db8991b`. At `b8f60166b` that is no longer true, and the accurate replacement is narrower than "implemented" but larger than nothing. [code]

#### What landed: the wire shape {#08-dp-wire-shape}

What landed is the wire shape. `dp` lives in the `exn` query/modifier section — the placement the branch requires — and is required on `apply` and `offer`: stage 2 of `IpexHandler.verify` rejects a message whose `q` lacks `dp`, whose `dp` is not a one-element outer list, or whose single element fails the triple check (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L419-425 @b8f60166b). The outer one-element list is deliberate future-proofing for [section 11](#08-dag-soup)'s multi-DAG case: "We currently only support one DAG (until Multi DAG), so exactly one entry is required" (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, _validSingleDagList, L223 @b8f60166b). The grammar checks each entry is a triple of "[schema SAID, DAG path, ACDC paths]", that the DAG path is either the root `"/"` or a prefix that "terminates at the far-node hop `\"_/\"` such as `\"/e/holder/_/\"`", and that the third element is a list of non-empty path strings. The builders refuse to construct a message without one, raising rather than returning false. So keripy at this pin agrees with the branch about where `dp` goes, what shape it has, and that the hop is spelled `_`. [code]

#### What did not land: enforcement {#08-dp-not-enforced}

What did not land is enforcement, and this is the distinction the whole tier story turns on. No verb checks a disclosed DAG against its `dp` plan. `dp` is validated for `apply` and `offer` only; `grant` — the verb that actually discloses — never reads it. A grant's stage-5 check walks the disclosed graph for internal closure and evaluates edge semantics over it, both of which are about the DAG's own shape, not about whether it matches what was asked for. A grant disclosing more than the agreed paths, or less, is accepted by this code. Nor is the machinery that would produce a targeted partial wired up: `Compactor.compact(paths=…)` exists and is tested, but the `paths=` form has no caller anywhere in `src/`, and nothing in the tree translates a `dp` path into a `Compactor` path — they are not obviously the same language, and no code reconciles them. `dp` is negotiated, not enforced. A reader who takes "`dp` is implemented" to mean a verifier will catch a mismatched disclosure would be wrong, and would be wrong about the one property that would make the negotiation load-bearing. [code]

#### Re-stamped 2026-10-03: still negotiated, not enforced {#08-dp-restamp}

Re-stamped 2026-10-03 at `80f77b73b`: still negotiated, not enforced. Every reference to `dp` in `src/keri` at the new pin is in `acdc/ipexing.py`: the `apply`/`offer` shape check in `verify` (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L497-503 @80f77b73b) and the two generators. `grant` still never reads it; its stage-5 path remains `_walkGraph(..., closed=True)` then `_verifyGraphSemantics` (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L591-596 @80f77b73b). `compact(paths=…)` still has no caller in `src/`. One generator change is new: an `offer` replying to an `apply` now inherits the apply's plan when the caller supplies none (`mods["dp"] = aq["dp"]`, keripy acdc/ipexing.py, offer, L1799 @80f77b73b). The month's commit titled "fix dp, add assertions" (`e8d4776ef`, 2026-09-29) touched only `tests/sedi/test_ipex_sedi.py`, and what it changed is evidence for the finding rather than against it: the tests' `dp` plans were rewritten from near-node schema SAIDs with absolute field paths to far-node schema SAIDs, multi-hop DAG paths such as `"/e/coreIdentity/_/e/utahAgent/_/"` and relative field paths such as `"a/state/"`, and the grants passed verification before and after (uncited — flagged by verification 2026-10-03: the tests were not run at either commit), because nothing checks what a plan means. The new relative, trailing-separator field-path form does resemble `Compactor`'s convention — "A trailing path separator keeps the whole node expanded" — but that is a convergence in test data, not code that translates one into the other. [code] (raw/09 section 7c, @`80f77b73b`)

## 5. Edges, operators, and edge groups {#08-edges}

The presentation model leans on the edge layer in two places: `I2I` closes the bespoke recipe ([section 3](#08-bespoke-origin)), and every proposal to signal multiple endorsement in the ACDC rather than in the exchange message is a proposal for a new edge-group operator ([section 9](#08-multiple-endorsement)).

### Block discrimination [spec] {#08-block-discrimination}

"An Edge MUST contain a node, `n` field. An Edge-group MUST NOT have a node, `n` field" (ACDC spec > Edge Section > Block Types, L1058 @f0bd097de). The Edge Section is itself the top-level edge-group. Edge-groups nest to arbitrary depth. Reserved labels are `[d, u, o, w]` for a group and `[d, u, n, s, o, w]` for an edge.

#### Unary operators: four are [spec], the fifth is [spec-next] {#08-unary-operators}

On `main` @`f0bd097de` the table is `I2I` (near issuer MUST be far issuee — the delegation link, and the default for a targeted far node), `NI2I` (relaxes it; default for untargeted), `DI2I` (near issuer MUST be far issuee or a delegated AID of far issuee) and `NOT` (inverts far-node validity) (ACDC spec > Edge Section > Edge > Operator, `o` field, L1190-1195 @f0bd097de). [spec] `v1.1` @`2362e48a1` adds a fifth row, `E1E`: near issuee MUST equal far issuee, "an identity relation on the two ACDCs' Issuees" that "places no constraint on either ACDC's Issuer" (ACDC spec > Edge Section > Edge > Operator, `o` field, L1206 @2362e48a1). Both ends MUST be targeted. Its motivating case is a core identity credential and a separate entitlement credential issued to the same subject by different issuers — a relation `I2I` cannot express, since `I2I` would require the entitlement's issuer to be the core credential's issuee. `E1E` occurs zero times on `main`, so it is [spec-next], and it also joins the default-inference gate on that branch while never being a default itself. `o` may be a list, and "When multiple unary Operators appear in the list, and there is a conflict between Operators, the latest Operator among the conflicting Operators in the list takes precedence" — that rule is [spec], on both branches.

#### The empty-operator default is to change in v1.1 {#08-default-change}

Added 2026-10-15. Both branches append `I2I` to an operator-less edge whose far node is targeted and `NI2I` to one whose far node is untargeted (ACDC spec > Edge Section > Edge > Operator, `o` field, L1209-1213 @2362e48a1). That rule is decided to change. Sam proposed it in ACDC issue #205: "we could change the default in v1.1 to be 'N121` for an empty unary operator list", where "N121" is a slip for `NI2I` (kswg-acdc-specification issue #205, body of 2026-08-11, R-030, https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-acdc-specification/issues/205). The next day he recorded the decision: "Based on the discussion in the maintainer call yesterday. The change of default is to land in v1.1 of the ACDC spec." Because vLEIs in production rely on the `I2I` default, "the v1.1 code must have a version switch that changes the default for v1.1 ACDCs but not for prior versions of the ACDC protocol." (issue #205, comment of 2026-08-12, R-030, https://github.com/trustoverip/kswg-acdc-specification/issues/205#issuecomment-5268897690). This is [proposal] with a maintainer-call decision behind it, and it is not carried: `v1.1` at `2362e48a1` keeps the `I2I`-if-targeted rule, and issue #205 is open. It changes the meaning of every operator-less edge in a v1.1 ACDC, and it reverses the position #1556 took in July against changing the global default ([section 9](#08-proposal-1556)). Once landed with the switch Sam describes, it would move the spec toward `acdc/ipexing.py`'s no-default behavior and away from `vdr/verifying.py`'s inferred `I2I` ([section 5](#08-three-axes)), for v1.1 ACDCs only (`raw/21` T-05).

#### M-ary operators {#08-mary-operators}

M-ary operators [spec] on an edge-group: `AND` (default), `OR`, `NAND`, `NOR`, `AVG`, `WAVG`. "When the Operator, `o`, field is missing in an Edge-group block, the default value for the Operator, `o`, field MUST be the `AND` Operator" (ACDC spec > Edge Section > Edge-group > Operator, `o` field, L1110 @f0bd097de; the m-ary table is unchanged between the branches).

#### No registry for operator tokens {#08-operator-namespace}

The operator-token namespace has no registry, and two specs are now writing into it. The Dossier spec @`6037adfb9` defines four further m-ary edge-group operators for joint issuance — `MxN`, `RMxN`, `MxQ`, `RMxQ` — "placed in the operator field (`o`) of an edge group within the dossier's edges block, following ACDC operator conventions" (Dossier spec > Joint Issuance > Threshold Operators, L364-372 @6037adfb9). They do not collide with the ACDC set or with the proposed `ME`, but nothing prevents a collision, and #1555 itself flags the risk in passing ("need to confirm no collisions"). Any argument that pivots away from edge operators toward exchange-message fields ([section 11](#08-dag-soup)) should weigh this: the operator namespace is a shared, unmanaged resource across at least two specifications.

#### keripy's operator enforcement {#08-keripy-operators}

[code] keripy recognizes five operators and enforces two of them, and the enforcement picture is mixed rather than empty. `Verifier.UnaryOps = ('I2I', 'NI2I', 'DI2I', 'E1E', 'NOT')` (keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier, L41 @b8f60166b). `I2I` and `E1E` are enforced — `I2I` as plain qb64 string equality of near-issuer against far-issuee, `E1E` as equality of the two issuees, with the code drawing the distinction explicitly: unlike `I2I`, `E1E` "says nothing about the issuer, so the common SEDI case -- both credentials issued by a third party to the same subject" is valid, which is exactly what `I2I` rejects. `NI2I` is a no-op binding check by construction — it requires the far node to exist and be in issued state, and constrains nothing about issuer or issuee. `DI2I` and `NOT` fail closed deliberately, raising `ValidationError` rather than escrowing, and the reason is written into the source: "DI2I and NOT are recognized but unimplemented: they are listed so they fail closed diagnosably instead of being dropped and silently defaulting" (keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier, L38-39 @b8f60166b), because "escrowing would promise a retry that can never succeed." A reviewer must not simplify either branch into a missing-chain error or into a silent skip. The edge `s` constraint is now enforced too, with "satisfy" rather than "equal" semantics: a direct SAID match short-circuits, otherwise the far node is validated against the edge's schema, and an uncached schema escrows and queries rather than failing.

#### Re-stamped 2026-10-03 at `80f77b73b` {#08-operators-restamp}

`vdr/verifying.py` has 17 changed lines between the two pins (10 insertions, 7 deletions; corrected 2026-10-03 (verification): previously "+17 lines"), all in comments, and every behavioral claim in the paragraph above still holds: the table is unchanged (`UnaryOps = ('I2I', 'NI2I', 'DI2I', 'E1E', 'NOT')`, keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier, L43 @80f77b73b; `DelegativeOps = ('I2I', 'NI2I', 'DI2I')`, L49), `DI2I` and `NOT` still raise at L449-455, the `E1E` branch is at L457-466, `I2I` equality at L481 (all keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier.verifyChain, @80f77b73b), edge `s` enforcement at L195-229 (keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier.processCredential, @80f77b73b). No new operator appeared. The two source comments quoted above were not separately re-quoted at the new pin and keep their `b8f60166b` stamp. [code] (raw/09 section 6c) Sam's own account of why `DI2I` exists, now on record in [#1515](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1515), bears on how much its fail-closed status matters: the QVI scaling case "came up in discussions with QVIs in the context of the EBA pilot, so we put it in the spec.  But the EBA backed out", and "That use case has yet been implemented by anyone AFAIK." (#1515, comment of 2026-07-18). That is his assessment, not a survey.

#### The read-but-unused shorthand {#08-read-but-unused}

The doctrinal shorthand "edge operators are read but unused" is no longer accurate at this pin, and the corpus's own shibboleth table still carries it. The replacement is the paragraph above, stated in full rather than compressed — two enforced, one vacuous, two failing closed on purpose — and the operator is still silently inferred when `o` is absent, now from a predicate that resolves an aggregate ACDC's issuee as well as an attributive one's.

#### A genuine inconsistency between two modules, which neither acknowledges {#08-module-inconsistency}

`vdr/verifying.py` drops an unrecognized operator token from a list-valued `o` and then applies the default rule; `acdc/ipexing.py` treats an unrecognized `o` as malformed and fails closed. The same edge can therefore pass credential processing and fail IPEX grant verification, or the reverse, depending only on which code path sees it. Nothing in either file mentions the other, and neither branch of the ACDC spec says what a validator should do with an operator token it does not recognize. This is the sharpest open code question in the chapter's area and is carried in [section 14](#08-open-questions).

#### Widened 2026-10-03: three axes of disagreement {#08-three-axes}

Widened 2026-10-03: at `80f77b73b` the two modules disagree on three axes, not one. [code] (raw/09 section 7e, section 9, section 11 item 1)

- Unrecognized tokens — unchanged. Dropped by `vdr/verifying.py` (keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier.verifyChain, L435 @80f77b73b); malformed in `acdc/ipexing.py`, now for every element of a list: `if any(operator not in UnaryEdgeOps for operator in recognizedOps): return None` (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._evaluateLeafEdge, L921-922 @80f77b73b).
- Conflicting operators in a list — new. `vdr/verifying.py` still resolves the delegative subset latest-wins (`op = next((cand for cand in reversed(ops) if cand in self.DelegativeOps), None)`, keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier.verifyChain, L436 @80f77b73b). `acdc/ipexing.py` deleted its `DelegativeEdgeOps` table and now conjoins: `E1E` and `I2I` each fire if they appear anywhere in the list, and "NI2I is explicitly non-delegative and therefore adds no issuer-to-Issuee equality." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._evaluateLeafEdge, L938-939 @80f77b73b). So `["I2I", "NI2I"]` is `NI2I` to one module and `I2I` to the other. The SEDI fixtures use `["E1E", "NI2I"]`, which both evaluate identically, so the tests do not exercise the divergence.
- Absent `o` — newly recorded. `vdr/verifying.py` infers `I2I` or `NI2I` (keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier.verifyChain, L443 @80f77b73b); `acdc/ipexing.py` applies no default — an absent leaf `o` yields no relation check at all (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._evaluateLeafEdge, L910-911 @80f77b73b). The same edge with no `o` is checked as `I2I` by credential processing and not checked by IPEX grant verification.

The second and third axes matter more than the first, because they are not about malformed input: they give two different answers for edges a conformant issuer may legitimately write. The `vdr/verifying.py` comment cites the ACDC spec for latest-wins; whether that citation holds is a `raw/03` check that has not been made, so the chapter does not yet say which module is right.

#### Where `E1E` came from {#08-e1e-origin}

#1515 is now read, and it settles where `E1E` came from. [#1515](https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1515), "New Unary Edge Operators to Support SEDI" (SmithSamuelM, opened 2026-07-17), is the origin: "E1E which means near side IssueE AID must equal far side IssueE AID." The opening post proposed a whole family — `I1I`, `I1E`, `E1I`, the "3" equivalence operators, and `DI1I` — and Sam then narrowed it to `E1E` alone: "The only concrete use case we have is for E1E, and we want to avoid it falling into the unknown operator trap." (#1515, comment of 2026-07-18). So `E1E`'s lineage is [proposal] in #1515, [code] in keripy, and [spec-next] in the ACDC `v1.1` branch, where `raw/03` read the row at `2362e48a1` in 2026-09; none of that changes this month. [proposal]

#### `I1I` and `DI1I` {#08-i1i-di1i}

New on 2026-10-01: `I1I` and `DI1I` are back, with a use case. [proposal] In a comment titled "Concrete Use Case in SEDI for I1I and DI1I operators" (2026-10-01), Sam argues that a SEDI leaf credential's edge to the core identity credential should be "both E1E and I1I  that is issuee is issuee and issuer is issuer." When `I1I` fails, "an alternate edge providing the chain of authority for the issuer is required"; `DI1I` is the delegated variant, used where "the delegation edge for the core is DI2I". He weighs an OR edge-group and prefers an optional schema edge instead: "Schema just needs to support the optional edge for delegation chain when the required E1E edge does not satisfy I1I". Neither operator exists in code at `80f77b73b`: both are absent from both operator tables and appear only in comments in `tests/sedi/test_sedi.py`. An edge carrying `o: "I1I"` today is silently dropped by `vdr/verifying.py` and is malformed to `acdc/ipexing.py` — the first axis above, which is exactly "the unknown operator trap" Sam named in July. One sentence in the comment says "I2I" where its context seems to call for "I1I"; raw/09 reads it as a probable slip and does not correct it, and neither does this chapter. [code] for the absence (raw/09 section 10 item 7, section 11 items 2 and 8).

#### M-ary operators in keripy {#08-mary-in-keripy}

M-ary operators are implemented in one module and absent from the other. The claim in the previous draft — that there is no m-ary concept at all in keripy and that every edge-group proposal is unbuildable — is superseded. The V2 IPEX module implements `EdgeGroupOps = ("AND", "OR")`, defaulting to `AND` as the spec requires, reducing a group with `any()`/`all()`, treating an empty group as malformed, and inheriting a group's edge-schema pin down to its children unless a child overrides it. `NAND`, `NOR`, `AVG` and `WAVG` remain unimplemented, and the Dossier spec's four threshold operators remain absent. The credential verifier in `vdr/verifying.py` is a separate matter: it resolves one hop and does not recurse, and the previous draft's `KeyError: 'n'` finding was made at `42db8991b` and was not re-verified at `b8f60166b` — treat it as standing at the old pin rather than as a current fact. What is verified at the new pin is that an ACDC's `e` section may now be either a single edge-block map or a list of them. Re-checked 2026-10-03: the V2 AND/OR reduction, schema-pin inheritance and closed edge label sets are unchanged in substance at `80f77b73b` (raw/09 section 7b), and the edge-list normalization in `vdr/verifying.py` sits at L165-171 (keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier.processCredential, L165-171 @80f77b73b).

One source comment worth knowing about when reading the code, and it is half right rather than stale: a comment in `vdr/verifying.py` says "E1E is a keripy extension not yet in the spec's normative operator table." (keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier, L40 @b8f60166b) Measured against the standardizing line that is accurate — `E1E` occurs zero times in `main` at `f0bd097de`. Measured against the forward branch it is behind, since `v1.1` at `2362e48a1` carries the row. The comment is therefore correct about what "normative" means today and out of date about where the design has gone, which is exactly the distinction this chapter's [spec]/[spec-next] split exists to preserve.
