Superseded 2026-10-03 — the comment has changed, and the paragraph above describes `b8f60166b` only. At `80f77b73b` it reads "E1E is normative on the spec's v1.1 branch (kswg-acdc-specification#197). It is absent from the 1.0 text currently under ToIP ratification" (keripy vdr/verifying.py, Verifier, L40-41 @80f77b73b). That now agrees with this chapter's tiering. It is not independent evidence for it: the change landed in `d9ba3d9da` (2026-09-11), a comments-only commit by Daniel Hardman, the corpus's own author, so the [spec-next] status of `E1E` continues to rest on `raw/03`'s reading of the `v1.1` branch, not on the code's say-so. (raw/09 section 6c)

## 6. Two IPEX state machines, and only one of them runs {#08-two-ipex}

### New 2026-09-15 {#08-two-ipex-new}

Every [code] claim about IPEX in this chapter now needs to say which IPEX, because keripy at `b8f60166b` contains two implementations of the protocol and they have begun to diverge. This section exists so that the rest of the chapter can cite one or the other without re-explaining the split.

#### V1, the handler keripy wires {#08-ipex-v1}

V1, `src/keri/vc/protocoling.py`, is the one keripy actually wires. Its handler is what the CLI loads. Its state machine is a legal-predecessor table: `offer` ← `apply`, `agree` ← `offer`, `grant` ← `agree`, `admit` ← `grant`, and `spurn` ← any of the four. `apply` may only open an exchange; `admit`, `agree` and `spurn` may never open one; `offer` and `grant` may open one or must answer a legal predecessor; the prior message must exist; and a second response to the same prior is rejected outright. An unmatched route returns false, so the machine fails closed. All of these claims were re-read at `b8f60166b` and are still true — they are rescoped, not superseded. What has changed is their scope: they describe the V1 handler, which is now one of two. [code]

#### V2, library and tests only {#08-ipex-v2}

V2, `src/keri/acdc/ipexing.py`, is library and tests only. `loadHandlers` has no caller anywhere in `src/keri` at this pin. The module is exported and exercised by tests, and it more than doubled in size in the two weeks before this pass, but nothing any shipped keripy command does goes through it. Claims sourced from it are [code] about code that exists in the reference implementation, not about behavior the reference implementation performs. Do not upgrade them past that, and do not cite V2 behavior as what "keripy does" without the qualifier.

#### Re-checked 2026-10-03: the split holds {#08-split-recheck}

Re-checked 2026-10-03 at `80f77b73b`: both halves of the split still hold. `loadHandlers` is now at `acdc/ipexing.py` L2149-2167 (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, loadHandlers, L2149-2167 @80f77b73b) and still registers six routes; a search of `src/keri` for `ipexing` and for imports of `acdc.loadHandlers` finds only the `acdc/__init__.py` re-export and the module's own docstring. The module has 913 changed lines in the window (729 insertions, 184 deletions, net +545; corrected 2026-10-03 (verification): previously "grew by another ~900 lines"). The CLI still loads V1: `cli/commands/ipex/list.py` L25 reads `from ....vc import loadHandlers, Ipex` (keripy cli/commands/ipex/list.py, L25 @80f77b73b), and the CLI changes in the window are V1 transport fixes. `vc/protocoling.py` itself is byte-identical between the two pins, so the V1 paragraph above carries forward unread. [code] (raw/09 section 7, section 7b)

#### The split is deliberate, and v1 exchanges will not be anchored {#08-split-deliberate}

Added 2026-10-15. The two modules were planned, not drifted into. Sam's PR that created the `acdc` subpackage in February says it "provides a place to support the new features in acdc v2 while leaving support for acdc v1 in the vc subpackage." (keripy PR #1170, body of 2026-02-04, R-078, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1170). And anchoring stays on the V2 side by policy: "Its only with v2 exchange messages that we plan to anchor exchanges. We really don't want to be anchoring v1 exchanges." (keripy PR #1492, comment of 2026-07-27, R-057, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1492#issuecomment-5093267019). The same comment puts the burden on deployments to move production branches to v2 for IPEX. That answers part of [question 14](#08-q-surviving-ipex) as intent: V2 is the module meant to carry IPEX forward, though nothing yet wires it. [proposal]

#### Where the two disagree, and it is not cosmetic {#08-v1-v2-differences}

V2's table lets a `grant` reply directly to an `apply`, skipping `offer` and `agree` entirely; V1 still requires `agree` first. Whether that shortcut reflects a spec intention or an implementation convenience is unsettled — neither branch of the ACDC spec's route table speaks to legal predecessors at all, so there is no text to appeal to. V2 also adds checks V1 has no equivalent of: role symmetry, so a reply must target the prior sender and come from the prior receiver, with a fourth test on the exchange id; ~~a refusal to spurn a thread-opening grant~~ a refusal to spurn a grant that answers a prior message, so that only a flow-starting grant may be spurned (corrected 2026-10-15; the struck phrase inverted the code, see [Spurning a grant](#08-spurn-grant)); m-ary edge-group evaluation over the disclosed DAG ([section 5](#08-edges)); rejection of orphan nests and, for a grant, of dangling edges, since "grant must disclose one fully closed reachable DAG rooted at the message's `a.o[0]`"; a one-nest-per-node rule stated as an anti-substitution guard, so "the node body cannot appear twice with conflicting attachment groups"; and a KEL-anchor check for `ax` ([section 10](#08-anchoring)). Its verification runs as six numbered stages, every failure path returning false. [code]

Re-checked 2026-10-03 at `80f77b73b`. The predecessor table is unchanged — `Ipex.grant: (Ipex.apply, Ipex.agree),` (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, PreviousRoutes, L35 @80f77b73b) — as are the role-symmetry and single-response checks, the anchoring-negotiation invariants, the closed-DAG walk and orphan-nest rejection, and the one-nest-per-node guard (raw/09 section 7b). Two V2 checks changed in substance and are covered where they bear: anchoring for a `grant` now accepts a set of anchorers rather than only the sender ([section 10](#08-anchoring)), and per-node issuer authentication now runs on every disclosed node rather than only registry-backed ones ([section 7](#08-authentication-factors)). A further stage, presentation-registry authentication, runs on every `grant` after those ([section 10](#08-anchoring); [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md)). [code]

#### Spurning a grant: corrected 2026-10-15 {#08-spurn-grant}

Until 2026-10-15 this section said V2 adds "a refusal to spurn a thread-opening grant", and `raw/09` section 7b said the same. Both inverted the code. The check rejects a spurn of a grant only when that grant has a prior: `if verb == Ipex.spurn and pverb == Ipex.grant and pserder.ked.get("p", ""):` (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._verifyReplyChain, L761 @80f77b73b), and the builder states the rule outright, raising "only flow-starting grants may be spurned" (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, spurn, L2120-2121 @80f77b73b). The same predicate was already there at `b8f60166b`, so the error was a misreading, not a change in the code, and the code is unchanged at upstream `c102367ea`. [code] V1 is different again: its table lets a spurn answer any of the four verbs, a grant after an agree included ([section 6](#08-ipex-v1)).

The rule is Sam's. keripy #1517 had removed `grant` from the routes a spurn can answer, on his reasoning that a grant after an agree cannot be taken back. Issue #1628 argued that the reasoning does not reach an unsolicited grant, which nobody agreed to, and he agreed: "an unsolicited grant i.e using a xip message should be spurnable. that is nuance i did not anticipate." (keripy issue #1628, comment of 2026-08-19, R-051, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/issues/1628#issuecomment-5349282926). The same comment extends it to a bare `exn` with an empty `p`, if KRAM supports one. So a disclosee who never asked for a credential can refuse it, and one who agreed to terms cannot repudiate them after the grant. [proposal] for the ruling, [code] for the code that carries it.

Neither ACDC branch speaks to the case. The route table lists `spurn` as rejecting `apply`, `offer` and `agree`, with no row for a spurn of a `grant` (ACDC spec > IPEX Protocol Messages, L1812-1816 @f0bd097de; L2005-2009 @2362e48a1). The spec is silent on exactly the case both Sam and the code allow; see [question 22](#08-q-spurn-grant).

#### What IPEX preserves and what it rejects {#08-defer-vs-refuse}

"IPEX rejects what it preserves" needs qualifying rather than cutting. The chapter has used that phrase for the shape of the KRAM gap in [section 8](#08-freshness-kram), and at `b8f60166b` the accurate form is sharper and is a statement about the handler generally: IPEX preserves what it defers on, and drops what it refuses. A missing chain escrows the message and cues a proof fetch, returning `None`, because "Registry-backed IPEX grants may arrive before the disclosee has fetched the issuer's TEL history from observers" — the message survives for replay. A behavior `verify` that returns false returns before the event is logged, so a permanently-invalid message is never persisted. The two outcomes are not variants of one rejection; they are a deferral and a refusal, and only the deferral preserves anything. [code] Re-verified 2026-10-03 at `80f77b73b` (keripy peer/exchanging.py, Exchanger.processEvent, L389-410 @80f77b73b; raw/09 section 7d), with one addition that softens the deferral for one verb: a route may now opt out of fail-closed handling of unresolved foreign evidence — "Opted routes request the KEL and continue with known factors." (keripy peer/exchanging.py, Exchanger.processEvent, L167 @80f77b73b) — and in IPEX only the grant route opts in (`self.acceptsMissingEvidence = resource == "/ipex/grant"`, keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.__init__, L438 @80f77b73b). So a `grant` carrying an endorsement whose endorser's KEL is not yet local proceeds on the factors it can verify, rather than waiting. [code]

## 7. Authentication factors: the second problem {#08-authentication-factors}

The DAG solves data integrity and authority structure. It does not, by itself, establish that the party sending the presentation controls anything at the moment of sending. Discussion #1613, "Authentication Factors in IPEX," is the systematic treatment. All of it is [proposal]; none of it is in any spec.

### Two purposes, never conflated {#08-two-purposes}

Every ACDC in a granted DAG needs an Issuer authentication factor — proof it was authentically issued. The `grant` needs a Grantor authentication factor — fresh proof of control by whoever is presenting. "For a given ACDC, a Grantor may be the Issuee, Issuer, both, or neither."

#### Three factor types, strictly ranked {#08-factor-ranking}

Three factor types, strictly ranked: registry (TEL) anchor, KEL anchor, bare signature. The ranking is not stylistic — registry and KEL anchors "enable perpetual verifiability and detectability of impersonation fraud. Whereas a bare signature does not," and a registry anchor additionally carries lifecycle state. The composition rule is absorption: "when multiple authentication factors are either required or provided for the same purpose, the highest-preference factor is used, and the others are ignored."

#### Bare signatures are ephemeral {#08-bare-signatures}

Bare signatures are ephemeral in a strong sense. "as soon as the Issuer rotates its keystate, any ACDCs it issued using a bare signature as the Issuer authentication factor with a prior keystate become unverifiable and must be reissued. This is only useful for truly temporary use (ephemeral) ACDCs." This is worth flagging against [section 3](#08-bespoke-origin)'s claim that a bespoke origin "does not need to be anchored or use a registry": a registryless, signature-only bespoke origin is disposable by construction, which is fine for a one-time recipe and is not fine if anyone later needs to prove what was presented.

#### The issuer factor for every disclosed node {#08-issuer-factor-every-node}

New 2026-10-03: the issuer factor is now [code] for every disclosed node, in the V2 module. At `b8f60166b` the V2 handler checked issuer authentication only for registry-backed nodes, and a node without a top-level `rd` passed that stage unconditionally. At `80f77b73b` `_verifyIssuerAuthGraph` requires "one valid issuer authentication factor per node" (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._verifyIssuerAuthGraph, L1132 @80f77b73b), and `_verifyIssuerAuthNode` (L1139) selects exactly one of three, in #1613's order and without falling through once one is chosen: the issuer registry when a top-level `rd` is present (L1142-1152); a seal anchor in the issuer's KEL (L1159-1201), where "An invalid anchor must not silently downgrade the ACDC to signature authentication." (L1199-1200); or signatures (L1203-1263), kept only if they "already name the current state" (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._verifyIssuerAuthNode, L1237-1240 @80f77b73b). That last restriction is the code's version of the ephemerality #1613 describes: an ACDC signed under issuer keys that have since rotated, with no registry and no anchor, should no longer authenticate in a V2 grant. That consequence is raw/09's inference from the code, not behavior anyone has run, and the code states the filter without stating the reason ([section 14](#08-open-questions)). [code] (raw/09 section 7e; V2-only per [section 6](#08-two-ipex))

#### Vocabulary {#08-ipex-vocabulary}

The Discloser sends `offer` and `grant` (Offerer, Grantor); the Disclosee sends `apply`, `agree`, `admit` (Applicant, Agreent, Admittant). "In common parlance, a Grantor is a Presentor, and the grant is a presentation." Where several AIDs endorse one grant, "there is a set of Grantors that each must be uniquely authenticated."

#### The receiver AID is never empty {#08-receiver-aid}

Added 2026-10-15. Every IPEX message names both parties. Asked why a draft left `ri` empty on several verbs, Sam answered: "The `ri` field is meant to carry the receiver AID." The negotiating AIDs are a correlation point by construction, and he argues that is the price of a binding contract rather than a leak: the verifier can correlate on the presenter's negotiating AID but "can't prove it is the same as the Issuee until the Grant", and "Proof of participation is not the same as correlation." (keripy discussion #1542, comment of 2026-07-23, R-054, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1542#discussioncomment-17755467). Contract law wants "a clear intent to engage in legal relations", which needs identity, so graduated disclosure governs the ACDC content and not the pair of AIDs negotiating over it. [proposal] keripy's V2 module already refuses a reply whose prior names no receiver (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._verifyReplyChain, L766-768 @80f77b73b). [code]

## 8. Freshness: KRAM, and what rests on it {#08-freshness-kram}

Everything about multiply-endorsed presentation rests on KRAM, so its status matters more than any other single fact in this chapter.

> This section is an audit of KRAM's status as it bears on presentation, not an account of what KRAM is. For the mechanism itself — the problem it solves, simple vs full KRAM, the monotonic timeliness cache, the v0.7.6 redesign, and its relationship to BADA-RUN — see [chapter 09](09-kram-and-request-authentication.md), which is built from Sam's whitepaper rather than from #1613's paraphrase of it. Two claims below are corrected there and are marked in place.

### The problem {#08-replay-problem}

A signature is a bearer token: "Any holder of both the document and its signature can replay them, and the signature will verify" (#1613). That phrasing is #1613's, and [proposal]. The KERI spec states the general form and prefers non-interactive mitigation — "Because non-interactive mitigations are asynchronous, however, they do not have the latency and scalability limitations of interactive mitigations and are therefore preferred" (KERI spec > Annex A > BADA (Best-Available-Data-Acceptance) Policy > Security Issues, L2878 @be618e7dc). [spec] for the problem and the preference; the spec says it about data-at-rest under BADA, not about presentations, so applying it here is this chapter's step. (Retiered 2026-10-15: this heading carried an ad hoc marker, `[N-adjacent]`, now said in words; the locator previously named a "Replay attack" heading that does not exist at that pin.)

#### The proposed mechanism [proposal] {#08-kram-mechanism}

As #1613 describes it, KRAM (KERI Request Authentication Mechanism) uses "a message SAID `d` field, a sender AID `i` field, a receiver AID `ri` field, a salty nonce `u` field, and a datetime stamp relative to the receiver's clock `dt` field." Corrected — the nonce is not part of KRAM. The whitepaper builds uniqueness from monotonic ordering of receiver-clock datetimes, and argues at length that nonce-based mechanisms are what KRAM replaces; keripy reads `msg.stamp` and never touches `u`. See [chapter 09, section 4](#09-redesign) and [chapter 09, section 8](#09-load-bearing). Its properties are otherwise as stated: one play or none, within a window measured on the receiver's clock, so "The sender cannot therefore lie about the datetime in the message." A same-message replay inside the window is either ignored or, for a multisig sender, contributes its signature to an escrow — "This elegantly solves the multi-sig problem without requiring a pre-protocol to collect signatures. The receiver's KRAM escrow does the signature collection."

#### Three findings about KRAM's actual status, each verified {#08-kram-status-findings}

KRAM is not in the KERI specification. A search for "KRAM" across KERI spec `main` @`be618e7dc` returns nothing in `spec/spec-body.md`. The spec discusses replay attacks and BADA-RUN at length and never names this mechanism. So the freshness guarantee the entire multiply-endorsed design depends on is, at the specification layer, absent. (One near-miss, found later: the rendered v1 artifact carries a glossary cross-reference imported from `trustoverip/kerisuite-glossary`, defining simple KRAM in a single sentence. It is not spec text, and it describes the variant that cannot support multisig — see [chapter 09, section 5](#09-normative-status).)

The `u` field KRAM is described as using does not exist on an `exn`. This puzzle probably dissolves — `u` is #1613's paraphrase, not the whitepaper's mechanism, per the correction above. The observation about message shapes stands on its own terms and is worth keeping, so it is recorded unchanged below. The KERI spec fixes both message shapes exactly: `xip` is `[v, t, d, u, i, ri, dt, r, q, a]` and `exn` is `[v, t, d, i, ri, x, p, dt, r, q, a]`, and for both, "All are REQUIRED. No other top-level fields are allowed (MUST NOT appear)" (KERI spec > Routed Messages > Exchange Transaction Inception Message Body, L1154 @be618e7dc; KERI spec > Routed Messages > Exchange Message Body, L1197 @be618e7dc). `u` is present on `xip` and absent on `exn`; the spec says `u` "appears in exchange transaction inception messages to ensure that the associated transaction ID is also universally unique" (KERI spec > Routed Messages > Reserved field labels in routed messages > UUID Salty Nonce field, L963 @be618e7dc). #1613 describes KRAM as using `u` and as applying "to each `xip` or `exn` individually." For an `exn` the uniqueness comes from `x` ⧺ `p` chaining instead. This may be a slip in the prose rather than a design gap, but it is not currently reconcilable as written.

keripy is further along than the July reading suggested, and the gap has moved. [code] `Kramer` (`src/keri/core/kraming.py`) is real, exn-aware — its cache-type cascade is keyed by message ilk and route, `_fetchCacheType(msgType, route)` with "`exn`" named explicitly (keripy core/kraming.py, Kramer._fetchCacheType, L282 @4df8e4a86) — and it deliberately distinguishes sender from non-sender attachments. `_normalizeSenderSeals` "leaves only non-sender triples in ssts for non-auth forwarding / escrow" (keripy core/kraming.py, Kramer._normalizeSenderSeals, L386 @4df8e4a86), and `_normalizeCurrentSenderTsgs` notes that "downstream exn/rpy handling still needs the[m]" (keripy core/kraming.py, Kramer._normalizeCurrentSenderTsgs, L448 @4df8e4a86). It is instantiated inside `Kevery` (keripy core/eventing.py, Kevery.__init__, L4176-4178 @4df8e4a86) and is default-disabled: "KRAM enforcement remains controlled by the provided configuration, defaulting to disabled without one." Sharpen that at `upstream/main` @`4df8e4a86` (2026-09-01): `Kevery.__init__` still takes `enableKram=False`, but the two runtimes that matter both pass `enableKram=True` — `app/directing.py` (keripy app/directing.py, Reactant.__init__, L470 @4df8e4a86) and `app/indirecting.py` (keripy app/indirecting.py, setupWitness, L76 @4df8e4a86). Default-disabled is a fact about the class, not about deployed agents and witnesses.

So KRAM now does exactly what #1613 says it does — passes non-sender endorsements along. And then `Exchanger.processEvent` throws them away, along with the whole message:

```python
if sender != prefixer.qb64:  # sig not by aid
    ...
    raise MissingSignatureError(msg)
```
(keripy peer/exchanging.py, Exchanger.processEvent, L88-95 @42db8991b.) `peer/exchanging.py` contained no reference to `kraming` or `Kramer` at all. The July-2026 reading of this gap was "KRAM is not wired to exn." The accurate August reading is sharper and more actionable: KRAM is exn-aware and preserves non-sender endorsements specifically so a downstream handler can use them, and the downstream handler rejects the message for carrying them. That is a two-sided gap in one code path, not an absent feature.

#### Amended 2026-09-15: the evidence policy {#08-evidence-policy}

Amended 2026-09-15, and the amendment is a real movement on the half of the gap that matters. At `b8f60166b`, `peer/exchanging.py` was reworked around a per-route evidence policy: `Exchanger.processEvent` looks for a `verifyEvidence` method on the route's behavior. A route without one keeps the old treatment — "Routes without an evidence policy preserve the existing TSG-over-cigar precedence" — and rejects foreign evidence outright, which is the behavior the paragraph above describes. A route with one receives only the validated foreign subset and gets to accept or refuse it, and refusing means the message is not persisted. The V2 IPEX handler supplies such a policy, and for a `grant` specifically it keeps what verifies: "Grant evidence is optional, so retain the valid subset despite invalid extras." Every other verb still rejects any non-sender evidence at all. So the downstream half of the two-sided gap — the handler that threw non-sender endorsements away — is closed for grants in the V2 module, which is exactly the message multiple endorsement attaches to ([section 9](#08-multiple-endorsement)). The qualification that keeps this honest is [section 6](#08-two-ipex)'s: the V2 module has no caller in `src/keri`, so this is capability in the reference implementation rather than behavior in the shipped path, and the V1 handler keripy actually wires has no evidence policy and therefore still refuses. [code] Sender authentication also gained a second independent satisfier at this pin — a valid source seal authenticates an `exn` on its own, and an invalid optional sender signature group is then tolerated rather than fatal, which a reviewer should not "simplify" into a conjunction. The KRAM-side claims above were not re-read at `b8f60166b` — `core/kraming.py` belongs to a different note and its last verification stands at `4df8e4a86` (2026-09-01). Treat the `Kramer` details, and the default-disabled-but-enabled-in-deployment finding, as pinned there.

#### Amended again 2026-10-03, at `80f77b73b` {#08-evidence-policy-1003}

The structure of the paragraph above still holds — routes without an evidence policy reject foreign evidence, and the V2 grant route keeps a validated subset (keripy peer/exchanging.py, Exchanger.processEvent, L140, L183-186, L211-213 @80f77b73b; raw/09 section 7d). What it quotes for the grant policy does not. The sentence "Grant evidence is optional, so retain the valid subset despite invalid extras." describes `b8f60166b`; at `80f77b73b` `verifyEvidence` is stricter about which subset it keeps. "Only Grant accepts supplemental grantor evidence." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verifyEvidence, L1574 @80f77b73b), and of that evidence it keeps only signatures tied to the endorser's current establishment event — "Require exact current establishment coordinates." (L1581) — and only fresh source seals, dropping an AID's signature when the same AID also supplied a valid seal (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verifyEvidence, L1608-1613 @80f77b73b). Every other verb still refuses any non-sender evidence. Accepted non-sender endorsements are now reverse-indexed by AID in a new `eidx` store, which takes "Only behavior-approved non-sender endorsements" (keripy peer/exchanging.py, Exchanger.logEvent, L616-617 @80f77b73b). What the grant verifier then does with them is [section 9](#08-multiple-endorsement)'s subject, and the answer is less than this paragraph might suggest. [code]

#### One KRAM-side change that IPEX now depends on, at `80f77b73b` {#08-kram-rdt}

KRAM's transactioned-message cache now records the receiver time at which it accepted the complete message, `rdt`, and sets it for a multi-key sender only once the threshold is met (keripy core/kraming.py, Kramer.kramit, L1655-1661 @80f77b73b). Its consumer is IPEX, not KRAM: the V2 presentation-registry check refuses a grant that declares a presentation registry unless KRAM completed acceptance — "A presentation requirement needs a completed KRAM acceptance." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._verifyPresentationAuthGraph, L1524 @80f77b73b) — and uses `rdt` as the cutoff for registry history. So at this pin KRAM is no longer only a replay filter in keripy; one verification path reads its acceptance timestamp. `raw/15` infers that a deployment with KRAM disabled therefore cannot accept a grant carrying a presentation-registry declaration; that is an inference from two code sites, not something a test was found to exercise. [code] (raw/15 section 4.8) The rest of the KRAM material above stays pinned at `4df8e4a86`.

#### Tethering [proposal] {#08-tethering}

Given multi-endorsement-aware KRAM, #1613 defines a derived property. The `grant` carries the origin SAID in an origin `o` field, and because the origin commits to every ACDC in its DAG, "when any Grantor AID appears anywhere in the DAG of ACDCs originating at the origin ACDC, then we say that that ACDC is *tethered* to the `grant`." Tethering means only that: fresh proof of control over that AID, wherever it appears. "Tethering implies no other relationship besides fresh (timely) proof-of-control over an AID so tethered." Its motivating case is entitlement replay — Bob's movie coupon, where Cal must know Bob and not the thief Ian is presenting.

#### A vocabulary trap in the code, as of `80f77b73b` {#08-tethered-set}

The V2 IPEX module has a set called `tethered`, and it is not #1613's tethering. It holds the Issuees a presentation registry authenticated, and it is consumed only by the `ax` anchoring rule ([section 10](#08-anchoring)). Nothing in the code requires an Issuee appearing in the DAG to be a Grantor, which is what #1613's tethering would check (raw/16 section 7.3, section 7.7). So tethering as #1613 defines it remains unimplemented, and a reader grepping for the word will find something else. [code]

Note that the origin `o` field is [proposal] and appears in no spec. Note also that `o` is already the reserved label for Operator throughout the ACDC edge and edge-group blocks. The two live in different namespaces — an `exn` attribute section versus an ACDC edge block — so this is an overload rather than a collision, but it is an overload in a protocol family where `o` otherwise means exactly one thing.

## 9. Multiply endorsed presentation: the proposal that moved {#08-multiple-endorsement}

This is the clearest case in the corpus of a design that was superseded, and reading the superseded version as current is the most likely way to be wrong about it.

### #1555 (2026-07-29) [proposal] {#08-proposal-1555}

Superseded in large part by #1613 below, though not its `ME` operator. (Retiered 2026-10-15: the heading carried an ad hoc marker, `[P, superseded]`, now said in words.) Non-sender AIDs attach signature groups (`-X`/`-Y` for transferable, and seal-source equivalents) to a single `grant`; KRAM's timeliness extends to them. The signal that endorsement is required should live in the ACDC, not the `exn`, because "An exchange message is relatively simple in comparison to an ACDC. There is no normative cryptographic commitment in an exchange message to a given schema." The mechanism: a new M-ary edge-group operator, `ME`, on a bespoke origin, meaning each far ACDC in the group must be endorsed by its issuee via signatures attached to the grant. Multi-DAG presentation explicitly out of scope.

#### #1556 (2026-07-29) [proposal] {#08-proposal-1556}

The companion. The global `I2I` default is a backward-compatibility accommodation for pre-operator vLEIs, and it fits the new non-delegative operators badly — an `ME` group would need explicit `NI2I` on every edge. Proposal: make unary defaults a function of the enclosing m-ary group operator (`ME` group → `NI2I` default), and add an `IAND` group whose edges default to `E1E`. Not changing the global default, which "might break vLEIs in the wild." Superseded in part 2026-10-15: two weeks later Sam proposed changing the global default after all, and a maintainer call decided that it becomes `NI2I` for v1.1 ACDCs behind a version switch, which answers the vLEI concern by leaving older ACDCs on `I2I` ([section 5](#08-default-change)). The group-scoped defaults and `IAND` are not withdrawn, but the problem they were built around is now proposed to be solved globally.

#### #1613 (2026-08-12, revised to v1.5 on 2026-08-18) [proposal] {#08-proposal-1613}

The current proposal. (Retiered 2026-10-15: the heading carried an ad hoc marker, `[P, current]`, now said in words.) Opens by superseding its predecessor: "As of version 1.1, this discussion supersedes much of the 'Multiply Endorsed' discussion... This discussion solves for the proxy negotiator for another AID use case without needing a new edge operator." What it does not supersede is `ME` itself — "It does not supersede the proposal for a new edge operator" — and it explicitly does not solve "the more generic use cases of a proxy negotiator for multiple other AID nor the more generic case where multiple simultaneous AIDs are negotiating in concert."

#### The motivating case: correlation, not convenience {#08-proxy-motivation}

The motivating case is correlation, not convenience. "a given controller may use one AID it controls as a proxy to negotiate on behalf of another AID it controls so that this other AID is not disclosed until after contractual protection is in place... Only the first AID needs to participate in the failed negotiation and is the only one exposed by it." Sam (proxy negotiator) fronts for Bob (coupon issuee); Bob's AID appears for the first time in the `grant`.

#### The processing rule [proposal] {#08-endorsement-processing}

KRAM validates sender-AID groups and passes non-sender groups through; "to support multiply endorsed IPEX, the IPEX processor MUST validate all non-sender endorsements after KRAM." Signatures must verify against the endorser's current key state and satisfy its threshold; seal-source references must be found in the endorser's KEL against the message SAID; where both are supplied, "the seal source reference is preferred."

#### One limitation stated plainly, and it is the sharp edge {#08-multisig-endorser-limit}

A non-sender multisig endorser gets no help from KRAM's escrow-collects-signatures trick, "therefore, the Grantor must employ some pre-protocol to collect a threshold-satisfying set of signatures and then attach them to the grant." The offered mitigation is that a proxy and its principal are the same controller and can be given matching multisig infrastructure and threshold, in which case collection happens "serendipitously." That is a real constraint on deployment topology dressed as a coincidence.

#### The `grant` only {#08-grant-only}

Multiple endorsement attaches to the `grant` and to nothing else — "A valid IPEX could consist of only a `grant` message. This means that multiple endorsements cannot depend on some combined effect of multiple messages."

#### New 2026-10-03: what keripy does with a multiply-endorsed grant, and the gap in it [code] {#08-keripy-endorsement}

At `80f77b73b`, in the V2 module only ([section 6](#08-two-ipex)), the generator supports the design. Commit `790797bcd` ("add multiply endorse support, add presentation registry support") gave `grant` two new parameters: endorsers are "Additional local habitats that sign the same outer exchange as non-sender grantors (e.g proxy AIDs)." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, _sign, L291-292 @80f77b73b), and anchorers are "Additional local transferable habitats whose KELs seal the same outer exchange." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, _sign, L293-294 @80f77b73b), attached as explicit source triples naming the anchoring AID. On the receiving side, the processing rule above is followed as far as filtering goes: non-sender evidence is validated after KRAM, against the endorser's current establishment state, and a valid seal from an AID is preferred to that AID's signatures — the code's version of "the seal source reference is preferred" from the processing rule above. Accepted endorsements are persisted and indexed.

#### Endorsement signatures do not decide validity {#08-signatures-discarded}

But endorsement signatures do not decide whether a grant is valid. `IpexHandler.verify` unpacks the accepted evidence as `_, _, extraSeals = evidence` (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L605 @80f77b73b) and discards the signature groups. Only the source seals are used, and only toward the anchoring requirement of [section 10](#08-anchoring). Under the default policy, then, an endorsement signature on a grant is recorded and has no effect on acceptance; an endorsement seal can satisfy `ax`. The #1613 obligation that each Grantor's endorsement verify and satisfy its threshold therefore has no consumer in the verdict. Whether non-sender signature groups are threshold-checked at all is unverified (raw/16 section 7.3 did not read `verifyAttachments`), and whichever way that falls, the result is not used. The limitation stated above — that a non-sender multisig endorser needs a signature-collection pre-protocol — is moot in the code for the same reason, because the signatures such a pre-protocol would collect are not counted. Whether discarding them is the intended endpoint or a stage in progress is not said anywhere in the tree ([section 14](#08-open-questions)). (raw/09 section 7e, section 10 item 9)

#### Live co-presence versus durable consent {#08-copresence-vs-consent}

`ME`-style endorsement requires every issuee online and signing at presentation time. It does not cover presentation on behalf of an offline party — a guardian for a dependent, an agent for a traveller. That case closes under plain `I2I` with a consent ACDC in the middle, and does so today at v2 with no new operator: `bespoke(issuer=A, issuee=V) --I2I--> consent(issuer=B, issuee=A) --I2I--> credential(issuer=HA, issuee=B)`. Both links satisfy `I2I`, and A cannot manufacture the bridge because the middle link demands B be the issuer of the consent. These are complementary halves — live freshness versus durable delegation bounded by revocation — and conflating them is easy. (Established by measurement, keripy v2, 2026-07-29; see #1555's comment stream.)

## 10. Anchoring: the `ax` field, presentation registries, origin-AID anchoring {#08-anchoring}

### Mostly [proposal], from #1613, but no longer all of it {#08-anchoring-tiers}

The section was written when every construct in it was a proposal. At keripy `b8f60166b` one of the three legs is [code], and saying which one is the point: direct KEL anchoring of a truthy `ax` is implemented, and presentation-registry anchoring is not. The sub-claims are marked individually below.

#### Superseded 2026-10-03 {#08-anchoring-superseded}

At keripy `80f77b73b` all three legs are [code] in the V2 module: direct KEL anchoring, presentation-registry anchoring, and #1613's origin-AID fallback rule, under which the origin's Issuee or Issuer may anchor in place of the sender. The 2026-09-15 sentence above is kept as the record of where the code stood two weeks earlier. Every one of these remains absent from both ACDC spec branches, and every one is subject to [section 6](#08-two-ipex)'s qualifier: the module that implements them has no caller in `src/keri`.

#### The gap `ax` fills {#08-ax-gap}

KRAM proves timeliness but "gives neither party a way to signal to the IPEX that the relevant messages MUST be perpetually verifiable and hence anchored. Anchoring via KRAM is solely determined by the set of endorsers at the time the message is transmitted."

#### The field {#08-ax-field}

`ax` is a boolean in the attribute `a` section of `apply`, `offer`, and `grant`; truthy only if present and `True`. An IPEX may begin with any of those three, so any of them may carry it. Satisfying it means the Grantor anchors the `grant` and the Applicant anchors `agree` and `admit`, with an exception where a `grant` arrives without an enabling `agree`.

Note the placement asymmetry against [section 4](#08-disclosure-paths): `dp` is in `q` on the forward branch and never in a `grant`; `ax` and the origin `o` are proposed for `a` and do appear in a `grant`. Any proposal that amends all three uniformly has to account for this.

#### `ax` in keripy {#08-ax-keripy}

`ax` is now [code], as a negotiated bit with a real anchor check behind it. At `b8f60166b` the V2 IPEX handler treats anchoring as negotiated state that a reply may not silently change: for `agree`, `grant` and `admit`, "Binding replies must exactly preserve the negotiated state," and an `offer` "may initiate anchoring, but may not drop it." That one-sidedness is an invariant a reviewer must not relax into a symmetric check. Where anchoring is required, the handler demands a real seal in the sender's own KEL: a source-seal couple naming an event at or after the sender's last establishment event, matching that event's SAID at the same sequence number, required to be an interaction event beyond it, and containing a seal whose digest is this exn's SAID. Missing KEL evidence raises a retryable missing-key-state error rather than a rejection — a deferral, in [section 6](#08-two-ipex)'s terms, not a refusal. [code]

#### Narrowed 2026-10-03 {#08-ax-narrowed}

Narrowed 2026-10-03: at `80f77b73b` the sender-KEL requirement applies to `agree` and `admit` only. The negotiation invariants are unchanged (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L561-568 @80f77b73b), and the seal checks moved into `_verifySourceAnchor` (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._verifySourceAnchor, L656-703 @80f77b73b) unchanged in substance. But "Agree and Admit satisfy anchoring directly through their sender." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L573 @80f77b73b), and a `grant` no longer must: "A truthy ax requires one permitted Grant anchorer." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L620 @80f77b73b). The verifier collects every AID that anchored the grant — the sender if its own seal verifies, every non-sender whose source seal verifies against its own KEL, and every Issuee a presentation registry authenticated — and accepts if any of them is one of three: `candidates = (serder.pre, origin.iseaid, origin.israid)` (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L648 @80f77b73b), the sender and the Issuee and Issuer of the origin named by `a.o[0]`. The comment draws the boundary as policy: "Default IPEX policy deliberately stops at these three AIDs; credential-specific policy may impose a narrower requirement." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L645-646 @80f77b73b). So a grant with `ax` true can now be valid with no sender anchor at all, provided the origin's Issuee or Issuer sealed it. The generator side matches: `grant(..., anchorers=[])` suppresses the default sender anchor and "leaves anchoring to a presentation registry." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, grant, L1948-1950 @80f77b73b). [code] (raw/09 section 7e; raw/16 section 2.5)

#### One-item lists on the wire {#08-one-item-lists}

And `o` and `ax` are one-item lists on the wire, which settles a conflict raised on the discussion. `_validSingleDagList` rejects any non-list and requires exactly one entry, with the source saying why: "We currently only support one DAG (until Multi DAG), so exactly one entry is required." On 2026-09-01 dhh1128 flagged on #1627 that keripy had merged `o` as a scalar string while the validator rejected lists outright, which contradicted #1627's preferred list form ([section 11](#08-dag-soup)). The code went the list way within ten days. That is worth noticing as a fact about this design conversation's tempo: a conflict between a discussion's preferred design and the implementation was resolved, in the discussion's favour, by the implementation rather than by the discussion. [code]

#### An origin `o` on the `offer` too {#08-offer-origin}

Added 2026-10-15. Sam wants the `offer` to carry an origin as well: "The offer message also needs to have an origin `o` field to replace the ACDC field." (keripy PR #1629, review of 2026-08-20, R-053, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1629#pullrequestreview-4987948288). Its value is "just the SAID of the Metadata ACDC DAG origin. The actual metadata ACDCs are attached in a substream." (keripy PR #1629, review comment of 2026-08-21, R-053, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1629#discussion_r3832392219). The reason is the agreement step: the metadata ACDC discloses the rule section and withholds the attributes, so "the only way for the agreent to know what it is agreeing to is for it to see the metadata ACDC DAG". So an `offer` looks structurally like the `grant` it anticipates. Neither ACDC branch has an `o` on either message. [proposal] This bears on [question 4](#08-q-dag-ordering): if the `offer` carries an origin, one message before the `grant` names a DAG, though the `apply` still does not.

#### The third leg, as of 2026-09-15 {#08-third-leg}

The third leg did not move, and chapter 10 owns it. #1618 frames presentation authentication as three factors — a signed grant, a grant anchored in an Issuee-controlled presentation registry, and a grant anchored directly in a KEL without one. Leg 3 is the one that just became [code]; leg 2 is not implemented at all, and the merged PR that added the anchoring work says so of itself, stating that presentation-registry anchoring "will come in a follow up PR." The three legs have moved apart, and the one that moved is the one needing no registry, no Issuee cooperation and no new infrastructure — which is what cost predicts and is not evidence about the design's merits either way. See [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md) for the registry leg, its three-part signal, the self-issuance hole in its fraud protection, and a check in the registry layer that a presentation registry would fail by construction. This chapter does not restate that material.

#### Superseded 2026-10-03: the third leg moved {#08-third-leg-moved}

Superseded 2026-10-03 — the third leg moved within three weeks. The paragraph above describes `b8f60166b`. At `80f77b73b` the verifier side of presentation-registry authentication is built, on `grant` only, in the V2 module: "Verify every presentation registry declared across the DAG." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler.verify, L609 @80f77b73b). Every registry an Issuer declares in a disclosed node must bind this grant's SAID, as of KRAM's acceptance time, with a KEL source reference from the Issuee; any failure rejects the grant, and the Issuees so authenticated count as anchorers for `ax` above. The registry-layer check that a presentation registry "would fail by construction" was scoped rather than removed, so the Issuer-equality test now applies only to an Issuer registry (raw/16 section 7.4). Discovery of a foreign registry is still not built: the verifier must already hold the Issuee's TEL (raw/16 section 7.8). The cost-predicts-order observation above still describes the order the legs arrived in, but it no longer describes a gap. All of this is [code] at `80f77b73b` and is recorded in full in `raw/16` section 7 and [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md); it is summarized here only because it changes what satisfies `ax`.

#### Who must act in a presentation {#08-who-must-act}

One part of it changes who must act in a presentation, and chapter 10 owns the argument. Between 2026-09-21 and 2026-09-25 the code required a presentation registry's Issuee also to be a sender, endorser or anchorer of the grant — "A registry supplements, but never replaces, a Grant endorsement." — and commit `b7c170f93` ("remove grantor requisite") deleted that check before the work merged. At `80f77b73b` a presentation-registry binding authenticates its Issuee on its own: "The declaration is the issuer's signal that this Issuee must authenticate the grant through this node-local registry." (keripy acdc/ipexing.py, IpexHandler._verifyPresentationAuthGraph, L1516-1517 @80f77b73b). #1613 says the opposite for every presentation-registry-anchored grant (not only the proxy case — scope corrected 2026-10-03 (verification) against the #1613 snapshot), that the grant "must be endorsed by each Grantor" and is therefore "always double-authenticated". In effect the code lets a registry anchor make the Issuee a Grantor without an endorsement. raw/16 judges that coherent, since the anchor is a KEL-anchored commitment to the exact grant SAID, and a design change that #1613 does not record. [code] against [proposal] (raw/09 section 7e; raw/16 section 2.6)

#### Why anchor at all {#08-why-anchor}

Anchoring `agree` gives the Discloser perpetually verifiable proof of agreement before disclosure; anchoring `grant` gives the Disclosee proof of "what was granted and, as importantly, what was not granted"; anchoring `admit` "removes plausible deniability regarding the Disclosee's knowledge of the disclosed information and could trigger safe harbor protections."

#### The contractual logic: agree binds, admit removes the easy defense {#08-contract-logic}

Added 2026-10-15. Sam's July comments on the CLC worked example give the contract reasoning that #1613's anchoring rules rest on. The `agree` is the binding act, and a missing `admit` does not undo it: "An agree is legally binding not sending an admit does not convey backing out." The `admit` exists for enforcement: "The admit is a corner case that enables easy enforcement by removing plausible deniablity." To make a disclosee send one, the grantor's terms can carry an escape clause: "The grantor gets an escape clause unless the admitter verifiably admits." (keripy PR #1505, comment of 2026-07-17, R-049, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1505#issuecomment-4997904242). He ties it to the duty of data loyalty: "So CLC and DDL are mutually reinforcing." [proposal]

Multiple anchors in one exchange are contingencies, not redundancy. Because the messages of an exchange are hash-chained, "anchoring the tail also anchors the whole transation including the head", and "Multiple anchors are not meant to anchor multiple transactions but as continencies for the transaction to proceed." (keripy PR #1505, comment of 2026-07-16, R-050, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/pull/1505#issuecomment-4996894599; "continencies" means contingencies). The sequence of anchors is what lets two peers settle without a trusted third party: the discloser wants an anchored `agree` before it grants, and the disclosee wants an anchored `grant` before it admits. In his words, "So the Offer/Agree/Grant/Admit removes plausible deniability which is the bane of peer-to-peer interactions." [proposal]

#### Four tiers of IPEX {#08-four-tiers}

Added 2026-10-15. Before #1613, Sam laid out four tiers as a decision aid, in captions to four diagrams (keripy discussion #1512, comment of 2026-07-22, R-062, https://github.com/WebOfTrust/keripy/discussions/1512#discussioncomment-17737728). The low-stakes, signed-only tier: "Only the granted ACDC is itself perpetually verifiable, Not the IPEX transaction". The same plus a presentation registry, which lets the presenter detect use of its compromised keys ([chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md)). The high-stakes anchored tier: "The Agree, and Admit exchange messages are anchored by the Disclosee. The Grant is anchored by the Discloser." And the high-stakes tier with a presentation registry, in which the ACDC itself requires the grant to be anchored through the `rd` in its attribute section. The anchoring rules above are #1613's later and more detailed form of the third and fourth tiers; the taxonomy is the part #1613 does not restate. [proposal]

#### Presentation registries {#08-presentation-registries}

Summarized here because they bear on anchoring; treated in full in [chapter 10](10-presentation-registries.md), which is built from the concept's origin document — keripy discussion #1095, ACDC Issuee Usage Registry, ten months older than #1613 and filed under a different name, which is why earlier passes over this corpus missed it. A registry controlled by the Issuee, whose latest non-vacuous blinded state binds the `grant` SAID. Signalled by the issuer at issuance through a populated `rd` and `i` at the top level of the ACDC's attribute `a` section — note, not the ACDC's own top-level `rd`, which names the ACDC state registry.

Two benefits, and only one is a security property. Impersonation-fraud detection: because the registry's events anchor in the Grantor's KEL, the Grantor can see events it did not create, and "an imposter that merely compromises the Grantor's signing infrastructure can't avoid the requirement without also compromising the Issuer." This works only when the Issuer differs from the Grantor — for a self-issued ACDC an imposter with the signing keys simply issues one that requires nothing. Correlation resistance: an anchored grant whose SAID appears only inside a blinded registry event means "a correlator walking the Grantor's KEL would not be able to observe it," so the exchange can be perpetually verifiable without giving a KEL-scanning third party a join key between Grantor and Grantee.

#### Restricting `rd`-in-`a` to presentation registries {#08-rd-in-a}

#1613 floats restricting `rd`-in-`a` to presentation registries. The v1 spec also permits it as a hidden ACDC state registry, and #1613 judges that case "potentially dubious" and suggests forbidding it in v1.1. That question is live and touches the independent-registry bulk-issuance work directly enough to be worth watching.

#### Origin AID anchoring: the resolution {#08-origin-aid-anchoring}

With multiple Grantors, who must anchor? The complications are real: in a delegation chain, "Issuee AIDs that are not at the tail (leaf) of a delegation chain (tree) do not need a fresh proof-of-control"; and a Dossier-style evidence presentation may name an issuee wholly unrelated to the Discloser. Rather than enumerate, #1613 picks a rule: "either the sender must anchor the grant or the Issuee or Issuer of the origin ACDC of the grant must anchor the grant," checked in that order of priority. This is what lets the sender AID stay absent from the disclosed DAG entirely while the principal's anchor still satisfies the requirement. [proposal] Implemented 2026-10-03, with one difference. keripy at `80f77b73b` realizes this rule in the V2 module (see the `ax` paragraph above), but as membership in a set rather than a priority order — any one of the three suffices, so "in that order of priority" has no operational effect. raw/16 reads that as consistent with #1613's own next sentence. [code]

#### The layering {#08-anchoring-layering}

The layering is explicit and worth preserving in any critique: the anchoring rule "is a loose business logic requirement... enforced after the grant passes KRAM and IPEX multiple endorsement but before other business logic requirements." Cal's coupon rule — that Bob specifically must anchor — is EGF business logic riding above the protocol rule, not a substitute for it. A grant can pass KRAM, pass multiple endorsement, satisfy `ax`, and still be refused by the verifier's own policy, and #1613 treats that as correct.

## 11. DAG soup: the list form, and what remains open {#08-dag-soup}

#1627's only concrete proposal. [proposal]

### The argument for needing it at all {#08-why-dag-soup}

A bespoke origin converts a soup into a DAG, so why keep soup? "When the ingredients are sourced from different cupboards, i.e., each have different Issuee, then the presentation must be multiply endorsed." And the practical case: presenting several DAGs in parallel in one exchange beats a series of IPEXes, since "A series of IPEX presentations adds more failure modes, and if the business logic requires all to complete for processing to continue, now the parties to the exchange have to keep state across multiple IPEXes. This requires a meta IPEX protocol."

#### The pivot away from edge operators {#08-pivot-from-operators}

#1555 put the multi-endorsement signal in the ACDC. #1627 reconsiders, because anchoring joined the picture: "#1555 predates #1613 which largely superseded #1555... now a fully multiply endorsed exchange gets more complicated with respect to anchoring, as there would be more than one effective origin node to which the anchoring requirement... must be applied. Following down the path of using new edge operators would require defining yet another edge operator that signaled the anchoring requirement." Conclusion: "the complications of a combination of multiply-endorsed and multiply-anchored presentations may flip the trade-space away from using edge operators as the primary way to signal either or both."

#### The amendment, as it now stands {#08-list-form-amendment}

The body of #1627 was revised in place on 2026-08-25, after this chapter was first drafted, and now offers two options in this order. The field-map option — each of `dp`, `o`, `ax` may become "a field map, with a unique informative label for each DAG" — is presented as deferrable: "This proposal does not change the current definitions but allows a future option to replace the field definitions with a field map. This is possible because none of the current field values is a field map so the data type removes ambiguity." The list option makes `dp` "a list of a list of tuples," `o` "a list of SAIDs," and `ax` "a list of Booleans," with one element per DAG and exactly one element in the single-DAG case. It is presented as not deferrable — "The proposal requires the change now because it uses lists, and the `dp` field is already a list. So it would be ambiguous" — and it is the one marked "the preferred approach at the time of this writing." dhh1128 endorsed the list form on the discussion, 2026-08-25. [proposal] #1627's body has since been edited again, on 2026-09-11, and the list form remains its preferred option.

#### The list form in keripy {#08-list-form-keripy}

The list form is now also [code], which is the strongest evidence it has. keripy at `b8f60166b` carries `o` and `ax` as one-element lists on the wire and rejects anything that is not a list, with the single-DAG restriction stated as temporary "until Multi DAG" ([section 10](#08-anchoring)). `dp` is likewise an outer one-element list of path plans. So the wire shape the code enforces today is the list form's degenerate case, laid out so the multi-DAG generalization needs no type change. That does not make the proposal normative anywhere — it is absent from both spec branches — but it does mean the trade-space question below is no longer purely hypothetical: an implementation has committed to one side of it.

#### What the list form settles {#08-list-form-settles}

Identity by position rather than by a minted label. That removes the join-key problem the field-map form created, and it removes a graduated-disclosure leak that was specific to the word informative: a meaningful label (`employment`, `utah-sedi`) is semantic content about the evidence, written in the clear in an `apply` or `offer`, before terms are agreed, so a disclosee that walks away from the negotiation keeps a description of what it declined. Position discloses only a count. Note the symmetry that makes this a genuine trade rather than a rout: across disconnected DAGs there is no edge to walk, so an ordering is stipulated rather than derived, exactly as a label is. Position's advantage over labels here is that it leaks nothing, not that it is canonical; labels retain a real advantage on optionality, since a positional gap cannot say which requested DAG is missing.

#### What the list form does not settle {#08-list-form-open}

Cross-message correspondence. No message carries both `dp` and `o`. `dp` is in the query section `q` of `apply` and `offer` only, on the forward branch; `o` is proposed for the attribute section `a` of the `grant`. So the disclosee fixes an ordering in the apply and the discloser fixes one in the grant, and nothing binds them together. The concrete form of the question: what does the `ax` list index against in an `apply` or `offer`, when the DAG set is fixed by the discloser at grant time and no origin exists yet? Asked on the discussion 2026-09-01; answered in part on 2026-09-02, and the answer does not close it. Sam replied that the KEL anchor "only applies when their is not a presentation registry being used by DAG ACDCs" whose issuees match one of the three eligible anchoring AIDs — which says which anchoring obligation applies to which AID, and says nothing about what an index in an `apply` refers to before any origin exists. The reply was subsequently promoted almost verbatim into #1613's body, so it now reads as standing design text in a discussion it was never posted to. The indexing question stays open; see [section 14, question 4](#08-q-dag-ordering).

`ax` binds three messages and only one of them is per-DAG. "the Grantor must anchor its `grant` message and the Applicant must anchor both its `agree` and `admit` messages when either is provided" (#1613). The `grant` carries `o` and can be spoken of per DAG. There is one `agree` and one `admit` for the whole exchange. So a per-DAG `ax` has no reading for the disclosee's half of the obligation it creates.

Whether the break must happen now. The "it would be ambiguous" claim looks checkable and may not hold: `o` is a string or a list, `ax` is a Boolean or a list, and `dp`'s first element's first element is a string in the flat form and an array in the nested one — one type probe each, which is the same discrimination argument used to call the field-map option deferrable. If that is right, the preferred form need not break the `dp` text that just landed in `v1.1`, nor force rework of the worked examples that build the flat form. Overtaken in practice, though not answered. keripy resolved the question by fiat in the list form's favour, wrapping `dp`, `o` and `ax` each in a one-element outer list at `b8f60166b` — so the code now presumes the break, while the `v1.1` text it would break still says a `dp` value is a list of tuples rather than a list of lists of tuples. The two are already out of step, which is a smaller version of exactly the branch-divergence problem this chapter's markers exist to track, and it should be re-checked at the next pass on both sides.

What DAG soup earns. Unchanged by the move to lists, and worth keeping separate from it. All three fields must change in a multi-DAG exchange — `o` cannot carry N commitments in one SAID, and `dp`'s prefixes have no unambiguous root once there are N origins — but only `ax` earns a capability by it. The one thing a single bespoke origin cannot express is a negotiated anchoring obligation bound to a particular body of evidence. Issuer-signalled per-ACDC anchoring already works inside one DAG: "When multiple ACDCs in the granted DAG each have a different presentation registry ID field value in the `rd` field in their attribute `a` section, the verifier must verify all of the anchors" (#1613). So the prize is real but narrow, and `o` and `dp` change as plumbing.

#### Superseded, recorded for provenance {#08-field-map-superseded}

Against the earlier field-map-only text this chapter argued that the labels were an unowned join key spanning three fields, and that a map reinstated the shape `dp` rejects. The first objection is answered by the list form. The second was always the weaker one and should not be revived: the rejection — which is [spec-next], not [spec] — is of a map keyed by schema SAID, a value the ACDCs determine and which therefore collides, whereas a presenter-chosen label can always be made unique.

## 12. The two SEDI recipes, and the reissuance cascade {#08-sedi-recipes}

#1627's applied section. Both are [proposal]; the trade is genuine and is the most decision- ready material in the discussion.

### Bespoke origin as recipe {#08-recipe-bespoke}

See [section 3](#08-bespoke-origin). Maximum flexibility. Relationships form only at presentation time, so "Data changes in each isolated ACDC that cause reissuance do not trigger a cascade of reissuance of other ACDCs." Cost: a bespoke ACDC per presentation, and no memorialization — "A bespoke on-the-fly ACDC does not have any ability to memorialize the state of the graph at the time."

#### Chained ontology as recipe {#08-recipe-ontology}

Pre-build the DAG as a standing labeled property graph, so that "All presentations are just branches of this master recipe." Edges are non-delegative (`NI2I` or `E1E`) since the issuee is constant. Simplest tooling; strongest normative structure for interop. Cost: the cascade — "whenever data changes in the root ACDC or in ACDCs that lie in upper branches of the graph... then all dependent ACDCs in lower branches or leaves must be reissued," mitigated by pushing volatile data to the leaves, and by a transfer registry whose state change forward-references a replacement rather than revoking.

#### What is not tradeable {#08-not-tradeable}

"secure delegation requires a DAG that represents the authority structure. A bespoke ACDC can not replace it. The delegation chain is inescapable." So guardianship and every other genuinely delegative use case needs the delegative DAG regardless of which recipe style is chosen, and the realistic answer is a combination.

#### A tension this chapter has not seen addressed {#08-ontology-origin-tension}

Under the ontology recipe you present a branch, and a branch's local source node is not the ontology's origin. But [section 10](#08-anchoring)'s anchoring rule and [section 8](#08-freshness-kram)'s tethering are both stated in terms of "the origin ACDC" of the grant. If the origin is whichever node roots the presented branch, then which party can satisfy `ax` changes with the branch selected — and if instead the ontology's own source node must always be the origin, then every presentation drags the whole upper graph along, which is most of what the ontology approach was supposed to avoid. #1627 does not say which.
